cards.front:
The INDUS VALLEY CIVILIZATION is also known as the:

(A) Ganga Civilization
(B) Harappan Civilization
(C) Aryan Civilization
(D) Mughal Civilization
cards.back:
(B) Harappan Civilization

Ancient India — After the site of Harappa (Pakistan's Punjab), excavated by Daya Ram Sahni in 1921. Mohenjo-Daro followed in 1922 (R. D. Banerji).
cards.storedExplanation: After the site of Harappa (Pakistan's Punjab), excavated by Daya Ram Sahni in 1921. Mohenjo-Daro followed in 1922 (R. D. Banerji).

cards.front:
Ashoka the Great embraced Buddhism after the Battle of:

(A) Panipat
(B) Kalinga
(C) Talikota
(D) Haldighati
cards.back:
(B) Kalinga

Ancient India — Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE) is mentioned in Rock Edict XIII where Ashoka expresses remorse for the bloodshed — the turning point to Dhamma.
cards.storedExplanation: Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE) is mentioned in Rock Edict XIII where Ashoka expresses remorse for the bloodshed — the turning point to Dhamma.

cards.front:
'ARTHASHASTRA', the classical treatise on statecraft, was authored by:

(A) Kalidasa
(B) Kautilya (Chanakya)
(C) Vishakhadatta
(D) Banabhatta
cards.back:
(B) Kautilya (Chanakya)

Ancient India — Kautilya, also called Chanakya or Vishnugupta, was the chief minister of Chandragupta Maurya. The Arthashastra, found by R. Shamashastry in 1905 (published 1909), covers statecraft, economics, military strategy.

cards.front:
Consider the following statements about the GUPTA AGE. 1. Gupta era began with Chandragupta I's accession, c. 319-320 CE. 2. The decimal place-value system (including zero) and Aryabhata's work on mathematics and astronomy belong to this period. 3. Kalidasa was a court poet of Samudragupta. 4. The Iron Pillar at Mehrauli, inscribed in the name of 'Chandra', is attributed to Chandragupta II. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 4 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 1 and 3 only
(D) 2 and 3 only
cards.back:
(A) 1, 2 and 4 only

Ancient India — Statement 3 is likely WRONG — tradition most commonly associates Kalidasa with the court of CHANDRAGUPTA II VIKRAMADITYA (not Samudragupta). Some historians disagree, but the exam answer follows tradition. Other three are correct.

cards.front:
Match List-I (foreign traveller) with List-II (Indian court visited). A. Megasthenes. B. Fa-Hien. C. Hiuen Tsang. D. Al-Biruni. List-II: 1. Chandragupta Maurya. 2. Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya). 3. Harsha Vardhana. 4. Mahmud of Ghazni.

(A) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4
(B) A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3
(C) A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4
(D) A-3, B-2, C-1, D-4
cards.back:
(A) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4

Ancient India — Megasthenes — Greek envoy to Chandragupta Maurya's court (c. 302 BCE), wrote 'Indica'. Fa-Hien — Chinese Buddhist pilgrim during Chandragupta II's reign (c. 399-414 CE). Hiuen Tsang — Chinese pilgrim during Harsha's reign (c. 630 CE), studied at Nalanda. Al-Biruni — Persian scholar who came with Mahmud of Ghazni c. 1017 CE, wrote 'Kitab-ul-Hind'.

cards.front:
Which ancient Indian text is considered the OLDEST of the four Vedas?

(A) Yajur Veda
(B) Rig Veda
(C) Sama Veda
(D) Atharva Veda
cards.back:
(B) Rig Veda

Ancient India — Rig Veda — oldest, composed c. 1500-1000 BCE, 10 Mandalas with 1,028 hymns. Order of composition (traditionally): Rig → Sama → Yajur → Atharva. The Atharva Veda was latest + included only after considerable debate.

cards.front:
The city of PATALIPUTRA (modern Patna) served as the capital of the following dynasties, EXCEPT:

(A) Mauryas
(B) Guptas (for a significant period)
(C) Shungas
(D) Mughals
cards.back:
(D) Mughals

Ancient India — Pataliputra served as capital for Mauryas, Shungas, Kanvas, Guptas, Palas (for a period). The Mughals ruled from Delhi/Agra/Fatehpur Sikri/Shahjahanabad — never from Patna. Patna was a provincial capital under Sher Shah Suri and the British.

cards.front:
The HARAPPAN civilization's decline is attributed to several factors. Which of the following are plausible contributors (as per current archaeological consensus)? 1. Gradual drying up of the Saraswati-Ghaggar river system. 2. Invasion by 'Aryan' hordes (the OLD theory, now largely discredited in its dramatic form). 3. Climate change and weakening monsoons c. 2000-1800 BCE. 4. Internal socio-economic stress and urban decay.

(A) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(B) 1, 3 and 4 only
(C) 2 and 3 only
(D) 1 and 2 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 3 and 4 only

Ancient India — Modern consensus favours a COMBINATION of climatic shift (weakening monsoons, drying rivers) + internal urban decay. The 'Aryan invasion' theory in its dramatic Wheeler-era form (1947) is no longer accepted; the encounter with Indo-Aryan speakers is now seen as much more gradual and complex. So statement 2 as an invasion theory is NOT part of the current consensus.

cards.front:
The famous Brihadisvara (Rajarajesvaram) temple at Thanjavur was built by which Chola king?

(A) Rajendra Chola I
(B) Rajaraja Chola I
(C) Vijayalaya Chola
(D) Kulottunga I
cards.back:
(B) Rajaraja Chola I

Ancient India — Rajaraja I (r. 985-1014) built the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. His son Rajendra I expanded the empire across South-East Asia and built the Gangaikonda Cholapuram. Vijayalaya founded the dynasty around 850. Kulottunga I merged the Chola and Chalukya lineages. The Cholas are known for their maritime reach — their navy raided Srivijaya (modern Sumatra) in 1025.

cards.front:
The Pandya kingdom of ancient Tamilakam had its capital at:

(A) Kanchipuram
(B) Madurai
(C) Thanjavur
(D) Karur
cards.back:
(B) Madurai

Ancient India — The Pandyas ruled from Madurai — the famous Tamil Sangams (assemblies of poets) were held under their patronage in the early centuries CE. Kanchipuram was the Pallava capital; Thanjavur was Chola territory; Karur / Vanchi was the Chera capital. Megasthenes (c. 300 BCE) mentions the Pandyas. The Meenakshi temple at Madurai was largely expanded by later Pandyas and Nayaks.

cards.front:
Match the southern dynasty with its capital. A. Cholas (imperial). B. Pallavas. C. Cheras. D. Satavahanas. List-II: 1. Thanjavur, 2. Kanchipuram, 3. Vanchi (Karur), 4. Pratishthana (Paithan).

(A) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4
(B) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4
(C) A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4
(D) A-1, B-2, C-4, D-3
cards.back:
(A) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4

Ancient India — Cholas — Thanjavur (later also Gangaikonda Cholapuram). Pallavas — Kanchipuram, today in Tamil Nadu. Cheras — Vanchi / Karur (modern Kerala and western TN). Satavahanas — Pratishthana / Paithan in modern Maharashtra — the dominant power in the Deccan from ~1st century BCE to 3rd century CE. Other key southern capitals — Badami (Chalukyas), Mahabalipuram (coastal Pallava port).

cards.front:
The rock-cut temples at Mahabalipuram (Mamallapuram) — a UNESCO World Heritage Site — were built by the:

(A) Cholas
(B) Pallavas
(C) Vijayanagara rulers
(D) Satavahanas
cards.back:
(B) Pallavas

Ancient India — Mamallapuram's rock-cut Rathas, Shore Temple and the 'Descent of the Ganges' relief were commissioned under the Pallava rulers Narasimhavarman I ('Mamalla', r. 630-668) and his successors. Kanchipuram's Kailasanatha temple (built by Rajasimha) is another major Pallava monument. UNESCO WHS since 1984.

cards.front:
The Satavahana dynasty, which dominated the Deccan in the early centuries of the common era, had its greatest ruler in:

(A) Simuka
(B) Gautamiputra Satakarni
(C) Kanishka
(D) Rudradaman I
cards.back:
(B) Gautamiputra Satakarni

Ancient India — Gautamiputra Satakarni (r. c. 78-102 CE) — the most celebrated Satavahana ruler; he defeated the Shakas and recovered the dynasty's position. The Nasik prashasti of his mother Gautami Balashri records his victories. Simuka founded the line around 230 BCE. Kanishka was a Kushan (not Satavahana). Rudradaman I was a Shaka ruler (Junagadh Rock Inscription) and a rival of the Satavahanas.

cards.front:
The Chola king who sent a naval expedition to South-East Asia (1025 CE) against the maritime kingdom of Srivijaya (modern Sumatra) was:

(A) Rajaraja I
(B) Rajendra I
(C) Kulottunga I
(D) Parantaka I
cards.back:
(B) Rajendra I

Ancient India — Rajendra I (r. 1014-44) — son of Rajaraja I — led the famous naval expedition against Srivijaya in 1025. After his northern campaign he was given the title 'Gangaikonda' (bringer of the Ganga). He founded the new capital Gangaikonda Cholapuram, complete with a great temple. His empire stretched from the Bay of Bengal to the Maldives, and included coastal parts of Sri Lanka.

cards.front:
The 'Sangam' literature of ancient Tamilakam flourished under the patronage of:

(A) Mauryan rulers
(B) The Pandyas
(C) Harshavardhana
(D) The Gupta emperors
cards.back:
(B) The Pandyas

Ancient India — Sangam literature (~300 BCE to 300 CE) — assemblies of Tamil poets held at Madurai under the Pandyas, but also patronised by the Cholas and Cheras. Major works — Tolkappiyam (grammar), Ettutokai (Eight Anthologies), Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls), Silappatikaram (one of the five great epics). The tradition is a key source for the political, social and cultural life of early historic Tamilakam. along with Cheras and Cholas.

cards.front:
Most of Ashoka's Rock and Pillar edicts were written in which script?

(A) Sanskrit
(B) Brahmi
(C) Devanagari
(D) Nagari
cards.back:
(B) Brahmi

Ancient India — Most Ashokan edicts are in Brahmi script (reading left to right) — used for Prakrit, the spoken language. Some NW edicts use Kharoshthi (right to left, Aramaic-derived); two bilinguals in Greek / Aramaic (Kandahar, in modern Afghanistan). Brahmi was deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837, unlocking the edicts. Brahmi is the ancestor of most Indian scripts, including Devanagari (a later medieval script).

cards.front:
The Ashokan pillar which bears the four-lion capital now used as India's national emblem is at:

(A) Vaishali
(B) Sarnath
(C) Lumbini
(D) Sanchi
cards.back:
(B) Sarnath

Ancient India — The Lion Capital at Sarnath — adopted as India's state emblem on 26 January 1950 — has four Asiatic lions back-to-back on an abacus with an elephant, horse, bull and lion (each representing a direction). The 'Satyameva Jayate' motto below is from the Mundaka Upanishad. Sanchi has its own great Stupa, and Vaishali has the single-lion pillar.

cards.front:
The 13th Major Rock Edict of Ashoka is chiefly about:

(A) Trade with China
(B) The Kalinga War and Ashoka's remorse
(C) Construction of roads
(D) Census of the empire
cards.back:
(B) The Kalinga War and Ashoka's remorse

Ancient India — The 13th Rock Edict — Ashoka's most famous — describes the bloodshed of the Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE), 100,000 killed and many more deported, and his resulting remorse, his adoption of dhamma-vijaya (conquest by righteousness). It also names 5 Hellenistic kings (Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus Gonatas, Magas of Cyrene, Alexander of Epirus) to whom he sent missions, establishing the date of Ashoka's reign.

cards.front:
The Ashokan edicts were deciphered in 1837 by:

(A) William Jones
(B) James Prinsep
(C) Alexander Cunningham
(D) Charles Wilkins
cards.back:
(B) James Prinsep

Ancient India — James Prinsep (Assay Master at the Calcutta Mint) cracked the Brahmi script in 1837, making the Ashokan edicts readable for the first time in nearly two millennia. Sir William Jones (1746-94) founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784). Alexander Cunningham (1814-93) was the first DG of the Archaeological Survey of India. Charles Wilkins first translated the Bhagavad Gita into English (1785).

cards.front:
Ashokan edicts are mostly written in which language family?

(A) Tamil
(B) Prakrit
(C) Avestan
(D) Pali
cards.back:
(B) Prakrit

Ancient India — Most Ashokan edicts are in varieties of Prakrit — the Middle Indo-Aryan spoken languages of the time. The Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra edicts (both in modern Pakistan) are in Prakrit but in Kharoshthi script. Two bilinguals in Aramaic + Greek (Kandahar). Not Sanskrit (the scholarly language). Pali is a specific Prakrit — Ashokan edicts are not, strictly speaking, in Pali.

cards.front:
The Ashokan pillar at Lumbini marks:

(A) The enlightenment of the Buddha
(B) The birthplace of the Buddha
(C) The first sermon of the Buddha
(D) The Buddha's death
cards.back:
(B) The birthplace of the Buddha

Ancient India — The Lumbini Pillar (in modern Nepal) records Ashoka's visit in the 21st year of his reign to honour the Buddha's birthplace and exempts Lumbini from most taxes. Bodh Gaya — enlightenment; Sarnath — first sermon; Kushinagar — mahaparinirvana. Lumbini has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.

cards.front:
The original name of Emperor Ashoka — based on inscriptions and literature — was:

(A) Priyadarsi
(B) Chandragupta
(C) Bimbisara
(D) Harshavardhana
cards.back:
(A) Priyadarsi

Ancient India — 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' ('Beloved of the gods, he who looks on lovingly') is the title Ashoka uses for himself in his edicts. The name 'Ashoka' is known from Buddhist texts (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa of Sri Lanka). The Maski Edict (Karnataka) is the crucial one that contains BOTH names and thus confirms they refer to the same person. Chandragupta — founder of the Mauryan dynasty. Bimbisara — Haryanka ruler of Magadha (6th century BCE). Harshavardhana — 7th-century emperor.

cards.front:
The Gupta Empire is often called the 'Golden Age' of India. Who was its founder?

(A) Chandragupta I
(B) Samudragupta
(C) Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
(D) Sri Gupta
cards.back:
(A) Chandragupta I

Ancient India — Sri Gupta (c. 240-280 CE) founded the Gupta dynasty but was a minor king. Ghatotkacha (280-319) followed. But the EMPIRE-builder — the first major imperial Gupta — was CHANDRAGUPTA I (r. 319-335 CE), who took the imperial title 'Maharajadhiraja' and started the GUPTA ERA (319 CE). He married LICCHAVI princess Kumaradevi — a political marriage that greatly enhanced Gupta influence in the Ganga valley. His son SAMUDRAGUPTA (335-375) hugely expanded the empire; called the 'Indian Napoleon' by V. A. Smith. CHANDRAGUPTA II VIKRAMADITYA (375-414) reached Gupta's zenith — defeated Western Kshatrapas, Fa-Hien visited, nine gems 'Navaratna' flourished. Decline after Skandagupta (455-467) who repelled Hun invasions.

cards.front:
Samudragupta's military achievements are inscribed in which famous prashasti (eulogy)?

(A) Aihole inscription
(B) Allahabad Prashasti (Prayag Prashasti), composed by Harisena
(C) Mandsaur inscription
(D) Junagadh rock inscription
cards.back:
(B) Allahabad Prashasti (Prayag Prashasti), composed by Harisena

Ancient India — The ALLAHABAD PRASHASTI (Prayag Prashasti), inscribed on an ASHOKAN PILLAR at Prayag (Allahabad/Prayagraj) by court poet HARISENA, is the primary source on Samudragupta's conquests. In Sanskrit, it lists 4 groups of kings defeated: (1) 9 of Aryavarta (uprooted); (2) 12 of Dakshinapatha (defeated and released — the 'Dharma-vijaya' policy); (3) 5 frontier kingdoms (submission); (4) 9 tribal republics. AIHOLE INSCRIPTION — by Ravikirti for Chalukya Pulakeshin II. MANDSAUR — by Vatsabhatti on Kumaragupta era. JUNAGADH — by Rudradaman (Saka), later appended by Skandagupta recording repair of Sudarshana Lake. Fun fact: the Allahabad pillar originally had Ashoka's edict; Samudragupta, Jahangir, and the British all added inscriptions.

cards.front:
Which Gupta king is associated with the title 'Vikramaditya' and whose court hosted the 'Nine Gems' (Navaratnas)?

(A) Chandragupta I
(B) Samudragupta
(C) Chandragupta II
(D) Skandagupta
cards.back:
(C) Chandragupta II

Ancient India — CHANDRAGUPTA II VIKRAMADITYA (r. 375-414 CE) — the Gupta zenith. The 'Nine Gems' (NAVARATNA) at his court (per later tradition) included: KALIDASA (playwright — Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Meghaduta; greatest Sanskrit poet), AMARASIMHA (lexicographer — Amarakosha dictionary), DHANVANTARI (physician), VARAHAMIHIRA (astronomer — Brihat Samhita, Panch Siddhantika), VETALA BHATTA, GHATAKARPARA, SHANKU, KSHAPANAKA, VARARUCHI. cards.front:
The IRON PILLAR at Delhi (Mehrauli, near Qutb Complex), famous for its rust-resistant composition over 1600+ years, is from which era?

(A) Maurya period
(B) Gupta period
(C) Delhi Sultanate
(D) Mughal period
cards.back:
(B) Gupta period

Ancient India — The Iron Pillar at Mehrauli (Delhi) dates to the Gupta period — inscription on it is in Sanskrit Brahmi script referring to a king 'Chandra' (generally identified as CHANDRAGUPTA II Vikramaditya). ~7 m tall, ~6 tonnes, 98% wrought iron. Its remarkable rust-resistance is due to a thin protective layer of 'misawite' (hydrogen phosphate) formed by catalytic action of phosphorus present in the iron (~1%) reacting with air — a marvel of ancient Indian metallurgy. Originally stood at a Vishnu temple in Udayagiri (MP), later moved to Delhi by Anangpal Tomar or Iltutmish. In the Qutb Complex since 1200s. Iltutmish's Qutb Minar built around it. Another Gupta masterpiece: BHITARI and ERAN pillars, the DASHAVATARA TEMPLE at Deogarh (oldest surviving Hindu stone temple, 500 CE). attributed to Chandragupta II.

cards.front:
ARYABHATA, the astronomer-mathematician who proposed heliocentrism and authored 'Aryabhatiya' in 499 CE, flourished under which dynasty?

(A) Maurya
(B) Gupta
(C) Chola
(D) Vakataka
cards.back:
(B) Gupta

Ancient India — ARYABHATA (476-550 CE) — lived during the later Gupta era under Budhagupta — composed the 'ARYABHATIYA' in 499 CE at age 23 at Kusumapura (Pataliputra). Key contributions: (1) Proposed Earth rotates on its axis (heliocentrism hints); (2) Used place-value notation WITHOUT zero as a written symbol (Brahmagupta, 628 CE, formalised zero and negative numbers); (3) Value of π (pi) ≈ 3.1416, close to modern; (4) Accurate calculation of solar year (365.25858 days); (5) Explained lunar eclipse (moon in Earth's shadow) and solar eclipse rationally (moon blocks sun) against prevailing demonic theories. Other Gupta-era scientists: VARAHAMIHIRA, BRAHMAGUPTA (7th c. actually Post-Gupta but influenced by Gupta tradition), DHANVANTARI. India's first satellite (1975) named 'Aryabhata' in his honour.

cards.front:
The decline of the Gupta Empire began mainly due to invasions by which foreign tribe in the 5th-6th century CE?

(A) Kushans
(B) Hunas
(C) Sakas
(D) Parthians
cards.back:
(B) Hunas

Ancient India — The HUNAS (White Huns / Hephthalites) — a Central Asian nomadic people — invaded India from the NW in the mid-5th c. CE. Initially REPELLED by SKANDAGUPTA (c. 455-467 CE — hailed as 'Vikramaditya' for this victory; Bhitari pillar inscription records it). After Skandagupta's death, subsequent weaker Gupta rulers (Buddhagupta, Narasimhagupta, Vishnugupta) lost ground. Hun chieftains TORAMANA (c. 500 CE, captured Malwa region) and his son MIHIRAKULA (c. 515-540 CE, notorious persecutor of Buddhists — defeated by Yashodharman of Malwa in 528). Gupta fragmentation complete by c. 550 CE. Sakas had been defeated by Chandragupta II earlier (4th c.). Kushans preceded Guptas (1st-3rd c.). Parthians — short-lived 1st c. BCE Indo-Parthian kingdom in NW.

cards.front:
Which of the following is considered the OLDEST surviving Hindu stone temple in India, dating to the Gupta era?

(A) Kailasa Temple, Ellora
(B) Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh (c. 500 CE)
(C) Brihadeshwara Temple, Thanjavur
(D) Sun Temple, Konark
cards.back:
(B) Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh (c. 500 CE)

Ancient India — The DASHAVATARA TEMPLE at Deogarh (Lalitpur district, UP), built c. 500 CE — the oldest surviving Hindu STONE temple in its original form. Dedicated to Vishnu (hence 'Dashavatara' — ten incarnations). Features magnificent relief panels: (1) Gajendra Moksha (rescue of the elephant); (2) Nara-Narayana; (3) Sheshashayi Vishnu (Vishnu on cosmic serpent Ananta). Introduced the SHIKHARA (curvilinear tower) architectural element that became the cornerstone of Nagara temple style. Other early Gupta temples: Tigawa (c. 400 CE) and Sanchi Temple 17 (c. 400 CE) — simpler flat-roof. KAILASA at Ellora (8th c. Rashtrakuta), BRIHADESHWARA (1010 CE Chola), KONARK (13th c. Eastern Ganga) — all much later.

cards.front:
The decimal place-value system and the concept of ZERO as a number were systematised in India during which period?

(A) The Mauryan period under Ashoka the Great
(B) The Gupta and post-Gupta period (roughly 4th-7th c. CE)
(C) The Vedic period of pre-Buddha sacred literature
(D) The Mughal period under Akbar's court patronage
cards.back:
(B) The Gupta and post-Gupta period (roughly 4th-7th c. CE)

Ancient India — Zero as a number + place-value notation — developed in India during the Gupta + post-Gupta era. Brahmagupta (628 CE, 'Brahmasphutasiddhanta') gave first systematic rules for ZERO and NEGATIVE numbers. Aryabhata used place-value implicitly. Bakhshali manuscript (~3rd-4th c. or later) contains the earliest known dot-symbol for zero. The 'Indo-Arabic numerals' (1, 2, 3, ..., 9, 0) were transmitted to the Arab world (al-Khwarizmi, ~825 CE) and from there to Europe (Fibonacci, ~1200 CE) — revolutionising mathematics. Distractor 1 — too early. Distractor 3 — Vedic math used a base-10 system but no formal zero. Distractor 4 — too late.

NALANDA UNIVERSITY — one of the world's earliest residential universities — was founded in the:

(A) 1st century BCE under the Mauryan dynasty
(B) 5th century CE under Kumaragupta I of the Gupta dynasty
(C) 10th century CE under the Pala dynasty in Bengal
(D) 12th century CE under the Delhi Sultanate
cards.back:
(B) 5th century CE under Kumaragupta I of the Gupta dynasty

Ancient India — Nalanda Mahavihara — founded c. 5th c. CE under KUMARAGUPTA I (~427 CE). Continued patronage by later Gupta + Pala kings. At its peak: ~10,000 students, 2,000 teachers, 9-storey library 'Dharmaganja'. Subjects: Buddhism, Vedas, logic, grammar, medicine, astronomy. Visited by Hiuen Tsang (early 7th c.) who studied here for years. SACKED + BURNED by BAKHTIYAR KHILJI (~1193 CE), library destroyed. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2016). Modern Nalanda University (2014) revived as international university near the ancient site.

Key contributions: π ≈ 3.1416 ('asanna' = approximate); concept of zero as a placeholder; place-value decimal system fully formed; Earth rotates on its axis (heliocentric ideas anticipating Copernicus); approximate sin(x) tables; lengths of solar / sidereal year. Bhaskara I (~600 CE) wrote commentaries. Brahmagupta (628 CE) gave first explicit rules for arithmetic with zero + negative numbers. Bhaskara II (12th C) wrote Lilavati. Varahamihira (~505 CE) — astronomy + meteorology (Brihat Samhita, Pancha Siddhantika).

cards.front:
Kalidasa — Sanskrit's greatest dramatist — wrote which of the following plays?

(A) Mricchakatika
(B) Abhijnanasakuntalam (Recognition of Sakuntala) and Meghaduta (Cloud Messenger)
(C) Mudrarakshasa
(D) Gita Govinda
cards.back:
(B) Abhijnanasakuntalam (Recognition of Sakuntala) and Meghaduta (Cloud Messenger)

Ancient India — Kalidasa's major works: Plays — Abhijnanasakuntalam (most celebrated), Vikramorvashiyam, Malavikagnimitram. Epic poems — Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava. Lyric — Meghaduta (Cloud Messenger), Ritusamhara. Translated to English by William Jones (1789) — Sakuntala caused a sensation in Europe; Goethe famously praised it. Mricchakatika ('The Little Clay Cart') — by Sudraka. Mudrarakshasa (about Chanakya overthrow of Nandas) — by Vishakhadatta. Gita Govinda — by Jayadeva (12th C, Krishna theme). Kalidasa is identified by tradition with court of Vikramaditya.

cards.front:
Nalanda University — one of the world's first major residential universities — was at its peak under the Guptas. Located in modern:

(A) West Bengal
(B) Bihar (Nalanda district)
(C) Uttar Pradesh
(D) Odisha
cards.back:
(B) Bihar (Nalanda district)

Ancient India — Nalanda — Bihar, ~95 km SE of Patna. Founded under Kumaragupta I (5th C). Peak in 7th C — 10,000 students + 1,500 teachers. Specialised in Buddhist studies, medicine, astronomy, mathematics, philosophy, logic. Visited by Chinese pilgrims Xuanzang (Hiuen-Tsang, 7th C) and Yijing (I-Tsing). Library was 9-storeys tall — Dharmaganja. Sacked + burnt by Bakhtiyar Khilji (~1193 CE) — fire said to have lasted months. UNESCO WHS 2016. Modern Nalanda University revived 2014 (international university near old site). Other ancient universities — Takshashila (Taxila, Pakistan), Vikramshila, Odantapuri.

cards.front:
The Gupta Empire's decline began with the invasions of:

(A) Mongols
(B) Hunas (White Huns) under Toramana and Mihirakula in late 5th-6th C
(C) Arabs
(D) Greek satraps
cards.back:
(B) Hunas (White Huns) under Toramana and Mihirakula in late 5th-6th C

Ancient India — Skandagupta (455-467 CE) — last great Gupta. Junagadh inscription mentions repair of Sudarshana lake (built by Chandragupta Maurya). Defeated the Hunas during his reign. After Skandagupta, successive Hun invasions weakened the empire — Toramana (early 6th C) and his son Mihirakula (~510-540 CE). Yashodharman of Malwa is credited with defeating Mihirakula (~528 CE). Combined with succession disputes + economic decline + rise of regional kingdoms (Vakatakas, Maukharis, later Harsha), Gupta empire dissolved by ~550 CE. Brief revival under Harshavardhana (606-647 CE) of Pushyabhuti dynasty.

cards.front:
HARSHA VARDHANA was the ruler of which dynasty in the early 7th century?

(A) Gupta dynasty, the golden-age dynasty
(B) Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty of Thanesar
(C) Pala dynasty of eastern Bengal area
(D) Chola dynasty of southern Tamil region
cards.back:
(B) Pushyabhuti (Vardhana) dynasty of Thanesar

Ancient India — Harsha (r. 606-647 CE) — Pushyabhuti / VARDHANA dynasty, capital initially at THANESAR (Haryana), shifted to KANAUJ. Came to throne after his elder brother Rajya Vardhana was killed by Sasanka of Gauda. United north India after the post-Gupta fragmentation. Was DEFEATED by PULAKESIN II (Chalukya of Vatapi) at Narmada (~630 CE) — limit of his southern advance. Distractor 1 — Guptas declined ~550 CE. Distractor 3 — Palas were ~750-1150. Distractor 4 — Cholas were southern.
cards.option2: Pala dynasty of eastern Bengal area
cards.option3: Chola dynasty of southern Tamil region

The Chinese pilgrim HIUEN TSANG (Xuanzang) visited India during the reign of:

(A) Chandragupta II, the Gupta emperor
(B) Harsha Vardhana, between 629 and 645 CE
(C) Akbar, the Mughal emperor of 16th century
(D) Ashoka, the Mauryan emperor of 3rd c. BCE
cards.back:
(B) Harsha Vardhana, between 629 and 645 CE

Ancient India — HIUEN TSANG / Xuanzang (~602-664 CE) — Chinese Buddhist monk; visited India 629-645 CE, much of it during Harsha's reign. Studied at NALANDA university (~5 years). Wrote 'Si-Yu-Ki' (Records of the Western Regions). Praised Harsha's administration; described religious assemblies he attended (the famous Kanauj assembly + Prayag Mahamoksha Parishad — held every 5 years, where Harsha donated his wealth). BANABHATTA was the COURT POET of Harsha, famous for writing:

(A) Mricchakatika, the famous play of love
(B) Harshacharita and Kadambari (in Sanskrit)
(C) Mudrarakshasa, a political play of Maurya
(D) Akbarnama, the chronicle of Akbar's reign

(B) Harshacharita and Kadambari (in Sanskrit)

One of India's earliest historical biographies. (2) KADAMBARI — Sanskrit romance novel; one of the world's earliest novels. Distractor 1 = Mricchakatika, by Shudraka (~ 5th c., Gupta period). Harsha was DEFEATED by which southern emperor at the Narmada around 630 CE?

(A) Krishnadeva Raya, the Vijayanagara emperor
(B) Pulakesin II, of the Chalukya dynasty (Vatapi)
(C) Rajaraja Chola, the great Chola emperor
(D) Nrip Tunga, the Rashtrakuta emperor
cards.back:
(B) Pulakesin II, of the Chalukya dynasty (Vatapi)

Ancient India — Pulakesin II (r. 610-642 CE) — greatest Chalukya king of Vatapi (modern Badami, Karnataka). Defeated Harsha at the BANKS OF NARMADA (~630 CE) → halted Harsha's southward advance. Pulakesin's Aihole inscription (composed by RAVIKIRTI) celebrates his victory + other achievements. Pulakesin received an embassy from Khusrau II of Persia. Was eventually defeated + killed by NARASIMHAVARMAN I (Pallava king) ~642 CE. Distractor 1 — Vijayanagara was 14-16th c. Distractor 3 — Chola peak was 11th c. Distractor 4 — Rashtrakutas came after Chalukyas.

Harsha shifted his capital from Thanesar to:

(A) Pataliputra, the old Mauryan capital
(B) Kanauj (Kanyakubja), in present-day UP
(C) Ujjain, an ancient cultural centre
(D) Tamralipti, an ancient port city
cards.back:
(B) Kanauj (Kanyakubja), in present-day UP

Ancient India — Harsha shifted his capital to KANAUJ / Kanyakubja (modern Kannauj, UP) — strategic location commanding the Doab. Inherited from his sister Rajyashri's husband (Maukhari king Grahavarman, killed by Sasanka). Kanauj remained politically important for centuries — TRIPARTITE STRUGGLE (8th-9th c.) between Pratiharas, Palas, Rashtrakutas was over Kanauj. Distractor 1 = Pataliputra (Mauryan/Gupta). Distractor 3 = Ujjain (Avanti, also a notable ancient city, but not Harsha's). Distractor 4 = Tamralipti (port in Bengal, Mauryan-Gupta era).

cards.front:
Harsha was a generous patron of which religion in his later years?

(A) Jainism, the ahimsa-focused Indian tradition
(B) Mahayana Buddhism, under Hiuen Tsang's influence
(C) Zoroastrianism, the Persian Parsi religion
(D) Christianity, with an early Indian connection
cards.back:
(B) Mahayana Buddhism, under Hiuen Tsang's influence

Ancient India — Harsha — initially follower of Shaivism (his earlier inscriptions), later turned to MAHAYANA BUDDHISM under Hiuen Tsang's influence. Held the famous KANAUJ ASSEMBLY (643 CE) to honour Mahayana Buddhism — 18 days, attended by Hiuen Tsang as chief of the Mahayana school. Held PRAYAG MAHAMOKSHA PARISHAD every 5 years at Allahabad — donated his wealth (alms to monks, Brahmins, the poor). Plays attributed to Harsha himself: NAGANANDA (Buddhist, plot from Jataka), PRIYADARSIKA, RATNAVALI (Sanskrit love-comedies). Tolerant patron — supported Hinduism + Jainism too.

cards.front:
After Harsha died (647 CE) without an heir, his minister Arjuna usurped the throne but was defeated by:

(A) Pulakesin II of the Chalukya dynasty
(B) A Tibet-Chinese expedition under Wang Xuance
(C) Khusrau II of the Persian Sassanid empire
(D) Bhaskaravarman of the Kamarupa dynasty
cards.back:
(B) A Tibet-Chinese expedition under Wang Xuance

Ancient India — WANG XUANCE — Chinese envoy from Tang court (visiting newly-vacant Harsha's court). Arjuna (the usurper) attacked the Chinese embassy + killed many. Wang escaped to Nepal + Tibet, raised an army (Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo's troops + Nepalese), returned, defeated Arjuna, captured him, took him back to China as prisoner. UNUSUAL military intervention from China in north India. Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa (Assam) was Harsha's ally + was given an honorary territory after Harsha's death; he was a contemporary, not the conqueror of Arjuna.

cards.front:
Who was the founder of the HARYANKA dynasty of Magadha?

(A) Bimbisara, contemporary of Buddha
(B) Ajatashatru, son of Bimbisara.
(C) Udayin, builder of Pataliputra.
(D) Mahapadma Nanda, the Shudra.
cards.back:
(A) Bimbisara, contemporary of Buddha

Ancient India — BIMBISARA (r. ~544-492 BCE) founded the Haryanka dynasty after consolidating Magadha (modern Bihar). He was a contemporary of both BUDDHA (Gautama Siddhartha) and MAHAVIRA (Vardhamana). MAJOR ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) Made Rajgir (Rajagriha) the capital, with its 5 hills providing natural fortification. (2) Expanded Magadha through MARRIAGE ALLIANCES — wives from Kosala (Mahakosala's daughter), Vaishali (Lichchhavi princess Chellana), Punjab (Madra princess) — giving him diplomatic + dowry territories. (3) ANNEXED ANGA (eastern Bihar) — first to do so. (4) Patronized Buddha — donated Veluvana (Bamboo Grove) monastery. SUCCESSION DRAMA: BIMBISARA was IMPRISONED AND KILLED by his own son AJATASHATRU (~492 BCE) — a notorious patricide noted in Buddhist Pali texts. EXAM ANGLE: Bimbisara as 'founder of imperial Magadha' is a high-frequency PYQ — appears in CGL, UPSC Prelims, and NDA at least 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing the FOUNDATION CHRONOLOGY of pre-Mauryan India.

cards.front:
AJATASHATRU is best known for which two military innovations?

(A) Mahashilakantaka and Rathamusala weapons
(B) Cavalry units and chariots alone
(C) War elephants and bows alone.
(D) Naval fleet and chariots alone
cards.back:
(A) Mahashilakantaka and Rathamusala weapons

Ancient India — AJATASHATRU (r. ~492-460 BCE) used two innovative weapons in his wars against Kosala and the Vaishali Lichchhavis: (1) MAHASHILAKANTAKA — a giant catapult that hurled large stones (an early siege engine). (2) RATHAMUSALA — a chariot fitted with rotating blades or 'mace-wheels' that mowed down infantry as it rolled. These tools, plus diplomacy, enabled Ajatashatru to defeat the Lichchhavi confederacy after a 16-year war. ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) Annexed Kashi (Varanasi) from his Kosalan grandfather Prasenjit. (2) Defeated Vaishali after splitting the confederacy via spies. (3) Convened the FIRST BUDDHIST COUNCIL at Rajagriha (~483 BCE, just after Buddha's death) — recorded the Sutta and Vinaya Pitakas. PERSONAL: Buddhist texts call him remorseful for killing Bimbisara; converted to Buddhism. SUCCESSORS: Udayin (founded PATALIPUTRA on the confluence of Ganga, Son, Gandak — strategic riverine trade hub). PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 Magadha Qs per UPSC/SSC paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing knowledge of innovative pre-Mauryan war-tech and diplomatic-warfare hybrid.

cards.front:
Who founded the city of PATALIPUTRA, future capital of multiple empires?

(A) Udayin (Haryanka, son of Ajatashatru)
(B) Bimbisara, the dynasty founder.
(C) Mahapadma Nanda, the Shudra king.
(D) Chandragupta Maurya, the empire-builder.
cards.back:
(A) Udayin (Haryanka, son of Ajatashatru)

Ancient India — UDAYIN (Udayabhadra), son of Ajatashatru, founded PATALIPUTRA (c. 460 BCE) at the confluence of Ganga, Son, and (then) Gandak rivers — a strategic position controlling east-west and north-south river commerce. The site replaced Rajgir as Magadhan capital. SUBSEQUENT CAPITAL ROLE: Pataliputra was the seat of (1) Nanda dynasty, (2) Mauryan empire (Chandragupta, Bindusara, Ashoka), (3) Sunga, (4) Gupta empire (Chandragupta I, II, Samudragupta), and (5) Pala (briefly). MODERN: today's PATNA (Bihar capital) sits on the same site. ARCHAEOLOGICAL: Megasthenes (Greek ambassador to Chandragupta Maurya) described Pataliputra as a city ~14.5 km long, 2.4 km wide, fortified with 64 gates and 570 towers (Indica). ETYMOLOGY: 'Putra' = son, with various theories: 'son of Patali' (a tree/plant) or 'son of Patali-grama' (an older village). EXAM ANGLE: Pataliputra-related questions are EXTREMELY HIGH-FREQUENCY in UPSC (it covers 4-5 dynasties), SSC, NDA. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing knowledge of dynasty-capital chronology — a foundational exam skill.

cards.front:
MAHAPADMA NANDA, founder of the Nanda dynasty, is historically notable for being:

(A) First non-Kshatriya emperor of Magadha
(B) Builder of Sanchi Buddhist stupa
(C) Patron of Mahavira directly alone
(D) Defeater of Alexander the Great
cards.back:
(A) First non-Kshatriya emperor of Magadha

Ancient India — MAHAPADMA NANDA (r. ~345-321 BCE) overthrew the Shishunagas (successors to Haryankas) and founded the NANDA dynasty. UNIQUE: he was a SHUDRA (or possibly a barber's son) — making him the first NON-KSHATRIYA emperor of north India, defying the Vedic varna hierarchy. He's called 'Ekarat' (sole sovereign) in Puranas — the first to bring all of north India under one rule. CONQUESTS: subjugated Kalinga (modern Odisha — see Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela mentioning Nanda's irrigation canal there); Kosala; Avanti; possibly Mysore. WEALTH: legendary — Greek sources call them 'Nava Nandas' (nine Nandas) and describe vast treasury. ARMY: Plutarch says Dhana Nanda (last Nanda king) had 200,000 infantry, 80,000 cavalry, 8,000 chariots, 6,000 war elephants — terrified Alexander's troops, leading to the famous mutiny on the Beas River (326 BCE). SUCCESSOR: Dhana Nanda was overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya (with Chanakya/Kautilya's strategy, ~321 BCE). PYQ ANGLE: 'first Shudra emperor' is a perennial CGL/UPSC test question.

UNIQUE: he was a SHUDRA (or possibly a barber's son) — making him the first NON-KSHATRIYA emperor of north India, defying the Vedic varna hierarchy. He's called 'Ekarat' (sole sovereign) in Puranas — the first to bring all of north India under one rule. CONQUESTS: subjugated Kalinga (modern Odisha — see Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela mentioning Nanda's irrigation canal there); Kosala; Avanti; possibly Mysore. WEALTH: legendary — Greek sources call them 'Nava Nandas' (nine Nandas) and describe vast treasury. ARMY: Plutarch says Dhana Nanda (last Nanda king) had 200,000 infantry, 80,000 cavalry, 8,000 chariots, 6,000 war elephants — terrified Alexander's troops, leading to the famous mutiny on the Beas River (326 BCE). cards.front:
DHANA NANDA, last Nanda emperor, was overthrown by:

(A) Chandragupta Maurya guided by Chanakya
(B) Alexander of Macedon's invasion
(C) Kharavela of Kalinga's army.
(D) Pushyamitra Sunga's coup d'état.
cards.back:
(A) Chandragupta Maurya guided by Chanakya

Ancient India — CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA, with the strategic mentorship of CHANAKYA (also Kautilya/Vishnugupta), overthrew DHANA NANDA around 321 BCE — founding the MAURYAN EMPIRE. The story is dramatized in 'Mudra-Rakshasa' (a Sanskrit play by Vishakhadatta, 4th century CE). MOTIVATION (per legend): Chanakya was insulted at Dhana Nanda's court — he vowed to overthrow the dynasty. He recruited young Chandragupta (whose origins are debated — possibly a Maurya/Moriya tribe member, possibly low-born) and trained him at Taxila in statecraft + military strategy. The pair then waged a guerrilla campaign from the northwest, gradually capturing territory. SOURCES: Greek (Justin's Epitome calls Chandragupta 'Sandrocottos'), Buddhist (Mahavamsa, Dipavamsa), Jain (Parishishtaparvan), and Puranas all confirm this overthrow. CHRONOLOGY: Mauryan rule 321-185 BCE; Chandragupta abdicated in old age, became a Jain monk, fasted to death at Sravanabelagola (Karnataka). EXAM-FAVORITE: 'Maurya foundation date 321 BCE' + Chanakya's role appears in UPSC, SSC, RRB ancient-history sections virtually every cycle.

cards.front:
Which Magadhan king convened the FIRST BUDDHIST COUNCIL at Rajagriha?

(A) Ajatashatru, soon after Buddha's parinirvana
(B) Bimbisara, during Buddha's lifetime
(C) Kalashoka of the Shishunaga dynasty
(D) Ashoka the Great of Mauryan empire
cards.back:
(A) Ajatashatru, soon after Buddha's parinirvana

Ancient India — FIRST BUDDHIST COUNCIL — convened at RAJAGRIHA (Rajgir, Bihar), c. 483 BCE, soon after Buddha's death (parinirvana). Patron: AJATASHATRU. President: Mahakasyapa. ~500 monks attended; goal was to compile Buddha's teachings. OUTPUTS: (1) Vinaya Pitaka (rules of monastic discipline) — recited by Upali. (2) Sutta Pitaka (Buddha's discourses) — recited by Ananda. (Abhidhamma added later.) FOUR BUDDHIST COUNCILS — full list: 1st: Rajagriha (483 BCE) — Ajatashatru patron. 2nd: Vaishali (383 BCE) — Kalashoka patron; led to schism (Sthaviravada vs Mahasanghika). 3rd: Pataliputra (250 BCE) — ASHOKA patron; finalized the Tripitaka, sent missionaries (Mahinda to Sri Lanka, etc.). 4th: Kashmir (~78 CE) — KANISHKA patron; led to Mahayana-Hinayana split. PYQ EXTREME-HIGH-FREQUENCY: 'patron of Buddhist council' appears in UPSC Prelims 1-2× per year, also in CGL/CHSL. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests cross-mapping of dynasty + religious patronage + chronology.

cards.front:
What was the CAPITAL of Magadha under BIMBISARA before it shifted to Pataliputra?

(A) Rajagriha, the city of five hills
(B) Vaishali of the Lichchhavis
(C) Kashi (modern Varanasi) alone
(D) Champa, capital of Anga.
cards.back:
(A) Rajagriha, the city of five hills

Ancient India — RAJAGRIHA (Rajgir, Nalanda district, Bihar) was the capital of Magadha under Bimbisara and Ajatashatru. Surrounded by FIVE HILLS — Vaibhar, Vipula, Saptaparni, Ratnagiri, and Udaygiri — making it naturally fortified, hence its name 'Giri-vraja' (girdle of hills). HISTORICAL SIGNIFICANCE: (1) Buddha frequently visited and preached here; the Saptaparni cave hosted the First Buddhist Council. (2) Mahavira spent ~14 monsoons here. (3) Bimbisara built the famous 'Cyclopean Wall' — one of the oldest known stone fortifications in India (~5th century BCE). MOVE TO PATALIPUTRA: under Udayin (~460 BCE), capital shifted to the strategically superior riverine site. MODERN RAJGIR: tourist circuit includes hot springs (Brahmakund), Vulture's Peak (Gridhrakuta — Buddha's preaching mount), Saptaparni cave, ancient university Nalanda nearby. UNESCO TENTATIVE LIST: Rajgir + Nalanda + Vikramshila are bid for World Heritage status. PYQ ANGLE: 'Magadha capital chronology' (Rajgir → Pataliputra) appears in UPSC, SSC ancient-history every 2 cycles.

cards.front:
The Harappan civilisation was discovered in 1921. Who led the initial excavation at Harappa?

(A) Sir John Marshall
(B) Daya Ram Sahni
(C) R. D. Banerji
(D) Mortimer Wheeler
cards.back:
(B) Daya Ram Sahni

Ancient India — Harappa (Punjab, now Pakistan) was excavated in 1921 by Daya Ram Sahni (under ASI). Mohenjo-daro (Sindh, now Pakistan) was excavated in 1922 by R. D. Banerji. Sir JOHN MARSHALL (ASI Director General) announced the discovery of this civilisation in 1924 through a landmark article in The Illustrated London News, giving it the name 'Indus Valley Civilisation'. Mortimer Wheeler excavated in the 1940s, refining chronology. Now called Harappan or Indus-Sarasvati Civilisation. Flourished 2600-1900 BCE (Mature phase). Spread over ~1.25 million sq km — across modern Pakistan, NW India, and eastern Afghanistan.

cards.front:
Lothal, famous for what specific feature, is an Indus Valley site located in which state?

(A) Earliest known dockyard; Gujarat
(B) Great Bath; Sindh (Pakistan)
(C) Fire altars; Rajasthan
(D) Largest size; Haryana
cards.back:
(A) Earliest known dockyard; Gujarat

Ancient India — LOTHAL (Bhal region of Gujarat, near Gulf of Khambhat) is FAMOUS for the world's oldest known dockyard (c. 2400 BCE) — confirming Harappan maritime trade with Mesopotamia. Also notable: fire altars (7), a bead-making factory, a chess-like board game. Excavated by S. R. Rao (1954-63). Tidal dockyard of 214 × 36 m with sluice gates. Contrast site features: Great Bath = Mohenjo-daro (Sindh, Pakistan); Fire altars = Kalibangan (Rajasthan) AND Lothal; Ploughed field = Kalibangan (oldest-known ploughed field, earthquake evidence); Largest site = Rakhigarhi (Haryana, ~350 ha); Harbour/coastal = Lothal, Dholavira, Surkotada.

cards.front:
Which Indus Valley site yielded the famous 'Dancing Girl' bronze statue?

(A) Harappa
(B) Mohenjo-daro
(C) Dholavira
(D) Kalibangan
cards.back:
(B) Mohenjo-daro

Ancient India — The 'DANCING GIRL' (10.5 cm tall, bronze, lost-wax casting technique) was excavated from Mohenjo-daro in 1926 by Ernest Mackay. Dated ~2500 BCE. Shows a nude young female with bangles on her left arm, hand on hip in a dance posture. Currently in the National Museum, New Delhi. Other famous Mohenjo-daro artefacts: 'Priest-King' bust (now in Karachi National Museum, Pakistan — disputed artefact), the Great Bath, the Great Granary. Harappa yielded: the 'Red Jasper Male Torso' (the 'Harappan Dancing Figure' or the Red-stone male figure, 10 cm).

cards.front:
Rakhigarhi, now considered the LARGEST Harappan site, is in which state?

(A) Punjab
(B) Haryana
(C) Rajasthan
(D) Uttar Pradesh
cards.back:
(B) Haryana

Ancient India — Rakhigarhi (Hisar district, Haryana) is now recognised as the LARGEST Harappan site (~350 ha — surpassing Mohenjo-daro's ~250 ha; sometimes called 'Rakhi-Shahpur' after the twin villages). Excavations by Vasant Shinde (Deccan College) and ASI have uncovered planned streets, drains, burials, seals, a jewellery workshop, and most famously — ANCIENT DNA from a 4500-year-old female skeleton (2018-19 study by Shinde & Niraj Rai), showing Harappan people had NO Steppe/Aryan ancestry — supporting the 'Aryan migration post-Harappa' theory. Previous 'largest site' status shifted: Mohenjo-daro > Harappa > Ganweriwala (Pakistan) > Dholavira > Rakhigarhi.

cards.front:
Kalibangan, known for its pre-Harappan ploughed field and fire altars, is located in which state?

(A) Gujarat
(B) Rajasthan
(C) Punjab
(D) Haryana
cards.back:
(B) Rajasthan

Ancient India — Kalibangan ('black bangles' in Punjabi — named after black terracotta bangles found in abundance) is located on the left bank of the Ghaggar river in Hanumangarh district, Rajasthan. Excavated by B. B. Lal and B. K. Thapar (1961-69). Unique for: (1) the world's EARLIEST EVIDENCE of a ploughed field (pre-Harappan, c. 2800 BCE — crisscross furrow pattern suggesting two crops grown simultaneously); (2) SEVEN FIRE ALTARS (suggesting fire-worship, a rare religious clue); (3) evidence of the OLDEST recorded EARTHQUAKE (c. 2600 BCE, may have caused abandonment); (4) lower town also fortified (unusual). Kalibangan sits on the now-dry Saraswati river.

cards.front:
Surkotada, a Harappan site in Gujarat, provided the ONLY conclusive evidence from Indus sites of the presence of:

(A) Domesticated horses
(B) Iron smelting
(C) Writing in Brahmi script
(D) Coinage
cards.back:
(A) Domesticated horses

Ancient India — Surkotada (Kutch, Gujarat), excavated by J. P. Joshi (1964-68), yielded the ONLY confirmed Harappan-era HORSE bones (dated c. 2000 BCE) — a significant finding because the absence of horses in Harappan art/bones was long cited as evidence that the Harappan people were NOT Aryan/Indo-European. The horse remains at Surkotada were verified by archaeo-zoologist Sándor Bökönyi (Hungarian expert). Horses are prominent in Vedic Aryan culture, which developed AFTER the Harappan civilisation declined. Iron came much later (c. 1200 BCE PGW culture). Harappans used pictographic seals, not Brahmi. Coinage dates only to ~6th c. BCE (Mahajanapadas).

cards.front:
The Harappan civilisation is best known for its town planning. Which of the following is NOT characteristic of a typical Indus city layout?

(A) Grid pattern streets intersecting at right angles
(B) A 'Citadel' (upper town) and 'Lower Town'
(C) Advanced underground drainage with soak pits
(D) Monumental temples and royal palaces
cards.back:
(D) Monumental temples and royal palaces

Ancient India — The HARAPPANS are notable for having NO monumental temples or palaces — unlike contemporary Mesopotamia and Egypt. This puzzles archaeologists: was it an egalitarian society, or was their religion domestic? Characteristic features: (a) GRID-pattern streets; (b) Citadel + Lower Town division (upper western citadel for public/administrative buildings, lower eastern for residences); (c) Standardised burnt bricks (ratio 1:2:4 — length:breadth:height); (d) ADVANCED drainage — covered drains, soak pits, manholes; (e) Granaries; (f) Uniform weights and measures; (g) Seals with pictographic script (~400 characters, undeciphered); (h) No large stone sculptures. Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro is the closest to a 'public' structure but not a temple.
cards.option1: Grid pattern streets intersecting at right angles
cards.option3: Advanced underground drainage with soak pits

cards.front:
Dholavira, a 2021 UNESCO WHS, uniquely had which advanced engineering feature?

(A) Iron smelting furnaces
(B) Sophisticated water conservation system with 16 reservoirs
(C) Animal-driven mills
(D) Underground nuclear shelters
cards.back:
(B) Sophisticated water conservation system with 16 reservoirs

Ancient India — DHOLAVIRA (Khadir Bet, Rann of Kutch, Gujarat) is famed for its INGENIOUS WATER HARVESTING system — 16 stone-lined reservoirs comprising ~10% of the city area, collecting monsoon runoff and water from two seasonal streams (Mansar and Manhar). Also known for: (1) tripartite city plan (Citadel + Middle Town + Lower Town — unique among Indus sites); (2) the DHOLAVIRA SIGNBOARD — a 10-sign inscription above a gateway, possibly the oldest 'signboard' in history; (3) rock-cut architecture; (4) declining phase shows gradual settlement of a much-reduced population. Inscribed as India's 40th UNESCO WHS on 27 July 2021.

INDUS VALLEY CIVILISATION (also Harappan) flourished approximately:

(A) 2600-1900 BCE (Mature phase)
(B) 10000-5000 BCE (much earlier)
(C) 1000 BCE-500 CE (much later)
(D) 500 BCE-100 CE (Mauryan era)
cards.back:
(A) 2600-1900 BCE (Mature phase)

Contemporary with EGYPT, MESOPOTAMIA, CHINA — 'cradle' civilisations. Major sites in INDIA: Lothal, Dholavira (Gujarat), Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Banawali, Rakhigarhi (Haryana — possibly LARGEST IVC site). RAKHIGARHI now considered 'capital' candidate.

MOHENJO-DARO (now in Pakistan) literally means:

(A) Mound of the Dead (Sindhi)
(B) City of Light (Urdu/Persian)
(C) King's Fort (Arabic)
(D) Sacred River (Sindhi)
cards.back:
(A) Mound of the Dead (Sindhi)

Ancient India — MOHENJO-DARO = Sindhi for 'MOUND OF THE DEAD' (where bodies / remains were thought to be). DISCOVERED by RD Banerji 1922; excavated by John Marshall (ASI Director-General) + colleagues. KEY FEATURES: GREAT BATH (large public swimming pool, water-resistant — religious purification?); GRANARY (large structure, possibly food storage); CITADEL (raised area for elites); LOWER TOWN (residences, planned grid). NO PALACES, NO TEMPLES (or unidentified) — egalitarian society? UNESCO WHS (1980). HARAPPA — twin city; both lay along then-active SARASWATI / SARASVATI (now dry GHAGGAR-HAKRA). Mohenjo-daro discovered through CHANCE (Buddhist stupa on top led to dig).

DHOLAVIRA (an IVC site in India) is located in which state?

(A) Gujarat (Kutch district, Khadir Bet island)
(B) Rajasthan (Hanumangarh near Kalibangan)
(C) Haryana (near Rakhigarhi) alone
(D) Punjab (near Indian Harappa region)
cards.back:
(A) Gujarat (Kutch district, Khadir Bet island)

Ancient India — DHOLAVIRA — Khadir Bet (an island in Rann of Kutch), GUJARAT. UNESCO WORLD HERITAGE SITE since 2021 — INDIA's 40th. Discovered by JP Joshi (1968), excavated extensively by RS Bisht (1989-2005). UNIQUE FEATURES: stone construction (most IVC was brick); 16+ reservoirs (sophisticated WATER MANAGEMENT — vital for arid Kutch); 3-PART city (Castle, Middle Town, Lower Town); 10 INDUS-SCRIPT SIGNS (largest known sign-board, on gateway). Inhabited ~3000-1500 BCE. OTHER major IVC sites in INDIA: KALIBANGAN (Rajasthan; world's earliest ploughed field; fire altars); LOTHAL (Gujarat; world's earliest known DOCKYARD); RAKHIGARHI (Haryana; possibly LARGEST IVC site, ~350 hectares; ancient DNA studies on skeletons).

cards.front:

(A) World's earliest known DOCKYARD
(B) Largest GRAIN STORAGE structure
(C) Highest CITADEL elevation
(D) Indus SCRIPT decipherment site
cards.back:

Ancient India — LOTHAL — Gujarat (Bhāl region, near Bhogavo + Sabarmati rivers). Discovered by SR Rao (1957). World's EARLIEST KNOWN DOCKYARD (~2400 BCE): rectangular brick basin (~37×22 m) with sluice gate connecting to river; for boats / cargo handling. Indicates IVC's MARITIME TRADE with Mesopotamia, Persian Gulf — Indus seals + beads found in Sumer. Famous artifacts: TERRACOTTA HORSE figurine (controversial — could rewrite chronology if confirmed), STANDARDISED weights + measures, FIRE altars, BEAD-MAKING workshop. Also has lower town + acropolis. NATIONAL MARITIME HERITAGE COMPLEX being developed at Lothal (announced 2022). NEAR Ahmedabad — easy day-trip.

cards.front:
INDUS SCRIPT (used by IVC) has:

(A) NOT been deciphered (~400 signs, undeciphered)
(B) Been deciphered as Sanskrit (definitive)
(C) Been deciphered as Tamil (proven)
(D) Been deciphered as Sumerian (alien)
cards.back:
(A) NOT been deciphered (~400 signs, undeciphered)

Ancient India — INDUS SCRIPT remains UNDECIPHERED despite 100+ years of effort. ~400 SIGNS used; most inscriptions VERY SHORT (avg 5 signs). NO BILINGUAL TEXT (like Rosetta Stone for Egyptian) found yet. Theories: PROTO-DRAVIDIAN, EARLY SANSKRIT, AUSTROASIATIC, or NOT a true language at all (just symbols). KEY scholars: Asko Parpola (Finnish, Dravidian theory), Iravatham Mahadevan (Tamil-Brahmi expert), Steve Farmer (challenges it as language at all). SAMPLE SCRIPT: appears on SEALS (esp. UNICORN motifs — most common on seals, ~60% of seal images), pottery, copper tablets. RECENT: Asko Parpola Indus Project + computational linguistics (entropy analysis suggests structured language); but full decipherment elusive. INDUS SCRIPT is one of world's GREAT undeciphered scripts (along with Linear A, Rongorongo).

cards.front:
IVC TOWNS were notable for:

(A) Grid layout, drainage system, standardised bricks
(B) Random organic streets (no plan) too
(C) Massive royal palaces + temples alone
(D) Elaborate fortifications + walls (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Grid layout, drainage system, standardised bricks

Ancient India — TOWN PLANNING was IVC's hallmark (~4500 years ago!): (1) GRID PATTERN — streets at right angles, N-S + E-W; (2) STANDARDISED bricks (ratio 1:2:4 — uniform across cities, possibly THE world's earliest standardisation); (3) UNDERGROUND DRAINAGE — covered drains, soak pits, regular cleaning provisions; (4) DUAL CITY structure — CITADEL (raised, west, fortified — elites/admin) + LOWER TOWN (east, residential); (5) PUBLIC GRANARIES; (6) WELLS in most houses + public ones; (7) BATHROOMS in each house — IVC had hygiene awareness millennia before others. CONTRAST: Egypt + Mesopotamia of same era didn't have such systematic urban planning. NO MEGA-PALACES + temples (or not identified) → suggests EGALITARIAN, possibly oligarchic society — different from contemporary 'pharaoh-style' civilisations. INDIAN town planners study IVC even today.

cards.front:
DECLINE of IVC (~1900 BCE) is most likely attributed to:

(A) Climate change + drying of Saraswati river system
(B) Aryan invasion (now disputed theory)
(C) Single massive earthquake at one site
(D) Plague / pandemic across all sites (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Climate change + drying of Saraswati river system

Ancient India — IVC DECLINE — modern consensus: GRADUAL CLIMATE CHANGE (~2200-1900 BCE) → weakened monsoon → drying of GHAGGAR-HAKRA / SARASWATI river system. Many IVC sites were on this river → without water, urban centres collapsed. Also: shifts in trade routes, possibly increased flooding then drought, soil salinisation (from over-irrigation), declining trade with Mesopotamia. ARYAN INVASION THEORY (proposed by Mortimer Wheeler 1947, popular for decades) is now LARGELY DISCREDITED — no archaeological evidence of mass violence; languages + people shifted gradually. INDO-ARYAN MIGRATION from Central Asia (~1800-1500 BCE) likely peaceful + gradual. Recent ANCIENT DNA studies (Rakhigarhi 2019, Reich Lab) suggest IVC people share ancestry with modern South Asians, with Indo-European steppe ancestry added later. CULTURAL CONTINUITY: many IVC elements likely persist in modern Indian culture.
cards.option2: Single massive earthquake at one site
cards.option3: Plague / pandemic across all sites (option here)

cards.front:
Which Indus Valley site, located on the Ravi river, was the FIRST to be discovered (1921)?

(A) Mohenjodaro
(B) Harappa
(C) Lothal
(D) Dholavira
cards.back:
(B) Harappa

Ancient India — Harappa (modern Sahiwal district, Punjab, Pakistan) — discovered by Daya Ram Sahni in 1921 under leadership of John Marshall (then ASI Director-General). Lent name to the entire 'Harappan Civilization' (preferred over IVC since sites span beyond Indus river). Located on the bank of the Ravi. Mohenjodaro (Larkana district, Sindh, Pakistan) — discovered next year, 1922, by R.D. Banerji. Carbon-dated mature phase: ~2600-1900 BCE.

cards.front:
The 'Great Bath' — most famous structure of the Indus Valley — is at:

(A) Harappa
(B) Mohenjodaro
(C) Kalibangan
(D) Lothal
cards.back:
(B) Mohenjodaro

Ancient India — Great Bath at Mohenjodaro — 11.88 m × 7.01 m × 2.43 m deep. Probably used for ritual bathing. Made watertight using gypsum mortar, lime plaster, and bitumen layers. Located in the citadel area. Also at Mohenjodaro: 'Granary' (largest building), 'College of Priests', 'Assembly Hall', dancing-girl bronze statuette, priest-king bust. Layout follows the grid (chess-board) plan with Citadel + Lower Town. UNESCO WHS since 1980.

(B) Gujarat (Bhal region, near Sabarmati estuary)

cards.back:

Other Gujarat IVC sites: Dholavira (Kutch — UNESCO WHS 2021), Surkotada (with horse remains), Kuntasi, Rojdi. Indus's reach far beyond the Indus — modern India: 1,500+ sites identified; 6 are major (Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Ganweriwal, Mehrgarh).

(B) Haryana (Hisar district)
(C) Punjab

cards.back:

The famous 'Pashupati Seal' — depicting a horned figure surrounded by animals (often interpreted as proto-Shiva) — was found at:

(A) Harappa
(B) Mohenjodaro
(C) Dholavira
(D) Banawali
cards.back:

Ancient India — Pashupati Seal — found at Mohenjodaro by John Marshall in 1928-29. Steatite (soapstone) seal, cross-legged horned deity, surrounded by elephant, tiger, rhino, water buffalo. cards.back:

The Kalinga War, a turning point in Indian history, was fought by Ashoka in:

(A) 261 BCE
(B) 232 BCE
(C) 305 BCE

cards.back:

Ancient India — The Kalinga War was fought c. 261 BCE — the 8th regnal year of Ashoka, who had been crowned c. 269 BCE. cards.front:
The Mauryan Empire declined and fragmented after the death of which ruler?

(A) Chandragupta Maurya
(B) Bindusara
(C) Ashoka
(D) Brihadratha (the last Mauryan)
cards.back:
(C) Ashoka

Ancient India — After Ashoka's death (c. 232 BCE), the Mauryan Empire declined rapidly. His successors (Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan, Brihadratha) were weaker; administrative costs were huge; provincial governors rebelled. The LAST Mauryan, Brihadratha, was assassinated by his commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga c. 185 BCE, founding the Shunga dynasty. So Ashoka's death BEGAN the decline; Brihadratha's assassination ENDED the empire.

cards.back:

Ancient India — ASHOKA (r. 268-232 BCE) — initially traditional Hindu / aggressive ruler. KALINGA WAR (261 BCE) — bloody victory horrified him → embraced BUDDHISM. Spread it through: ROCK + PILLAR EDICTS (across India, in Brahmi + Kharoshthi scripts; also Greek + Aramaic in Afghanistan); MISSIONS to Sri Lanka (son Mahindra + daughter Sanghamitra), Burma, Central Asia; THIRD BUDDHIST COUNCIL at Pataliputra (250 BCE, under Moggaliputta Tissa); state policy of DHAMMA (ethical code, non-violence, tolerance). His emblem (4-lion capital, Sarnath) = India's national emblem. Distractor 3: Chandragupta MAURYA (his grandfather) is said to have embraced JAINISM in old age, abdicating to die in Shravanabelagola.

GUPTA AGE is famously called the 'Golden Age of India' because of:

(A) Massive territorial expansion (largest empire)
(B) Cultural + scientific + literary flourishing
(C) Adoption of Christianity by Guptas
(D) Discovery + use of pure gold mines

cards.front:
The MAURYAN administration was famous for which detailed treatise on statecraft?

(A) Nyaya Sutras of Gautama (philosophy)
(B) Arthashastra by Kautilya / Chanakya
(C) Mahabharata of Vyasa (epic)
(D) Manusmriti by Manu (law book)
cards.back:
(B) Arthashastra by Kautilya / Chanakya

Ancient India — ARTHASHASTRA — comprehensive treatise on STATECRAFT, economics, military strategy, espionage, diplomacy, taxation, foreign policy. Written by KAUTILYA (also known as Chanakya / Vishnugupta) — Chandragupta Maurya's chief advisor (~4th c. BCE; rediscovered 1905). Themes: importance of dharma, importance of king's safety, MANDALA THEORY of foreign policy (concentric circle of ally / enemy), SPY networks, taxation. Often compared with Machiavelli's 'The Prince' (much earlier, more comprehensive). Contains the famous saying: 'an enemy of an enemy is a friend' (mandala).

Chinese pilgrim FA-HIEN (Faxian) visited India during the reign of which Gupta emperor?

(A) Samudragupta, the conqueror emperor
(B) Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
(C) Skandagupta, defender of empire
(D) Kumaragupta, the middle emperor
cards.back:
(B) Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)

Ancient India — FA-HIEN / FAXIAN (Chinese Buddhist monk) — visited India ~399-414 CE, during reign of CHANDRAGUPTA II VIKRAMADITYA (r. 380-415 CE). Travelled to study Buddhist texts. Wrote 'FOGUOJI' (Records of Buddhist Kingdoms) — described Indian society, Buddhism, customs. Praised peaceful + prosperous life. Other Chinese visitors: HIUEN TSANG (Xuanzang) ~629-645 CE — Harsha's reign; I-TSING (Yijing) ~671-695 CE — Pala period (later, after Guptas).

cards.front:
Which empire had MEGASTHENES (Greek ambassador to Indian court) as a foreign visitor?

(A) Gupta empire (during Chandragupta II)
(B) Mauryan empire (during Chandragupta Maurya)
(C) Harsha's empire (during 7th century CE)
(D) Kushan empire (during Kanishka's reign)
cards.back:
(B) Mauryan empire (during Chandragupta Maurya)

Ancient India — MEGASTHENES — Greek envoy sent by SELEUCUS NICATOR (Alexander's general, founder of Seleucid empire) to the court of CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA at Pataliputra (~302 BCE). Stayed several years. Wrote 'INDIKA' (now lost; survives in fragments quoted by later Greek writers — Strabo, Arrian, Diodorus). Described India's society, geography, government, army (~600,000 infantry + 30,000 cavalry + 9000 elephants — likely exaggerated). Famous descriptions: '7 castes' (his classification), Pataliputra's grandeur. Distractor 1 — Fa-Hien visited Gupta. Distractor 3 — Hiuen Tsang visited Harsha.

cards.front:
The Maurya empire was founded in around 321 BCE by:

(A) Ashoka
(B) Chandragupta Maurya
(C) Bimbisara
(D) Bindusara
cards.back:
(B) Chandragupta Maurya

Ancient India — Chandragupta Maurya — mentored by Chanakya (Kautilya) — overthrew the last Nanda king, Dhana Nanda, around 321 BCE and founded the Mauryan dynasty at Pataliputra. Bindusara was his son; Ashoka his grandson. Bimbisara had ruled Magadha three centuries earlier under the Haryanka dynasty. Greek sources knew Chandragupta as 'Sandrakottos'.

cards.front:
Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism was triggered by which war described in his 13th Rock Edict?

(A) Battle of Magadha
(B) Kalinga War
(C) Battle of Hydaspes
(D) Battle of Taxila
cards.back:
(B) Kalinga War

Ancient India — The Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE) — Ashoka's bloody conquest of Kalinga (modern Odisha) — moved him to abandon violent conquest and adopt Buddhism, dhamma-vijaya (victory through righteousness), and a pan-imperial message of non-violence. Described in the 13th Rock Edict. The Battle of Hydaspes (326 BCE) was Alexander vs Porus. Taxila was Chandragupta's earlier campaign location, not a battle with Ashoka.

Samudragupta, often called the 'Napoleon of India' by the historian V. A. Smith, is chiefly praised for his:

(A) Religious tolerance
(B) Military campaigns across India
(C) Revenue reforms
(D) Maritime expeditions overseas
cards.back:
(B) Military campaigns across India

Ancient India — Samudragupta (c. 335-375 CE) — son of Chandragupta I — led extensive military campaigns across northern, eastern and southern India, recorded on the Allahabad Pillar Prashasti (composed by his court poet Harishena). He was also a noted vina player and is shown on some coins with that instrument. Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya), his son, is the one associated with a court of learning (Nine Jewels / Navaratnas).

cards.front:
The mathematician-astronomer Aryabhata, who lived during the Gupta age, is credited with:

(A) Discovery of penicillin
(B) Early use of zero and an approximation of π
(C) Invention of the telescope
(D) Writing the Charaka Samhita
cards.back:
(B) Early use of zero and an approximation of π

Ancient India — Aryabhata (b. 476 CE) wrote the Aryabhatiya (499 CE), which used place-value notation including a placeholder for zero (later formalised as a distinct number by Brahmagupta in 628 CE). He approximated π as 3.1416 and proposed that the Earth rotates on its own axis, causing the apparent motion of the stars. Penicillin was discovered by Fleming in 1928; the telescope by Galileo in 1609; the Charaka Samhita is a text on Ayurveda by Charaka (redacted c. 1st-2nd century CE).

cards.front:
The dynasty that IMMEDIATELY succeeded the Mauryas in Magadha (after the last Mauryan emperor Brihadratha was killed in 185 BCE) was the:

(A) Kushana dynasty
(B) Satavahana dynasty
(C) SHUNGA DYNASTY
(D) Gupta dynasty
cards.back:
(C) SHUNGA DYNASTY

Ancient India — SHUNGA DYNASTY (185-73 BCE, ~112 years) — founded when PUSHYAMITRA SHUNGA (the Brahmin senapati / commander-in-chief of the Mauryan army) ASSASSINATED the last Mauryan emperor BRIHADRATHA during a military PARADE in Pataliputra in 185 BCE. Pushyamitra Shunga established himself as the new king of Magadha; his capital was PATALIPUTRA. SIGNIFICANCE: (1) End of Mauryan empire, 137 years after Chandragupta Maurya founded it; (2) Began a period of PERIPHERAL INVASIONS and FRAGMENTATION of north India. PUSHYAMITRA SHUNGA: (a) celebrated HINDU REVIVAL after Ashokan Buddhism; reportedly persecuted Buddhists (per Buddhist texts like Ashokavadana/Divyavadana) though historical veracity is debated; (b) performed two ASHVAMEDHA YAJNAS (horse sacrifices) as claimed in Ayodhya inscription; (c) faced Greek (Indo-Greek) invasions — DEMETRIUS of Bactria, then MENANDER I (MILINDA) who reached as far as Sagala (Sialkot); famous ‘MILINDA PANHA’ is dialogue of Milinda with Buddhist monk NAGASENA. (d) Pushyamitra's court patronised Sanskrit: PATANJALI (the grammarian, author of Mahabhashya — commentary on Panini's Ashtadhyayi) was contemporary — some say court scholar; Patanjali also credited with Yoga Sutras (may be same/different person). Pushyamitra was succeeded by AGNIMITRA (subject of Kalidasa's MALAVIKAGNIMITRAM play, though Kalidasa is much later, 4th-5th century CE), Vasujyestha, Vasumitra, Andhraka, Pulindaka, Ghosha, Vajramitra, Bhagabhadra, Devabhuti (last Shunga, killed ~73 BCE by Vasudeva Kanva of the Kanva dynasty — who then ruled 73-28 BCE for just 45 years). BUILDING legacy: despite alleged anti-Buddhism, Shunga ART FLOURISHED — BHARHUT STUPA (MP) railings and torana, SANCHI STUPA (MP, originally built by Ashoka; enlarged+encased in Shunga period with stone railing); the medallions and reliefs of these stupas are Shunga art (2nd-1st c. BCE). Religious literature: Shunga era is when MANU SMRITI was composed (uncertain, 2nd BCE - 2nd CE); later sections of RAMAYANA + MAHABHARATA + Puranas were compiled. KANVAS succeeded Shungas 73-28 BCE (4 rulers: Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana, Susarman); then SATAVAHANAS of Deccan swept north and ended them in 28 BCE. founded by PUSHYAMITRA SHUNGA, a Brahmin commander-in-chief of the Mauryan army who killed Brihadratha during a military parade; ruled Magadha ~185-73 BCE.

cards.front:
The SATAVAHANA DYNASTY, which ruled the DECCAN for nearly 4 centuries from ~230 BCE to 220 CE, had its capital at:

(A) Pataliputra
(B) PRATISHTHANA (modern PAITHAN on the Godavari river, in Aurangabad district, Maharashtra); also used Amaravati (on Krishna, AP) as secondary capital
(C) Kaveripattinam
(D) Madurai
cards.back:
(B) PRATISHTHANA (modern PAITHAN on the Godavari river, in Aurangabad district, Maharashtra); also used Amaravati (on Krishna, AP) as secondary capital

Ancient India — SATAVAHANA DYNASTY (~230 BCE - 220 CE, ~450 years) — the GREATEST early DECCAN dynasty; also known as ANDHRAS (mentioned in Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII as vassals, and in the Puranas as ‘ANDHRAS’ and ‘ANDHRABHRTYAS’). FOUNDER: SIMUKA (c. 230 BCE). CAPITAL: PRATISHTHANA (modern PAITHAN in Maharashtra, on the Godavari, still a pilgrimage site); also AMARAVATI (on Krishna, near Guntur, Andhra Pradesh) was a major political + Buddhist centre; DHANYAKATAKA / Dharanikota nearby. LANGUAGE of records: mostly PRAKRIT (Brahmi script); occasional Sanskrit. DOMAIN: at peak, covered Maharashtra, MP, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Gujarat, Konkan. GREATEST RULERS: (1) SATAKARNI I (c. 70 BCE) — performed 2 Ashvamedhas, 1 Rajasuya; mentioned in NANAGHAT inscription (Naneghat Caves, Maharashtra — where his wife Naganika inscribed his reign). (2) HALA (c. 20-24 CE) — a SCHOLAR-KING; compiled ‘GATHA SAPTASHATI’ / GATHASATTASAI — an ANTHOLOGY of 700 PRAKRIT love poems by various poets; one of oldest Indian literary anthologies. (3) GAUTAMIPUTRA SATAKARNI (c. 106-130 CE) — regarded as the greatest Satavahana; defeated the Saka KSHAHARATA chief NAHAPANA (Kshatrapa satrap) and took back Deccan + Gujarat + Malwa; his mother GAUTAMI BALASHRI composed the NASIK CAVE INSCRIPTION (a eulogy calling him ‘destroyer of the pride of Kshatriyas, conqueror of Sakas-Yavanas-Pahlavas’). (4) VASHISHTHIPUTRA PULUMAYI (130-158 CE) — son of Gautamiputra; his coins bear ship images (maritime trade). (5) YAJNA SATAKARNI (c. 170-190 CE) — last strong ruler; after him the empire fragmented; Ikshvakus, Abhiras, Vakatakas, etc., rose. ART & ARCHITECTURE: Satavahanas were great patrons of BUDDHISM (despite being Vedic/Hindu rulers themselves). Built/patronised: (1) AMARAVATI STUPA (AP) — MAHACHAITYA — famous for marble drum-slab reliefs, now mostly in British Museum and Madras Museum. (2) NAGARJUNAKONDA (AP) — Buddhist centre; but peak was under Ikshvakus successor. (3) KARLE, BHAJA, NASIK, KANHERI CAVES — ROCK-CUT BUDDHIST CAVES (chaitya halls + viharas) in Western Ghats; cathedral-like Karla chaitya is stunning. (4) AJANTA — earliest caves (9, 10) begun in Satavahana times (though famous paintings are Vakataka/Gupta era). ECONOMY: issued LEAD, POTIN, COPPER, SILVER coins; controlled Indo-Roman maritime trade via ports (Broach/Bharukaccha, Sopara, Kalyan); Pliny and Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st c. CE Roman text) describe brisk trade in silk, cotton, muslin, spices, ivory, gems. DECLINE: weakened after 2nd c. CE; IKSHVAKUS of AP, ABHIRAS of Maharashtra, VAKATAKAS of Vidarbha, PALLAVAS of Kanchi emerged.

Built/patronised: (1) AMARAVATI STUPA (AP) — MAHACHAITYA — famous for marble drum-slab reliefs, now mostly in British Museum and Madras Museum. (2) NAGARJUNAKONDA (AP) — Buddhist centre; but peak was under Ikshvakus successor. (3) KARLE, BHAJA, NASIK, KANHERI CAVES — ROCK-CUT BUDDHIST CAVES (chaitya halls + viharas) in Western Ghats; cathedral-like Karla chaitya is stunning. (4) AJANTA — earliest caves (9, 10) begun in Satavahana times (though famous paintings are Vakataka/Gupta era). ECONOMY: issued LEAD, POTIN, COPPER, SILVER coins; controlled Indo-Roman maritime trade via ports (Broach/Bharukaccha, Sopara, Kalyan); Pliny and Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st c. CE Roman text) describe brisk trade in silk, cotton, muslin, spices, ivory, gems. DECLINE: weakened after 2nd c. CE; IKSHVAKUS of AP, ABHIRAS of Maharashtra, VAKATAKAS of Vidarbha, PALLAVAS of Kanchi emerged.

cards.front:
The greatest KUSHANA ruler, under whom Buddhism received royal patronage and the 4th Buddhist Council was held in Kashmir, was:

(A) Vima Kadphises
(B) Kujula Kadphises
(C) KANISHKA I
(D) Huvishka
cards.back:
(C) KANISHKA I

Ancient India — KANISHKA I (KANISHKA THE GREAT) — the most famous KUSHANA emperor. Ruled c. 78-144 CE (dates long debated). Kushanas were a branch of the YUEH-CHI tribe (of Central Asian / Chinese origin) who migrated west into Bactria (Afghanistan) and then entered India through the NW. KANISHKA'S EMPIRE: vast — from Central Asia (parts of Tajikistan + Uzbekistan) + Afghanistan + Pakistan + N India down to Mathura + Sanchi + Bihar. CAPITALS: two — PURUSHAPURA (PESHAWAR, Pakistan) + MATHURA (UP). ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) ADOPTED + PATRONISED MAHAYANA BUDDHISM (though Kanishka was tolerant of all — his coins depict Greek + Iranian + Indian deities). (2) CONVENED the 4TH BUDDHIST COUNCIL at KUNDALAVANA (KASHMIR), ~78 CE (or thereabouts); presided by VASUMITRA, with poet-philosopher ASVAGHOSHA as vice-president. This council: (a) compiled Buddhist texts in SANSKRIT (earlier councils in Pali/Magadhi); (b) produced the MAHAVIBHASHA commentary on the Abhidharma; (c) accelerated the rise of MAHAYANA Buddhism over Theravada/Hinayana. (3) STARTED THE SAKA ERA on 22 March 78 CE — still used as INDIA'S NATIONAL CIVIL CALENDAR (SHAKA SAMVAT), adopted officially in 1957; 78 years behind Gregorian. (4) First Indian ruler to issue GOLD COINS (Roman-style, high quality) along with copper coins — gold from Roman trade + Central Asian mines. (5) Patronised BUDDHIST ART — GANDHARA school (Greco-Buddhist hybrid, Afghanistan-Pakistan, wavy hair + Greek robes, standing/seated Buddha statues — first physical representations of Buddha) and MATHURA school (indigenous red-sandstone, kapotaka style). (6) Patronised scholars: ASVAGHOSHA (poet, wrote BUDDHACHARITA + SAUNDARANANDA — Buddhist Sanskrit mahakavyas; first Indian Sanskrit ‘drama’); NAGARJUNA (founder of MADHYAMIKA philosophy + SUNYATA doctrine); VASUMITRA; CHARAKA (physician, author of Charaka Samhita); Mathara/Parsva. (7) KANISHKA'S STUPA at PESHAWAR — one of the tallest stupas of ancient world (reported 13-storey or 400 ft) — contained Buddha relics (excavated 1908, relics now in Burma). (8) Kanishka's HEADLESS STATUE at MATHURA MUSEUM — famously preserved (head broken off by iconoclasts later). INSCRIPTION: RABATAK (discovered 1993 in Afghanistan) — gives GENEALOGY of Kushanas: KUJULA KADPHISES (founder, c. 30-80 CE) → VIMA TAKTO → VIMA KADPHISES → KANISHKA I → HUVISHKA → VASUDEVA I (last great, after whom empire declined). KUSHANAS collapsed after 230 CE due to Sasanian invasions from Persia; smaller Kushano-Sasanian kingdoms continued; remnants absorbed by GUPTAS.

cards.front:
India's NATIONAL CALENDAR, the SAKA ERA, begins from the year:

(A) 312 BCE (Seleucid)
(B) 58 BCE (Vikrami Samvat)
(C) 78 CE — started by Kushana emperor KANISHKA I; adopted as India’s National Civil Calendar by GoI in 1957, alongside Gregorian; 78 years behind Gregorian
(D) 606 CE (Harsha era)
cards.back:
(C) 78 CE — started by Kushana emperor KANISHKA I; adopted as India’s National Civil Calendar by GoI in 1957, alongside Gregorian; 78 years behind Gregorian

Ancient India — SAKA SAMVAT / SAKA ERA — INDIA'S NATIONAL CIVIL CALENDAR (Rashtriya Panchang). STARTED: 22 March 78 CE, the traditional date of KANISHKA I's accession / the vernal equinox of that year. Thus Saka Year = Gregorian Year − 78 (for dates after 22 March). E.g., 2026 CE → 1948 Saka; 20 April 2026 → 30 Chaitra 1948 Saka. Saka is BEHIND Gregorian by 78 years. MONTHS of Saka (based on tropical signs of zodiac, 12 months): CHAITRA (Mar-Apr, 30 days; 31 in leap year) → VAISHAKHA → JYESTHA → ASHADHA → SHRAVANA → BHADRA → ASHVIN → KARTIKA → AGRAHAYANA (Margashira) → PAUSHA → MAGHA → PHALGUNA. NEW YEAR's DAY: 1 CHAITRA = 22 March (or 21 March in Gregorian leap years). LEAP YEAR rule same as Gregorian (adds 1 day to Chaitra). ADOPTED on 22 March 1957 by Government of India, alongside Gregorian, based on recommendations of CALENDAR REFORM COMMITTEE (1952) chaired by MEGHNAD SAHA (astrophysicist). Saka dates appear in: (1) Gazette of India; (2) All India Radio (AIR) national news announcements; (3) Government communications; (4) Calendars issued by GoI. OTHER PROMINENT INDIAN ERAS: (I) VIKRAMA SAMVAT (VS) — started 58/57 BCE; traditionally by King VIKRAMADITYA of Ujjain after defeating Sakas; used in N India, Nepal (official Nepali calendar Bikram Sambat). 2026 CE = 2083 VS. (II) KALI YUGA — started 3102 BCE (traditional Hindu astronomical era); age of Kali (4,32,000 years); current year 5127 (2026). (III) GUPTA ERA — 319/320 CE (start of Chandragupta I's reign); used in Gupta + Vakataka inscriptions. (IV) HARSHA ERA — 606 CE (start of Harshavardhana's reign). (V) HIJRI (ISLAMIC) — 622 CE (Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina); lunar; 622 CE = 1 AH; 2026 CE ≈ 1447-1448 AH. (VI) BUDDHIST ERA — 544/543 BCE (Buddha's Mahaparinirvana by Theravada reckoning); 2026 CE = 2569 BE. (VII) BANGLA SAMBAT / Bengali calendar — 594 CE (claimed link to King Shashanka of Gauda, or revised by Akbar from Islamic era); 2026 CE = 1432-1433 BS; 14/15 April = Pohela Boishakh (Bengali New Year). (VIII) KOLLAM ERA — 825 CE, used in Kerala (Kollavarsham). (IX) SAPTA-RISHI era — used in Kashmir. GLOBAL CIVIL CALENDAR: GREGORIAN, introduced 15 Oct 1582 by Pope Gregory XIII (reformed Julian calendar of Julius Caesar 46 BCE). India followed British adoption in 1752 (when UK finally shifted). Leap year rule: every 4 yrs, except century years not divisible by 400 (so 1900 NOT leap, 2000 LEAP, 2100 NOT leap).

cards.front:
The INDO-GREEK ruler MENANDER I (MILINDA, c. 165-130 BCE), remembered for his dialogue with Buddhist monk NAGASENA, had his capital at:

(A) Taxila
(B) Pataliputra
(C) SAGALA
(D) Mathura
cards.back:
(C) SAGALA

Ancient India — MENANDER I SOTER (‘Saviour’) / MILINDA (c. 165-130 BCE) — greatest INDO-GREEK ruler. Indo-Greeks (also called Yavanas in Sanskrit) were successors of ALEXANDER THE GREAT's conquests of Bactria (Afghanistan) + NW India. They established kingdoms in Bactria (c. 250 BCE by DIODOTUS) and later spread into India. Menander ruled from SAGALA (modern SIALKOT, Punjab, Pakistan). EMPIRE: stretched from Bactria + Arachosia to Gandhara + Taxila + Punjab + as far east as Mathura. He is CELEBRATED in Buddhist literature as a CONVERT TO BUDDHISM. The ‘MILINDA PANHA’ (‘QUESTIONS OF MILINDA’) is a famous PALI text (1st c. BCE or later) recording a series of DIALOGUES between King Milinda and the Buddhist sage NAGASENA on doctrinal questions — self, soul, rebirth, nirvana; one of the best-known Indian Buddhist non-canonical works. Like the dialogues of Socrates, but in Buddhist philosophical tradition. Menander's COINS (bilingual, Greek + Kharoshthi; silver drachms) have been found widely. GREEK HISTORIAN STRABO claimed Menander's conquests ‘exceeded even those of Alexander’. Menander also sent ambassadors and had contact with Central Asia. After his death (130 BCE), his empire began to fragment; his widow Agathokleia served as regent for his son Strato I. Other notable Indo-Greek kings: DEMETRIUS I (‘king of India’), ANTIALKIDAS (sent HELIODORUS as envoy to SHUNGA king at Vidisha — Heliodorus converted to Bhagavata Vaishnavism and erected the HELIODORUS PILLAR at Besnagar/Vidisha, MP, with Garuda, dedicated to Vasudeva-Krishna — one of earliest evidence of devotional Vaishnavism). INDO-GREEKS were eventually displaced by: (1) SAKAS / Scythians (Indo-Scythians, from Central Asia, c. 1st c. BCE; MAUES was first king); (2) PAHLAVAS / Parthians; (3) KUSHANAS (Yueh-Chi). Indo-Greeks RETREATED to Hindu Kush by c. 10 CE. CULTURAL IMPACT: Hellenistic art + GANDHARAN sculpture (Greco-Buddhist style — Buddha depicted with Apollo-like features, wavy hair, toga-drapes); ASTRONOMY (Indian astronomy borrowed zodiac signs — Rashi names like Mesha = Aries, Vrishabha = Taurus — from Greek); GEOMETRY; COINAGE (Indian kings adopted Greek coin design conventions); POSSIBLY Indian theatre structure (though disputed). The ‘YAVANAS’ / ‘YAVANI’ script/language (= Greek) is mentioned in Patanjali's Mahabhashya and Kamasutra. Rock edicts of Ashoka mention Greek kings Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Magas, Antigonus, Alexander as recipients of his dhamma messengers. Thus Indo-Greeks bridged the cross-cultural Indo-Mediterranean exchange for ~250 years. ruled over most of NW India down to Mathura; the dialogue forms the ‘MILINDA PANHA’ (Questions of Milinda) in Pali, a Buddhist classic; SIALKOT, Punjab, Pakistan.
