cards.front:
The art school famous for its HELLENISTIC / GRAECO-BUDDHIST style, depicting the Buddha with WAVY HAIR and GRECIAN ROBES, is the:

(A) Mathura school (red sandstone)
(B) Amaravati school (marble)
(C) GANDHARA SCHOOL — flourished in present-day NW Pakistan + E Afghanistan; 1st-5th c. CE; Greek-Roman + Indian + Central Asian fusion; patronised under Kushanas (esp. Kanishka); first physical Buddha images here
(D) Pallava school
cards.back:
(C) GANDHARA SCHOOL — flourished in present-day NW Pakistan + E Afghanistan; 1st-5th c. CE; Greek-Roman + Indian + Central Asian fusion; patronised under Kushanas (esp. Kanishka); first physical Buddha images here

Ancient India — GANDHARA SCHOOL OF ART (1st c. BCE - 5th c. CE) — one of three great SCHOOLS OF INDIAN BUDDHIST ART (along with Mathura + Amaravati). Named after the region GANDHARA (modern TAKHT-I-BAHI, Peshawar, Swat, Taxila in Pakistan + parts of E Afghanistan). DEFINING FEATURES: (1) HELLENISTIC GRECO-ROMAN INFLUENCE due to Indo-Greek presence + exposure to Roman trade + Kushana patronage; (2) BUDDHA STATUES with APOLLO-LIKE face (oval, sharp nose, wavy curly hair, serene gaze, half-closed meditative eyes); (3) drapery — TOGA-STYLE FLOWING ROBES (sanghati) with heavy folds (imitating Greek/Roman sculpture); (4) HALOS (nimbus) behind head — derived from sun-god imagery; (5) anatomically realistic body (Greek human proportions); (6) MATERIAL: grey-black SCHIST stone (Gandhara) + later STUCCO + terracotta. LEADING SITES: (a) TAKHT-I-BAHI (Pakistan, UNESCO WHS 1980) — rock-cut Buddhist monastery; (b) TAXILA (Pakistan, UNESCO WHS 1980) — includes Dharmarajika Stupa, Sirkap city, Sirsukh, Jaulian, Mohra Moradu monasteries; (c) SWAT VALLEY (Butkara, Saidu Sharif); (d) HADDA + BAMIYAN (Afghanistan) — the BAMIYAN BUDDHAS (2 colossal Buddhas, 6th c. CE, 53 m + 35 m tall) were destroyed by the Taliban in March 2001 — one of the great cultural losses of our time. Reconstruction debated. PATRONS: (I) Indo-Greeks + Indo-Scythian rulers; (II) KUSHANAS — esp. KANISHKA I + HUVISHKA (2nd c. CE) — the golden age of Gandhara. MATHURA SCHOOL (2nd c. BCE - 7th c. CE) — contemporary, INDIGENOUS SCHOOL centred at Mathura (UP). Features: (a) RED SANDSTONE from Sikri/Kasupa quarries; (b) INDIAN aesthetic — fuller body, CURLY KNOT OF HAIR (USHNISHA), URNA (mark between brows), earlobe elongation, erect posture, smiling face, THINNER-TRANSPARENT drapery (not layered like Gandhara); (c) depicted not just Buddha but JAIN tirthankaras, Hindu gods (Krishna, Shiva), and KUSHANA PORTRAIT sculptures (famous HEADLESS KANISHKA statue); (d) developed iconographic conventions that became Pan-Indian (lotus seat, mudras, parasol); (e) mass-production of images that travelled widely. AMARAVATI SCHOOL (2nd c. BCE - 3rd c. CE) — in the DECCAN, patronised by SATAVAHANAS + IKSHVAKUS. Features: (a) WHITE LIMESTONE / MARBLE; (b) narrative reliefs on stupa DRUM-SLABS showing Jataka tales + Buddha's life; (c) dynamic poses, slender graceful bodies, crowded compositions; (d) early aniconic (symbols — footprints, empty throne) transitioning to anthropomorphic Buddha. AMARAVATI STUPA reliefs now in British Museum (London) + Government Museum Chennai + Amaravati Archaeological Museum. OTHER SCHOOLS that emerged later: SARNATH (late Gupta), PALA (Bihar-Bengal, 8-12th c.), HOYSALA (Karnataka, 11-14th c.).

cards.front:
RUDRADAMAN I, the Shaka (Western Kshatrapa) ruler of Saurashtra, is famous for the:

(A) Aihole inscription
(B) Allahabad Pillar inscription
(C) JUNAGADH (Girnar) ROCK INSCRIPTION (150 CE)
(D) Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription
cards.back:
(C) JUNAGADH (Girnar) ROCK INSCRIPTION (150 CE)

Ancient India — JUNAGADH ROCK INSCRIPTION of RUDRADAMAN I (150 CE) — inscribed on the same ROCK near GIRNAR HILL (Junagadh, Gujarat) that already carried Ashoka's earlier rock edicts. Considered the EARLIEST LONG SANSKRIT INSCRIPTION (earlier Sanskrit inscriptions are much shorter). CONTENTS: (1) Records in chaste Sanskrit (influenced by Panini's grammar; kavya style with poetry + prose alternating) the REPAIR of the SUDARSHANA LAKE (Reservoir) — originally built by PUSHYAGUPTA, a Mauryan viceroy under CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA (4th c. cards.front:
The SANGAM AGE of Tamil literature flourished in the FAR SOUTH (Tamilakam) approximately during which period?

(A) 500-200 BCE
(B) ~3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE
(C) 5th-8th century CE
(D) 10th-12th century CE
cards.back:
(B) ~3rd century BCE to 3rd century CE

Ancient India — SANGAM AGE — classical age of TAMIL literature + history; named after SANGAMS (Tamil ‘Sangam’ means assembly/academy — from Sanskrit ‘Sangha’). Traditional Tamil legend speaks of THREE SANGAMS held at Madurai/Kapatapuram under the PANDYA patronage: First Sangam — 4,400 years, lost to a deluge; Second Sangam — 3,700 years, also lost; Third Sangam — 1,850 years, whose output SURVIVED. The Third Sangam (~3rd c. BCE to 3rd c. CE) is what scholars identify as the historical Sangam period. CONTEMPORARY to: Mauryas (their mention in Sangam poems + Ashoka's edict II and XIII referring to south Indian kingdoms), Satavahanas, Sakas. LOCATION: TAMILAKAM — comprised modern Tamil Nadu, Kerala, parts of Karnataka + Andhra; also Sri Lanka had presence. THREE DYNASTIES: (I) CHERAS — west coast (Kerala + west TN); capital VANJI (later KARUR); emblem BOW; greatest king SENGUTTUVAN (‘the Just’) — hero of SILAPPADIKARAM; performed Aryan-influenced ceremonies + led expedition to Himalayas to get stone for KANNAGI (the chaste wife) statue. (II) CHOLAS — central TN, Kaveri delta; capitals UPHUR + KAVERIPOOMPATTINAM / PUHAR (port); emblem TIGER; greatest: KARIKALA (‘the one with the charred leg’) — defeated Cheras + Pandyas at battle of Venni, built the GRAND ANICUT (Kallanai dam across Kaveri, ~1st-2nd c. CE — oldest functional DAM in the world still in use). (III) PANDYAS — southern TN + Kerala; capital MADURAI; emblem FISH; presided over the Tamil Sangams; known for pearl fishery of Korkai port. SANGAM LITERATURE — ~473 poets, ~2,381 poems survive; in ancient Tamil (before Brahmi adaptation to Tamil-Brahmi script). DIVIDED INTO: (I) ETTUTHOKAI (‘Eight Anthologies’) — AKANANURU (love poetry on ‘akam’ — inner life); PURANANURU (heroic/public poetry on ‘puram’); NARRINAI; KURUNTOKAI; KALITOKAI; AINKURUNURU; PARIPATAL; PATIRRUPPATTU. (II) PATTUPPATTU (‘Ten Idylls’) — long narrative poems incl. TIRUMURUGARRUPPATAI, POR UNARATRUPPATAI, MALAIPATUKATAM. (III) PATINENKILKANAKKU (18 minor works) — shorter; includes TIRUKKURAL by TIRUVALLUVAR (!!! though most scholars date Kural to post-Sangam 4-5th c. CE). (IV) TWO GREAT EPICS (later, c. 5th-6th CE but part of extended Sangam tradition): SILAPPADIKARAM (‘The Tale of the Anklet’) by ILANGO ADIGAL — heroine Kannagi, husband Kovalan murdered unjustly by Pandya king, she burns Madurai down; MANIMEKALAI by SATTANAR — Buddhist, sequel about Kovalan's daughter Manimekalai. Plus JIVAKA-CHINTAMANI (Jain, by Tiruttakkadevar) + SILAPPADIKARAM + VALAIYAPATI + KUNDALAKESI = ‘FIVE GREAT EPICS of Tamil’. CULTURE from Sangam: 5 TINAIS (landscape types — kurinji hills, mullai forest/pastoral, marudam farmland, neydal seashore, palai arid); each associated with specific deity + mood of love. Religion: a mix of indigenous Tamil worship + later-adopted Hindu deities + Jain + Buddhist presence (Nagarjunakonda, Amaravati). After Sangam era: KALABHRA interregnum (3rd-6th c.), then PALLAVAS rose + Pandya revival + Early Cholas. roughly parallel to the post-Mauryan / Satavahana period in the north; ‘Sangam’ = assembly of poets/scholars under Pandya patronage; produced a vast body of secular Tamil poetry.

cards.front:
The GRAND ANICUT (Kallanai), regarded as one of the OLDEST WATER-DIVERSION STRUCTURES in the world STILL IN USE, was built by:

(A) Ashoka on the Sindhu
(B) Samudragupta on the Ganges
(C) KARIKALA CHOLA (c. 1st-2nd c. CE) across the KAVERI RIVER near TIRUCHIRAPPALLI, Tamil Nadu
(D) Rajaraja Chola I in the 11th century
cards.back:
(C) KARIKALA CHOLA (c. 1st-2nd c. CE) across the KAVERI RIVER near TIRUCHIRAPPALLI, Tamil Nadu

Ancient India — GRAND ANICUT / KALLANAI (Tamil ‘kal’ = stone + ‘anai’ = dam) — ancient water-diversion dam across the KAVERI (Cauvery) RIVER at a point where the river branches into many distributaries, near TIRUCHIRAPPALLI (modern Trichy), Tamil Nadu. BUILT BY: KARIKALA CHOLA — greatest EARLY CHOLA king, SANGAM AGE; c. 1st-2nd century CE (exact date debated; could be 2nd c. BCE to 2nd c. CE). STRUCTURE: originally ~329 m (1,080 ft) LONG, ~20 m wide, ~5 m high; built of LARGE STONES (unhewn granite) packed together without mortar; engineered to REGULATE Kaveri waters into 4 distributaries, prevent floods, and irrigate the KAVERI DELTA agricultural heartland. STILL IN USE today, 2,000 years later — one of the OLDEST WATER-ENGINEERING structures on Earth still in regular service (probably only the MARIB DAM of Yemen 8th c. BCE is older; that one collapsed). British engineer Sir Arthur Cotton (who built LOWER ANICUT + modern Dowleswaram dam) studied and ADMIRED the Grand Anicut; incorporated its principles into the UPPER ANICUT (1836-38). Today the Kallanai is a protected ancient monument; enlarged Mettur Dam (1934) upstream + modern works. The Kaveri delta it irrigates is called the ‘RICE BOWL OF SOUTH INDIA’ — produces 3 crops/year. OTHER ANCIENT INDIAN WATER ENGINEERING: (1) SUDARSHANA LAKE at Girnar (Gujarat) — Mauryan period, repaired by Rudradaman (as per Junagadh inscription). (2) Indus Valley DOCKS at LOTHAL (2400 BCE) + water reservoirs at DHOLAVIRA (world's first known rainwater harvesting system with 16 reservoirs, step-wells). (3) Vijayanagara's extensive canal + tank systems including KAMALAPUR tank, ANANTARAJA TANK. (4) KAREZ / QANAT underground water channels (Persia + Deccan sultanates). (5) KAIL HAUZ / BAOLIS (stepwells) of Delhi, Gujarat (RANI KI VAV at Patan, UNESCO WHS — 11th c. Solanki), Rajasthan (CHAND BAORI, ADI KUMBESHWARA). (6) BHOJPAL / BHOJ TAL of Bhopal — built by Raja Bhoja of Malwa, 11th century. (7) BASTI in Karnataka — Jain temple reservoirs. KARIKALA CHOLA also conquered Chera + Pandya + fought to defeat; his fame is such that even Rajaraja Chola I (11th c.) referred to himself as Karikala's ‘descendant’. His capital was KAVERIPATTINAM / PUHAR — a great trading port (destroyed by a tsunami later, as per Tamil tradition; Roman amphorae + ceramics have been excavated there). Karikala also celebrated in SANGAM poetry — PORUNARATRUPPATTAI (a pattuppattu) extols him. ~329 m long stone dam; still functional after ~2,000 years; irrigates ~10 lakh acres of Kaveri delta.

cards.front:
KHARAVELA, the great ruler of KALINGA who commissioned the HATHIGUMPHA INSCRIPTION at Udayagiri (near Bhubaneswar, Odisha), belonged to the:

(A) Satavahana dynasty
(B) Maurya dynasty
(C) MAHAMEGHAVAHANA / CHEDI dynasty
(D) Kushana dynasty
cards.back:
(C) MAHAMEGHAVAHANA / CHEDI dynasty

Ancient India — KHARAVELA (c. 193-170 BCE or 1st century BCE per modern scholarship) — greatest ruler of the MAHAMEGHAVAHANA / CHEDI dynasty of KALINGA (modern ODISHA). CAPITAL: KALINGANAGARI (near modern Bhubaneswar/Puri). JAINISM was his state religion — Kharavela was a devout JAIN (he recovered the JAIN image of ‘Kalinga Jina’ that Magadha king had taken during Mahapadma Nanda's raids centuries earlier, +other Jain relics). HATHIGUMPHA INSCRIPTION (‘Cave of the Elephant’ — named after its entrance) at UDAYAGIRI HILL, near Bhubaneswar, Odisha. One of the MOST IMPORTANT INSCRIPTIONS of ancient India. Inscribed in PRAKRIT (not Sanskrit); in BRAHMI SCRIPT; 17 lines; a PRASHASTI / eulogistic autobiography of Kharavela's reign year by year (up to 13 regnal years). Key content: (1) His military campaigns — defeated the SATAKARNI (Satavahana king), demarkated MATHURA (defeated some Yavana king), even reached GORATHAGIRI and captured RAJAGRIHA; (2) campaign to MAGADHA defeating its king BAHASATIMITRA / BRIHASPATIMITRA (identified by some scholars with Pushyamitra Shunga — though dates may not align); (3) brought back the JINA idol stolen by NANDAS; (4) public works — construction of canals, aqueducts, subsidies for 35 lakh Brahmins + ascetics; (5) religious + artistic patronage — theatrical performances, music, dance in court; (6) ‘GITA-VADITA-SAMSKITA-NRTYA’ — promotion of GANDHARVA-VEDA (music-dance); (7) convened a council of Jain ASCETICS at KUMARI PARVATA (Udayagiri-Khandagiri hills). Udayagiri-Khandagiri HILLS have ~18+15 = 33 caves hewn as shelters for Jain monks — Hathigumpha, Ranigumpha, Ganesh Gumpha, Swargapuri-Manchapuri, Bagha Gumpha, Sarpa Gumpha — famous as early examples of ROCK-CUT CAVE architecture in E India (~1st c. BCE). Decorated with ELEPHANT, TIGER, SERPENT motifs — precursors to later Chaitya style. JAINISM's three greatest royal patrons in ancient India: (a) CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA — converted to Jainism under BHADRABAHU in old age, migrated with him to Shravanabelagola (Karnataka) + fasted to death (Sallekhana). (b) KHARAVELA — as above. (c) Later, CHANDRAGUPTA II VIKRAMADITYA was tolerant but Hindu (Vaishnava); AMOGHAVARSHA I of RASHTRAKUTAS (9th c.) — famous as a Jain king who composed ‘KAVIRAJAMARGA’ in Kannada + renounced throne at end of life to become Jain monk. (d) SOUTH INDIAN Jain renaissance under GANGAS + HOYSALAS + WESTERN CHALUKYAS: BAHUBALI (GOMATESHWARA) statue at SHRAVANABELAGOLA (Karnataka, 57 ft, 981 CE) built by Chamundaraya, Ganga minister; Mahamastakabhisheka every 12 years. (e) CHANDELLAS + RAJPUTS patronised JAIN TEMPLES (Khajuraho Parshvanatha, Osian, Ranakpur (UNESCO Jain temple 1439 CE — 1,444 pillars), Dilwara at Mount Abu (11th-13th c. — marble craftsmanship), Palitana (Satrunjaya hill, 863 temples). ruled Kalinga c. 1st century BCE; Kharavela was a JAIN, patronised Jainism; Hathigumpha inscription is his famous prashasti.

cards.front:
The SHUNGA dynasty (185-73 BCE) was founded by:

(A) Chandragupta Maurya
(B) Pushyamitra Shunga
(C) Agnimitra
(D) Kanishka
cards.back:
(B) Pushyamitra Shunga

Ancient India — Pushyamitra Shunga — Mauryan commander-in-chief who assassinated the last Mauryan, Brihadratha, in 185 BCE and founded the Shunga dynasty. Ruled from Pataliputra. Agnimitra was his son (and subject of Kalidasa's play Malavikagnimitra). Sanchi Stupa was built/renovated in this period.

The KUSHAN king KANISHKA is remembered for:

cards.front:
Tolkappiyam — the oldest extant work of Tamil grammar — was composed by:

(A) Ilango Adigal
(B) Tolkappiyar
(C) Sattanar
(D) Thiruvalluvar
cards.back:
(B) Tolkappiyar

Ancient India — Tolkappiyam — composed by Tolkappiyar (real name disputed; possibly Trinadhumagni). Treats grammar in 3 sections — Eluttu (letters/phonology), Sol (words/morphology), Porul (subject matter / poetics). The Porul-adigaram is unique — it is essentially the world's oldest known sociolinguistic / poetics treatise. Often dated 3rd-2nd century BCE. Other Sangam authors: Ilango Adigal (Silappadikaram), Sattanar (Manimekalai), Thiruvalluvar (Tirukkural — post-Sangam, ~5th C CE).

cards.front:
Tirukkural — the celebrated Tamil treatise on ethics and life — was composed by:

(A) Tolkappiyar
(B) Thiruvalluvar
(C) Sattanar
(D) Kapilar
cards.back:
(B) Thiruvalluvar

Ancient India — Tirukkural — 1330 couplets (kurals) divided into three books: Aram (virtue/dharma), Porul (wealth/artha), Inbam (love/kama). cards.front:
The two main divisions of Sangam literature based on theme are:

(A) Saiva and Vaishnava
(B) Akam (love / interior) and Puram (war / exterior)
(C) Yapparungalakarigai and Iraiyanar Akapporul
(D) Vyakarana and Nirukta
cards.back:
(B) Akam (love / interior) and Puram (war / exterior)

Ancient India — Sangam poetry classified by theme into Akam ('inner / love') and Puram ('outer / public — war, valour, kingship, ethics'). The Akam tradition relates emotions to one of five 'tinai' (landscape archetypes): Kurinji (mountain — union of lovers), Mullai (forest — patient waiting), Marudam (cropland — quarrels), Neithal (coast — separation), Palai (desert — elopement / parting). Puram themes — Vetchi, Karandai, Vanji, Kanji, Ulinai, Tumbai, Vakai (each a stage of military expedition).

cards.front:
The VEDIC AGE in ancient India — marked by composition of the Vedas — lasted approximately:

(A) 600-200 BCE
(B) 1500 BCE - 600 BCE
(C) 3000-2000 BCE (this is Harappan)
(D) 500 BCE - 0 CE
cards.back:
(B) 1500 BCE - 600 BCE

Ancient India — VEDIC AGE (~1500 BCE - 600 BCE): divided into EARLY VEDIC (RIGVEDIC, ~1500-1000 BCE) + LATER VEDIC (~1000-600 BCE). Followed the decline of the HARAPPAN (INDUS VALLEY) civilisation. Sources: the 4 VEDAS — our primary knowledge. EARLY VEDIC — lived in 'SAPTA SINDHAVA' (land of seven rivers — Punjab region). Semi-nomadic, pastoral, cattle-rearing. Tribal polity (GANA). Worshipped nature gods — INDRA (god of war, storm), AGNI (fire), VARUNA (cosmic order), SURYA, USHA, etc. COMPOSED RIGVEDA (10 mandalas, 1028 hymns). LATER VEDIC — expanded eastward from Punjab to Ganga-Yamuna doab + onwards. Settled agriculture, iron tools (PGW culture = Painted Grey Ware). Rise of kingdoms (JANAPADAS). Composed SAMA-, YAJUR-, ATHARVA-VEDAS + BRAHMANAS + ARANYAKAS + UPANISHADS. Rise of VARNA system (4-fold caste: Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) based on birth. Period ended with the rise of MAHAJANAPADAS (600 BCE onwards — 16 great kingdoms) + heterodox religions (Buddhism + Jainism). Early Vedic 1500-1000 BCE; Later Vedic 1000-600 BCE.

cards.front:
The OLDEST and MOST IMPORTANT Veda is:

(A) Sama Veda
(B) RIG VEDA
(C) Yajur Veda
(D) Atharva Veda
cards.back:
(B) RIG VEDA

Ancient India — THE FOUR VEDAS (meaning 'KNOWLEDGE' in Sanskrit): (1) RIG VEDA (Rigveda, ~1500-1200 BCE) — OLDEST, most important. 10 MANDALAS (books), 1028 SUKTAS (hymns), ~10,600 verses. Mandalas 2-7 are the OLDEST 'Family Mandalas'. Famous hymns: GAYATRI MANTRA (3rd mandala, to Savitri), PURUSHA SUKTA (10th, on the creation + 4 varnas). Dedicated to gods — Agni (most hymns), Indra (2nd most). (2) SAMA VEDA ('Veda of Melodies/Chants') — musical rendering of Rig Veda verses for ritual chanting; considered the origin of INDIAN CLASSICAL MUSIC. (3) YAJUR VEDA ('Veda of Sacrificial Formulas') — prose + verse formulae for yajnas (sacrifices). Two recensions: Krishna (Taittiriya etc.) + Shukla (Vajasaneyi/Madhyandina). (4) ATHARVA VEDA ('Veda of Atharvan, a Priest') — LATEST, contains spells, charms, folk practices, medicine (Ayurveda origins), daily life issues. Considered by orthodox Brahmins as 'less holy' initially; later accepted. Each Veda has 4 divisions: SAMHITAS (mantras), BRAHMANAS (ritual commentary), ARANYAKAS ('forest books', mystical), UPANISHADS (philosophical, 'Vedanta — end of Vedas'). UPANISHADS (~108; 10-13 principal ones) are the philosophical core. 10 mandalas / books, 1028 hymns / suktas.

cards.front:
Which river is mentioned MOST frequently in the RIGVEDA, and is considered the 'MOTHER' of Vedic culture?

(A) Ganga (Ganges)
(B) Sarasvati
(C) Yamuna
(D) Brahmaputra
cards.back:
(B) Sarasvati

Ancient India — RIGVEDIC RIVERS — the Rig Veda mentions SAPTA SINDHAVA ('SEVEN RIVERS' — seven sacred rivers): Sindhu (Indus), Jhelum (Vitasta), Chenab (Asikni), Ravi (Parushni), Beas (Vipasa), Sutlej (Shutudri), and SARASVATI. SARASVATI is mentioned 72 TIMES in the Rigveda — FAR MORE than any other river — regarded as the 'MOTHER OF WATERS' + 'best of rivers'. Today SARASVATI is DRIED UP — identified with the GHAGGAR-HAKRA palaeo-channel (which flowed through NW India + Pakistan). GANGA is mentioned only ONCE in the Rigveda; YAMUNA thrice — suggesting Vedic society was centred in Punjab, with minimal early contact with eastern Ganga valley. Rig Veda also mentions: Kubha (Kabul), Gomati, Krumu (Kurram), Suvastu (Swat). LATER VEDAS show eastward shift — more references to Yamuna, Ganga. MAHABHARATA confirms Saraswati's drying up ('Saraswati Vinasanam'). ISRO satellite imaging has mapped ancient Saraswati palaeo-channels. Today observed as a 'mythical' river — supposedly the hidden third river at PRAYAGRAJ (Triveni Sangam). mentioned 72 times, most of any river.

cards.front:
The VARNA system — the 4-fold classification of society — is first mentioned in which hymn of the Rig Veda?

(A) Gayatri Mantra
(B) PURUSHA SUKTA
(C) Nasadiya Sukta
(D) Ushas Sukta
cards.back:
(B) PURUSHA SUKTA

Ancient India — PURUSHA SUKTA (Rig Veda 10.90) — one of the latest Rigvedic hymns. Describes the COSMIC PURUSHA (primeval man) whose sacrifice by the gods produced the universe. The four VARNAS emerge from different parts of his body: BRAHMIN (priests + scholars) from his MOUTH; KSHATRIYA (warriors + rulers) from his ARMS; VAISHYA (merchants + cultivators) from his THIGHS; SHUDRA (labourers + service) from his FEET. Later fossilised into the rigid JATI (caste) system with thousands of sub-castes. Original Vedic varna may have been occupation-based + flexible; became HEREDITARY + RIGID in later Vedic times. NOTE: DALITS / 'UNTOUCHABLES' originally outside varna system ('Panchama' 5th varna in some texts — below Shudras). Abolished by Article 17 of Constitution. Other famous Rig Vedic hymns: GAYATRI MANTRA (3.62.10, to Savitri — most chanted mantra in Hinduism); NASADIYA SUKTA (10.129 — the 'creation hymn' with philosophical speculation about origins — 'Who knows whence creation arose?'). USHAS SUKTA — dawn goddess. Rig Veda, 10th Mandala, 90th Sukta.

cards.front:
The UPANISHADS — philosophical texts at the end of each Veda — are also called:

(A) Puranas
(B) VEDANTA
(C) Smritis
(D) Tantras
cards.back:
(B) VEDANTA

Ancient India — UPANISHADS = 'VEDANTA' (from anta = 'end') — the concluding philosophical portions of each Veda. ~108 Upanishads traditionally accepted; 10-13 are considered 'PRINCIPAL UPANISHADS': Isha, Kena, Katha, Prashna, Mundaka, Mandukya, Taittiriya, Aitareya, Chandogya, Brihadaranyaka, Shvetashvatara, Kaushitaki, Maitri. Core ideas: BRAHMAN (ultimate reality), ATMAN (individual soul), their identity ('TAT TVAM ASI' — That Thou Art; 'AHAM BRAHMASMI' — I am Brahman); MOKSHA (liberation from cycle of birth-death); KARMA + SAMSARA. Rejected mechanical ritualism of earlier Vedic period in favour of inner knowledge. Shankaracharya (8th c. CE) expounded ADVAITA VEDANTA based on them. Translated by DARA SHIKOH (Mughal prince) in 1657 into Persian ('Sirr-i-Akbar'), introduced to Europe via Anquetil-Duperron's Latin translation — deeply influenced German philosopher Schopenhauer. OTHER HINDU TEXTS: PURANAS (mythological narratives — 18 Mahapuranas); SMRITIS (dharma codes — Manusmriti); EPICS (Ramayana, Mahabharata); AGAMAS + TANTRAS; 6 DARSHANAS (philosophical schools: Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta). 'End of the Vedas'.

Core ideas: BRAHMAN (ultimate reality), ATMAN (individual soul), their identity ('TAT TVAM ASI' — That Thou Art; 'AHAM BRAHMASMI' — I am Brahman); MOKSHA (liberation from cycle of birth-death); KARMA + SAMSARA. Rejected mechanical ritualism of earlier Vedic period in favour of inner knowledge. Shankaracharya (8th c. CE) expounded ADVAITA VEDANTA based on them. Translated by DARA SHIKOH (Mughal prince) in 1657 into Persian ('Sirr-i-Akbar'), introduced to Europe via Anquetil-Duperron's Latin translation — deeply influenced German philosopher Schopenhauer. cards.front:
In the EARLY VEDIC PERIOD, the political institution 'SABHA' was:

(A) A royal council of ministers
(B) An assembly of selected nobles / elders
(C) The army
(D) The priests' guild
cards.back:
(B) An assembly of selected nobles / elders

Ancient India — EARLY VEDIC POLITICAL INSTITUTIONS: (1) SABHA — an assembly of nobles + elders, sometimes with women present ('SABHAVATI' — dignified lady of sabha). (2) SAMITI — general assembly of tribal members (sometimes translated 'folk assembly'); larger than sabha. Both are considered democratic-like checks on royal power. (3) VIDATHA — oldest, earliest folk-assembly; possibly for religious/social/distributive functions. (4) GANA — the tribal group/nation itself. Later they declined in importance as kingship became hereditary + bureaucratised. RAJAN (king) — elected initially by the tribe, later hereditary. Helped by PUROHITA (priest — chief advisor), SENANI (army chief), GRAMINI (village head). No standing army (warriors called up as needed). Tribes mentioned: BHARATAS, PURUS, YADUS, TURVASAS, ANUS, DRUHYUS (the 'PANCHA-JANA' — five tribes). Famous BATTLE OF TEN KINGS (Dasarajna Yuddha) — described in Rig Veda; won by Sudas, king of Bharata-Tritsu confederacy against 10 other tribes including Purus. BHARATA tribe gave India its name ('BHARATA-VARSHA'). possibly the upper chamber of Vedic assembly; women could attend.

cards.front:
The WRITING SCRIPT used in the Vedic Sanskrit literature (centuries LATER when Vedas were finally written down) is:

(A) Brahmi
(B) Devanagari (a descendant of Brahmi, developed around 7th-8th c. CE); oldest surviving scripts of Sanskrit: Brahmi → Gupta → Siddham → Devanagari
(C) Indus script
(D) Kharosthi
cards.back:
(B) Devanagari (a descendant of Brahmi, developed around 7th-8th c. CE); oldest surviving scripts of Sanskrit: Brahmi → Gupta → Siddham → Devanagari

Ancient India — Vedic Sanskrit was initially transmitted ORALLY for centuries — the famous ŚRUTI tradition ('that which is heard'). Oral memorisation with strict phonetic + grammatical rules preserved the Vedas UNCHANGED across generations. Writing in India: (1) INDUS SCRIPT (~2500 BCE, Harappan) — undeciphered, possibly not Indo-European. (2) BRAHMI SCRIPT (~3rd c. BCE, Ashokan edicts) — ancestor of most modern Indian scripts + Southeast Asian (Thai, Burmese, Khmer, Balinese). Deciphered by James Prinsep 1837. (3) KHAROSHTHI — used in NW India/Pakistan (~3rd c. BCE - 3rd c. CE); right-to-left. (4) GUPTA BRAHMI — Gupta-era development. (5) SIDDHAM (Siddhamatrika) — 7th c. CE — used for Buddhist texts in Japan (Shingon). (6) DEVANAGARI — evolved from Nagari (~7th-10th c. CE) — now used for Sanskrit, Hindi, Marathi, Nepali, Konkani, Maithili, Bodo, Dogri. Scripts of Indian languages: Bengali-Assamese, Gurmukhi (Punjabi), Gujarati, Odia, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, etc. — all descend from Brahmi. KEY: Vedic knowledge OLDER THAN WRITING — preserved orally for possibly 1000+ years.

cards.front:
The OLDEST and most sacred among the four Vedas is the:

(A) Atharvaveda, with magical and folk elements
(B) Rigveda, containing 1028 hymns to Indo-Aryan deities
(C) Yajurveda, the manual of sacrificial rituals
(D) Samaveda, the songs to be chanted at rituals
cards.back:
(B) Rigveda, containing 1028 hymns to Indo-Aryan deities

Ancient India — Four Vedas (in order of antiquity): RIGVEDA (oldest, ~1500-1000 BCE; 1,028 hymns in 10 'mandalas' to deities — Indra, Agni, Varuna, Soma), SAMAVEDA (chants), YAJURVEDA (ritual formulas), ATHARVAVEDA (later, includes folk + magical elements). UNESCO Memory of the World register 2007. Each Veda has 4 parts: Samhitas (hymns), Brahmanas (ritual texts), Aranyakas (forest texts), Upanishads (philosophy). Memory transmitted orally for millennia with extreme accuracy via 'pathas' (recitation methods).

cards.option2: Yajurveda, the manual of sacrificial rituals
cards.option3: Samaveda, the songs to be chanted at rituals

cards.front:
The MAIN occupation in the EARLY VEDIC PERIOD (Rigvedic, ~1500-1000 BCE) was:

(A) Settled agriculture with iron tools used widely
(B) Pastoralism (cattle-rearing) and limited agriculture
(C) Long-distance trade by sea with foreign nations
(D) Iron-smelting industries and complex urban crafts
cards.back:
(B) Pastoralism (cattle-rearing) and limited agriculture

Ancient India — Early Vedic — semi-nomadic pastoralists. CATTLE = primary measure of wealth ('gomat' = wealthy = owner of cattle). 'Yuddha' (war) literally meant 'fight for cows'. Rigveda has many hymns about cattle. Late Vedic period (~1000-600 BCE) saw shift to settled AGRICULTURE (iron tools — the 'Iron Age' shift), expansion eastward into Ganga plains, varna stratification, urbanisation. Distractor 1, 3, 4 describe later periods.

cards.option2: Long-distance trade by sea with foreign nations
cards.option3: Iron-smelting industries and complex urban crafts

cards.front:
Two important POPULAR ASSEMBLIES of the early Vedic age were:

(A) Maha Sabha and Lok Sabha as later constitutional forms
(B) Sabha (council of elders) and Samiti (general assembly)
(C) Mantri Parishad and Council of advisers under the king
(D) Gana and Sangha, the early republican-state forms
cards.back:
(B) Sabha (council of elders) and Samiti (general assembly)

Ancient India — Early Vedic polity: TRIBAL CHIEF (rajan/raja), assisted by: SABHA — council of elders, restricted membership, advisory body. SAMITI — larger general assembly, all adult tribesmen, where the rajan was sometimes elected and approved. VIDATHA — religious + economic council. Both Sabha and Samiti became less important in the Later Vedic period as monarchy strengthened. Distractor 4 (Gana / Sangha) — ancient republican states like Vajji, but these are POST-Vedic (Mahajanapada period).

cards.front:
The most PROMINENT deity in the Rigveda, with the most hymns dedicated to him, is:

(A) Vishnu, the preserver in later mythology
(B) Indra, the god of thunder and warfare
(C) Shiva, the destroyer in later Hinduism
(D) Brahma, the creator in later cosmology
cards.back:
(B) Indra, the god of thunder and warfare

Ancient India — INDRA — most-praised in Rigveda, ~250 hymns dedicated. King of gods, thunderbolt-wielder, slayer of Vritra (drought-demon), 'Purandara' (fort-breaker). Reflected the warrior-pastoralist values of early Vedic society. AGNI — second most important (~200 hymns), the fire god, intermediary between humans + gods. VARUNA — guardian of cosmic order (rita). Vishnu, Shiva, Brahma — minor in the Rigveda; gained dominance in later Puranic Hinduism (~500 BCE onward).

cards.option3: Brahma, the creator in later cosmology

cards.front:
The four-fold VARNA system (Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) is mentioned for the first time in the:

(A) Atharvaveda, in its folk-magical hymns
(B) Rigveda's Purusha Sukta hymn (10th mandala)
(C) Manusmriti, written around 200 BCE in Sanskrit
(D) Bhagavad Gita, written around 200 BCE
cards.back:
(B) Rigveda's Purusha Sukta hymn (10th mandala)

Ancient India — PURUSHA SUKTA (Rigveda 10.90) — first explicit mention of four varnas. Allegorical: Brahmana from Purusha's mouth (priests), Kshatriya from arms (warriors), Vaishya from thighs (merchants/farmers), Shudra from feet (servants). Considered a LATER addition (10th mandala is the youngest). MANUSMRITI (~200 BCE-200 CE) elaborated the varna system into a rigid law-code. The 'Purusha Sukta' is also notable for envisioning a divine cosmic Person dismembered to create the universe. Distractor 1 — Atharvaveda has caste mentions but not the original. Distractor 3 = Manusmriti (later codification). Distractor 4 = Gita.
cards.option2: Manusmriti, written around 200 BCE in Sanskrit

cards.front:
The famous 'Battle of Ten Kings' (Dasarajna), described in the Rigveda, was fought on the banks of which river?

(A) Yamuna, near present-day Delhi region
(B) Parushni (modern Ravi) river in the Punjab area
(C) Ganga, near present-day Varanasi area
(D) Saraswati, the lost ancient mythical river
cards.back:
(B) Parushni (modern Ravi) river in the Punjab area

Ancient India — Dasarajna — described in Rigveda 7.18 — battle between Bharatas (under Sudas, with priest Vasishtha) and a confederation of 10 tribes (under priest Vishvamitra) on the banks of PARUSHNI (modern RAVI) river. Sudas of the Bharata tribe won. The 'Bharata' tribe gave its name to BHARAT — original India. Considered one of the earliest references to the political geography of north-west India in literature.
cards.option3: Saraswati, the lost ancient mythical river

cards.front:
GAYATRI MANTRA — one of the most sacred Vedic verses — appears in which Veda?

(A) Atharvaveda, in a magical-protection chant
(B) Rigveda (3.62.10), composed by sage Vishvamitra
(C) Yajurveda, in a household ritual section
(D) Samaveda, in a melodic chanting section
cards.back:
(B) Rigveda (3.62.10), composed by sage Vishvamitra

Ancient India — Gayatri Mantra — Rigveda 3.62.10. 'Om bhur bhuvah svah, tat savitur varenyam, bhargo devasya dhimahi, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat.' Composed by sage VISHVAMITRA. Addressed to the solar deity Savitr. 24 syllables in the Gayatri meter (3 lines of 8 syllables). Considered the most sacred Vedic mantra. Recitation is part of daily Brahminical practice + sandhya rituals.

cards.option3: Samaveda, in a melodic chanting section

cards.front:
The oldest of the four Vedas is the:

(A) Yajur Veda
(B) Rigveda
(C) Sama Veda
(D) Atharva Veda
cards.back:
(B) Rigveda

Ancient India — The Rigveda — ~1,500-1,200 BCE — is the oldest of the four Vedas and one of the oldest religious texts in the world. It has 10 mandalas and 1,028 hymns. Sama Veda (musical chants derived from the Rigveda), Yajur Veda (sacrificial formulae) and Atharva Veda (spells, domestic rituals) came later. Rigveda's Book 9 is dedicated to Soma.

cards.front:
The famous 'Gayatri Mantra' of the Rigveda is dedicated to:

(A) Indra
(B) Savitr
(C) Agni
(D) Varuna
cards.back:
(B) Savitr

Ancient India — The Gayatri Mantra (Rigveda 3.62.10, attributed to sage Vishvamitra) is addressed to Savitr, the 'inspirer' Sun god. Indra is the Rigveda's most-mentioned deity — god of war and thunder. Agni (fire) and Varuna (cosmic order, waters) are other prominent Vedic gods. The Gayatri's metre (gayatri chhanda) has 3 lines of 8 syllables each. a form of the Sun.

The social fourfold division (varna system) was first mentioned in which hymn?

(A) Gayatri Mantra
(B) Purusha Sukta
(C) Nasadiya Sukta
(D) Ushas Sukta
cards.back:
(B) Purusha Sukta

Ancient India — The Purusha Sukta (Rigveda 10.90) — probably a late Rigvedic addition — describes the four varnas (Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) as arising from the cosmic sacrifice of Purusha's mouth, arms, thighs and feet respectively. Nasadiya Sukta (10.129) is a celebrated philosophical 'creation hymn'. Ushas Sukta hymns praise the dawn goddess.

cards.front:
The Upanishads, philosophical texts usually attached to each Veda, are primarily concerned with:

(A) Sacrificial rituals
(B) Knowledge of the self (Atman) and the ultimate reality (Brahman)
(C) Rules for social conduct
(D) Astronomical observations
cards.back:
(B) Knowledge of the self (Atman) and the ultimate reality (Brahman)

Ancient India — The Upanishads (c. 800-500 BCE) — the philosophical core of the later Vedic corpus, the 'end' of the Vedas ('Vedanta') — explore the identity of the individual Self (Atman) with the cosmic Absolute (Brahman). Major Upanishads include Isha, Kena, Katha, Mundaka, Chhandogya, Brihadaranyaka. The sacrificial / ritual portions are the Brahmanas; rules for conduct are in the Dharmasutras / Smritis.

cards.front:
The 'Sapta Sindhu' of the Rigveda — the 'land of seven rivers' — chiefly corresponds to present-day:

(A) Ganga plain
(B) Punjab / NW India and eastern Pakistan
(C) Gujarat coast
(D) Deccan plateau
cards.back:
(B) Punjab / NW India and eastern Pakistan

Ancient India — The Rigvedic 'Sapta Sindhava' — seven rivers — are usually taken as the Indus and its main tributaries (Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) plus either the Saraswati or the Kabul. This places the Rigvedic 'Aryans' chiefly in the Punjab and NW Indian region (including today's eastern Pakistan). Later Vedic peoples shifted eastwards into the Ganga-Yamuna doab.

The 'Satapatha Brahmana', a text of later Vedic ritual, is attached to the:

(A) Rigveda
(B) Yajur Veda
(C) Sama Veda
(D) Atharva Veda
cards.back:
(B) Yajur Veda

Aitareya Brahmana — Rigveda. Tandya and Jaiminiya Brahmanas — Sama Veda. Gopatha Brahmana — Atharva Veda. The Shatapatha is a major source for later Vedic social and religious life.

cards.front:
The tribal assembly of the Rigvedic period, which discussed matters of common concern, was called the:

(A) Samiti only
(B) Sabha and Samiti
(C) Janapada
(D) Gana
cards.back:
(B) Sabha and Samiti

Ancient India — Rigvedic polity had two main assemblies — the Sabha (a smaller, possibly older council of senior tribesmen) and the Samiti (a larger assembly of the tribe, often involved in electing the king). They are referred to as the 'twin daughters of Prajapati' in the Atharva Veda. 'Janapada' and 'Mahajanapada' are later territorial units of the 6th century BCE. 'Gana' / 'sangha' became tribal republics in the pre-Mauryan period.

Gautama Buddha was born in which year (traditional date) and at which place?

(A) 563 BCE at Bodh Gaya
(B) 563 BCE at Lumbini, Nepal (then Kapilavastu's territory)
(C) 486 BCE at Kushinagar
(D) 400 BCE at Kapilavastu
cards.back:
(B) 563 BCE at Lumbini, Nepal (then Kapilavastu's territory)

Buddhism & Jainism — Traditional date — 563 BCE (some sources 480 BCE). Born at LUMBINI (in modern Nepal, near Indo-Nepal border) under a sal tree. Mother Mahamaya, father Suddhodana (King of the Shakya clan). Childhood name — Siddhartha Gautama. Lumbini is a UNESCO WHS (1997) — the actual birthplace marked by Ashoka's pillar (~249 BCE) bearing inscription confirming it. Bodh Gaya is where ENLIGHTENMENT happened, not birth. Kushinagar is where he died.

(A) King, queen, prince, princess
(B) An old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic
(C) Sun, moon, stars, planets
(D) Hunger, thirst, cold, heat
cards.back:
(B) An old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic

Buddhism & Jainism — While Siddhartha lived in palace luxury (insulated from suffering by his father), he encountered FOUR SIGHTS during chariot rides outside: 1. An old, frail man (suffering of aging), 2. A diseased man (suffering of illness), 3. A dead body (mortality), 4. A serene wandering ascetic (path to liberation). These triggered his renunciation ('Mahabhinishkramana' = the Great Going Forth) at age 29. Six years of asceticism followed before enlightenment.

(B) 483 BCE
(C) 563 BCE

cards.back:

Scholarly estimates vary (some say 563 BCE based on other dating methods). 483 BCE is typically cited as his year of MAHAPARINIRVANA (death) at Kushinagar. The NCERT textbook variant often uses 563 BCE; ISI/ASI and Buddhist sources use 623 BCE.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT one of the Four Noble Truths?

(A) Dukkha — life is suffering
(B) Samudaya — cause of suffering is craving (tanha)
(C) Karma — one reaps what one sows
(D) Nirodha — cessation of suffering is possible
cards.back:
(C) Karma — one reaps what one sows

Buddhism & Jainism — The FOUR NOBLE TRUTHS (Arya-satyas) are: (1) DUKKHA — suffering exists; (2) SAMUDAYA — cause is craving/tanha; (3) NIRODHA — cessation is possible by extinguishing craving; (4) MAGGA/Marga — the Eightfold Path leads to cessation. KARMA is a general Indian concept of moral causation shared with Hinduism/Jainism, NOT a Noble Truth itself. The Eightfold Path (Magga) has 8 components: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.

cards.front:
The Third Buddhist Council was held during the reign of which emperor?

(A) Ajatashatru
(B) Kalashoka
(C) Ashoka
(D) Kanishka
cards.back:
(C) Ashoka

Buddhism & Jainism — FOUR Buddhist Councils: (1) First — 483 BCE at Rajgriha under Ajatashatru, presided by Mahakassapa; (2) Second — 383 BCE at Vaishali under Kalashoka; (3) THIRD — 250 BCE at Pataliputra under ASHOKA, presided by Moggaliputta Tissa (led to codification of Tripitaka and Buddhist missions abroad); (4) Fourth — ~72 CE at Kundalvana (Kashmir) under Kanishka, marked the Mahayana-Hinayana split. Fifth council (19th c.) and Sixth (1954 Yangon) are modern.

Which of the following are the 'Three Jewels' (Triratna) of Buddhism?

(A) Truth, Non-violence, Compassion
(B) Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha
(C) Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva
(D) Body, Mind, Soul
cards.back:
(B) Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha

Buddhism & Jainism — The Triratna (Three Jewels / Three Refuges) of Buddhism are: (1) BUDDHA — the enlightened one; (2) DHAMMA/DHARMA — his teachings; (3) SANGHA — the community of monks and nuns. A Buddhist is formally one who takes refuge in all three: 'Buddham saranam gacchami, Dhammam saranam gacchami, Sangham saranam gacchami'. Ashoka adopted this formula in many of his rock edicts.

cards.front:
Which Buddhist school believed in the Bodhisattva ideal and the worship of Buddha as a deity, and spread to China, Japan, and Korea?

(A) Theravada (Hinayana)
(B) Mahayana
(C) Vajrayana
(D) Zen
cards.back:
(B) Mahayana

Buddhism & Jainism — MAHAYANA ('Greater Vehicle'), which emerged in the 1st c. CE (crystallized at Kanishka's 4th Council), emphasises the Bodhisattva ideal (compassionate enlightened beings postponing own Nirvana to save others) and treats Buddha as divine. Spread to China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam. THERAVADA (formerly 'Hinayana') is older, more conservative, treats Buddha as a human teacher, uses Pali canon — widespread in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar. VAJRAYANA (Tibetan/Tantric) is a sub-school of Mahayana. ZEN is a Japanese Mahayana school.

(C) Tivara and Karuvaki

cards.front:
Nalanda — the great Buddhist university destroyed in the 12th century by Bakhtiyar Khilji — flourished chiefly under:

(A) Mauryan rulers
(B) Gupta rulers
(C) Kushan rulers
(D) Satavahana rulers
cards.back:
(B) Gupta rulers

Buddhism & Jainism — Nalanda Mahavihara — founded in the 5th century CE under the Guptas (Kumaragupta I), further expanded by Harshavardhana and the Palas. At its peak it had 10,000 students (including from China, Korea, Japan, Tibet, South-East Asia), a nine-storey library, and was India's leading centre of Buddhist learning. Destroyed in 1193 by Bakhtiyar Khilji. A modern Nalanda University was re-established in 2014. and later the Palas.

(B) Right faith, Right knowledge, Right conduct

Buddhism & Jainism — Jain Triratna (or Ratnatraya): Samyak Darshana (right faith), Samyak Gyana (right knowledge), Samyak Charitra (right conduct). Path to moksha. (Buddha-Dhamma-Sangha = Buddhist Tisarana, or 'Three Refuges'.) Pancha-Mahavrat (5 vows): Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Aparigraha, Brahmacharya.

cards.front:
The FIRST BUDDHIST COUNCIL was held at:

(A) Vaishali (c. 383 BCE)
(B) Rajagriha (c. 483 BCE, just after Buddha's death)
(C) Pataliputra (c. 250 BCE)
(D) Kashmir (c. 72 CE)
cards.back:
(B) Rajagriha (c. 483 BCE, just after Buddha's death)

Buddhism & Jainism — 1st Council: Rajagriha, soon after Buddha's Parinirvana (under Ajatshatru). 2nd: Vaishali, ~100 years later (schism — Sthaviras vs Mahasanghikas). 3rd: Pataliputra, under Ashoka (~250 BCE, Moggaliputta Tissa). 4th: Kashmir, under Kanishka (~72 CE, Mahayana emerges).

Buddhism split into MAHAYANA and HINAYANA at the:

(A) First Buddhist Council
(B) Second Buddhist Council
(C) Fourth Buddhist Council
(D) Third Buddhist Council (under Ashoka)
cards.back:
(C) Fourth Buddhist Council

Buddhism & Jainism — 4th Council held during Kanishka's reign (~1st century CE, Kashmir) formally split Buddhism into Mahayana ('Great Vehicle') and Hinayana ('Lesser Vehicle') — Theravada is a surviving Hinayana school. Earlier, 2nd Council had produced the Sthavira-Mahasanghika split — the root of these two branches. under Kanishka.

cards.front:
The Jain community is divided into two main sects:

(A) Theravada and Mahayana
(B) Digambara and Svetambara
(C) Shaiva and Vaishnava
(D) Hinayana and Mahayana
cards.back:
(B) Digambara and Svetambara

Buddhism & Jainism — Digambara ('sky-clad', ascetics go nude as a symbol of total renunciation). Svetambara ('white-clad', wear white robes). Schism around 3rd century BCE during the famine in Magadha. Digambaras concentrated in South India; Svetambaras in Gujarat / Rajasthan.

cards.front:
Jainism has 24 TIRTHANKARAS ('ford-makers'). The FIRST Tirthankara was:

(A) Parshvanatha
(B) RISHABHANATHA
(C) Mahavira
(D) Neminatha
cards.back:
(B) RISHABHANATHA

Buddhism & Jainism — TIRTHANKARAS of JAINISM — 24 great teachers who crossed the 'ocean of samsara' + helped others across ('tirtha' = ford). (1) RISHABHANATHA / ADINATHA / ADISHWARA — FIRST, founder of Jainism; mentioned in Rig Veda (as Vrishabha) + Bhagavata Purana. Symbol: BULL. (2)-(22) include Ajitnatha, Sambhavanatha, Chandraprabha (moon), Suparshvanatha, Shantinatha, Kunthunatha, Aranatha, Mallinatha (only female in Shvetambara; but male per Digambara), Munisuvrata, Neminatha/Arishtanemi (22nd, cousin of Krishna per Jain tradition). (23) PARSHVANATHA — 23rd, HISTORICAL figure (c. 872-772 BCE); preached 4 vows (ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha); symbol: SNAKE. (24) MAHAVIRA — 24th + LAST (c. 540-468 BCE); added brahmacharya (celibacy) as 5th vow. SYMBOLS (lanchanas) of each Tirthankara are distinct (bull, elephant, lotus, snake, etc.). PANCH MAHAVRATAS (5 great vows): (a) AHIMSA (non-violence); (b) SATYA (truth); (c) ASTEYA (non-stealing); (d) BRAHMACHARYA (celibacy/continence); (e) APARIGRAHA (non-possession / non-attachment). TRIRATNA (3 jewels of Jainism): samyak darshana (right faith), samyak gnyana (right knowledge), samyak charitra (right conduct). Jainism rejects Vedic authority; denies creator God; accepts karma + soul (jiva) but not supreme deity. COSMOLOGY: eternal cycle of utsarpini (ascending) + avasarpini (descending) eras, each with 24 Tirthankaras. the founder; mentioned in Rig Veda + Vishnu Purana as a great ascetic; also called ADINATHA.

cards.front:
MAHAVIRA, the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism, was born in:

(A) Lumbini, Nepal
(B) KUNDAGRAMA (near Vaishali, modern Bihar) in 540 BCE
(C) Kapilavastu
(D) Pataliputra
cards.back:
(B) KUNDAGRAMA (near Vaishali, modern Bihar) in 540 BCE

Buddhism & Jainism — MAHAVIRA (540-468 BCE per traditional dating; some give 599-527 BCE) — 24th + last Tirthankara of Jainism. BIRTH: KUNDAGRAMA / KSHATRIYAKUND — a suburb of VAISHALI (modern Basokund, Muzaffarpur district, BIHAR). PARENTS: King SIDDHARTHA (of the Jnatrika / Jnatrika Kshatriya clan) + Queen TRISHALA (sister of Chetaka, king of Vaishali; so Mahavira was a prince by birth). Chetaka's daughter Chellana married Bimbisara of Magadha → Mahavira + Buddha's royal circles overlapped. ORIGINAL NAME: VARDHAMANA (meaning 'prosperity-increasing'). Married YASHODA, had a daughter PRIYADARSHANA. At AGE 30, after parents' death, renounced the world; wandered 12 YEARS as an ascetic. KAIVALYA (omniscient enlightenment) attained at 42 at JRIMBHIKAGRAMA (near Rijupalika River) under a SAL TREE. Given title 'MAHAVIRA' ('great hero') + 'JINA' ('conqueror of passions') — hence JAINISM. Preached for 30 years; attained NIRVANA / MOKSHA at age 72 at PAVAPURI (modern Pawapuri, Nalanda district, Bihar — where Jalmandir stands today) in 468 BCE (per traditional). TITLES: Mahavira, Jina, Arihanta, Nirgrantha (bondless), Kevalin. MAIN DISCIPLES: 11 GANADHARAS (chief disciples) — INDRABHUTI GAUTAMA was the chief; SUDHARMAN / SUDHARMA was the last surviving, whose successor JAMBU was the last Jain to attain Kevala Jnana in our age. CONTEMPORARY of BUDDHA (566/480 BCE). Both in BIHAR, both from Kshatriya royal families, both rejected Vedic ritual + caste hierarchy. to Kshatriya parents Siddhartha + Trishala of the Jnatrika clan.

cards.front:
The FIVE GREAT VOWS (Panch Mahavratas) of Jainism include ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha + a fifth added by Mahavira:

(A) Santosha (contentment)
(B) BRAHMACHARYA
(C) Saucha (purity)
(D) Tapas (austerity)
cards.back:
(B) BRAHMACHARYA

Buddhism & Jainism — PANCH MAHAVRATAS ('5 great vows') of JAINISM (for monks + nuns; laypeople observe lighter 'anuvratas'): (1) AHIMSA — NON-VIOLENCE in thought, word + deed. Core of Jainism — extends to NOT harming any life form including microbes. Jain monks sweep the path ahead with soft brush (rajoharana), strain water, wear face masks (muhpatti) to avoid inhaling insects. (2) SATYA — truthfulness. (3) ASTEYA — non-stealing; not taking anything not freely given. (4) APARIGRAHA — non-possession / non-attachment; some Jain monks (Digambara) renounce even clothes. (5) BRAHMACHARYA — celibacy/continence. ADDED by MAHAVIRA to Parshvanatha's ORIGINAL FOUR vows (chauryam: the 5th was not codified earlier). PARSHVANATHA (23rd Tirthankara, c. 872-772 BCE) was a HISTORICAL figure, 250 years before Mahavira; his original chaturyama included four vows; Mahavira added the 5th to strengthen sexual discipline. JAINISM PHILOSOPHY: (a) KARMA theory — much more atomistic/particulate than Hindu view; karmic particles stick to soul; ascetic practice burns them off (nirjara) + prevents new influx (samvara) + leads to moksha. (b) ANEKANTAVADA — 'doctrine of many-sidedness' / non-absolutism; reality has multiple aspects; no single view is complete. (c) SYADVADA — 'doctrine of may-be' / 7-fold predication; every statement qualified with 'syat' ('perhaps'). (d) NAYAVADA — theory of standpoints. Jainism champions PLURALISM + epistemological humility. ALL life has SOUL (jiva) — organised in 5 categories by senses (1-sense microbes to 5-sense humans); 3 worlds of samsara. celibacy/continence; added by Mahavira to Parshvanatha's original 4 vows.

cards.front:
After Mahavira's death (468 BCE), Jainism SPLIT into two major sects. They are:

(A) Sthavira + Mahasanghika
(B) DIGAMBARA (sky-clad/nude monks) + SHVETAMBARA
(C) Hinayana + Mahayana
(D) Sthaulabhadra + Bhadrabahu
cards.back:
(B) DIGAMBARA (sky-clad/nude monks) + SHVETAMBARA

Buddhism & Jainism — JAIN SCHISM — SECTS formed ~1st c. BCE / CE: (1) DIGAMBARA ('sky-clad' / nude) — monks go naked; believe COMPLETE renunciation requires shedding of ALL possessions including clothes. Hold that: (a) WOMEN CANNOT achieve moksha (must be reborn as man first); (b) 19th Tirthankara MALLI was MALE (not female as Shvetambara holds); (c) Mahavira did not marry (vs Shvetambara view that he did); (d) A kevalin does not need food. Dominant in KARNATAKA + parts of MP/Rajasthan. Key figures: Kundakunda, Umaswami (author of Tattvartha Sutra). (2) SHVETAMBARA ('white-clad') — monks + nuns wear simple WHITE ROBES + keep minimum possessions (bowl, brush, muhpatti). Allow WOMEN's ordination + liberation. Dominant in GUJARAT + Rajasthan. Main canonical scriptures: AGAMAS (~45 texts). CAUSE of SCHISM: great FAMINE in Magadha (~298 BCE) during Chandragupta Maurya's reign. Jain leader BHADRABAHU migrated with a group of monks SOUTH to Sravanabelagola (Karnataka); STHULABHADRA stayed in Magadha + held First Jain Council there. When Bhadrabahu's group returned, they found the Magadha Jains had relaxed some rules (adopting white robes) — conflict widened over centuries + formalised into Digambara (southern group) vs Shvetambara (Magadha/later migration). LATER sub-sects: Shvetambara → Murtipujaka (idol-worshippers) + Sthanakvasi (non-idolatrous, 17th c. Lonka Shah) + Terapanthi. Digambara → Bisapanthi, Terapanthi (Dig), Taranpanthi (no idols). NOTE: Digambara-Terapanthi + Shvetambara-Terapanthi are DIFFERENT. split around 1st c. BCE / CE over migration to south + monastic robes; white-clad monks.

cards.front:
The FIRST JAIN COUNCIL (Prathama Samiti) was held around 300 BCE at:

(A) Vaishali
(B) PATALIPUTRA
(C) Sravanabelagola
(D) Valabhi
cards.back:
(B) PATALIPUTRA

Buddhism & Jainism — JAIN COUNCILS — two major canonical councils. (1) FIRST JAIN COUNCIL (Prathama Samiti) — held ~300 BCE at PATALIPUTRA under the presidency of STHULABHADRA during the reign of CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA. CONTEXT: great Magadha famine prompted BHADRABAHU to migrate south with half of the sangha to Sravanabelagola (modern Karnataka). The monks who remained in Magadha convened the council to compile the canon — compiled 12 ANGAS (canonical texts) but the 12th (Drishtivada) was already lost, so only 11 were preserved. The returning Digambara faction rejected this compilation (saying it was incomplete + corrupted). This ASSEMBLY'S failure to be universally accepted was the SEED of the Digambara-Shvetambara schism. (2) SECOND JAIN COUNCIL — held at VALABHI (Gujarat) ~5th-6th c. CE (453 or 466 CE) under DEVARDDHI KSHAMASHRAMANA. Final RE-compilation of Jain canon — 45 AGAMAS (canonical texts) of Shvetambara tradition committed to writing for the first time (till then oral). Digambara tradition holds that original Mahavira teachings were LOST in toto; no canonical agreement with Shvetambara. NOTABLE JAIN LITERATURE: (a) KALPA SUTRA (by Bhadrabahu, lives of Tirthankaras); (b) TATTVARTHA SUTRA (by Umaswami, ~2nd c. CE, common to both sects); (c) PRAKRIT language used for most early Jain texts (Ardhamagadhi dialect); (d) later Sanskrit + regional languages. JAINISM FLOURISHED in KARNATAKA, GUJARAT, RAJASTHAN, MAHARASHTRA + TAMIL NADU (Sangam era). Royal patrons: Chandragupta Maurya (convert in old age per tradition), Kharavela of Kalinga (Hathigumpha inscription 150 BCE), Amoghavarsha (Rashtrakuta), Kumarapala (Chalukya Gujarat), Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagar. Famous Jain temples: Mount Abu (Dilwara), Shravanabelagola (Gommateshwara statue), Palitana (Gujarat — 863 temples on Shatrunjaya hill), Ranakpur, Khajuraho (Parshvanatha temple). presided by STHULABHADRA during Chandragupta Maurya's reign; compiled 12 Angas of canonical literature.

cards.front:
The MONOLITHIC STATUE OF BAHUBALI (Gommateshwara), 57-ft tall, at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka was erected by:

(A) Rajaraja Chola
(B) CHAMUNDARAYA
(C) Ashoka
(D) Harshavardhana
cards.back:
(B) CHAMUNDARAYA

Buddhism & Jainism — GOMMATESHWARA / BAHUBALI MONOLITH at SHRAVANABELAGOLA (Hassan district, KARNATAKA) — a 57-FOOT (17.4m) tall single-stone GRANITE statue of BAHUBALI (a son of Rishabhanatha, first Tirthankara). ERECTED: 981 CE by CHAMUNDARAYA, the Jain minister + commander of Ganga king Rachamalla IV (Western Ganga dynasty). Sculptor: Aristanemi. At the time, one of the world's largest monolithic sculptures. Stands atop VINDHYAGIRI HILL; Chandragiri hill nearby is believed to be the site where Emperor CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA ended his life by sallekhana (fasting to death) in his final years as a Jain monk under Acharya Bhadrabahu. MAHAMASTAKABHISHEKA — the grand head-anointing ceremony held every 12 YEARS — milk, saffron, ghee, sugarcane juice, sandal paste + 10008 kalashas of water poured over the statue from scaffolding; attracts millions of pilgrims + tourists. 12-year interval ceremonies: 2006, 2018, next in 2030. KARNATAKA STATE HERITAGE list's jewel; candidate for UNESCO World Heritage. OTHER major JAIN HERITAGE: (1) DILWARA TEMPLES, Mount Abu (Rajasthan) — 11th-13th c., marble work among the finest in world; 5 main temples incl. Vimal Vasahi (for Adinath), Luna Vasahi (for Neminath). (2) RANAKPUR Chaturmukha temple (Rajasthan) — 1444 pillars, no two alike; one of largest + busiest Jain temples. (3) SHIKHAR JI / PARASNATH HILL (Jharkhand) — 20 of 24 Tirthankaras attained moksha here; holiest Jain pilgrimage. (4) PALITANA (Shatrunjaya Hill, Gujarat) — 863 Jain temples; Shvetambara holy site. (5) KHAJURAHO (MP) — Jain temple group (Parshvanatha etc.) along with Hindu temples (UNESCO since 1986). (6) UDAYAGIRI + KHANDAGIRI caves (Odisha) — from Kharavela's era (c. 150 BCE); Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela = only Jain royal inscription of magnitude. minister of the Ganga king Rachamalla IV, in 981 CE; world's largest monolithic statue at the time.

Stands atop VINDHYAGIRI HILL; Chandragiri hill nearby is believed to be the site where Emperor CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA ended his life by sallekhana (fasting to death) in his final years as a Jain monk under Acharya Bhadrabahu. MAHAMASTAKABHISHEKA — the grand head-anointing ceremony held every 12 YEARS — milk, saffron, ghee, sugarcane juice, sandal paste + 10008 kalashas of water poured over the statue from scaffolding; attracts millions of pilgrims + tourists. 12-year interval ceremonies: 2006, 2018, next in 2030. KARNATAKA STATE HERITAGE list's jewel; candidate for UNESCO World Heritage. OTHER major JAIN HERITAGE: (1) DILWARA TEMPLES, Mount Abu (Rajasthan) — 11th-13th c., marble work among the finest in world; 5 main temples incl. Vimal Vasahi (for Adinath), Luna Vasahi (for Neminath). (2) RANAKPUR Chaturmukha temple (Rajasthan) — 1444 pillars, no two alike; one of largest + busiest Jain temples. (3) SHIKHAR JI / PARASNATH HILL (Jharkhand) — 20 of 24 Tirthankaras attained moksha here; holiest Jain pilgrimage. (4) PALITANA (Shatrunjaya Hill, Gujarat) — 863 Jain temples; Shvetambara holy site. (5) KHAJURAHO (MP) — Jain temple group (Parshvanatha etc.) along with Hindu temples (UNESCO since 1986). (6) UDAYAGIRI + KHANDAGIRI caves (Odisha) — from Kharavela's era (c. 150 BCE); Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela = only Jain royal inscription of magnitude. minister of the Ganga king Rachamalla IV, in 981 CE; world's largest monolithic statue at the time.

cards.front:
KHARAVELA, the great Jain king of KALINGA, is known for which famous inscription?

(A) Allahabad Prashasti
(B) HATHIGUMPHA INSCRIPTION
(C) Aihole inscription
(D) Mehrauli Iron Pillar inscription
cards.back:
(B) HATHIGUMPHA INSCRIPTION

Buddhism & Jainism — KHARAVELA (c. 193-170 BCE, approx) — great Jain king of KALINGA (modern Odisha), 3rd ruler of CHEDI / MAHAMEGHAVAHANA dynasty. Ascended throne at 24. HATHIGUMPHA ('Elephant Cave') INSCRIPTION — at UDAYAGIRI + KHANDAGIRI twin-hill Jain caves near Bhubaneswar (Odisha), dated ~150 BCE. The inscription is in PRAKRIT + BRAHMI script; 17 lines; records Kharavela's achievements in chronological order year-wise (first such autobiography-like record in India). CONTENTS: (1) Kharavela's education + early career. (2) 5th year — extended Tansulya Canal (dug by a Nanda king) — CHATTEENMETE (400 km canal). (3) 8th year — attacked Rajagriha (Magadha). (4) 12th year — humbled Magadhan king + extended empire; brought back the Jain IDOL (carried away by Nandas earlier) — SIGNIFICANT as Kalinga was recovering spiritual icons. (5) 13th year — renovation of JAIN CAVES on Kumari Hill (Udayagiri-Khandagiri). (6) Built temples, aqueducts, pleasure-parks. FOUND (rediscovered) by British archaeologist ALEXANDER CUNNINGHAM + Lt. Markham Kittoe in 1837; deciphered by James Prinsep (who decoded Brahmi ~1837). SIGNIFICANCE: (1) only extensive Jain royal inscription from early India; (2) shows Jainism's vigor in Odisha in 2nd c. BCE; (3) provides historical picture of post-Ashokan period — Kharavela defeated Demetrius (Yavana = Indo-Greek) in Mathura (per some readings); (4) mentions BRIHADRATHAS, MAGADHAS, musicians + poets; (5) mentions recovery of the Kalinga-Jina from Nanda-period spoliation. UDAYAGIRI + KHANDAGIRI caves — 18 + 15 caves respectively; rock-cut residential + meditational chambers for Jain monks; famous caves include RANI GUMPHA (Queen's cave, two-storeyed, sculpted reliefs), GANESHA GUMPHA, HATHIGUMPHA. Protected monuments; major tourist site. Kharavela ranks alongside Ashoka + Samudragupta as one of ancient India's greatest empire-builders of Indian east. carved in Udayagiri Caves near Bhubaneswar (~150 BCE); earliest known biographical rock edict of a Jain king.

cards.front:
SALLEKHANA / SANTHARA in Jainism refers to:

(A) A festival
(B) RITUAL FASTING to death
(C) A pilgrimage
(D) A tax on ahimsa violators
cards.back:
(B) RITUAL FASTING to death

Buddhism & Jainism — SALLEKHANA (also called SANTHARA / SAMADHI MARANA) — ritual practice in Jainism of voluntary, gradual CESSATION of food + water as one nears death (old age, incurable illness, or facing unavoidable death). Seen as the SPIRITUAL CULMINATION of a Jain life — dying with equanimity, without fear, freeing soul from bodily attachments, burning off remaining karma. Performed with guidance of a Jain monk + family. TAKES weeks / months of gradual reduction (rather than abrupt). Distinguished from suicide (which is rejected in Jainism as karmic bondage) — sallekhana is: (a) gradual, not abrupt; (b) chosen when death is INEVITABLE anyway; (c) performed with awareness + detachment; (d) not from passion/despair. HISTORICAL: CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA is believed to have practiced sallekhana at CHANDRAGIRI hill, Shravanabelagola, under BHADRABAHU's guidance (c. 298 BCE); his inscription there (Bhadrabahu cave). About 200-300 Jains still practice sallekhana annually in India (mostly Digambara + Shvetambara Terapanthi). LEGAL CONTROVERSY: (1) 2015 — RAJASTHAN HC in Nikhil Soni v. UoI ruled sallekhana was SUICIDE under IPC 306/309 + banned the practice. (2) Major Jain community protests; rallies in Delhi, Mumbai, Jaipur. (3) SUPREME COURT STAYED the Rajasthan HC ruling (31 Aug 2015) recognising sallekhana as a legitimate religious practice under Article 25 (freedom of religion). CASE STILL PENDING. (4) Compare with KARUNA MERCY KILLING / ACTIVE EUTHANASIA debate (Aruna Shanbaug case 2011 + 2018 Common Cause v. UOI — passive euthanasia + living wills ALLOWED). Sallekhana falls between suicide + euthanasia, occupying a unique religious-cultural-legal space. ALMOST all world faiths have analogues: Hindu sanyasin's renunciation unto death, Buddhist self-starvation (rare), Vaishnavite Samadhi. KEY to Jainism's emphasis on ahimsa — self-directed non-violence + peaceful exit.

cards.front:
CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA, founder of the Mauryan Empire, is said to have become a JAIN monk in his final years + died by sallekhana at:

(A) Pataliputra
(B) SHRAVANABELAGOLA (Chandragiri Hill) in Karnataka
(C) Taxila
(D) Ujjain
cards.back:
(B) SHRAVANABELAGOLA (Chandragiri Hill) in Karnataka

Buddhism & Jainism — CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA (c. 340-298 BCE) — founder of MAURYAN EMPIRE (322 BCE); mentored by CHANAKYA/KAUTILYA (author of Arthashastra); overthrew Nanda dynasty; built India's first subcontinental empire (Hindu Kush to Bengal, Himalayas to Deccan); defeated SELEUCUS NICATOR (Alexander's successor) in 305 BCE, gained Afghanistan + married his daughter Helen; received Seleucus's ambassador MEGASTHENES (author of 'Indika'). JAIN CONVERSION: per Jain tradition (Digambara), Chandragupta abdicated the throne ~298 BCE (after a 24-year reign), became disciple of JAIN ACHARYA BHADRABAHU, + migrated SOUTH with him when a great famine struck Magadha. Lived final years at Shravanabelagola (Karnataka) + died by SALLEKHANA (ritual fast to death) at CHANDRAGIRI HILL. Chandragiri inscription (attributed to later period but references BHADRABAHU's cave) supports this. Succeeded by son BINDUSARA. HISTORICAL DEBATE: not all scholars accept the Jain tradition; some (like V.A. Smith) held it legendary. But (a) the Sravanabelagola tradition is ancient + consistent; (b) cave named for Bhadrabahu at Chandragiri; (c) Chandragupta's name inscribed in later record. BROADLY ACCEPTED as historically plausible. SIGNIFICANCE: (1) shows Jainism's appeal to royal elite in 4th c. BCE; (2) indicates Jain presence in south India TWO centuries before Ashoka's missions; (3) bridges Magadha + Deccan Jainism historically. OTHER royal Jain patrons: BIMBISARA (Magadha), AJATASHATRU (Magadha, met Mahavira), CHANDANA (first female disciple of Mahavira, daughter of King Dadhivahana of Champa), SUPRATIBUDDHA, KHARAVELA (Kalinga), KUMARAPALA (Chalukya, 12th c.), AMOGHAVARSHA (Rashtrakuta, 9th c. — patronised Jinasena + Gunabhadra; author of 'Kavirajamarga' in Kannada; abdicated himself in Jain style). JAIN POPULATION TODAY: ~0.4% of Indian population (~45 lakh), but DISPROPORTIONATELY affluent + influential in trade + philanthropy + minoritystatus (2014). under the guidance of Jain acharya BHADRABAHU, around 298 BCE.

cards.front:
The TRIRATNA (three jewels) of Jainism for attaining moksha are:

(A) Ahimsa, satya, asteya
(B) SAMYAK DARSHAN (right faith), SAMYAK GNYANA (right knowledge), SAMYAK CHARITRA
(C) Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva
(D) Karma, dharma, moksha
cards.back:
(B) SAMYAK DARSHAN (right faith), SAMYAK GNYANA (right knowledge), SAMYAK CHARITRA

Buddhism & Jainism — TRIRATNA ('three jewels') or RATNATRAYA of JAINISM — the path to MOKSHA (liberation from samsara): (1) SAMYAK DARSHANA — 'right faith' / right vision / right perception; seeing reality as it is (through the 9 tattvas — soul, non-soul, asrava, bandha, samvara, nirjara, moksha, punya, papa); belief in Tirthankaras + their teachings. (2) SAMYAK GNYANA — 'right knowledge' / scriptural + experiential comprehension; understanding through anekantavada (multi-perspectival). (3) SAMYAK CHARITRA — 'right conduct' / ethical practice; following the 5 mahavratas + the 5 samitis (carefulness) + 3 guptis (restraint) + 10 dharmas + 12 reflections (bhavanas). All 3 together → moksha; one alone insufficient. JAIN COSMOLOGY: the universe is ETERNAL (no creator God); has 6 eternal substances (dravyas) — soul (jiva), matter (pudgala), motion principle (dharma), rest principle (adharma), space (akasha), time (kala). Souls are INFINITE in number, each potentially capable of liberation. LOKA (universe) is shaped like a STANDING HUMAN — Urdhvaloka (upper), Madhyaloka (middle — where we are), Adholoka (lower hells). 14 gunasthanas (stages of spiritual progress). JAIN CALENDAR: Vira Nirvana Samvat starts 527 BCE from Mahavira's nirvana — currently VS 2552. PARYUSHANA — 8-day holiest Jain festival (Aug-Sep); fasting, prayer, CONFESSION of faults; ends with KSHAMAVANI (forgiveness day) — 'Michhami Dukkadam' (asking/giving forgiveness). MAHAVIR JAYANTI — 13th day of Chaitra Shukla paksha; public holiday in India. JAIN FESTIVALS: Diwali (Mahavira's nirvana day!), Bhogali Purnima, Akshaya Tritiya (Rishabhanatha's end of year-long fast).

cards.front:
The greatest of the CHOLA emperors, who conquered Lanka + parts of SE Asia, was:

(A) Karikala
(B) RAJARAJA CHOLA I (985-1014) + his son RAJENDRA CHOLA I (1014-1044)
(C) Parantaka I
(D) Kulottunga
cards.back:
(B) RAJARAJA CHOLA I (985-1014) + his son RAJENDRA CHOLA I (1014-1044)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — CHOLA EMPIRE (9th-13th c. CE) — TAMIL dynasty ruling from THANJAVUR; one of the LONGEST-ruling dynasties in world history (reviving from 9th c.). GREATEST RULERS: (1) RAJARAJA CHOLA I (985-1014) — original name Arulmozhivarman; 'Rajaraja' = 'King of Kings'. Conquered (a) Pandyas of Madurai, (b) Cheras of Kerala, (c) Western Chalukyas, (d) Sri Lanka (northern, incl. Anuradhapura — renamed 'Mummudi Chola Mandalam'), (e) Maldives (first Indian empire to conquer beyond South Asia). Built THE BRIHADESHVARA TEMPLE (Rajarajeshwaram) at THANJAVUR (1010 CE) — UNESCO World Heritage; 66m tall vimana; one of India's tallest temples; 80-tonne granite capstone on top; 130-ton Nandi; massive stone carved. Undertook great LAND SURVEY + centralised revenue. (2) RAJENDRA CHOLA I (1014-1044) — son + successor; EXPANDED further. Defeated PALAS of Bengal (Mahipala); marched to GANGES + took Ganges water home — built GANGAIKONDACHOLAPURAM (new capital); took title 'Gangaikonda' (conqueror of Ganges) + 'Kadaram-kondan' (conqueror of Kadaram). NAVAL EXPEDITION TO SOUTHEAST ASIA (1025) — defeated SRIVIJAYA EMPIRE (Malaya-Sumatra); took tribute from Kadaram (Kedah), Sri Vishaya (Palembang), Srivijaya, Pannai, Malaiyur, Mayirudingam, Ilangasoga, Mapappalam, Valaippandur, Takkola, Madamalingam, Ilamurideham, Manakkavaram (Nicobar), KADARAM — across Malaysia, Indonesia, Myanmar. FIRST INDIAN MARITIME EMPIRE of substance. Built CHOLAMANDALAM (Coromandel Coast). PATRONISED ART + literature — Tamil Bhakti (Tevaram saints canonised under him); 63 Nayanar + 12 Alvar hymns; Nataraja bronzes peak. (3) KULOTTUNGA I (1070-1122), RAJENDRA II, KULOTTUNGA III maintained empire till 1279 when PANDYAS overran. together made Cholas South + SE Asia's greatest power.

cards.front:
The BRIHADESHVARA TEMPLE at THANJAVUR (a UNESCO World Heritage site) was built by:

(A) Rajendra Chola
(B) RAJARAJA CHOLA I
(C) Kulottunga
(D) Parantaka
cards.back:
(B) RAJARAJA CHOLA I

South India & Regional Kingdoms — BRIHADESHVARA TEMPLE / 'RajaRajeswaram' / 'Peruvudaiyar Kovil' at THANJAVUR (Tanjore), Tamil Nadu — ARCHITECTURAL MARVEL of CHOLA era. BUILT by RAJARAJA CHOLA I; completed in 1010 CE. DEDICATED to LORD SHIVA. FEATURES: (1) VIMANA (tower above sanctum) — 66 METRES (216 ft) tall, made of granite — one of the tallest in India; (2) capped by a single 80-tonne granite stone (some say 130 tonnes via ramp up a 6km earthen slope per legend); (3) LARGE NANDI (monolithic seated bull) — 6 m long, 2.7 m tall, 360 tonnes; (4) SANCTUM houses a 3.7m Shiva lingam; (5) fresco paintings in Chola + later Nayak layers on walls; (6) inscriptions in Tamil + Grantha detailing the temple's administration, donations, dancing girls (devadasis — 400 employed), staff, grants. Financed by tribute + loot from Rajaraja's conquests. UNESCO listed 1987 as part of 'GREAT LIVING CHOLA TEMPLES' group with two others: (a) BRIHADESHVARA at GANGAIKONDACHOLAPURAM (built by Rajendra Chola c. 1035 CE to celebrate his Ganges victory — slightly smaller but more ornate); (b) AIRAVATESHVARA TEMPLE at DARASURAM (built by Rajaraja II c. 1166 CE). All 3 showcase DRAVIDA architectural style at peak. DRAVIDA (SOUTHERN) vs NAGARA (NORTHERN) vs VESARA (HYBRID) are 3 Indian temple styles (classified in Shilpa texts). DRAVIDA features: (a) square/rectangular plan; (b) TALL vimana above garbha-griha (sanctum); (c) PYRAMIDAL + tiered vimana; (d) GOPURAMS (gateway towers) at cardinal entrances (became increasingly tall, surpassing vimana in later centuries); (e) COMPOUND walls with multiple courts; (f) MANDAPAS (pillared halls); (g) temple TANK (kalyani); (h) Dravidian stupi (finial). Famous Dravida temples: Pallava (Kailasanatha Kanchipuram), Chola (Brihadeshvara), Chalukya (Badami), Pandya (Meenakshi Madurai), Vijayanagar (Hampi), Nayak era (Meenakshi + Ranganathaswamy Srirangam). dedicated to Lord Shiva; part of 'Great Living Chola Temples' UNESCO site; completed 1010 CE.

BUILT by RAJARAJA CHOLA I; completed in 1010 CE. DEDICATED to LORD SHIVA. FEATURES: (1) VIMANA (tower above sanctum) — 66 METRES (216 ft) tall, made of granite — one of the tallest in India; (2) capped by a single 80-tonne granite stone (some say 130 tonnes via ramp up a 6km earthen slope per legend); (3) LARGE NANDI (monolithic seated bull) — 6 m long, 2.7 m tall, 360 tonnes; (4) SANCTUM houses a 3.7m Shiva lingam; (5) fresco paintings in Chola + later Nayak layers on walls; (6) inscriptions in Tamil + Grantha detailing the temple's administration, donations, dancing girls (devadasis — 400 employed), staff, grants. Financed by tribute + loot from Rajaraja's conquests. UNESCO listed 1987 as part of 'GREAT LIVING CHOLA TEMPLES' group with two others: (a) BRIHADESHVARA at GANGAIKONDACHOLAPURAM (built by Rajendra Chola c. 1035 CE to celebrate his Ganges victory — slightly smaller but more ornate); (b) AIRAVATESHVARA TEMPLE at DARASURAM (built by Rajaraja II c. 1166 CE). All 3 showcase DRAVIDA architectural style at peak. DRAVIDA (SOUTHERN) vs NAGARA (NORTHERN) vs VESARA (HYBRID) are 3 Indian temple styles (classified in Shilpa texts). DRAVIDA features: (a) square/rectangular plan; (b) TALL vimana above garbha-griha (sanctum); (c) PYRAMIDAL + tiered vimana; (d) GOPURAMS (gateway towers) at cardinal entrances (became increasingly tall, surpassing vimana in later centuries); (e) COMPOUND walls with multiple courts; (f) MANDAPAS (pillared halls); (g) temple TANK (kalyani); (h) Dravidian stupi (finial). Famous Dravida temples: Pallava (Kailasanatha Kanchipuram), Chola (Brihadeshvara), Chalukya (Badami), Pandya (Meenakshi Madurai), Vijayanagar (Hampi), Nayak era (Meenakshi + Ranganathaswamy Srirangam). dedicated to Lord Shiva; part of 'Great Living Chola Temples' UNESCO site; completed 1010 CE.

cards.front:
The CHOLA local government had a highly developed VILLAGE ASSEMBLY system. The assembly of a Brahmadeya (Brahmin-settled village) was called:

(A) Panchayat
(B) SABHA / MAHASABHA
(C) Jati
(D) Nadu
cards.back:
(B) SABHA / MAHASABHA

South India & Regional Kingdoms — CHOLA LOCAL SELF-GOVERNMENT — one of the most developed systems of medieval world. THREE TYPES of village assemblies: (1) UR — regular village of non-Brahmin cultivators; general assembly of all adult male landholders. (2) SABHA / MAHASABHA — assembly of BRAHMADEYA (Brahmin-settled village); exclusively for learned Brahmins + involved complex elected committees. (3) NAGARAM — assembly of merchant towns; like NAGARATTAR commercial guilds. UTTIRAMERUR INSCRIPTIONS (c. 919 CE, near Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu) by PARANTAKA CHOLA I — detail elaborate ELECTION PROCEDURE of SABHA: (a) Qualifications — (i) own land of 1/4 veli; (ii) reside in own house on that land; (iii) age 35-70; (iv) knowledge of Vedas + Dharmashastra; (v) honest + good character. (b) Disqualifications — embezzlers of public funds, those with close relatives in office, defaulters of taxes. (c) Selection by KUDAVOLAI ('pot ticket' — LOTTERY) system: names written on palm-leaf tickets, placed in pot, a young priest drew names; rotation ensured broad participation; prevented oligarchy. (d) 30 wards of village → 30 members chosen annually. (e) 6 VARIYAM (committees) — Samvatsara-variyam (annual committee), Totta-variyam (garden committee), Eri-variyam (TANK committee — maintenance of IRRIGATION tank was sacred!), Pancha-vara-variyam (standing committee of 5), Pon-variyam (gold committee / treasury), Nyaya-variyam (justice committee). (f) 1-YEAR term; those who committed fraud disqualified for life + 7 generations. REMARKABLE for: (1) PRESCRIBED qualifications + DISQUALIFICATIONS; (2) secret ballot / lottery — innovative for 10th c.; (3) PUBLIC ACCOUNTABILITY — regular audit; (4) committees for SPECIFIC FUNCTIONS. Dr B.R. AMBEDKAR + framers of Indian Constitution studied this system for PANCHAYATI RAJ — Art 40 DPSP. UTTIRAMERUR remains a PILGRIMAGE of DEMOCRACY. Cholas' decentralised governance = secret of long rule. elected by Kudavolai (lottery/pot) system; UTTIRAMERUR inscriptions (c. 919 CE) detail procedure + qualifications.

cards.front:
The CHOLA BRONZES (lost-wax cast bronze figures) are most famously represented by:

(A) Terracotta images of Ganesha
(B) NATARAJA (Shiva as cosmic dancer in TANDAVA pose) — CHIDAMBARAM; now iconic symbol of Indian art globally
(C) Buddha in meditation
(D) Tirthankara seated in padmasana
cards.back:
(B) NATARAJA (Shiva as cosmic dancer in TANDAVA pose) — CHIDAMBARAM; now iconic symbol of Indian art globally

South India & Regional Kingdoms — CHOLA BRONZES — unrivalled tradition of Lost-wax casting (Cire Perdue / Madhuchchhishta Vidhana) that peaked during 10th-12th centuries. MOST ICONIC: NATARAJA ('King of Dance') — Shiva as cosmic dancer performing the TANDAVA. ATTRIBUTES: (1) 4 ARMS — upper right holds DAMARU (drum, creation + sound/time), upper left holds AGNI (fire, destruction + transformation), lower right in ABHAYA mudra (fear-not / protection), lower left points to raised foot (moksha / liberation); (2) raised LEFT foot — 'raising of consciousness'; (3) right foot CRUSHING APASMARA (dwarf-demon of ignorance); (4) dancing within a PRABHAMANDALA (circle of FIRE) representing the cosmos; (5) JATAMUKUTA (dread-locks flowing); (6) GANGA in hair; (7) snake around waist; (8) 'ANANDATANDAVA' = dance of bliss. LOCATION: primary Nataraja shrine = CHIDAMBARAM (Tamil Nadu), one of Panch Bhoota Sthalams representing AKASHA (space/ether); Nataraja in temple gold-plated; called 'Thillai Nataraja'. PHILOSOPHICAL: symbolises 5 cosmic activities of Shiva (Panchakritya) — creation, preservation, destruction, concealment, liberation. Universal symbol — CERN's Geneva campus has a Nataraja statue (donated by India 2004) honoring the 'cosmic dance' analogy with particle physics. OTHER CHOLA BRONZES: Parvati (Uma), Shiva-Parvati-Skanda (Somaskanda), Rama-Sita-Lakshmana (Ram-setu), Krishna, saints (Nayanars, Alvars — 63 canonised under Rajaraja), dancing Shiva variants. CASTING TECHNIQUE: (1) wax model sculpted; (2) coated in clay; (3) heated to melt wax out ('lost wax'); (4) molten bronze poured in; (5) clay broken + bronze cleaned. Each piece UNIQUE. Chola bronzes display perfect ANATOMICAL precision + graceful contrapposto; IDEALISED proportions per SILPA SHASTRA; incredible realism + sinuous motion. MODERN MUSEUMS: Govt Museum Chennai, Thanjavur Royal Art Gallery, National Museum Delhi, British Museum, Louvre, MET NYC, Asian Civilisations Museum Singapore — all have Chola bronzes. India has SEIZED BACK many looted Chola bronzes (Suthamalli Nataraja 2015, Sripuranthan Nataraja 2015 — from Australia, US smugglers).

cards.front:
The three MAJOR SOUTH INDIAN DYNASTIES of the Sangam Age (3rd c. BCE – 3rd c. CE) were:

(A) Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Pallavas
(B) CHERAS (Kerala + W.TN), CHOLAS (central + E.TN Cauvery delta), PANDYAS
(C) Vijayanagar, Bahmani, Hoysala
(D) Mauryas, Guptas, Kushans
cards.back:
(B) CHERAS (Kerala + W.TN), CHOLAS (central + E.TN Cauvery delta), PANDYAS

South India & Regional Kingdoms — THREE CROWNED KINGS (MUVENDAR) of Sangam Age South India: (1) CHERAS (Keralaputra) — ruled KERALA + western Tamil Nadu; capital VANJI / Karur; emblems: bow + arrow; greatest king SENGUTTUVAN (the Cheran warrior-prince who invaded north India per Silappadikaram). (2) CHOLAS — central + eastern Tamil Nadu (CAUVERY Delta, Thanjavur region); capital URAIYUR (Tiruchirapalli); emblem: tiger; greatest king KARIKALA (built Grand Anicut / Kallanai dam on Kaveri — one of world's oldest working dams, still in use!). (3) PANDYAS — southern Tamil Nadu; capital MADURAI; emblem: fish; patrons of TAMIL SANGAMS (literary academies) — 3 Sangams in Madurai, 1st + 2nd mythical, 3rd (c. 3 BCE-3 CE) historical; Pandyas = 'PERUMBANARRUPPADAI' + TAMIL SANGAM patrons. SANGAM LITERATURE — ETTUTHOKAI (Eight Anthologies: Natrinai, Kurunthokai, Ainkurunuru, Padirrupathu, Paripadal, Kalithokai, Akananuru, Purananuru), PATTUPATTU (Ten Idylls), TOLKAPPIYAM (earliest Tamil grammar by Tolkappiyar, ~3rd c. BCE). 5 TINAI (ecological regions) — Kurinji (hill), Mullai (pastoral), Marudam (cropland), Neydal (coast), Palai (desert). TRADE: Tamil Nadu's ARIKAMEDU (near Puducherry) was major ROMAN TRADE PORT (1st-2nd c. CE) — Roman coins, amphorae, rouletted ware, pottery found; mentioned in Periplus of the Erythraean Sea + Ptolemy as 'Poduke'. Tamil ports — Muziris (Kerala, Cranganore/Kodungallur), Korkai, Kaveripoompattinam/Puhar. Exports: spices (pepper, cardamom, cinnamon), pearls, gems, silk, teak, peacocks; imports: Roman gold + wine. Sangam era ENDED ~3rd c. CE (Kalabhra interregnum) → MEDIEVAL Cholas (Vijayalaya 848 CE), PALLAVAS (Kanchi), PANDYAS (revival) emerged. CHENNAI + MADURAI remain ancient urban centres. Sangam age epics: SILAPPADIKARAM (story of Kannagi + Kovalan), MANIMEKALAI (Buddhist sequel), CHIVAKA CHINTAMANI (Jain). southern TN, Madurai.
