cards.front:
The PALLAVA dynasty, who ruled from KANCHIPURAM (4th-9th c. CE), is credited with:

(A) Building the Brihadeshvara Temple
(B) Founding ROCK-CUT + STRUCTURAL temple architecture in South India
(C) Defeating the Cholas permanently
(D) Establishing Tamil as court language
cards.back:
(B) Founding ROCK-CUT + STRUCTURAL temple architecture in South India

South India & Regional Kingdoms — PALLAVA DYNASTY (c. 275-897 CE) — Tamil dynasty ruling NORTHERN Tamil Nadu + parts of AP from KANCHIPURAM. Initiated DRAVIDA TEMPLE ARCHITECTURE evolution. FOUR PHASES of Pallava art: (1) MAHENDRA group (7th c.) — rock-cut cave temples. (2) NARASIMHA group / MAHABALIPURAM — monolithic ratha temples + bas-reliefs. (3) RAJASIMHA / STRUCTURAL period — first free-standing structural temples (Shore Temple, Kailasanatha). (4) NANDIVARMAN / LATER Pallava. KEY RULERS: (1) MAHENDRAVARMAN I (600-630) — scholar-king, author of 'MATTAVILASA PRAHASANA' (Sanskrit satirical drama); initial rock-cut caves; converted from Jainism to Shaivism under Appar. (2) NARASIMHAVARMAN I 'MAMALLA' (630-668) — defeated Chalukya PULAKESIN II in epic battles; founded MAHABALIPURAM / MAMALLAPURAM port; built Pancha Rathas (5 monolithic temples carved from single rocks — Dharmaraja, Bhima, Arjuna, Draupadi, Nakul-Sahadeva Rathas). (3) RAJASIMHA / NARASIMHAVARMAN II (700-728) — built the SHORE TEMPLE at Mahabalipuram + KAILASANATHA TEMPLE at Kanchipuram. (4) NANDIVARMAN II (731-796) — built VAIKUNTHA PERUMAL temple. MAHABALIPURAM (Mamallapuram) — UNESCO WHS 1984. Monuments: (a) SHORE TEMPLE — 8th c., two shikharas, oceanfront, battered by cyclones; (b) FIVE RATHAS (Pancha Rathas) — monoliths, each different Dravida temple form; (c) ARJUNA'S PENANCE / Descent of the Ganga — massive open-air BAS-RELIEF (27m × 9m) — one of the world's largest; (d) cave temples — Varaha, Mahishasuramardini, Trimurti, Krishna; (e) KRISHNA'S BUTTERBALL — precariously balanced granite boulder. KANCHIPURAM — 'City of 1000 Temples'; KAILASANATHA TEMPLE (Rajasimha) — earliest structural temple; Vaikuntha Perumal; Ekambareshwara; Varadaraja; Kamakshi Amman. Kanchipuram also a major BUDDHIST + JAIN centre; seat of Shankaracharya MATHA (one of the four original). ENDED by CHOLAS — ADITYA I defeated last Pallava APARAJITAVARMAN at TIRUPPURAMBIYAM (897 CE). Pallavas influenced CAMBODIA + INDONESIA — Shailendra + Khmer temples derive from Pallava grammar. MAHABALIPURAM monuments (UNESCO); KAILASANATHA Kanchipuram.

cards.front:
The GRAND ANICUT (Kallanai), one of the world's OLDEST functioning dams, was built on the Kaveri River (~150 CE) by:

(A) Rajaraja Chola
(B) KARIKALA CHOLA
(C) Krishnadevaraya
(D) Parantaka I
cards.back:
(B) KARIKALA CHOLA

South India & Regional Kingdoms — GRAND ANICUT / KALLANAI — ~2000-year-old DAM + diversion weir on the KAVERI (Cauvery) river, near TIRUCHIRAPPALLI (Trichy), Tamil Nadu. Built by KARIKALA CHOLA (~150 CE), early Chola of the Sangam age. STRUCTURE: originally a rubble-masonry weir, 329m long × 20m wide × 5m deep; designed to divert Kaveri's waters to irrigate Thanjavur delta — 'rice bowl of South India'. Still FUNCTIONS TODAY (after many renovations — British in 1804 by Sir Arthur Cotton who studied Kallanai + adapted its design for his Godavari + Krishna deltas; modern concrete reinforcement). One of the OLDEST WATER-REGULATION structures in the world still in use. Irrigates ~400,000 hectares today. KARIKALA CHOLA — early Chola king; famous for defeating Cheras + Pandyas (Venni battle); credited with: (a) building Kallanai; (b) felling forests + bringing large tracts under rice cultivation; (c) founding Puhar (Kaveripoompattinam) as port; (d) building grand palace at Uraiyur. Mentioned in SANGAM LITERATURE (Pattinappalai by Kadialur Uruttirangannanar describes his Puhar's splendor). ORIGIN LEGEND: 'Karikala' = 'charred leg' — burned as an infant. Known as 'Tiruvalangadan' + great warrior + visionary ruler. OTHER ANCIENT INDIAN DAMS + IRRIGATION: (1) SUDARSHANA LAKE at Girnar, Gujarat — built by CHANDRAGUPTA MAURYA's governor PUSHYAGUPTA (~321 BCE); repaired by Ashoka + later Rudradaman (rock inscription 150 CE) + Skandagupta — celebrated Junagadh Rock Inscription. (2) HAUZ KHAS (Alauddin's reservoir) + HAUZ-I-SULTANI + Firoz Shah's canals. (3) HALEBIDU + HOYSALA tanks in Karnataka. (4) Kakatiya tanks in Telangana — PAKHAL, LAKNAVARAM, Ramappa — UNESCO since 2021 ('Kakatiya Rudreshwara Ramappa Temple'). (5) Mughal canal on Yamuna (Firoz Shah's revived by Shah Jahan's Ali Mardan Khan). Indian water-management expertise is OLD + DEEP. early Chola king of the Sangam age; dam still in use 2000 years later near Trichy.

cards.front:
The CHALUKYAS of BADAMI (6th-8th c.) reached their peak under which king?

(A) Kirtivarman I
(B) PULAKESIN II (609-642)
(C) Vikramaditya VI
(D) Somesvara III
cards.back:
(B) PULAKESIN II (609-642)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — CHALUKYAS OF BADAMI / VATAPI (543-757 CE) — Kannada dynasty ruling from BADAMI (modern Bagalkot district, KARNATAKA). Greatest ruler: PULAKESIN II (609-642) — perhaps the most powerful Deccan king of his time. ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) defeated HARSHA of Kanauj at NARMADA (~630 CE) — Harsha stopped at Narmada, Deccan remained independent; Pulakesin assumed title 'Dakshinapatheswara' ('Lord of South'); 'Maharajadhiraja'. (2) Defeated Pallavas repeatedly; took Kanchi (briefly). (3) Received emissary from KHUSRAU II of PERSIAN SASSANID Empire (Ajanta cave 1 has a famous painting depicting this); sent one to Khusrau. (4) Conquered Gujarat, parts of MP. (5) Chinese traveller HIUEN TSANG (Xuanzang, 631 CE) visited his court; praised his just rule. LIMITS: eventually DEFEATED + KILLED by Pallava NARASIMHAVARMAN I 'MAMALLA' at Vatapi (642 CE) — hence 'Vatapi-kondan' title of Pallava. BADAMI TEMPLES: (a) 4 Rock-Cut Cave temples (Vaishnavite, Shaivite, Jain), 6th-7th c., early Dravida + Nagara fusion; (b) AIHOLE — 125+ temples (6th-9th c.), 'cradle of Hindu temple architecture' — Durga temple, Lad Khan temple, Ravana Phadi cave; (c) PATTADAKAL — 10 temples of later Chalukyas (UNESCO since 1987), Virupaksha temple mahalayas. LATER CHALUKYAS: (1) WESTERN CHALUKYAS of KALYANI (973-1189) — dynasty revived by Tailapa II; greatest king VIKRAMADITYA VI (1076-1126) — started Chalukya-Vikrama era. Court poet BILHANA (Vikramankadevacharita), jurist VIJNANESWARA (Mitakshara — classical Hindu law commentary, still used in legal reference). (2) EASTERN CHALUKYAS of VENGI (624-1189) — ruled coastal Andhra; branch founded by Kubja Vishnuvardhana, brother of Pulakesin II; Telugu literature flowered under them — NANNAYA's Mahabharata (11th c.). (3) CHALUKYAS of GUJARAT / Solanki (950-1300) — separate. Chalukyas succeeded by RASHTRAKUTAS (753-982) who defeated Badami Chalukyas. DANTIDURGA founded Rashtrakuta; AMOGHAVARSHA I (814-878) — great Rashtrakuta king, author of 'Kavirajamarga' (earliest Kannada poetics); Jain patron; Sanskrit + Kannada literature flowered. ELLORA's Kailasa Temple (rock-cut, monolithic, 8th c.) built by Rashtrakuta KRISHNA I — a pinnacle of Indian architecture. defeated HARSHA at Narmada (630); received emissaries from Persia; eventually defeated by Pallava Narasimhavarman I.

cards.front:
The famous KAILASA TEMPLE (Cave 16) at ELLORA — carved from a SINGLE ROCK top-down — was commissioned by:

(A) Pulakesin II
(B) RASHTRAKUTA king KRISHNA I (757-773)
(C) Rajendra Chola
(D) Narasimhavarman I
cards.back:
(B) RASHTRAKUTA king KRISHNA I (757-773)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — KAILASA TEMPLE (Cave 16 of ELLORA caves, AURANGABAD district, MAHARASHTRA) — one of the most astonishing architectural feats of ANCIENT INDIA; considered one of the greatest monolithic structures in world. COMMISSIONED by RASHTRAKUTA KING KRISHNA I (757-773 CE). DEDICATED to Lord SHIVA, representing MT KAILASA (Shiva's abode). STRUCTURE: carved from a SINGLE block of BASALT rock, TOP-DOWN (starting from top + excavating downward + inward); ~2,00,000 TONNES of rock removed; estimated ~150 years of continuous labour. DIMENSIONS: 30 m tall, 46 m wide, 82 m long. FEATURES: (1) Free-standing structural form despite being monolithic; (2) 2-storey GOPURAM entrance; (3) NANDI mandapa; (4) FIVE subsidiary shrines representing Mt Meru; (5) 16-pillared MAHAMANDAPA; (6) GARBHA-GRIHA (sanctum) with Shivalingam; (7) Elaborate SCULPTURES including RAVANA shaking Mt Kailasa (Ravananugrahamurti), Mahishasuramardini, Dashavatara, epic scenes from Ramayana + Mahabharata + Puranas. ELLORA CAVES — UNESCO WHS 1983 — 34 CAVES along 2km basalt cliff: (1) Caves 1-12 = BUDDHIST (6th-7th c.) — Vishwakarma (chaitya with stupa), Tin Thal (3-storeyed); (2) Caves 13-29 = HINDU (7th-10th c.) — Kailasa, Dasavatara, Rameshwara; (3) Caves 30-34 = JAIN (8th-10th c.) — Indra Sabha, Jagannatha Sabha, Chota Kailasa. UNIQUE RELIGIOUS COEXISTENCE — Buddhist, Hindu, Jain shrines side-by-side showing medieval religious pluralism. AJANTA CAVES (MH, Aurangabad — UNESCO WHS 1983) — 30 cave temples (Buddhist only, 2nd c. BCE to 6th c. CE) — famous for MURAL PAINTINGS (Jataka tales, Bodhisattvas; 'Padmapani' + 'Vajrapani' in Cave 1). Rediscovered 1819 by British hunting officer Captain John Smith. AJANTA + ELLORA together = the 2 wondrous rock-cut traditions of India. OTHER major rock-cut sites: Elephanta (Maharashtra, UNESCO 1987); Bagh (MP); Badami (Karnataka); Mahabalipuram (TN); Udayagiri-Khandagiri (Odisha); Bhaja, Karle, Bedse (MH). monolithic rock-cut temple, single largest stone excavation ever; 200,000 tonnes of basalt removed.

cards.front:
The VIJAYANAGAR EMPIRE (1336-1646) was founded by:

(A) Krishnadevaraya alone
(B) HARIHARA + BUKKA (Sangama brothers) in 1336, with guidance of sage VIDYARANYA
(C) Kempe Gowda
(D) Ballaladeva
cards.back:
(B) HARIHARA + BUKKA (Sangama brothers) in 1336, with guidance of sage VIDYARANYA

South India & Regional Kingdoms — VIJAYANAGAR EMPIRE (1336-1646) — great Hindu empire of SOUTH INDIA; bulwark against Bahmani + Delhi Sultanate southward expansion; capital HAMPI (modern Karnataka, UNESCO WHS 1986). FOUNDED in 1336 by two brothers: HARIHARA I + BUKKA (SANGAMA BROTHERS), per tradition with spiritual guidance of sage VIDYARANYA (of Sringeri Math) — 'Vidyanagara' (city of learning), renamed VIJAYANAGAR ('city of victory'). Brothers had been captured by Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq, forcibly converted to Islam, then sent back south to quell rebellions; Vidyaranya reconverted them back to Hinduism — they founded the empire instead. FOUR DYNASTIES: (1) SANGAMA (1336-1485) — founders; Harihara I, Bukka I, Harihara II, Bukka II, Devaraya I + II. (2) SALUVA (1485-1505) — founded by Saluva Narasimha; short-lived. (3) TULUVA (1505-1570) — the GOLDEN AGE; KRISHNADEVARAYA (1509-1529) — emperor par excellence; poet, patron, conqueror; defeated Bahmani sultans, Gajapatis of Orissa; built HAZARA RAMA temple + VITTALA temple. Author of 'AMUKTAMALYADA' (Telugu — advice-cum-love-story on ideal kingship + 8 duties). Court of 'ASHTADIGGAJAS' (8 poets) — Allasani Peddana (Andhra-Kavita-Pitamaha, 'grandfather of Telugu poetry'), Nandi Timmana, Mukku Timmana, Madayyagari Mallana, Pingali Surana (Kalapurnodayam), Dhurjati, Ayyalaraju Ramabhadrudu, Ramaraja Bhushanudu (Bhattumurti). (4) ARAVIDU (1570-1646) — last dynasty; after BATTLE OF TALIKOTA (23 Jan 1565) where combined DECCAN SULTANATES (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) DESTROYED Vijayanagar forces + RAMA RAYA killed; Hampi razed over 6 months. Empire limped on from Penukonda + Chandragiri till 1646. HAMPI is a UNESCO WHS — spectacular ruins, Vittala temple with STONE CHARIOT + musical pillars (SaReGa), Virupaksha temple (still functional), Lotus Mahal, Elephant Stables, Hazara Rama, Krishna temple. Famous foreign VISITORS to Vijayanagar: Nicolo Conti (Italian 1420), Abdur Razzaq (Persian 1440-1445), Duarte Barbosa + DOMINGO PAES (Portuguese 1520-22), Fernao Nuniz (Portuguese 1530s). Paes called Hampi 'as large as Rome' + 'the best-provided city in the world'. CURRENCY: PAGODA (gold coin) + VARAHA. BANKING developed well. COROMANDEL + MALABAR trade. as bulwark against Delhi Sultanate southern expansion.

cards.front:
The greatest Chola emperor who built the Brihadeeswara (Rajarajeshwara) temple at Thanjavur was:

(A) Aditya Chola, the dynasty founder
(B) Rajaraja Chola I, who reigned 985-1014
(C) Rajendra Chola I, the naval emperor
(D) Kulottunga Chola I, of later phase
cards.back:
(B) Rajaraja Chola I, who reigned 985-1014

South India & Regional Kingdoms — RAJARAJA CHOLA I (r. 985-1014 CE) — built the magnificent BRIHADEESWARA TEMPLE / Rajarajeshwaram (1010 CE) at Thanjavur (UNESCO World Heritage; 'Great Living Chola Temples'). Granite shikhara ~66 m, single capstone weighs ~80 tonnes. Conquered: Kerala, Sri Lanka (north), Maldives. Standardised Chola revenue + administration. Distractor 1: Aditya Chola I (c. 871-907) was the founder of imperial line. Distractor 3: Rajendra (his son) built temple at Gangaikondacholapuram. Distractor 4: Kulottunga (1070-1120) was later.
cards.option2: Rajendra Chola I, the naval emperor
cards.option3: Kulottunga Chola I, of later phase

cards.front:
Rajendra Chola I, son of Rajaraja, took which title after his triumphant Ganga expedition?

(A) Mummudi Chola, the three-crowned king
(B) Gangaikonda Chola, conqueror of the Ganges
(C) Trailokyavardhana, the world expander
(D) Vikrama Chola, the brave conqueror title
cards.back:
(B) Gangaikonda Chola, conqueror of the Ganges

South India & Regional Kingdoms — RAJENDRA CHOLA I (r. 1014-1044 CE) — most famous Chola. ~1019-22 CE marched north, defeated Pala king Mahipala (Bengal), brought Ganga water back to his capital. Took title GANGAIKONDA CHOLA (= 'Chola who conquered the Ganges'). Built new capital GANGAIKONDA CHOLAPURAM with a great Shiva temple + a giant tank ('Cholaganga'). Also led NAVAL EXPEDITIONS to Srivijaya (Sumatra, Malaya) ~1025 CE — first Indian to project sea power that far. Distractor 1 is Aditya II Karikala's title.
cards.option3: Vikrama Chola, the brave conqueror title

cards.front:
Chola local self-government was famously developed at the village level via:

(A) Vidatha, the tribal Vedic council
(B) Ur and Sabha (Mahasabha) assemblies
(C) Mantri Parishad of central capital
(D) Rajya Sabha modern federal house
cards.back:
(B) Ur and Sabha (Mahasabha) assemblies

South India & Regional Kingdoms — Chola village government — 3 tiers: UR (general village assembly of all classes); SABHA (or Mahasabha) — assembly of brahmin agraharas (brahmin-only Brahmadeya villages); NAGARAM — assembly of merchants/traders. UTTIRAMERUR INSCRIPTIONS (Parantaka I, 919 + 921 CE) — fascinating record of how Sabhas were elected: kuda-olai (pot-ticket) lottery from qualified candidates' names written on palm leaves. Variyams (committees) for irrigation, gardens, justice, treasury. Local self-government ahead of its time. Distractor 1 is Vedic-age. Distractor 3 is central, not village.

cards.front:
Cholas were the most powerful naval force in their day. Rajendra Chola's naval expedition reached:

(A) Persia and the Arabian peninsula
(B) Srivijaya (Sumatra, Malaya, SE Asia)
(C) Mediterranean Roman empire trade
(D) Eastern Africa via Indian Ocean
cards.back:
(B) Srivijaya (Sumatra, Malaya, SE Asia)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — Rajendra I led naval expedition (~1025 CE) against SRIVIJAYA empire (Sumatra-Malaya-Java; Buddhist thalassocracy controlling Strait of Malacca). Defeated king Sangrama Vijayottunga Varman, captured Kadaram (Kedah), wealth + ports. Aim: secure trade routes to China. The Cholas dominated Indian Ocean trade for ~200 years. Also expanded to Sri Lanka. Distractor 1: Cholas didn't go to Persia. Distractor 4: Indian-East Africa trade existed but was Arab-mediated, not Chola-led.

cards.front:
The famous CHOLA BRONZES (Nataraja, etc.) were cast using which technique?

(A) Stone-mould casting, common technique
(B) Lost-wax (cire perdue) bronze casting
(C) Forging by heavy hammer-strikes
(D) Die-cast manufacturing process used
cards.back:
(B) Lost-wax (cire perdue) bronze casting

South India & Regional Kingdoms — LOST-WAX (cire perdue) method — wax sculpture made first → coated with clay → fired (wax melts out, leaving cavity) → molten bronze poured in → clay broken to reveal final bronze. Allows fine detail. CHOLA BRONZES — pinnacle of Indian sculpture. Most famous: NATARAJA (Shiva as Lord of Dance) — multi-armed, leg raised in dance pose, fire halo, Apasmara (demon of ignorance) trampled. Also Parvati, Vishnu, saints (Bhakti period — Alvars + Nayanars). Adopted from earlier Pallava + Ganga work but perfected by Cholas.

cards.front:
Chola kingdom's CAPITAL CITY founded by Rajendra I was:

(A) Madurai, the older Pandyan capital
(B) Gangaikonda Cholapuram, his new city
(C) Kanchipuram, Pallava-era capital
(D) Kaveripattanam, ancient port city
cards.back:
(B) Gangaikonda Cholapuram, his new city

South India & Regional Kingdoms — Original Chola capital — THANJAVUR (under Rajaraja). Rajendra I shifted to GANGAIKONDA CHOLAPURAM after his Ganga expedition (~1025 CE). Built a great Shiva temple there (Brihadeeswara II). Also built a vast tank — Cholaganga — by carrying water from the Ganga (symbolic). Capital remained until late Chola period. Now in Ariyalur district, Tamil Nadu (UNESCO Great Living Chola Temples, 2004). Distractor 1: Madurai = Pandyan capital. Distractor 3: Kanchipuram = Pallava capital.

cards.front:
The Chola dynasty's eventual DECLINE in 13th century was mainly due to:

(A) Defeat by the rising Mughal empire
(B) Rise of Pandyas and Hoysalas in south
(C) Black plague pandemic spread of era
(D) Internal Buddhist religious conflict
cards.back:
(B) Rise of Pandyas and Hoysalas in south

South India & Regional Kingdoms — Cholas declined ~late 12th-early 13th c. CE under combined pressure from rising PANDYAS (Madurai, especially Maravarman Sundara Pandya, Jatavarman Sundara Pandya) and HOYSALAS (Karnataka, esp. Vira Ballala II). Rajadhiraja Chola III defeated by Pandyas ~1279 CE — last Chola king. Distractor 1 — Mughals came centuries later (16th c.). Distractor 3 — Black Death was 14th c., Eurasia-wide, not Chola-centric. Distractor 4 — Cholas were Shaivites; Buddhism had declined long before.

cards.option2: Black plague pandemic spread of era

(B) Chandragupta II
(C) Samudragupta
(D) Kumaragupta I

(B) Chandragupta II

South India & Regional Kingdoms — Chandragupta II / Vikramaditya (r. ~380-415 CE) — conquered western Saka kingdoms, Gupta empire at peak extent. Navaratna court (including Kalidasa). Fa-Hien (Chinese pilgrim) visited India during his reign. Samudragupta was his father — also great conqueror ('Indian Napoleon').

Samudragupta's achievements are documented in the:

(B) Prayag Prashasti

(B) Prayag Prashasti

cards.front:
Prithviraj Chauhan was defeated by Muhammad Ghori at which battle?

(A) First Battle of Tarain, 1191
(B) Second Battle of Tarain, 1192
(C) First Battle of Panipat, 1526
(D) Battle of Khanwa, 1527
cards.back:
(B) Second Battle of Tarain, 1192

South India & Regional Kingdoms — First Tarain (1191) — Prithviraj defeated Ghori. Second Tarain (1192) — Ghori returned a year later with fresh forces, defeated and captured Prithviraj. This opened the door to Turkish rule in North India and the Delhi Sultanate (Qutb-ud-din Aibak, 1206). Panipat 1526 (Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi) and Khanwa 1527 (Babur vs Rana Sanga) are later battles.

cards.front:
The VIJAYANAGARA empire was founded in 1336 CE by:

(A) Krishnadevaraya and Achyutadevaraya
(B) HARIHARA I and BUKKA RAYA I
(C) Saluva Narasimha
(D) Deva Raya I and II
cards.back:
(B) HARIHARA I and BUKKA RAYA I

South India & Regional Kingdoms — VIJAYANAGARA EMPIRE (1336-1646 CE) — south Indian kingdom on the TUNGABHADRA river; capital HAMPI (modern Karnataka). FOUNDED by brothers HARIHARA I and BUKKA RAYA I (also called Hakka and Bukka), originally treasury officials of KAKATIYAS of Warangal; captured by DELHI SULTANATE (Muhammad bin Tughluq), converted to Islam, sent south to govern; re-converted back to Hinduism under sage VIDYARANYA of Sringeri Math; raised the banner of Hindu resurgence against Islamic expansion. ORIGINAL NAME of the city: VIJAYANAGARA (‘City of Victory’); also called ‘Bidarahalli’ ‘Virupakshapura’. Four DYNASTIES ruled successively: (1) SANGAMA (1336-1485) — founders; included Harihara, Bukka, Deva Raya I & II. (2) SALUVA (1485-1505) — founded by Saluva Narasimha. (3) TULUVA (1491-1570) — KRISHNADEVARAYA (1509-1529) the GREATEST; golden age. (4) ARAVIDU (1542-1646) — last dynasty after Battle of Talikota. Empire became the southernmost HINDU bastion against Bahmani/Deccan Sultanates; lasted 310 years. Foreign travellers: NICOLO DE CONTI (Italian, Deva Raya II's court), ABDUR RAZZAQ (Persian, Deva Raya II's court), DOMINGO PAES (Portuguese, Krishnadevaraya's), FERNAO NUNIZ (Portuguese, Achyutadevaraya's) — all left detailed accounts. founded under the guidance of sage VIDYARANYA of Sringeri; Sangama dynasty.

cards.front:
The GREATEST ruler of the Vijayanagara empire, who presided over its golden age (1509-1529), was:

(A) Harihara II
(B) Deva Raya II
(C) KRISHNADEVARAYA
(D) Sadashiva Raya
cards.back:
(C) KRISHNADEVARAYA

South India & Regional Kingdoms — KRISHNADEVARAYA (1509-1529) — son of Tuluva Narasa Nayaka; the MOST CELEBRATED Vijayanagara ruler; empire reached its ZENITH politically, militarily, culturally, commercially. MILITARY: (1) Defeated GAJAPATIS of Odisha (Prataparudra Deva) and took Udayagiri, Kondavidu; (2) crushed ADIL SHAH of Bijapur at battle of Raichur (1520) — pivotal Deccan victory; (3) extended empire from Krishna-Godavari in north to Cape Comorin in south, west to Konkan, east to Bay of Bengal. LITERATURE & LEARNING: (1) himself a scholar — patronised TELUGU, KANNADA, TAMIL, SANSKRIT. (2) His AMUKTAMALYADA (Telugu) a manual of kingship — ‘a king should always be mindful of his subjects’ welfare’; also Sanskrit JAMBAVATI KALYANAM. (3) Court had ASHTADIGGAJAS (‘eight elephants of literature’) — ALLASANI PEDDANA (‘Andhra Kavita Pitamaha’, author of Manucharitra), NANDI THIMMANA, MADAYYAGARI MALLANA, DHURJATI, AYYALARAJU RAMABHADRUDU, PINGALI SURANA, RAMARAJABHUSHANA, TENALI RAMAKRISHNA (the wit). (4) Patronised HARIHARA KANAKADASA, VYASARAYA (Madhva saint-composer). ARCHITECTURE: built HAZARA RAMA temple, VITTHALA (with Stone Chariot), KRISHNA temple (to house Krishna idol brought from Udayagiri), upgraded VIRUPAKSHA; built suburb NAGALAPURAM (after queen Nagala Devi). DIPLOMACY: cordial relations with PORTUGUESE (Albuquerque); exchanged embassies. TRADE: Goa/ Bhatkal / Mangalore ports bustling. poet-king, author of ‘Amuktamalyada’ (Telugu); patron of the ASHTADIGGAJAS; Tuluva dynasty.

cards.front:
The battle of TALIKOTA (1565) that led to the DOWNFALL of Vijayanagara was fought between:

(A) Vijayanagara and Portuguese
(B) Vijayanagara and the Bahmani Sultanate (still undivided)
(C) VIJAYANAGARA (under RAMA RAYA, regent of Sadashiva Raya) vs a CONFEDERACY of four Deccan Sultanates: BIJAPUR (Adil Shahi) + AHMADNAGAR (Nizam Shahi) + GOLCONDA (Qutb Shahi) + BIDAR
(D) Vijayanagara and Mughals under Akbar
cards.back:
(C) VIJAYANAGARA (under RAMA RAYA, regent of Sadashiva Raya) vs a CONFEDERACY of four Deccan Sultanates: BIJAPUR (Adil Shahi) + AHMADNAGAR (Nizam Shahi) + GOLCONDA (Qutb Shahi) + BIDAR

South India & Regional Kingdoms — BATTLE OF TALIKOTA / RAKKASA-TANGADI (23 January 1565) — fought on the banks of KRISHNA river at a place variously called TALIKOTA, RAKKASI-TANGADI, or BANNIHATTI (near Bijapur). KEY DETAILS: (1) VIJAYANAGARA was then ruled by SADASHIVA RAYA (nominal), with RAMA RAYA the de facto regent — an aggressive statesman who had earlier played Deccan Sultans off against each other. (2) Alarmed by his dominance, FOUR DECCAN SULTANATES formed a CONFEDERACY — BIJAPUR (Ali Adil Shah I), AHMADNAGAR (Hussain Nizam Shah I), GOLCONDA (Ibrahim Qutb Shah), BIDAR (Ali Barid Shah). (Berar’s Imad Shahi had been absorbed earlier.) Cemented via marriages. (3) VIJAYANAGARA army (c. 1.4 lakh) initially had the upper hand; but TWO Muslim COMMANDERS in Rama Raya's army (Gilani brothers) DEFECTED mid-battle, tipping the tide. (4) RAMA RAYA was captured and BEHEADED on the spot by Hussain Nizam Shah. (5) Defeated army fled; the SULTAN armies SACKED HAMPI for 6 months — temples demolished, idols broken, statues defaced, libraries burnt — the ONE-TIME ‘greatest city in the world’ (per Domingo Paes) reduced to ruins; never reoccupied as a capital. (6) TIRUMALA (brother of Rama Raya) spirited away Sadashiva Raya + treasury to PENUKONDA (new capital), later shifted to CHANDRAGIRI, then VELLORE. (7) Last Vijayanagara dynasty ARAVIDU continued till 1646. HAMPI ruins: UNESCO World Heritage (1986); Virupaksha, Vitthala, Stone Chariot still stand as testimony. Barid Shahi.

cards.front:
The ‘AMUKTAMALYADA’, a Telugu literary classic written by Krishnadevaraya, is about:

(A) A story of wars between Pandavas and Kauravas
(B) ANDAL (TAMIL ALVAR SAINT-POETESS) — her devotion to Vishnu; also incorporates a detailed MANUAL OF STATECRAFT (Rajadharma)
(C) A biography of Krishnadevaraya
(D) A treatise on architecture
cards.back:
(B) ANDAL (TAMIL ALVAR SAINT-POETESS) — her devotion to Vishnu; also incorporates a detailed MANUAL OF STATECRAFT (Rajadharma)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — AMUKTAMALYADA (literally ‘she who gives the garland she has worn’) — TELUGU kavya in 6 cantos by KRISHNADEVARAYA himself; one of the FIVE great Telugu kavyas (Pancha Mahakavyas). CONTENT: (1) narrates the legend of GODA DEVI / ANDAL — the 9th-c. Tamil ALVAR saint-poetess of Srivilliputhur, daughter of Periyalvar; she wove a garland daily, wore it herself briefly, and offered it to Lord Vishnu (Ranganatha of Srirangam) — considered sacrilege but accepted by the Lord as a mark of her devotion; she eventually merged into the Ranganatha idol. (2) Includes extensive INTERLUDES ON STATECRAFT (Rajadharma) — Krishnadevaraya’s advice on ministers, diplomacy, famine relief, treatment of subjects, military strategy, forts, water works, foreign trade — a primary source on Vijayanagara polity. Famous line: ‘A crowned king should always rule with an eye to dharma (righteousness)’. Inspired by Krishnadevaraya’s visit to SRIKAKULAM / his patron deity ANDHRA VISHNU appearing in a dream asking him to compose on Goda Devi. OTHER Krishnadevaraya work: JAMBAVATI KALYANAM (Sanskrit, on Krishna-Jambavati wedding).

CONTENT: (1) narrates the legend of GODA DEVI / ANDAL — the 9th-c. Tamil ALVAR saint-poetess of Srivilliputhur, daughter of Periyalvar; she wove a garland daily, wore it herself briefly, and offered it to Lord Vishnu (Ranganatha of Srirangam) — considered sacrilege but accepted by the Lord as a mark of her devotion; she eventually merged into the Ranganatha idol. (2) Includes extensive INTERLUDES ON STATECRAFT (Rajadharma) — Krishnadevaraya’s advice on ministers, diplomacy, famine relief, treatment of subjects, military strategy, forts, water works, foreign trade — a primary source on Vijayanagara polity. Famous line: ‘A crowned king should always rule with an eye to dharma (righteousness)’. cards.front:
The ‘Stone Chariot’, an iconic monument of Hampi, is part of the:

(A) Virupaksha Temple
(B) Hazara Rama Temple
(C) VITTHALA TEMPLE complex
(D) Lotus Mahal
cards.back:
(C) VITTHALA TEMPLE complex

South India & Regional Kingdoms — STONE CHARIOT at HAMPI — shrine of GARUDA (Vishnu’s mount) sculpted as a stone CHARIOT; ONE of three famous stone chariots in India (others: KONARK Sun Temple in Odisha, MAHABALIPURAM rathas in TN, and the temple chariot at MELKOTE). LOCATED inside the VITTHALA TEMPLE COMPLEX, Hampi; built in the 16th century under KRISHNADEVARAYA (extending work begun under Deva Raya II). ARCHITECTURAL FEATURES: (1) made of several BLOCKS of granite cleverly joined to look monolithic; (2) wheels were ORIGINALLY rotatable (locked now to prevent damage); (3) two elephants in front — originally horses (whose broken legs can still be seen, elephants added later); (4) depicts Garuda seated inside. Printed on the NEW ₹50 note (2017 Mahatma Gandhi series). Whole VITTHALA temple: famous for MUSICAL PILLARS (SAREGAMA pillars) — 56 pillars that produce different notes when struck. Other Hampi marvels: VIRUPAKSHA temple (oldest, continuously in worship), HAZARA RAMA (royal chapel, walls depict Ramayana), KING’S BALANCE (Tula-Purusha dana place), LOTUS MAHAL (Indo-Islamic), ELEPHANT STABLES, QUEEN’S BATH, MAHANAVAMI DIBBA (Dasara platform). HAMPI declared UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. built during Deva Raya II / expanded by Krishnadevaraya; dedicated to Vitthala (form of Vishnu); houses 56 musical pillars.

cards.front:
The ASHTADIGGAJAS (‘eight elephants of literature’) were Telugu poets in the court of:

(A) Harihara II
(B) KRISHNADEVARAYA
(C) Deva Raya II
(D) Sadashiva Raya
cards.back:
(B) KRISHNADEVARAYA

South India & Regional Kingdoms — ASHTADIGGAJAS (‘eight elephants’ symbolising the eight directions) — EIGHT celebrated TELUGU POETS in KRISHNADEVARAYA’s court (1509-1529), who led the ‘Prabandha era’ — the GOLDEN AGE of Telugu literature. NAMES + works: (1) ALLASANI PEDDANA — ‘ANDHRA KAVITA PITAMAHA’ (father of Telugu poetry); author of MANUCHARITRA / SVAROCHISHA SAMBHAVA. (2) NANDI THIMMANA — PARIJATAPAHARANAMU. (3) MADAYYAGARI MALLANA — RAJASHEKHARA CHARITRA. (4) DHURJATI — KALAHASTI MAHATMYAM, Kalahasti devotional. (5) AYYALARAJU RAMABHADRUDU — RAMABHYUDAYAMU. (6) PINGALI SURANA — RAGHAVAPANDAVIYAMU (simultaneously narrates Ramayana + Mahabharata via clever puns — shlesha poetry). (7) RAMARAJABHUSHANA / BHATTUMURTHI — VASUCHARITRA, NARAKASURA VIJAYAM. (8) TENALI RAMAKRISHNA — author of PANDURANGA MAHATMYA; wit, satirist — innumerable folk tales of his wisdom. Each was a master of a specific style; their works followed the PRABANDHA form (longer literary narrative). They elevated Telugu from an oral/bardic language to a fully classical literary medium. Krishnadevaraya’s court also hosted Sanskrit scholars like VYASATIRTHA (Madhva acharya, Krishnadevaraya's spiritual guide). TENALI RAMAKRISHNA (the famous jester-poet) was one of them.

cards.front:
Which Portuguese traveller visited the Vijayanagara court of Krishnadevaraya and left a DETAILED account of the capital?

(A) Marco Polo
(B) Vasco da Gama
(C) DOMINGO PAES
(D) Duarte Barbosa
cards.back:
(C) DOMINGO PAES

South India & Regional Kingdoms — DOMINGO PAES (Portuguese horse trader / chronicler) — visited Vijayanagara c. 1520 during KRISHNADEVARAYA’s reign; stayed several months; wrote ‘CHRONICA DOS REIS DE BISNAGA’ (Chronicle of the Kings of Bisnaga [Vijayanagara]). Remarks: (1) described Hampi as ‘AS LARGE AS ROME AND VERY BEAUTIFUL TO THE SIGHT…the best-provided city in the world’; (2) population ~5 lakh; 7 concentric walls; (3) detailed MAHANAVAMI (Dasara) festival with 9-day royal spectacle — elephant processions, wrestling, sacrifices; (4) described BAZAARS selling diamonds, pearls, rubies ‘as if they were breads’; (5) detailed KRISHNADEVARAYA’s physique, daily exercise, military parades. COMPANION FERNAO NUNIZ visited later (1535-37, Achyutadevaraya’s reign), continued the chronicle. OTHER foreign visitors: (1) NICCOLO DE CONTI (Venetian, c. 1420, Deva Raya II) — ‘City has a circumference of 60 miles, 90,000 men fit for arms’. (2) ABDUR RAZZAQ (Persian ambassador from Herat, 1443, Deva Raya II) — ‘The city is such that eye has not seen nor ear heard of any place resembling it upon the whole earth’; described the 7 fortifications, the Mahanavami pavilion. (3) ATHANASIUS NIKITIN (Russian, c. 1470) — Bidar-centric but passed through; noted Hindu-Muslim contrast. (4) LUDOVICO DI VARTHEMA (Italian, early 16th c.). (5) DUARTE BARBOSA (Portuguese, c. 1516). his ‘Chronica dos Reis de Bisnaga’ describes Hampi as ‘as large as Rome and very beautiful to the sight’; companion FERNAO NUNIZ visited later in Achyutadevaraya’s reign.

cards.front:
The capital city of Vijayanagara at HAMPI is situated on the banks of which river?

(A) Krishna
(B) Kaveri
(C) TUNGABHADRA
(D) Godavari
cards.back:
(C) TUNGABHADRA

South India & Regional Kingdoms — HAMPI lies on the SOUTHERN bank of the TUNGABHADRA RIVER in the BELLARY district of KARNATAKA (now part of VIJAYANAGARA district, carved out 2021 from Bellary). TUNGABHADRA (‘Pampa’ in ancient texts) — formed by confluence of TUNGA (rises at Gangamoola, Varaha Parvata, Western Ghats) + BHADRA (rises nearby) at KUDLI in Karnataka; flows ~531 km E/NE, joining KRISHNA at Sangameshwaram in Andhra Pradesh. Vijayanagara founders chose the site for its natural defences: (1) Tungabhadra on the north; (2) rocky granite HILLS (Anjana Parvat = Anegundi range) around; (3) strategic; (4) mythological — ancient PAMPA-kshetra where Shiva was worshipped (Virupaksha is Shiva = Pampapati, consort of river-goddess PAMPA). Hampi = corrupted form of Pampa. KISHKINDHA of Ramayana is identified with the Hampi-Anegundi region — monkey kingdom of Sugriva-Hanuman. ANEGUNDI (across the river from Hampi) was the ORIGINAL capital of early Sangamas, before they moved capital to Hampi proper. TUNGABHADRA DAM (Hospet, 1953) built across the river for irrigation + hydropower; joint Karnataka-Andhra project.

cards.front:
The CHIEF SOURCE OF REVENUE in the Vijayanagara empire was:

(A) Plunder from wars
(B) LAND REVENUE (siddhaya)
(C) Foreign tribute
(D) Mining royalties
cards.back:
(B) LAND REVENUE (siddhaya)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — VIJAYANAGARA ECONOMY — HIGHLY monetised, prosperous, with the land-revenue system called RAYARE-KANDAVARE (or SIDDHAYA). FEATURES: (1) Land revenue the chief income — 1/6 (on wet land, rice) to 1/3 (on irrigated/sugarcane land) of gross produce, paid in cash or kind; (2) AMARAM (military feudal) system: nobles called NAYAKAS / AMARA-NAYAKAS held land in return for maintaining troops — precursor of later Zamindari/Jagirdari system; (3) separate department NAYAKATTANAM administered it; (4) other taxes: SRUTHAYAM (customs), DAIVADAYA (religious), HORSE-TAX, FISHERY, WEAVERS' TAX; (5) EIGHTEEN DIFFERENT TAXES on various trades in major cities; (6) COINS — gold VARAHA / GADYANA (standard coin, ~52 grains), PAGODA (half-varaha), FANAM, PANAMS; copper JITAL; (7) Currency bore Hindu iconography — Garuda, Vishnu, Hanuman, boar (Varaha, royal emblem of Sangamas & Tuluvas). COMMERCE: FLOURISHING FOREIGN TRADE via ports GOA, BHATKAL, HONAVAR, MANGALORE, CAMBAY, PULICAT; (a) Exported textiles, rice, iron, diamonds, sandalwood, spices; (b) imported horses (from ARABIA/PERSIA via Portuguese trade — essential for cavalry), elephants, silks, pearls, gems, precious metals. Indigenous industries: weaving, metalwork, jewellery, dyeing. 1/6 to 1/3 of produce; supplemented by taxes on trade, tolls, pasture, fish, oil, potter, weaver, and a war-tax (bhandaravadha).

cards.front:
The FOUR successive dynasties that ruled Vijayanagara (in chronological order) were:

(A) Saluva → Sangama → Tuluva → Aravidu
(B) Tuluva → Sangama → Saluva → Aravidu
(C) SANGAMA (1336-1485) → SALUVA (1485-1505) → TULUVA (1491-1570) → ARAVIDU (1542-1646)
(D) Aravidu → Tuluva → Saluva → Sangama
cards.back:
(C) SANGAMA (1336-1485) → SALUVA (1485-1505) → TULUVA (1491-1570) → ARAVIDU (1542-1646)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — FOUR VIJAYANAGARA DYNASTIES: (1) SANGAMA (1336-1485, ~150 years) — founders; Harihara I, Bukka I, Harihara II, Deva Raya I (digged Tungabhadra-anicut), Deva Raya II (Prauda Deva, ‘Immadi Deva Raya’, Niccolo de Conti, Abdur Razzaq visited), Mallikarjuna, Virupaksha II. Named after Sangama (father of Harihara and Bukka). (2) SALUVA (1485-1505) — founded by SALUVA NARASIMHA, a noble who usurped throne in the ‘First usurpation’ (1485) amid Sangama weakness. Lasted only 20 years; Immadi Narasimha succeeded as a minor. (3) TULUVA (1491-1570) — founded by TULUVA NARASA NAYAKA, regent who usurped power in the ‘Second usurpation’ (1503-05) from the Saluvas. His sons Vira Narasimha, KRISHNADEVARAYA (1509-29, golden age), Achyutadevaraya (1529-42), Venkata I, and Sadashiva Raya (nominal till 1570; real power with Rama Raya of Aravidu family). (4) ARAVIDU (1542-1646) — founded by TIRUMALA (Rama Raya's brother) after Battle of Talikota (1565); fled with Sadashiva + treasury; ruled from PENUKONDA (Anantapur district) → CHANDRAGIRI (Chittoor) → VELLORE; Venkata II (height of Aravidu rule), Sriranga III (last). Empire finally extinguished by 1646 (Sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda dismembered it). VIJAYANAGARA = 310 years of continuous Hindu imperial rule in south India.

cards.front:
The Vijayanagara empire was founded in 1336 CE by:

(A) Krishnadeva Raya, the greatest emperor
(B) Harihara I + Bukka Raya I (brothers)
(C) Saluva Narasimha, of Saluva dynasty
(D) Hari Hara II, mid-Sangama emperor
cards.back:
(B) Harihara I + Bukka Raya I (brothers)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — VIJAYANAGARA empire — founded 1336 CE by HARIHARA I + BUKKA RAYA I (Sangama brothers; legend: blessed by Vidyaranya, the Shringeri Math saint). Capital: VIJAYANAGARA / HAMPI on Tungabhadra (Karnataka). Four DYNASTIES: SANGAMA (1336-1485), SALUVA (1485-1505), TULUVA (1505-1570 — including KRISHNADEVA RAYA, the greatest), ARAVIDU (1570-1646). Originally founded as a Hindu bulwark against Bahmani / Delhi sultanates expansion southward. Distractor 1 — Krishnadeva Raya was Tuluva dynasty (1509-29).

KRISHNADEVA RAYA (greatest Vijayanagara emperor) belonged to which dynasty?

(A) Sangama dynasty, the founders
(B) Tuluva dynasty (1505-1570 phase)
(C) Saluva dynasty, briefly in middle
(D) Aravidu dynasty, the last phase
cards.back:
(B) Tuluva dynasty (1505-1570 phase)

Wrote AMUKTAMALYADA (Telugu epic) + JAMBAVATI KALYANAM (Sanskrit). cards.front:
The BATTLE OF TALIKOTA (1565), which led to Vijayanagara's downfall, was fought against:

(A) Mughal empire under emperor Akbar
(B) Combined forces of Deccan sultanates
(C) Portuguese Goa-based traders force
(D) Marathas under early Bhonsle leaders
cards.back:
(B) Combined forces of Deccan sultanates

South India & Regional Kingdoms — BATTLE OF TALIKOTA (also called RAKSHASA-TANGADI / BANNIHATTI; 23 Jan 1565 CE) — DECCAN SULTANATES alliance vs Vijayanagara. Five Deccan sultanates briefly UNITED: Bijapur (Adil Shah) + Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shah) + Bidar (Barid Shah) + Golconda (Qutb Shah). Berar stayed neutral. Vijayanagara army led by RAMA RAYA (Aravidu, regent of TULUVA emperor Sadasiva) — defeated, captured + beheaded. CAPITAL HAMPI sacked + ruined for 5 months. Empire continued in reduced form under Aravidu dynasty for ~80 more years (Penukonda + Chandragiri capitals) but never recovered.

cards.front:
The Vijayanagara military was famous for its use of:

(A) Naval warships in the Arabian Sea
(B) Elephants, cavalry, and Portuguese cannons
(C) Gunpowder grenades and rifles only
(D) Camel cavalry from the desert nomads
cards.back:
(B) Elephants, cavalry, and Portuguese cannons

South India & Regional Kingdoms — Vijayanagara army components: (1) ELEPHANTS — psychological terror + breaking enemy lines. (2) CAVALRY — imported Arabian + Persian horses (via Portuguese in Goa, after 1510); cavalry critical for victories. (3) INFANTRY (foot soldiers, archers, swordsmen). (4) ARTILLERY / FIREARMS — guns + cannons, often supplied / operated by PORTUGUESE in alliance (esp. under Krishnadeva Raya). NAYANKARA SYSTEM — chiefs (NAYAKAS) granted land (AMARAM) in return for military service + revenue collection. Distractor 1 — Vijayanagara had limited naval forces.

cards.front:
Vijayanagara's official COURT LANGUAGE for literature was largely:

(A) Sanskrit, classical only with no other
(B) Telugu (esp. Krishnadeva Raya's era)
(C) Persian, the Mughal court language
(D) Portuguese, after Goa came under Portugal
cards.back:
(B) Telugu (esp. Krishnadeva Raya's era)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — Vijayanagara — multilingual but TELUGU rose to prominence, especially under KRISHNADEVA RAYA (himself a Telugu poet — 'Andhra Bhoja'). Often called the GOLDEN AGE OF TELUGU LITERATURE. Also patronised KANNADA (Kumara Vyasa, Sarvajna), TAMIL (Saiva + Vaishnava texts), SANSKRIT (philosophy, religious). ASHTADIGGAJAS = 8 great TELUGU poets in Krishnadeva Raya's court. Notable works: 'AMUKTAMALYADA' (by emperor himself), 'MANUCHARITRAMU' (Allasani Peddana). Distractor 4 — Portuguese were a TRADING partner via Goa, not Vijayanagara's language.

cards.front:
MAHANAVAMI festival, splendidly celebrated at Vijayanagara each year, marked the:

(A) Birthday of the reigning emperor
(B) Nine-night Navaratri (royal celebration)
(C) Autumn harvest at end of monsoon
(D) Spring festival of colours called Holi
cards.back:
(B) Nine-night Navaratri (royal celebration)

South India & Regional Kingdoms — MAHANAVAMI = '9-night' = NAVARATRI festival (devoted to goddess Durga + Mother goddess). Most important state festival of Vijayanagara, lasting 9 days; ended on Vijaya Dashami (10th day = Dussehra). Celebrated at the MAHANAVAMI DIBBA (a stone platform at Hampi, still visible) — emperor reviewed troops, received tribute, watched dance + music. Foreign travellers like Abdur Razzak + Paes wrote elaborate accounts of MAHANAVAMI. Continued tradition: MYSORE DASARA (Wodeyars who succeeded Vijayanagara in part of the territory adopted similar grand celebrations). Distractor 4 — Holi is north Indian, not a southern festival emphasised.
cards.option2: Autumn harvest at end of monsoon
cards.option3: Spring festival of colours called Holi

The BATTLE OF TALIKOTA (1565), which fatally weakened Vijayanagar, was fought against:

(A) The Mughals
(B) A confederacy of Deccan Sultanates
(C) The Portuguese
(D) The Cholas
cards.back:
(B) A confederacy of Deccan Sultanates

South India & Regional Kingdoms — 26 January 1565 at Talikota (Rakkasa-Tangadi). Four Deccan Sultanates (without Berar) united against Vijayanagar. Ramaraya (regent for Sadashiva Raya) was killed; Hampi was sacked. Empire survived on in a diminished form under the Aravidu dynasty until 1646. Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar.

cards.front:
The DELHI SULTANATE (1206-1526) comprised FIVE SUCCESSIVE dynasties. The FIRST was:

(A) Tughlaq
(B) SLAVE / MAMLUK dynasty (1206-1290)
(C) Khilji
(D) Lodi
cards.back:
(B) SLAVE / MAMLUK dynasty (1206-1290)

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — DELHI SULTANATE (1206-1526) — five successive dynasties of Muslim rulers in North India. (1) SLAVE / MAMLUK dynasty (1206-1290) — founded by QUTB-UD-DIN AIBAK (1206-1210), originally Turkic slave of MUHAMMAD GHORI. Succeeded by ILTUTMISH (1211-36, proper founder of sultanate), RAZIA SULTANA (1236-40, first + only female sultan), BALBAN (1266-87, 'iron-handed' — 'zil-i-ilahi' theory). (2) KHILJI dynasty (1290-1320) — founded by Jalal-ud-din Khilji; apex under ALA-UD-DIN KHILJI (1296-1316) who repelled Mongol invasions, conquered Gujarat, Malwa, Deccan (Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra, Madurai); introduced market price controls; built Siri fort, Alai Darwaza, Hauz Khas. Died after court intrigue. (3) TUGHLAQ dynasty (1320-1414) — GHIYAS-UD-DIN TUGHLAQ founded (1320). MUHAMMAD-BIN-TUGHLAQ (1325-51) — 'wise fool' — moved capital Delhi→Daulatabad (forced migration, disaster); issued token currency (copper coins as silver — counterfeited, withdrawn); ambitious failed projects. FIROZ SHAH TUGHLAQ (1351-88) — moderate reformer; restored Delhi; built canals, Firoz Shah Kotla; shifted Ashokan pillars to Delhi. TIMUR's INVASION 1398 destroyed Delhi — effectively ended Tughlaq power. (4) SAYYID dynasty (1414-51) — founded by Khizr Khan (Timur's appointee); 4 weak rulers; Delhi reduced to 'Delhi to Palam'. (5) LODI dynasty (1451-1526) — first AFGHAN dynasty; Bahlul Lodi founded. IBRAHIM LODI (1517-26) — defeated by BABUR at FIRST BATTLE OF PANIPAT (21 April 1526) — ended Delhi Sultanate, began MUGHAL empire. MNEMONIC 'SKTSL' — Slave, Khilji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi. founded by Qutb-ud-din Aibak, a slave-general of Muhammad Ghori.

cards.front:
The QUTB MINAR, Delhi's iconic 72.5m tower, was begun by Qutb-ud-din Aibak (1199) but COMPLETED by:

(A) Balban
(B) ILTUTMISH (1210-36) who added 3 storeys
(C) Alauddin Khilji
(D) Razia Sultana
cards.back:
(B) ILTUTMISH (1210-36) who added 3 storeys

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — QUTB MINAR — 72.5m tall (5-storey), RED SANDSTONE + marble tower in MEHRAULI, Delhi; UNESCO World Heritage Site (1993). CONSTRUCTION STAGES: (1) QUTB-UD-DIN AIBAK (1199-1210) — began foundation + first storey to celebrate Muslim victory over the last Hindu kingdom of Delhi; named after sufi saint QUTB-UD-DIN BAKHTIYAR KAKI (whose dargah is nearby). (2) ILTUTMISH (c. 1220) — added 2nd, 3rd + 4th storeys. (3) FIROZ SHAH TUGHLAQ (1368) — after lightning damaged top storey (1369), rebuilt TOP TWO storeys + replaced sandstone with white MARBLE + red sandstone. Cupola added. (4) SIKANDAR LODI (1505) — further repair after earthquake. (5) BRITISH era — iron railing added; small pavilion atop removed in 1848. PURPOSE: a victory tower + minaret for adjacent QUWWAT-UL-ISLAM MOSQUE (first built mosque in Delhi, using pillars from 27 Hindu + Jain temples — visible today). INSCRIPTIONS: Quranic verses + rulers' names in ornamental calligraphy. QUTB COMPLEX also has: (a) IRON PILLAR of Delhi — 7m cast iron pillar erected by CHANDRAGUPTA II 'Vikramaditya' (c. 400 CE) in honor of Vishnu; originally at Udayagiri; famous for its RUST-RESISTANCE (high P content ~1%, low S, Fe-P passive layer); tradition of 'encircling it with arms backwards' to make wishes (now fenced). (b) ALAI DARWAZA (1311) by ALAUDDIN KHILJI — gateway in Indo-Islamic style; first TRUE ARCH in India. (c) ALAI MINAR — Alauddin's attempt to build a minar DOUBLE Qutb's height; only 24m base completed at his death. (d) TOMB of ILTUTMISH (1235). (e) TOMB of IMAM ZAMIN (Lodi era). Qutb Complex = founding monument of INDO-ISLAMIC ARCHITECTURE in India. 5th + top storey rebuilt by FIROZ SHAH TUGHLAQ in 1368 after lightning strike.

cards.front:
RAZIA SULTANA (1236-1240), the FIRST + only female sultan of Delhi, was the daughter of:

(A) Qutb-ud-din Aibak
(B) ILTUTMISH
(C) Balban
(D) Muhammad Ghori
cards.back:
(B) ILTUTMISH

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — RAZIA SULTANA (Razia-uddin, 1205-1240) — FIRST + ONLY WOMAN SULTAN of Delhi. REIGN: 10 Nov 1236 – 14 Oct 1240 (3 years, 11 months). BACKGROUND: daughter of ILTUTMISH (3rd Slave-dynasty sultan). Her father was impressed by her abilities during her brothers' inadequate conduct; he NOMINATED her as successor, writing 'Razia is better than 20 sons'. Succeeded her brother Rukn-ud-din Firoz Shah (deposed + murdered after 6 months). FEATURES of her rule: (a) discarded purdah + female dress; appeared in court in male attire (qaba + kulah); rode elephant publicly. (b) Efficient administrator; suppressed rebellions; appointed non-Turks to high offices — enraged the TURKIC 'CHAHALGANI' (Forty) nobility. (c) Close association with YAQUT (Abyssinian slave, appointed Amir-i-Akhur / Master of Horse) — created jealousy, scandal. (d) Fought 2 civil wars. OVERTHROW: 1240 — Governor of Bhatinda, MALIK ALTUNIYA, revolted; Razia defeated + captured; Yaqut killed. She married Altuniya in prison; they attempted to reclaim Delhi; defeated by her brother Bahram Shah; both Razia + Altuniya killed near KAITHAL (Haryana, 1240) after reportedly being robbed by an Indian zamindar (some say a Hindu, Jat) after fleeing. Tomb in Turkman Gate area of Old Delhi (modest, often disputed location). SIGNIFICANCE: (1) progressive for her time; (2) challenge to medieval Islamic gender norms; (3) tragic end shows the limits of TURKIC NOBILITY ('CHAHALGANI' = Forty) + patriarchal court politics; (4) pop culture — Kamal Amrohi's 1983 film 'Razia Sultan' (Hema Malini); Rajesh Kumar TV serial 2015. First female Indian monarch (CHAND BIBI of Ahmednagar, DURGAVATI of Gondwana, ZEB-UN-NISSA, MANGAMMAL of Madurai, NUR JAHAN of Mughals, AHILYABAI HOLKAR of Indore later exercised power but mostly as regents or in smaller principalities). She is India's first politically de jure reigning female monarch. nominated by him as successor over his sons; overthrown by Turkish nobility after 4-year reign; killed Kaithal 1240.

(A) Mansabdars

(C) Jagirdars
(D) Zamindars
cards.back:
(B) DIWAN-I-RIYASAT (Malik Yaqub) + SHAHNA-I-MANDI

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — ALAUDDIN KHILJI (1296-1316) — 2nd Khilji sultan, one of Delhi Sultanate's most powerful + most feared rulers. KEY REFORMS: (1) MARKET CONTROL / PRICE REGULATION — unique in medieval world. Motivated by: need to maintain huge standing army against Mongol threat. 4 DELHI MARKETS (mandis) controlled: (a) grain (Mandi); (b) cloth, sugar, dry fruits, medicines (Sarai-Adl); (c) horses, slaves, cattle; (d) general goods. OFFICIALS: Diwan-i-Riyasat (headed by MALIK YAQUB) oversaw all markets; SHAHNA-I-MANDI was the chief market officer for grain; BARID + MUNHIYAN were spies who reported any price hike to Sultan. Fixed prices with HARSH punishments for overcharging — even light thumb on scale → loss of equivalent flesh. Resulted in (a) prices stable for 25 years; (b) soldiers' wages sufficient (low-cost food). System collapsed soon after his death. (2) MILITARY REFORMS — huge standing army under central pay (cash, not jagirs); horse-branding (DAGH) + descriptive roll of soldiers (HULIA) — to prevent corruption. (3) ECONOMIC reforms — increased land revenue from 1/3 to 1/2 in Delhi region; MEASURED land (masahat) for revenue; eliminated intermediaries. (4) REPELLED MONGOL invasions — 5 major Mongol attacks (1299, 1303, 1305, 1306, 1308) all repelled; built SIRI FORT as 2nd Delhi + HAUZ KHAS TANK. (5) CONQUESTS — Gujarat (1299, married widow of Gujarat king, Kamala Devi; brought Khusraw Khan + Malik Kafur from there), Ranthambore (1301, killed Hammir Dev + Rani Padmini per legend), Chittor (1303 — Rani PADMINI's jauhar per Padmavat of Malik Muhammad Jayasi 1540, largely legendary), Malwa (1305), DECCAN (Devagiri, Warangal, Dwarasamudra, Madurai — captured fabulous wealth incl. KOHINOOR). (6) BUILDINGS — Alai Darwaza (1311), Alai Minar (incomplete), SIRI CITY. (7) Spent last years paranoid, ill; Malik Kafur killed him 1316. AMIR KHUSRAU was his court poet. Declared himself 'Sikander Sani' (Second Alexander) on coins. ONE OF the great conquerors; ruthless but effective. controlled prices in 4 markets of Delhi for grain, cloth, horses, slaves.

cards.front:
MUHAMMAD-BIN-TUGHLAQ (1325-51) is famous for two BLUNDERS that inspired his nickname 'wise fool'. They were:

(A) Moving army to Persia + inviting Mongols
(B) (a) TRANSFER of CAPITAL from Delhi to DAULATABAD (Devagiri) + (b) TOKEN CURRENCY
(C) Burning of Taxila + Alexandria
(D) War against all Hindu kingdoms
cards.back:
(B) (a) TRANSFER of CAPITAL from Delhi to DAULATABAD (Devagiri) + (b) TOKEN CURRENCY

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — MUHAMMAD-BIN-TUGHLAQ (real name Jauna Khan / Ulugh Khan; son of Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq; r. 1325-51) — 2nd Tughlaq sultan; accomplished scholar (knew philosophy, medicine, math, Persian literature) but plagued by disastrous experiments. Called 'WISE FOOL'. KEY 'BLUNDERS' / SCHEMES: (1) TRANSFER OF CAPITAL (1327) — from Delhi to DAULATABAD (renamed Devagiri, Maharashtra), to centralise southern empire. FORCED MIGRATION of ENTIRE Delhi population (officials + families, not just court) — thousands died on the 700-mile march in summer. When Mongol threats resurged, reversed back to Delhi — ANOTHER forced march back. Delhi devastated. (2) TOKEN CURRENCY (1329-32) — issued COPPER / BRASS coins (jital, tanka) as legal tender equivalent to silver tanka. Masses counterfeited these at home; state treasury dried up; eventually had to REDEEM all tokens for silver — enormous loss. (3) KHURASAN EXPEDITION — raised a 370,000-strong army for invasion of Central Asia (Khurasan); disbanded when funds ran out — those troops returned + roamed countryside as bandits. (4) QARACHIL EXPEDITION into HIMALAYAN Kangra; most of army perished in mountains. (5) INCREASED tax rates on DOAB (already famine-struck) — widespread rebellions. RESULT: empire rebellions + breakaways — (a) BENGAL (1335 Fakhr-ud-din Mubarak Shah independent); (b) MADURAI (1335, Jalal-ud-din Ahsan Khan); (c) Vijayanagar (1336, founded by Harihara + Bukka — breakaway state with Hindu revival); (d) Bahmani Sultanate (1347, Hasan Gangu — breakaway in Deccan). KEY PRIMARY SOURCE: IBN BATTUTA — Moroccan traveller who served as Delhi qazi for 8 years, wrote 'RIHLA'; Tughlaq appointed him ambassador to China. ZIAUDDIN BARANI = other major chronicler. DIED in 1351 in Sind pursuing rebels; historian BADAUNI wrote 'the king was freed from his people + the people from their king'. Successor FIROZ SHAH TUGHLAQ was MUCH more moderate. copper coins as substitute for silver tankas.

cards.front:
FEROZ SHAH TUGHLAQ (1351-88) brought two ASHOKAN PILLARS to Delhi + built many public works. He is most famous for founding the city of:

(A) Agra
(B) FEROZABAD (Firoz Shah Kotla, near Yamuna in Delhi) + extensive public works: 4 Delhi canals (Yamuna-Hissar), Firozabad fort, Hissar + Fatehabad towns
(C) Lucknow
(D) Patna
cards.back:
(B) FEROZABAD (Firoz Shah Kotla, near Yamuna in Delhi) + extensive public works: 4 Delhi canals (Yamuna-Hissar), Firozabad fort, Hissar + Fatehabad towns

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — FIROZ SHAH TUGHLAQ (1351-88) — cousin + successor of Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq; most BENEVOLENT + PUBLIC-WORKS-focused Tughlaq sultan. 37-year reign. KEY POLICIES: (1) Abolished many oppressive taxes; collected only 4 legal Islamic taxes — Kharaj (land revenue), Khums (1/5 war booty), Jizya (on non-Muslims; first extended to BRAHMINS, causing protest), Zakat. (2) Built extensive PUBLIC WORKS: (a) FEROZABAD / Firoz Shah Kotla — his new capital on Yamuna banks (ruins near Delhi Gate, cricket stadium named after it). (b) 4 IRRIGATION CANALS — Yamuna-to-Hissar canal (a predecessor of modern Western Yamuna Canal), Rajab canal, Khadi-karan canal, Ulugh-Khani canal — irrigated millions of acres; first large-scale irrigation works in medieval India. (c) FOUNDED CITIES — FATEHABAD, HISSAR, FIROZPUR, JAUNPUR (named after his cousin Juna Khan), FIROZABAD. (d) Built ~40 MOSQUES, 30 COLLEGES, 100 HOSPITALS (DAR-UL-SHIFA), 100 public baths (hammams), 100 wells, 150 bridges, 1200 SARAIS (inns). (e) DAR-UL-SHAFA (free hospital, Delhi). (f) DIWAN-I-KHAIRAT (department of charity) — helped widows, orphans, dowries for poor girls. (3) BROUGHT TWO ASHOKAN PILLARS from Topra (Haryana) + Meerut (UP) to Delhi — by boats + bullock carts, despite not reading the inscriptions (later deciphered by James Prinsep 1837). One pillar stands at FIROZ SHAH KOTLA (Topra) + Delhi Ridge (Meerut, near Bara Hindu Rao). (4) HOWEVER, DESTROYED many Hindu temples (unlike his pragmatic predecessors). Imposed jizya on Brahmins (novel + controversial; Hindus demanded relief after huge hunger strike — he relented partially). (5) Continued JAGIR system — IQTAS made hereditary; led to decentralisation + weakening of central control — SEED of his dynasty's post-death collapse. (6) AUTHORED 'FUTUHAT-I-FIROZ SHAHI' — 30-page memoir. After his death 1388, TUGHLAQ dynasty disintegrated within a decade; TIMUR's invasion of 1398 finished them off.

cards.front:
TIMUR (Tamerlane) invaded India in 1398 and sacked Delhi. Who was the ruling sultan at the time?

(A) Alauddin Khilji
(B) NASIR-UD-DIN MAHMUD SHAH TUGHLAQ
(C) Firoz Shah Tughlaq
(D) Ibrahim Lodi
cards.back:
(B) NASIR-UD-DIN MAHMUD SHAH TUGHLAQ

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — TIMUR's INVASION of India (1398-99) — catastrophic sack of Delhi by the Turco-Mongol conqueror TIMUR (Tamerlane, 1336-1405) from Samarkand. ROUTE: crossed Indus Sep 1398; sacked Multan, Tulamba, Dipalpur, Bhatner (Hanumangarh), Panipat; reached Delhi on 17 Dec 1398. RULING SULTAN: NASIR-UD-DIN MAHMUD SHAH TUGHLAQ (1394-1413) — weak ruler, fled Delhi as Timur's forces entered. SACK OF DELHI (17-20 Dec 1398): one of the worst in Indian history. (1) 100,000 Hindu prisoners taken captive earlier were massacred (to prevent rebellion during assault). (2) Delhi LOOTED for 3 days — virtually every Delhi building + population affected; tens of thousands dead; city-wide fires; took skilled craftsmen (masons, artisans) back to SAMARKAND to build his famous monuments (incl. Bibi-Khanum mosque). (3) Took massive loot — jewels, gold, silver; elephants; slaves. (4) Left Delhi 30 Dec 1398, returned to Samarkand via Meerut, Haridwar (sacked), Kangra (sacked), Jammu (sacked); crossed Indus Mar 1399. Appointed KHIZR KHAN (governor of Multan, a Sayyid noble) as his viceroy — founder of SAYYID dynasty (1414-51). IMPACT: (1) Effectively ended TUGHLAQ sultanate. (2) Delhi DESOLATE for decades — 'Malwa, Gujarat, Khandesh, Jaunpur, Bengal', Sharqi rulers consolidated independent regional kingdoms. (3) REGIONAL STATES flourished — Gujarat Sultanate (1407), Malwa Sultanate (1392), Jaunpur Sharqi Sultanate (1394-1479 — Sharqi means 'east'; Jaunpur = 'Shiraz of India' for its scholars + architecture), Bengal Sultanate, Bahmani Sultanate (1347, Deccan), Vijayanagar Empire (1336, southern resistance). (4) Timur's descendant BABUR (5th gen) later founded MUGHAL empire (1526) — 'MUGHAL' = Persian for Mongol. POST-TIMUR legacy: Samarkand + Bukhara flourished; Timurid Renaissance in Central Asia; Ulugh Beg's observatory. AMIR TIMUR of Uzbekistan today venerated as national hero. the last effective Tughlaq ruler; fled Delhi as Timur entered.

cards.front:
The FIRST BATTLE OF PANIPAT (21 April 1526) ended the Delhi Sultanate + began the Mughal Empire. It was fought between:

(A) Akbar vs Hemu
(B) BABUR vs IBRAHIM LODI
(C) Sher Shah Suri vs Humayun
(D) Aurangzeb vs Shivaji
cards.back:
(B) BABUR vs IBRAHIM LODI

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — FIRST BATTLE OF PANIPAT — 21 APRIL 1526 — one of the most consequential battles in Indian history. COMBATANTS: (1) ZAHIR-UD-DIN MUHAMMAD BABUR (1483-1530, Timurid ruler of Kabul, descendant of TIMUR on father's side + GENGHIS KHAN on mother's side) with ~12,000 troops. (2) IBRAHIM LODI (last Lodi sultan of Delhi, 1517-26) with ~100,000 + 1,000 elephants. TERRAIN: Panipat plain north of Delhi (Haryana). BABUR'S FORMATION: (a) Center of army protected by 700 carts tied with rawhide thongs (TULGHMA system — central fortification, a Turco-Mongol tactic adopted from Ottomans). (b) Gaps between carts for MATCHLOCK GUNS (tufang) + CANNONS — fired by Ottoman-trained gunners Ustad Ali Quli + Mustafa Rumi. (c) Flanks used Turkic CAVALRY WHEEL (Tulghma) — rapid encirclement tactic. KEY FACTORS: (1) Babur's ARTILLERY was NEW to Indian warfare — Lodi had only swords, bows, elephants. (2) Ibrahim's troops were disciplined but slow; elephants panicked at gunfire. (3) Babur's flanking cavalry encircled Lodi's host. BY MIDDAY, Ibrahim Lodi + 15,000-20,000 men DEAD (including Ibrahim himself); Babur entered DELHI + AGRA; proclaimed emperor of 'Hindustan'. SIGNIFICANCE: (1) ENDED Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526, 320 years, 5 dynasties). (2) BEGAN MUGHAL EMPIRE (1526-1857, 331 years). (3) First major Indian battle decided by GUNPOWDER ARTILLERY — start of 'GUNPOWDER EMPIRES' in India. (4) KOHINOOR diamond changed hands — Babur received it from Raja Vikramaditya of Gwalior (who had taken it from Alauddin's loot), passed to Humayun, back + forth, eventually to Mughal Red Fort → Nadir Shah 1739 → Ahmad Shah Durrani → Ranjit Singh → British 1849 → Queen Victoria 1877 → Crown Jewels UK. BABUR wrote BABURNAMA (memoirs in Chaghatai Turkish) — famous autobiography. SECOND + THIRD battles of Panipat followed (1556 Akbar-Hemu, 1761 Marathas-Abdali). Babur's smaller force (~12,000) defeated Lodi's (~100,000) using ARTILLERY (matchlocks) + TULGHMA cavalry tactics.

cards.front:
Which Delhi Sultan was known as the 'SHADOW OF GOD ON EARTH' + formulated the 'ZIL-I-ILAHI' theory of kingship?

(A) Qutb-ud-din Aibak
(B) BALBAN
(C) Iltutmish
(D) Alauddin Khilji
cards.back:
(B) BALBAN

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — GHIYAS-UD-DIN BALBAN (r. 1266-1287) — 9th Mamluk / Slave dynasty sultan; one of the most POWERFUL + DESPOTIC sultans of Delhi. ORIGINAL name: BAHA-UD-DIN; born Turkic (Ilbari tribe); captured + sold to Khwaja Jamal-ud-din of Basra; brought to Delhi by Iltutmish. Rose through Iltutmish + Razia's court; served as NAIB-I-MAMLAKAT (regent) for Sultan Nasir-ud-din Mahmud (1246-66); married daughter to the sultan; ultimately ascended himself at age 60. KEY POLICIES: (1) 'ZIL-I-ILAHI' ('Shadow of God on Earth') theory — derived Sultan's authority from God DIRECTLY, not from the Caliphate; sultan superior to all mortals; elevated + distanced the monarchy from nobility. (2) Persian COURT CEREMONIAL — introduced SIJDA (prostration) + PAIBOS (kissing the feet / ground before the Sultan); court etiquette to awe subjects. Inspired by Iranian Sasanian court tradition. (3) CRUSHED the TURKISH CHAHALGANI (Forty) — the powerful 40-noble Turkic oligarchy Iltutmish had created; Balban systematically killed / exiled them; replaced by non-Turks + trusted men. (4) Restored law + order — the Mewatis + Doab bandits terrorising Delhi's outskirts crushed with ruthless force; reopened trade routes. (5) Built + strengthened FORTS — Lahore, Multan, Hisar, Delhi; raised CAVALRY + army; established DIWAN-I-ARZ (military dept). (6) Suppressed BENGAL rebellion (Tughril Khan, 1279-80) — personally led army. (7) Repelled Mongol raids — central Asian border stabilised. (8) SON MUHAMMAD (the 'Khan Shahid') KILLED while guarding against Mongols at Multan (1285) — broke Balban's spirit; died 1287 of grief. NOTABLE COURTIERS: AMIR KHUSRAU (poet, just beginning career), Amir Hasan. HISTORIAN: Ziauddin Barani (wrote Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, Fatawa-i-Jahandari). SUCCESSOR: grandson Kaiqubad (murdered 1290); LAST Slave sultan. 1290 — JALAL-UD-DIN KHILJI ended Slave dynasty. BALBAN's DESPOTISM + anti-noble purges = template for later Sultanate centralisation. Slave dynasty; introduced Persian court ceremonial (sijda + paibos); crushed Turkish Chahalgani; Ghiyas-ud-din Balban, 1266-87.

(3) CRUSHED the TURKISH CHAHALGANI (Forty) — the powerful 40-noble Turkic oligarchy Iltutmish had created; Balban systematically killed / exiled them; replaced by non-Turks + trusted men. (4) Restored law + order — the Mewatis + Doab bandits terrorising Delhi's outskirts crushed with ruthless force; reopened trade routes. (5) Built + strengthened FORTS — Lahore, Multan, Hisar, Delhi; raised CAVALRY + army; established DIWAN-I-ARZ (military dept). (6) Suppressed BENGAL rebellion (Tughril Khan, 1279-80) — personally led army. (7) Repelled Mongol raids — central Asian border stabilised. (8) SON MUHAMMAD (the 'Khan Shahid') KILLED while guarding against Mongols at Multan (1285) — broke Balban's spirit; died 1287 of grief. NOTABLE COURTIERS: AMIR KHUSRAU (poet, just beginning career), Amir Hasan. HISTORIAN: Ziauddin Barani (wrote Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi, Fatawa-i-Jahandari). SUCCESSOR: grandson Kaiqubad (murdered 1290); LAST Slave sultan. 1290 — JALAL-UD-DIN KHILJI ended Slave dynasty. BALBAN's DESPOTISM + anti-noble purges = template for later Sultanate centralisation. Slave dynasty; introduced Persian court ceremonial (sijda + paibos); crushed Turkish Chahalgani; Ghiyas-ud-din Balban, 1266-87.

cards.front:
The LAND REVENUE system 'IQTA' under the Delhi Sultanate was:

(A) Hereditary land ownership by peasants
(B) Assignment of LAND REVENUE from a territory to a noble / officer
(C) Salary paid in gold
(D) Temple lands tax-exempt
cards.back:
(B) Assignment of LAND REVENUE from a territory to a noble / officer

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — IQTA system — key ADMINISTRATIVE + MILITARY institution of the Delhi Sultanate. ORIGIN: Arabic 'iqta' = assignment / share. Borrowed from Abbasid Caliphate. CHARACTERISTICS: (1) the SULTAN granted to a noble / military officer (IQTADAR / MUQTI / WALI) the right to COLLECT LAND REVENUE of a specified territory instead of paying him a salary. (2) Revenue collected was expected to MAINTAIN a military contingent (soldiers + horses) + remit SURPLUS to central treasury. (3) NON-HEREDITARY — iqta-dar could be TRANSFERRED or removed at Sultan's pleasure → maintained central control (unlike European feudalism). (4) Officers were also expected to ADMINISTER the territory (judicial, civil). EVOLUTION: (1) Under ILTUTMISH — iqtas introduced widely; granted to Turkish soldiers to maintain cavalry. Created the '40 CHAHALGANI'. (2) BALBAN — tightened control; reclaimed many iqtas. (3) ALAUDDIN KHILJI — DRASTIC reforms; RESUMED many iqtas; paid cash salaries instead; maintained direct central army (lessons from Mongol threats). Land revenue raised to 50%; MEASURED land (masahat). (4) MUHAMMAD-BIN-TUGHLAQ — rebellions forced him to re-assign iqtas. (5) FIROZ SHAH TUGHLAQ — made iqtas HEREDITARY (huge mistake) — decentralised power to provincial iqtadars; after his death, iqtas became de facto principalities → break-up of Sultanate. (6) Mughal era — replaced by JAGIR + MANSABDARI system (Akbar). KEY OFFICIALS: MUQTI (iqta-dar/governor), AMIR (mid-rank), MALIK (senior), KHAN (royal rank — Amir Khusrau, Bahram Khan). REVENUE DEMAND historically: (a) Sultanate — 25% to 50% of produce (Alauddin raised to 50%); (b) Collected in cash + kind; (c) measured via MASAHAT (land survey by jarib); (d) BATAI (sharing crop between state + cultivator); (e) KANKUT (estimation). Nobles lived lavishly from iqta income; standing army supported. VILLAGE LEVEL: MUQADDAM (village headman), KHUT (big peasant, land-holding), BALAHAR (minor functionary), CHAUDHURIES (medium-large) — rural power intermediaries. PEASANT (RAIYAT) life was often hard; oppressive demands drove many to forest banditry (Rajputs, Meos). NON-hereditary; revenue basis of Sultanate administration; IQTADAR / MUQTI.

cards.front:
The founder of the Slave (Mamluk) dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate was:

(A) Iltutmish
(B) Qutb-ud-din Aibak
(C) Balban
(D) Muhammad Ghori
cards.back:
(B) Qutb-ud-din Aibak

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Qutb-ud-din Aibak, a slave-general of Muhammad Ghori, became the first Sultan of Delhi in 1206 after Ghori's death — founding the Slave or Mamluk dynasty. He began the Qutub Minar (completed by Iltutmish) and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque. Iltutmish (1211-36) was Aibak's son-in-law and successor; Balban (1266-87) consolidated the dynasty's power.

cards.front:
Market-control regulations and price-fixing in Delhi's bazaars were famously introduced by:

(A) Balban
(B) Alauddin Khilji
(C) Muhammad bin Tughlaq
(D) Firoz Shah Tughlaq
cards.back:
(B) Alauddin Khilji

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Alauddin Khilji (1296-1316) introduced sweeping market reforms — fixed prices for grain, cloth, horses and slaves; set up three separate markets under a Diwan-i-Riyasat; maintained buffer stocks. He did this mainly to pay a standing army cheaply. He also imposed a tax on produce (kharaj) at half the yield and a house tax (ghari).

The Tughlaq sultan who shifted his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad and issued token currency was:

(A) Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq
(B) Muhammad bin Tughlaq
(C) Firoz Shah Tughlaq
(D) Balban
cards.back:
(B) Muhammad bin Tughlaq

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325-51) tried to move the capital from Delhi to Devagiri (renamed Daulatabad) in 1327, forcing an unpopular mass migration, and issued copper/brass token coins that counterfeiters promptly forged, causing economic chaos. Ibn Battuta, the Moroccan traveller, visited his court. Ghiyas-ud-din founded the dynasty; Firoz Shah (1351-88) was his cousin and successor.

The only woman sultan of Delhi was:

(A) Nur Jahan
(B) Razia Sultana
(C) Chand Bibi
(D) Mumtaz Mahal
cards.back:
(B) Razia Sultana

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Razia Sultana (r. 1236-40), daughter of Iltutmish, was the only woman to sit on the throne of Delhi. She was overthrown by the Turkish nobility (the 'Forty' / Chahalgani) after a short reign. Nur Jahan was Jahangir's wife (Mughal, not Sultanate); Chand Bibi defended Ahmednagar against Akbar; Mumtaz Mahal was Shah Jahan's queen (the Taj's namesake).

The last ruler of the Lodi dynasty, defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat (1526), was:

(A) Sikandar Lodi
(B) Ibrahim Lodi
(C) Bahlol Lodi
(D) Daulat Khan Lodi
cards.back:
(B) Ibrahim Lodi

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Ibrahim Lodi (1517-26) was the last sultan of Delhi. Babur defeated and killed him at Panipat on 21 April 1526, using cannons and the 'tulughma' flanking tactic; the Mughal empire began. Bahlol (1451-89) founded the Lodi line; Sikandar (1489-1517) moved the capital to Agra and was Ibrahim's father. Daulat Khan Lodi, governor of Punjab, actually invited Babur to invade.

MUHAMMAD BIN TUGHLAQ is famous for which infamous decision?

(A) Building the Taj Mahal in Agra
(B) Capital shift Delhi to Daulatabad and back
(C) Religious conversion of Mongol invaders
(D) Abolition of all forms of taxation
cards.back:
(B) Capital shift Delhi to Daulatabad and back

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — MUHAMMAD BIN TUGHLAQ (r. 1325-1351) — eccentric ambitious sultan. Known for 5 'experiments' (mostly failures!): (1) Shifted CAPITAL from Delhi to DAULATABAD / Devagiri (1327; meant for better control of Deccan; forced entire population to march south — many died; abandoned + reverted to Delhi 1335). (2) TOKEN CURRENCY — copper / brass coins valued same as silver (1330; rampant counterfeiting → currency collapse). (3) TAXATION in Doab — sharply raised; then drought hit; revolts. (4) Plan to invade Khurasan (Persia) — never executed. (5) Plan to conquer Karachil (Tibet area) — disaster, army wiped out. Had vast learning + ambition but lacked judgement. Ibn Battuta visited his court.

Alauddin Khilji's most famous economic reform was:

(B) Market control / price-fixing system in Delhi
(C) Issuing token currency

cards.back:

Set up four markets — Mandi (grains), Sara-i-Adl (cloth), separate markets for horses/cattle and slaves. Officials: Diwan-i-Riyasat (controller), Shahna-i-Mandi (market officer), reporters (Barids, Munhiyans). Strict punishments for cheating. Token currency was Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiment (later, 1329-32). Land redistribution wasn't a Khilji reform; rather, kharaj raised to 50% of produce.

cards.back:

Firuz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351-88) is best remembered for:

Famous for benevolent civic projects: canals (notably Western Yamuna Canal — restored & later used by British), gardens, hospitals (Dar-ul-Shifa, free medical care), employment bureau (Diwan-i-Khairat), abolition of torture and mutilation. Alauddin Khilji's army system featured revolutionary measures including:

(A) Permanent land grants to soldiers
(B) Branding of horses (Dagh) and descriptive rolls of soldiers (Chehra) to prevent fraud
(C) Hereditary military offices
(D) Outsourcing army to mercenaries
cards.back:

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Alauddin Khilji's military reforms — first ruler to maintain a STANDING ARMY paid in CASH (not jagirs). Dagh (branding) — every horse branded with the state's mark to prevent substitution. Chehra (descriptive roll) — physical description of every soldier kept on file to prevent impersonation/proxy. These were later adopted by Sher Shah Suri and the Mughals (Akbar's mansabdari). The cash-paid army required Alauddin's market-control reforms — fixed low prices meant cash salary went further.

The Lodi Dynasty, the last ruling dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate, was founded in 1451 by:

(A) Sikandar Lodi
(B) Bahlul Lodi (an Afghan noble who deposed the last Sayyid sultan)
(C) Ibrahim Lodi
(D) Sher Shah Suri
cards.back:
(B) Bahlul Lodi (an Afghan noble who deposed the last Sayyid sultan)

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Lodi Dynasty (1451-1526) — Afghan in origin (most Sultanate dynasties were Turkic). Founder Bahlul Lodi (r. 1451-89) — was governor of Sirhind under the Sayyid sultans; deposed Alam Shah, the last Sayyid sultan, on 19 Apr 1451. Three rulers: Bahlul, Sikandar (1489-1517), Ibrahim (1517-26). The Lodis were the FIRST Afghan dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate. The dynasty ended with Ibrahim's defeat and death at the First Battle of Panipat (21 Apr 1526) by Babur — marking the start of the Mughal Empire.

cards.front:
Sikandar Lodi (r. 1489-1517), the most capable Lodi ruler, founded which present-day major city as his new capital?

(A) Lucknow
(B) Agra (founded 1504, became Lodi capital 1506)
(C) Hyderabad
(D) Lahore
cards.back:
(B) Agra (founded 1504, became Lodi capital 1506)

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Sikandar Lodi — founded the city of Agra in 1504 on the right bank of the Yamuna; shifted capital from Delhi to Agra in 1506. Reasons: better central location to control Doab + Bayana, Gwalior, central India; relief from Delhi's overcrowded politics. Agra later flourished as the Mughal capital (Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan). Sikandar's other achievements: stable administration; introduced 'Gaz-i-Sikandari' (Sikandari yard, ~30 inches, used as a measure for land); patronised Persian + Hindi literature; commissioned 'Lahjat-i-Sikandari' on music. Was an iconoclast — destroyed many Hindu temples in Mathura, Utgir, Jwalamukhi.

cards.front:
The First Battle of Panipat (21 April 1526) was fought between:

(A) Akbar and Hemu
(B) Babur (Mughals) and Ibrahim Lodi (Delhi Sultanate)
(C) Babur and Rana Sanga
(D) Sher Shah Suri and Humayun
cards.back:
(B) Babur (Mughals) and Ibrahim Lodi (Delhi Sultanate)

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — First Battle of Panipat — 21 April 1526; Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi. Babur was invited to invade by Daulat Khan Lodi (governor of Punjab) and Alam Khan (Ibrahim's uncle), both at odds with Ibrahim. Babur's force ~12,000-15,000 vs Ibrahim's ~100,000 + 1,000 elephants. Babur won decisively due to (1) tulughma — flanking-attack tactic; (2) artillery — first major use of gunpowder cannons in India (master-gunner Ustad Ali); (3) breast-defence with carts (araba). Ibrahim was killed in battle — only Delhi Sultan to die in battle. Babur founded the Mughal Empire (1526-1857). Battle of Khanwa (1527) — Babur vs Rana Sanga. Second Panipat (1556) — Akbar vs Hemu. Third Panipat (1761) — Marathas vs Ahmad Shah Abdali.

The 'Lodi Gardens' in central Delhi contain the tombs of Lodi-era rulers including the:

(A) Tomb of Iltutmish
(B) Tombs of Sikandar Lodi and Mohammad Shah (Sayyid)
(C) Tomb of Akbar

cards.back:
(B) Tombs of Sikandar Lodi and Mohammad Shah (Sayyid)

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Lodi Gardens (90-acre park, central Delhi, near Khan Market) — contains: (1) Tomb of Mohammad Shah (Sayyid sultan, 1444); (2) Tomb of Sikandar Lodi (1517); (3) Bara Gumbad (1490, prob a gateway to a missing mosque); (4) Sheesh Gumbad (Sikandar Lodi era). Ibrahim Lodi's tomb is at PANIPAT (where he died) — a simple unadorned structure. Iltutmish's tomb — in Qutb complex (Mehrauli), early 13th c. Akbar's tomb — Sikandra (Agra). Lodi tombs marked transition to octagonal + double-domed pattern that culminated in Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal — early experiments with the Indo-Islamic mausoleum form.

cards.front:
Daulat Khan Lodi, the governor of Punjab whose invitation indirectly brought Babur into India, did so because:

(A) He wanted Babur to be his son-in-law
(B) He resented Ibrahim Lodi's centralising and harsh policies toward the Afghan nobles
(C) Babur was his student
(D) Babur was the rightful heir to Delhi
cards.back:
(B) He resented Ibrahim Lodi's centralising and harsh policies toward the Afghan nobles

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Ibrahim Lodi (r. 1517-26) — tried to centralise authority and humiliated several senior Afghan nobles (a key error since Lodi rule rested on the consent of the Afghan tribal nobility). Daulat Khan Lodi (governor of Punjab) and Alam Khan (Ibrahim's own uncle, who claimed the throne) sent emissaries to Babur in Kabul, asking him to invade and depose Ibrahim. Babur — already familiar with Punjab from previous raids (1519-24) — accepted. By the time Babur reached Delhi, Daulat Khan had reconsidered and tried to oppose Babur — but his army melted away. The invitation–defection pattern was a classic Lodi-era weakness; Sher Shah Suri later exploited similar tribal disaffection against the Mughals.

(A) Mahabharata

cards.back:
(B) Ayurveda treatises (a work titled Tibb-i-Sikandari or Ma'din-ush-shifa-i-Sikandar Shahi was compiled in his time)

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Tibb-i-Sikandar Shahi / Ma'din-ush-shifa-i-Sikandar Shahi — a Persian compilation of Indian medicine commissioned during Sikandar Lodi's reign (compiled by Miyan Bhuwa, son of his minister). Ayurvedic remedies were translated from Sanskrit. Sikandar also patronised music — 'Lahjat-i-Sikandari' (treatise on music). Sanskrit-to-Persian translation traditions later flourished under the Mughals — Akbar's Razmnama (Mahabharata) and Ramayana translations; Dara Shukoh's translation of Upanishads (Sirr-i-Akbar, 1657). Lodi-era cultural sponsorship was modest but transitional, paving the way for the Mughal florescence.

cards.front:
Bahlul Lodi spent most of his reign (1451-89) consolidating control over which troublesome eastern principality, finally succeeding in 1483?

(A) Bengal Sultanate
(B) Sharqi Sultanate of Jaunpur
(C) Vijayanagara Empire
(D) Bahmani Sultanate
cards.back:
(B) Sharqi Sultanate of Jaunpur

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Bahlul Lodi spent most of his reign in long campaigns against the Sharqi Sultanate of Jaunpur (founded 1394 after Timur's invasion fragmented the Tughlaq empire; capital Jaunpur in eastern UP; also called the 'Shiraz of the East' for cultural patronage — Atala Masjid, Lal Darwaza Masjid, Jami Masjid). Bahlul finally annexed Jaunpur in 1483; the Sharqi sultans took refuge in Bihar. This expansion brought the Doab + eastern UP firmly under Lodi rule. Bahmani Sultanate — Deccan (1347-1527, fragmented into 5 sub-sultanates including Ahmednagar, Bijapur, Golconda).

cards.front:
The IQTA system in the Delhi Sultanate refers to:

(A) A tax on Hindu pilgrims
(B) Revenue-assignment grants to nobles in lieu of salary
(C) Religious endowments to Sufi saints

Medieval India & Delhi Sultanate — Iqta = territorial assignment whose land-revenue supported the noble (iqtadar) who held it. cards.front:
Which of Akbar's NAVRATNAS was famous as a court musician and singer?

(A) Tansen (originally Ramtanu Pandey)
(B) Birbal (a witty courtier alone)
(C) Abul Fazl (the chief biographer)
(D) Todar Mal (revenue minister here)
cards.back:
(A) Tansen (originally Ramtanu Pandey)

Mughal Empire — MIYAN TANSEN (originally Ramtanu Pandey, ~1500-1589) — one of Akbar's NAVRATNAS, regarded as the GREATEST musician in Indian history. Born in Behat, near Gwalior; trained under Swami Haridas of Vrindavan. Joined Akbar's court ~1562; granted title 'MIYAN' by Akbar. CONTRIBUTIONS: (1) Created RAGAS — Miyan ki Todi, Miyan ki Malhar, Darbari Kanada (still core of Hindustani classical music). (2) Master of DHRUPAD style. (3) Legend: Tansen sang Raga Deepak which lit oil lamps; Raga Megh Malhar to bring rain (mythological). DEATH: 1589; Akbar attended his funeral. SAMADHI: at Gwalior (annual Tansen Music Festival held there). LINEAGE: founder of the SENI GHARANA — many great musicians trace lineage to him (e.g., Ustad Bismillah Khan claims artistic ancestry). AKBAR'S NAVRATNAS — full list: (1) Birbal — wit/advisor. (2) Tansen — musician. (3) Abul Fazl — biographer (Akbarnama, Ain-i-Akbari). (4) Faizi — Persian poet, Abul Fazl's brother. (5) Todar Mal — revenue minister (Zabt system). (6) Raja Man Singh I — military general (Amber). (7) Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan — poet, military leader, son of Bairam Khan. (8) Mulla Do-Piyaza — court humorist. (9) Hakim Humam — physician. PYQ FREQUENCY: Navratnas appear in SSC CGL, UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.
