cards.front:
Who among Akbar's Navratnas wrote the AKBARNAMA and AIN-I-AKBARI?

(A) Abul Fazl ibn Mubarak
(B) Tansen, the famous singer
(C) Birbal, of witty court fame
(D) Raja Man Singh, the warrior
cards.back:
(A) Abul Fazl ibn Mubarak

Mughal Empire — ABUL FAZL ibn MUBARAK (1551-1602) — Akbar's chief biographer, vizier, and one of the Navratnas. WORKS: (1) AKBARNAMA — three-volume official chronicle of Akbar's reign in PERSIAN; the first two volumes cover history; the THIRD volume is the famous AIN-I-AKBARI ('Institutes of Akbar'). (2) AIN-I-AKBARI — comprehensive administrative report of Akbar's empire — including detailed accounts of revenue, military, court life, geography, weights/measures, statistics. Considered the gazetteer of Mughal India. ABUL FAZL'S BACKGROUND: father Sheikh Mubarak was a learned scholar; brother FAIZI was court poet. Abul Fazl was a champion of DIN-I-ILAHI (Akbar's syncretic religion, 1582) and tolerance — drew strong opposition from orthodox ulema. DEATH: assassinated at age 51 (1602) by VIR SINGH BUNDELA on the orders of PRINCE SALIM (Jahangir) — who resented Abul Fazl's influence over Akbar. KEY VALUE for HISTORIANS: Akbarnama remains one of the MOST DETAILED primary sources for Mughal history. Photographs of original manuscript pages (with Abul Fazl's elegant Persian) are in libraries worldwide. PYQ FREQUENCY: Akbarnama-Abul-Fazl link is a top UPSC, SSC CGL, NCERT staple.

cards.front:
RAJA TODAR MAL is famous for which administrative achievement under Akbar?

(A) Land revenue 'Zabt' system reform
(B) Constructing forts across the empire
(C) Translating Sanskrit texts to Persian
(D) Leading military campaign in Bengal
cards.back:
(A) Land revenue 'Zabt' system reform

Mughal Empire — RAJA TODAR MAL (1500-1589) — Akbar's REVENUE MINISTER (Diwan-i-Ashraf). Reformed the Mughal land revenue system, creating what's called the ZABT or DAHSALA system (1580). KEY PRINCIPLES: (1) MEASUREMENT of all cultivable land using a uniform unit (BIGHA). (2) CLASSIFICATION of land by FERTILITY: Polaj (annually cultivated), Parauti (rested), Chachar (fallow 3-4 yrs), Banjar (uncultivable for 5+ yrs). (3) FIXED TAX RATES based on AVERAGE PRICES of crops over previous TEN YEARS — hence DAH-SALA (Persian for 'ten years'). (4) Tax = ~ONE-THIRD of produce, payable in cash or kind. (5) Created the office of QANUNGO (record-keeper). KEY CONTRIBUTION: brought stability, predictability, and reduced peasant exploitation. Land records became extensive. PRECURSORS: SHER SHAH SURI's earlier reforms (1540s) were the foundation; Todar Mal extended and codified them. KEY TEXT: TODAR MAL also coordinated the translation of the MAHABHARATA into Persian (RAZMNAMA project). LATER: Todar Mal was elevated as Wazir; administered Bengal post-conquest. NOTABLE: a learned man fluent in Persian, Sanskrit, mathematics. PYQ FREQUENCY: Todar Mal-revenue link is a top SSC CGL, UPSC, MPSC fact — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
BIRBAL's original name was Mahesh Das. He served Akbar as a:

(A) Witty advisor and courtier
(B) Land revenue chief minister
(C) Senior military commander
(D) Persian translator scholar
cards.back:
(A) Witty advisor and courtier

Mughal Empire — BIRBAL (Mahesh Das, ~1528-1586) — RAJA Birbal — served as a WITTY ADVISOR and confidant of Akbar; held the title 'Raja' and the rank of military commander too. ORIGIN: born to a poor Brahmin family at Kanpur. Joined Akbar's court ~1556; rose due to wit, intelligence, and Persian-Hindi-Sanskrit fluency. ROLE: known for his SHARP REPARTEE, problem-solving wit, and ability to entertain the emperor — recorded in countless folk stories ('Akbar-Birbal' tales). RELIGIOUS POSITION: one of the few HINDUS to embrace DIN-I-ILAHI (Akbar's syncretic religion). DEATH: killed in 1586 in the YUSUFZAI Expedition (Afghanistan) — leading a Mughal force; ambushed and slaughtered with most of his troops. Akbar reportedly mourned for days. ACADEMIC CONSENSUS: Birbal's reputation as 'court jester' is largely FOLKLORE; in real history, he was a SERIOUS COMMANDER and political advisor, not merely a comedic figure. Many of the witty tales were composed long after his death. RECENT POPULAR CULTURE: numerous TV shows ('Akbar-Birbal'), films, comics. PYQ FREQUENCY: Birbal-Mahesh-Das identity test in SSC CGL, UPSC 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests beyond-folklore knowledge of Mughal courtiers.

(B) Tansen, the great musician

cards.back:
(A) Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan

Mughal Empire — ABDUL RAHIM KHAN-I-KHANAN (1556-1627) — son of BAIRAM KHAN (Akbar's regent). Despite being MUSLIM, he wrote prolific BRAJ BHASHA (Hindi dialect) DOHAS (couplets) — pen name 'RAHIM'. He's celebrated alongside KABIR, TULSIDAS, SURDAS as a major Bhakti-period poet. FAMOUS DOHAS: 'Rahiman dhaaga prem ka, mat todo chatkay; Toote se phir naa jude, jude gaanth padi jaay' (don't break the thread of love; once broken, even when rejoined, a knot remains). 'Rahiman paani rakhiye, bin paani sab soon; paani gaye na ubre, moti, manus, choon' (preserve water/honor; without it, pearl, person, lime are useless). MILITARY ROLE: Akbar's COMMANDER — led campaigns in Gujarat, conquered Sindh; later served Jahangir. Held title 'KHAN-I-KHANAN' (Khan of Khans). LANGUAGES: Persian, Arabic, Sanskrit, Turkish, Hindi, Braj. Translated BABURNAMA from Turkish to Persian. TOMB: built for himself in Delhi (now restored, near Humayun's tomb). LATER FATE: lost favor with Jahangir, died in poverty 1627. RAHIM is part of the Hindi school syllabus across India — students memorize his dohas. PYQ FREQUENCY: Rahim is a top UPSC, NCERT, MPSC fact — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
RAJA MAN SINGH I, one of Akbar's Navratnas, was the ruler of which kingdom?

(A) Amber (Amer/Jaipur in Rajasthan)
(B) Mewar of Maharana Pratap fame
(C) Marwar capital was Jodhpur
(D) Bundi-Kota Hadoti region area
cards.back:
(A) Amber (Amer/Jaipur in Rajasthan)

Mughal Empire — RAJA MAN SINGH I (1550-1614) — ruler of AMBER (Amer; modern-day Jaipur was founded later by his descendant Sawai Jai Singh II, 1727). KACHHWAHA RAJPUT clan. RELATIONSHIP TO AKBAR: nephew of Bharmal of Amber whose daughter Harkha Bai (Jodha Bai) married Akbar 1562 — so Man Singh became Akbar's grand-nephew by marriage. MILITARY CAREER: Mughal commander; led campaigns in Kabul, Bengal, Bihar, Orissa. KEY BATTLE — HALDIGHATI (1576): commanded Mughal forces against MAHARANA PRATAP of Mewar; tactical Mughal victory but Pratap escaped to continue resistance. ROLE: Mansabdar of 7000 (highest Hindu rank under Akbar); one of the FOUR PILLARS of empire (with Abul Fazl, Birbal, Todar Mal). RELIGIOUS: HINDU; Akbar's tolerance allowed top Hindu generals; built temples (Govind Dev temple in Vrindavan). DEATH: 1614 (Jahangir's reign). SUCCESSION: Amber kingdom continued; Sawai Jai Singh II (1693-1743) founded JAIPUR city (1727) with Vidyadhar Bhattacharya as architect. JAIPUR is the largest planned city of pre-modern India. CONTRAST — MEWAR (Udaipur) under Maharana Pratap RESISTED Mughals; Amber ALLIED with them — strategic disagreement among Rajputs. PYQ FREQUENCY: Man Singh-Amber link in SSC, UPSC.

cards.front:
FAIZI, one of Akbar's Navratnas, was famous as a:

(A) Persian-language court poet (poet laureate)
(B) Revenue and finance minister (option here)
(C) Builder of major Mughal forts (option here)
(D) Trader and silk-route merchant (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Persian-language court poet (poet laureate)

Mughal Empire — ABUL FAIZ FAIZI (1547-1595) — elder brother of ABUL FAZL; appointed Akbar's COURT POET (Malik-ush-Shu'ara, 1588). PERSIAN POETRY: composed ~101 books, famous for ELEGIES (marsiyas), ghazals, qasidas. Translated MAHABHARATA's BHISHMA PARVA from Sanskrit. Also translated LILAVATI (the famous Sanskrit math text by Bhaskaracharya) into Persian. NOTED WORKS: NAL-DAMAYANTI (Persian retelling of the Sanskrit love story); MARKAZ-I-ADWAR (rhetoric treatise). FAMILY BACKGROUND: father Sheikh Mubarak was a Sufi-influenced scholar; the family was hounded by orthodox ulema for liberal views. Faizi & Abul Fazl became core figures in Akbar's RELIGIOUS TOLERANCE policies. DEATH: 1595, age 48; broke Akbar's heart. AFTER FAIZI: Abul Fazl became Akbar's closest confidant. CONTRAST WITH OTHER POETS: Faizi was Persian poet; RAHIM was Braj Bhasha poet; both contemporaries. KEY EXAMPLE LINE: 'Be sure that your tongue does not utter that which your heart does not approve' (translated). HISTORICAL: Faizi's works survive in libraries (Bodleian, Tehran, Hyderabad). PYQ FREQUENCY: Faizi as poet/translator appears in UPSC History optional, NCERT-driven SSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
AKBAR became Mughal emperor at the age of:

(A) 10 years (very young) at coronation time
(B) 13 years (after Humayun's death in 1556)
(C) 15 years at the time of accession crown
(D) 18 years on coming of age formally crown
cards.back:
(B) 13 years (after Humayun's death in 1556)

Mughal Empire — AKBAR (1542-1605) — became emperor at AGE 13 in 1556, after father HUMAYUN's death (fell down library stairs). Coronation at KALANAUR (Punjab). BAIRAM KHAN was his regent for 4 years (1556-60); won SECOND BATTLE OF PANIPAT (1556) against Hemu (Hindu general of Adil Shah Suri) — re-established Mughal rule. Akbar took full charge of empire ~1560 (sent Bairam Khan to Mecca; later assassinated en route). Reigned 49 YEARS — one of longest in Indian history.
cards.option2: 15 years at the time of accession crown
cards.option3: 18 years on coming of age formally crown

cards.front:
Akbar's CAPITAL was MAINLY at:

(A) Delhi was his sole capital
(B) Agra (and briefly Fatehpur Sikri)
(C) Lahore was his only capital
(D) Kabul was the capital throughout
cards.back:
(B) Agra (and briefly Fatehpur Sikri)

Mughal Empire — Capital MOSTLY AGRA (built Agra Fort, 1565-73). FATEHPUR SIKRI (1571-85; ~14 years) — built to honour Sufi saint Sheikh Salim Chishti's blessing for a son (Salim, future Jahangir, born 1569). Beautiful Mughal-Rajput-Persian architecture: Buland Darwaza (entrance — tallest gateway in world, 54 m), Diwan-i-Khas (with central pillar — Akbar's throne), Panch Mahal, Salim Chishti's tomb, Jodha Bai's palace. Abandoned ~1585 (water shortage). LAHORE briefly capital 1585-1598 (during NW campaigns). Akbar died 1605 + buried at SIKANDRA (near Agra) in tomb he started + Jahangir completed.

cards.front:
Akbar's NINE GEMS (Navaratnas) included Birbal, Tansen, Abul Fazl, Faizi, Todar Mal + four others. Who was his FINANCE MINISTER?

(A) Birbal, the witty courtier-friend
(B) Raja Todar Mal, the revenue master
(C) Tansen, the legendary musician
(D) Abul Fazl, court historian-author
cards.back:
(B) Raja Todar Mal, the revenue master

Mughal Empire — RAJA TODAR MAL — Akbar's revenue minister (Diwan-i-Ashraf). Devised the ZABTI / DAHSALA system: land surveyed, classified by fertility, average revenue based on PAST 10 YEARS' yield → fixed assessment. Standardised TAX RATES + units (BIGHA). Made Persian the official record-keeping language. Died 1589. NAVARATNAS (9 Gems): (1) Abul Fazl (court historian — Akbarnama, Ain-i-Akbari); (2) Faizi (poet, Abul Fazl's brother); (3) Tansen (legendary musician, Gwalior); (4) Birbal (Mahesh Das — wit, advisor; killed 1586); (5) Raja Todar Mal (finance); (6) Raja Man Singh (general, Amber); (7) Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana (poet, Bairam Khan's son); (8) Fakir Aziao-Din (advisor); (9) Mullah Do Piaza (jokester).

cards.front:
Akbar's RELIGIOUS POLICY 'DIN-I-ILAHI' (Divine Faith) was:

(A) Sole worship of Allah, orthodox Islamic style
(B) Eclectic synthesis of Hindu, Islam, Christian ideas
(C) Conversion of Hindus to Islamic faith only
(D) Strict caste segregation system enforced strongly
cards.back:
(B) Eclectic synthesis of Hindu, Islam, Christian ideas

Mughal Empire — DIN-I-ILAHI (1582) — Akbar's syncretic religious experiment. Drew from Islam, Hinduism, Christianity, Zoroastrianism, Jainism. Emphasised: monotheism, ethical conduct, tolerance, reason. Few followers (~19; mostly courtiers) — never large movement. Ended with Akbar's death. SHOWCASED Akbar's tolerance: ABOLISHED JIZYA (poll-tax on non-Muslims, 1564); abolished pilgrimage tax (1563); allowed remarriage of widows; banned Sati (advised); MARRIED Rajput princess (Jodha Bai, mother of Jahangir); IBADAT KHANA (House of Worship, Fatehpur Sikri) — religious dialogue with all faiths. Issued MAHZAR-NAMA (1579) — declared Akbar arbiter on religious questions. (PYQ-favourite topic.)

cards.front:
Akbar's MANSABDARI system was:

(A) A taxation system on agricultural produce
(B) Ranking of nobles + officers (zat + sawar)
(C) A judicial system based on sharia
(D) An espionage and intelligence network
cards.back:
(B) Ranking of nobles + officers (zat + sawar)

Mughal Empire — MANSABDARI = Akbar's nobility + military rank system. MANSAB ('rank'). Each MANSABDAR had: (1) ZAT — personal rank, status + salary; (2) SAWAR — number of cavalry he must maintain. Ranks ranged 10 to 5000 (princes higher). Salary = JAGIR (assigned land revenue) or cash (from treasury). Built unified administrative + military hierarchy across diverse nobles (Turkish, Persian, Afghan, Indian Muslim, Rajput, etc.). Reduced fragmentation of medieval Iqta system. Continued under successors with modifications.

cards.front:
Major MILITARY conquests of Akbar included all EXCEPT:

(A) Gujarat (1572) and Bengal (1576)
(B) Conquest of all of South India + Ceylon
(C) Rajputana states (mostly via alliance)
(D) Sind (1591), Kashmir (1586), Kandahar (1595)
cards.back:
(B) Conquest of all of South India + Ceylon

Mughal Empire — Akbar's empire stretched from Kabul to Bengal, Kashmir to North Deccan — but NOT South India / Ceylon. South Deccan still under Vijayanagara remnants + Bahmani sultanate offshoots (Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golkonda, Berar) — these were partly absorbed by his successors (Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb). RAJPUTS — most submitted via alliance (matrimonial — Akbar married Jodha Bai of Amber); MEWAR alone resisted (Maharana Pratap — Battle of HALDIGHATI 1576, indecisive; Pratap retreated). MAJOR CONQUESTS: Malwa (1561), Gondwana (1564 — defeated Rani Durgavati), Chittor (1568), Ranthambore (1569), GUJARAT (1572), BENGAL (1576), KABUL (1581 from half-brother), Kashmir (1586), Sind (1591), Berar (1596), KANDAHAR (1595).

cards.front:
ABUL FAZL, Akbar's court historian, wrote:

(A) Babur-nama (memoirs of Babur)
(B) Akbarnama + Ain-i-Akbari
(C) Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (Jahangir's auto)
(D) Padshahnama (Shah Jahan's chronicle)
cards.back:
(B) Akbarnama + Ain-i-Akbari

Mughal Empire — ABUL FAZL — court historian, Akbar's confidant. Wrote: AKBARNAMA (3 vol; biography + history of Akbar's reign in Persian); AIN-I-AKBARI (vol 3 of Akbarnama; treatise on Akbar's administration, statistics, court customs, social life — invaluable historical source). Killed 1602 by Vir Singh Bundela (instigated by prince Salim/Jahangir, who saw Abul Fazl as obstacle). Distractor 1 = BABURNAMA by Babur himself (in Chagatai Turkish; auto-biography). Distractor 3 = JAHANGIRNAMA by Jahangir himself. Distractor 4 = PADSHAHNAMA by Abdul Hamid Lahori (under Shah Jahan).

cards.front:
Akbar's policy of 'SULH-I-KUL' is best translated as:

(A) Strict enforcement of Islamic religious orthodoxy
(B) Universal peace and tolerance of all religions
(C) Ban on all non-Persian languages used at court
(D) Heavy taxes on Hindu landholders to fund armies
cards.back:
(B) Universal peace and tolerance of all religions

Mughal Empire — SULH-I-KUL — Persian / Sufi-influenced phrase meaning 'absolute peace' or 'peace with all'. Akbar's foundational policy of religious tolerance: no one should be persecuted for faith; merit, not religion, decided imperial advancement. Practical expressions: abolition of pilgrim tax (1563), abolition of jizya on non-Muslims (1564), Rajput marriages (Mariam-uz-Zamani), Hindu generals (Raja Man Singh, Raja Todar Mal, Bhagwan Das). Counterpoint: Aurangzeb reversed many of these (re-imposed jizya 1679).

cards.front:
Akbar built the IBADAT KHANA at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 specifically as:

(A) A military headquarters for his Rajput cavalry units
(B) A hall for inter-religious philosophical debates and dialogue
(C) A public bathhouse with hot and cold water arrangements
(D) A burial chamber for the early imperial Mughal ancestors
cards.back:
(B) A hall for inter-religious philosophical debates and dialogue

Mughal Empire — Ibadat Khana ('House of Worship') — built 1575 inside Fatehpur Sikri. Initially for Sunni Muslim ulema; from 1578 opened to Shias, Sufis, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians (Parsis), Christian Jesuits (Aquaviva, Monserrate from Goa). Many notable theological debates held here. Akbar grew sceptical of orthodoxy, leading to his promulgation of DIN-I-ILAHI (1582), a syncretic ethical movement combining elements of multiple faiths — small following (~19 disciples), did not survive his death. Distractor 4 — Mughal tombs are separate (e.g., Humayun's tomb at Delhi, Akbar's own at Sikandra).

cards.option2: A public bathhouse with hot and cold water arrangements
cards.option3: A burial chamber for the early imperial Mughal ancestors

cards.front:
Akbar abolished the JIZYA tax — a tax historically levied on non-Muslims under Islamic rule — in:

(A) 1556, the year of his accession after Humayun's death
(B) 1564, eight years into his independent reign
(C) 1582, with the founding of the Din-i-Ilahi religion
(D) 1605, just before his death in October that year
cards.back:
(B) 1564, eight years into his independent reign

Mughal Empire — Akbar abolished the JIZYA in 1564 — eight years into his reign (became king 1556 at age 13; Bairam Khan's regency ended 1560). Earlier in 1563 he had abolished pilgrim tax on Hindus. These were politically symbolic moves to win Hindu support — particularly Rajputs whose cooperation was vital for empire. Aurangzeb RE-IMPOSED jizya in 1679 (alienating Rajputs and contributing to imperial decline). Distractor 1 — Akbar was a child then, regents ran the empire. Distractor 3 — Din-i-Ilahi was 1582. Distractor 4 — too late.

cards.option2: 1582, with the founding of the Din-i-Ilahi religion
cards.option3: 1605, just before his death in October that year

cards.front:
The MANSABDARI system, introduced by Akbar, was primarily a:

(A) System of land grants given outright to Hindu peasants
(B) Ranking system for nobles linking civil and military service
(C) Religious order encouraging mixed-faith Sufi devotion
(D) Trade guild that controlled all the spice trade routes
cards.back:
(B) Ranking system for nobles linking civil and military service

Mughal Empire — MANSABDARI — Persian 'mansab' (rank). Each noble (mansabdar) held a numerical rank, with two parts: ZAT (personal status / pay grade) and SAWAR (number of cavalry he must maintain for state service). Highest ranks (~5000+ zat) held by Mughal princes. Salaries paid in cash or as JAGIR (revenue assignment from a tract of land). System brought all civil + military officers into a single hierarchy, weakening hereditary tribal aristocracy. Continued and refined by successors. Distractor 1 = jagir / inam systems (different). Distractor 3 = sufi orders. Distractor 4 = guilds / European company analogy.
cards.option1: System of land grants given outright to Hindu peasants
cards.option2: Religious order encouraging mixed-faith Sufi devotion
cards.option3: Trade guild that controlled all the spice trade routes
cards.storedExplanation: MANSABDARI — Persian 'mansab' (rank). Each noble (mansabdar) held a numerical rank, with two parts: ZAT (personal status / pay grade) and SAWAR (number of cavalry he must maintain for state service). Highest ranks (~5000+ zat) held by Mughal princes. Salaries paid in cash or as JAGIR (revenue assignment from a tract of land). System brought all civil + military officers into a single hierarchy, weakening hereditary tribal aristocracy. Continued and refined by successors. Distractor 1 = jagir / inam systems (different). Distractor 3 = sufi orders. Distractor 4 = guilds / European company analogy.

cards.front:
Akbar's revenue system, refined under his finance minister, settled land tax based on:

(A) A simple flat-rate tax irrespective of crop or year
(B) Detailed survey of land + 10-year average yield (Dahsala)
(C) A share of village livestock paid to the local zamindar
(D) A poll tax based on the number of male family members
cards.back:
(B) Detailed survey of land + 10-year average yield (Dahsala)

Mughal Empire — DAHSALA SYSTEM (also called the ZABTI system) — designed by RAJA TODAR MAL (Akbar's revenue minister, originally served Sher Shah Suri). 1580s. STEPS — measure land (bigha), classify by quality (polaj — annual; parauti — fallow then back; chachar — fallow 3-4 yrs; banjar — barren), record 10-year average yield + price for each crop, fix demand at one-third of average produce, payable in cash. Replaced earlier ad-hoc collections. Continued under later Mughals. Distractor 1 — too crude. Distractor 3 — separate, livestock-based. Distractor 4 = jizya structure, not land revenue.
cards.option1: A simple flat-rate tax irrespective of crop or year
cards.option2: A share of village livestock paid to the local zamindar
cards.option3: A poll tax based on the number of male family members

cards.front:
The famous 'NINE GEMS' (Navaratnas) of Akbar's court included Abul Fazl, Birbal, Tansen, Todar Mal, Faizi, Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana, Mulla Do Piaza, Hakim Humam, and one more. Who was the ninth gem?

(A) Tulsidas, the Hindi poet of Ramcharitmanas fame
(B) Raja Man Singh, Akbar's Rajput general and Amber ruler
(C) Mirza Ghalib, the celebrated 19th-century Urdu poet
(D) Bairam Khan, the regent during Akbar's early years
cards.back:
(B) Raja Man Singh, Akbar's Rajput general and Amber ruler

Mughal Empire — Akbar's NAVARATNAS (Nine Gems): (1) ABUL FAZL — chronicler, author of Akbarnama + Ain-i-Akbari (assassinated 1602 by Bir Singh Bundela on Salim's orders); (2) FAIZI — poet, Abul Fazl's elder brother; (3) BIRBAL — court wit + counsellor (died 1586 in Yusufzai campaign); (4) TANSEN — court musician (originally Mian Tansen, from Gwalior, dhrupad master); (5) RAJA TODAR MAL — finance minister; (6) RAJA MAN SINGH — Rajput general (Amber); (7) ABDUR RAHIM KHAN-I-KHANA — poet, Bairam Khan's son; (8) FAQIR AZIAO-DIN; (9) MULLA DO PIAZA. Distractor 1 — Tulsidas was Akbar's contemporary but not in his court. Distractor 3 — much later (1797-1869). Distractor 4 — Bairam Khan was the regent (died 1561), not in the navaratnas.

cards.front:
Akbar's syncretic order DIN-I-ILAHI (1582) — sometimes called Tauhid-i-Ilahi — drew elements from many religions but was based ESSENTIALLY on:

(A) Strict orthodox Sunni Islam alone, with no other influences
(B) An ethical code emphasising piety, prudence, abstinence, sun-veneration
(C) The Bhakti devotional movement of medieval north India alone
(D) Christian doctrine introduced by Jesuit missionaries from Goa
cards.back:
(B) An ethical code emphasising piety, prudence, abstinence, sun-veneration

Mughal Empire — DIN-I-ILAHI ('Religion of God') / TAUHID-I-ILAHI ('Divine monotheism') — promulgated 1582. Drew from: Islam (especially Sufi monism), Hindu Vedanta + Bhakti, Zoroastrianism (sun + fire reverence), Jainism (vegetarianism, ahimsa), Christianity (love + reason). EMPHASES: piety, prudence, kindness, abstinence from meat / alcohol, abstinence from sensual indulgences, sun + fire veneration. NOT a mass religion — strictly elite court initiation; ~19 known disciples (incl. Birbal). Faded with Akbar's death (1605). Akbar himself viewed it as 'spiritual leadership of the empire' rather than displacement of existing faiths.

cards.option2: The Bhakti devotional movement of medieval north India alone
cards.option3: Christian doctrine introduced by Jesuit missionaries from Goa

cards.front:
AURANGZEB SPENT THE LAST 26 YEARS of his reign primarily campaigning in:

(A) Deccan (against Marathas + Bijapur)
(B) Bengal (against local rulers)
(C) Punjab (against Sikhs entirely)
(D) Northwest (against Persia only)
cards.back:
(A) Deccan (against Marathas + Bijapur)

Mughal Empire — AURANGZEB (r. 1658-1707) — last great Mughal emperor. The LAST 26 YEARS (1681-1707) were spent in the DECCAN, attempting to crush MARATHAS, conquer BIJAPUR & GOLCONDA. KEY CAMPAIGNS: (1) BIJAPUR — annexed 1686 (Adil Shahi dynasty extinguished). (2) GOLCONDA — annexed 1687 (Qutb Shahi dynasty extinguished); Aurangzeb captured the famous KOH-I-NOOR diamond and DECCAN GOLD here. (3) MARATHAS — eternal nemesis. Captured Sambhaji (Shivaji's son, 1689) and TORTURED him to death; but Maratha resistance only intensified under Rajaram, then Shahu. AURANGZEB DIED in 1707 in AHMADNAGAR, Deccan, age 88; never returned to Delhi. WHY DECCAN OBSESSION: (1) Religious — Sunni vs Shia (Bijapur, Golconda were Shia). (2) Strategic — Maratha raiders disrupted Mughal heartland. (3) Wealth — Deccan gold/diamonds. CONSEQUENCES: (1) MILITARY OVEREXTENSION — empire stretched thin. (2) HUGE FINANCIAL DRAIN — daily ~Rs 4 lakh on military. (3) PEASANT REVOLTS in north India (Sikhs, Jats, Satnamis). (4) MARATHAS NOT crushed — they regrouped post-1707, eventually became dominant power until 1818. AFTERMATH: 'AFTER AURANGZEB, THE DELUGE' — empire fragmented under weak successors; Mughal supremacy ended within 30 years. PYQ FREQUENCY: Aurangzeb-Deccan in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
AURANGZEB re-imposed JIZYA tax on which group in 1679?

(A) Non-Muslims (Hindus, others)
(B) Muslim peasants (Sunnis)
(C) Foreigners (European traders)
(D) Maratha soldiers (military)
cards.back:
(A) Non-Muslims (Hindus, others)

Mughal Empire — JIZYA — TAX on NON-MUSLIMS in Islamic states (in lieu of zakat which Muslims pay). Established in earlier Islamic kingdoms; ABOLISHED by AKBAR (1564). RE-IMPOSED by AURANGZEB on 2 APRIL 1679 — major break from Akbar's tolerant policy. RATES: rich paid 48 dirhams; middle class 24; poor 12. Brahmins, women, children, monks, disabled were exempt. WHY: Aurangzeb's ORTHODOX SUNNI ISLAMIC outlook + financial need (ongoing Deccan campaigns drained treasury). RESPONSE: PROTESTS — sit-ins by Hindu merchants in Delhi; widespread anger. RAJPUTS who had been Mughal allies (since Akbar's marriages) FELT BETRAYED — Mewar, Marwar (Jodhpur) rebellions. MARATHA ANGER fueled their revolt. SHIVAJI's son SAMBHAJI HARSHLY criticized Jizya. SIKHS — Guru Tegh Bahadur (9th Sikh Guru) was EXECUTED 1675 for protecting Kashmiri Pandits forced to convert; this preceded jizya but reflected same trend. ABOLITION: jizya was finally abolished by JAHANDAR SHAH (1712, briefly) and permanently by FARRUKHSIYAR (1717). AKBAR's POLICY: in Akbar's view, RULE OF LAW (suluh-i-kul, peace with all) ensured peasant cooperation, military strength via Rajput allies, prosperity. AURANGZEB reversed this — narrow religious base. RESULT: MUGHAL EMPIRE WEAKENED. PYQ FREQUENCY: jizya re-imposition in UPSC History optional, NCERT Class 12, MPSC.

cards.front:
Which Sikh Guru was executed by Aurangzeb in 1675 in Delhi?

(A) Guru Tegh Bahadur (the 9th Guru)
(B) Guru Arjan Dev (executed by Jahangir, 1606)
(C) Guru Gobind Singh (10th, died 1708)
(D) Guru Nanak Dev (the 1st Guru)
cards.back:
(A) Guru Tegh Bahadur (the 9th Guru)

Mughal Empire — GURU TEGH BAHADUR (1621-1675) — the 9TH SIKH GURU. Executed by Aurangzeb in DELHI on 24 NOVEMBER 1675 at GURUDWARA SIS GANJ SAHIB (built later at the execution site, near Chandni Chowk). REASON: Hindu BRAHMINS of Kashmir came to Guru Tegh Bahadur seeking protection from forced conversion to Islam under Mughal pressure. The Guru went to Delhi to confront Aurangzeb; refused to convert; was beheaded. Title: 'HIND DI CHADAR' (Shield of India / Protector of Hindus). HIS SON GURU GOBIND SINGH became the 10th Guru and TRANSFORMED Sikhism — created the KHALSA on Vaisakhi 1699 (Anandpur Sahib), establishing the warrior-saint tradition; died 1708 at Nanded. SIKH GURUS sequence: (1) Nanak (founder, 1469-1539). (2) Angad (1539-52). (3) Amar Das (1552-74). (4) Ram Das (1574-81). (5) Arjan (1581-1606, compiled Adi Granth, executed by Jahangir). (6) Hargobind (1606-44, militarized). (7) Har Rai (1644-61). (8) Har Krishan (1661-64, child Guru). (9) TEGH BAHADUR (1664-75, executed by Aurangzeb). (10) Gobind Singh (1675-1708, founded Khalsa). After Guru Gobind Singh, the GURU GRANTH SAHIB (sacred scripture) became the eternal Guru. PYQ FREQUENCY: Sikh Gurus, Mughal-Sikh conflict in UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Aurangzeb defeated and EXECUTED Shivaji's son SAMBHAJI in:

(A) 1689 (after capture at Sangameshwar)
(B) 1680 (Shivaji's death year)
(C) 1707 (Aurangzeb's death year)
(D) 1761 (Battle of Panipat)
cards.back:
(A) 1689 (after capture at Sangameshwar)

Mughal Empire — SAMBHAJI MAHARAJ (1657-1689) — Chhatrapati of the Maratha Empire after Shivaji's death (1680). Captured by Mughal forces under MUQARRAB KHAN at SANGAMESHWAR (Maharashtra) on 1 February 1689 — betrayed by his brother-in-law GANOJI SHIRKE who informed Mughals of his location. TORTURE + EXECUTION: Aurangzeb ordered his eyes plucked out, tongue cut, then beheading on 11 March 1689 at TULAPUR (near Pune). REASON CITED: refused to convert to Islam, accept Mughal subsidiary status. LEGACY: Maratha resistance INTENSIFIED, not weakened. His brother RAJARAM took over (1689-1700); then his widow TARABAI (regent for son Shivaji II, 1700-1707); then Shahu (Sambhaji's son, who was Mughal hostage and released after Aurangzeb's death) — under Shahu, Marathas became the dominant Indian power until 1818. SAMBHAJI's SHRINE — at Tulapur, near Pune; visited by lakhs of Marathi devotees. SAMBHAJI's COURT INCLUDED: KAVI BHUSHAN — Hindi poet who composed verses praising Sambhaji's bravery. Sambhaji was an ACCOMPLISHED SANSKRIT SCHOLAR — wrote 'BUDH BHUSHANAM' (Sanskrit treatise on rajaniti). AURANGZEB and SAMBHAJI battles: 1681-89 — multiple skirmishes; Aurangzeb committed enormous resources but Marathas evaded full defeat. PYQ FREQUENCY: Sambhaji-Aurangzeb in UPSC, MPSC, SSC modern history 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Aurangzeb's annexation of GOLCONDA in 1687 brought him control over which famous diamond mines?

(A) Golconda mines (Kollur, Andhra)
(B) Bidar (different mineral wealth)
(C) Bijapur (gold not diamonds)
(D) Surat (a port city only)
cards.back:
(A) Golconda mines (Kollur, Andhra)

Mughal Empire — GOLCONDA — capital of QUTB SHAHI dynasty (founded 1518); ruled Telangana region of southern India for nearly 170 years. MAJOR DIAMOND MINES: KOLLUR, PARITALA in present-day Andhra Pradesh — produced INDIA's most famous diamonds throughout history. WORLD-FAMOUS DIAMONDS from Golconda mines: (1) KOH-I-NOOR — 'Mountain of Light'; original ~793 carats, recut to 105 carats; through Mughals → Nadir Shah (1739) → Ahmad Shah Abdali → Maharaja Ranjit Singh → British (1849). Now in Queen Mother's crown (UK). (2) HOPE DIAMOND — blue 45.5-carat diamond; cursed legend; now in Smithsonian (USA). (3) DARYA-I-NOOR — pink ~182 carats; in Iranian crown jewels. (4) ORLOFF DIAMOND — 189.6 carats; in Russian Imperial Sceptre. (5) REGENT DIAMOND — 140.6 carats; now in Louvre. (6) NIZAM DIAMOND — owned by Nizams of Hyderabad. (7) JACOB DIAMOND — 184.5 carats. KEY: until ~1730 (when Brazilian + later South African mines opened), Golconda was the WORLD'S ONLY KNOWN SOURCE of diamonds. AURANGZEB'S CAMPAIGN: 1687 siege of Golconda Fort (8 months); ABUL HASAN QUTB SHAH (last Qutb Shahi sultan) was imprisoned in Daulatabad. Golconda's wealth funded Mughal coffers briefly. HYDERABAD founded by Quli Qutb Shah (1591). PYQ FREQUENCY: Golconda-diamond link in SSC, UPSC.

cards.front:
Aurangzeb's royal title (regnal name) was:

(A) Alamgir ('World Conqueror')
(B) Akbar ('The Great' before him)
(C) Jahangir ('World Seizer' before)
(D) Shah Jahan ('King of World')
cards.back:
(A) Alamgir ('World Conqueror')

Mughal Empire — AURANGZEB took the regnal title ALAMGIR — Persian for 'WORLD CONQUEROR' (or 'Conqueror of the Universe'). His full regnal name was MUHI-UD-DIN MUHAMMAD AURANGZEB ALAMGIR PADSHAH GHAZI. KEY TITLES of MUGHAL EMPERORS: (1) BABUR — adopted regnal name BABUR ('the tiger'), simple. (2) HUMAYUN — 'fortunate'. (3) AKBAR — 'great' (by his own designation). (4) JAHANGIR — 'world-seizer' (originally Salim, named after Sheikh Salim Chishti). (5) SHAH JAHAN — 'king of the world' (originally Khurram, after his father). (6) AURANGZEB — 'ALAMGIR' = world conqueror. (7) BAHADUR SHAH — 'brave king'. (8) FARRUKHSIYAR — 'auspicious figure'. (9) MUHAMMAD SHAH — 'praiseworthy king'. (10) BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR — last Mughal, executed/exiled to Burma 1858. AURANGZEB's wars EARNED him 'Alamgir' title — but he never quite conquered the world; Mughals never extended beyond India in his time. The IRONY: 'World Conqueror' title at the very moment Mughal empire began OVEREXTENDING and DECLINING. AURANGZEB IN HISTORICAL DEBATE: most controversial Mughal — destroyed temples (Kashi Vishwanath at Varanasi, Krishna Janmabhoomi at Mathura, Somnath); BUT also pragmatic, generous to many Hindu officials; Marathas had Hindu officers in his army. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'Alamgir' title in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1× per cycle.

Aurangzeb's grave is located in which city?

(A) Khuldabad (near Aurangabad, Maharashtra)
(B) Agra (near Taj Mahal complex) (option here)
(C) Delhi (Red Fort vicinity) (option here)
(D) Lahore (Pakistan currently) (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Khuldabad (near Aurangabad, Maharashtra)

Mughal Empire — AURANGZEB'S TOMB — located in KHULDABAD (also spelled Khuldābād, formerly Rauza), near the city of AURANGABAD (now SAMBHAJINAGAR after 2022 renaming) in MAHARASHTRA. SIMPLE GRAVE: as per his wishes — small, open-air, made of LIMESTONE; covered with white-marble jali (lattice screen) added later. PHILOSOPHY: Aurangzeb was a DEVOUT MUSLIM in his later years, lived austerely (sewed caps, copied Quran for income — refused royal stipend); his grave reflects this simplicity. CONTRAST with ELABORATE TOMBS: (a) HUMAYUN'S TOMB — Delhi (precursor to Taj). (b) AKBAR'S TOMB — Sikandra, near Agra (mix of styles). (c) JAHANGIR'S TOMB — Shahdara, Lahore (Pakistan). (d) SHAH JAHAN'S TOMB — Taj Mahal, Agra (next to Mumtaz). (e) AURANGZEB's — minimalist, Khuldabad. WHY KHULDABAD: he died in AHMADNAGAR (3 March 1707, age 88) during Deccan campaigns; never returned to north. Khuldabad is a historical Sufi center — site of revered Sufi saints' tombs (e.g., Zar Zari Zar Baksh). NEAR ATTRACTIONS: ELLORA + AJANTA caves (UNESCO Heritage), Daulatabad fort, Bibi-ka-Maqbara (Aurangzeb's son Azam Shah built it — 'mini Taj Mahal' in Aurangabad, 1660-1661). RECENT (2022): Aurangabad city renamed CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR by Maharashtra govt — political move honoring Sambhaji. PYQ FREQUENCY: Aurangzeb tomb location in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1× per 2 cycles.

cards.front:
AURANGZEB (r. 1658-1707) reached the Mughal throne by:

(A) Peaceful succession after father's death
(B) War of succession; killed brothers + jailed Shah Jahan
(C) Election by the Mughal nobles council here
(D) British East India Company support here
cards.back:
(B) War of succession; killed brothers + jailed Shah Jahan

Mughal Empire — WAR OF SUCCESSION (1657-58) — when Shah Jahan fell ill, his 4 sons (DARA SHIKOH eldest, the heir; SHAH SHUJA; AURANGZEB; MURAD BAKSH) fought. Aurangzeb defeated his brothers in battles of DHARMAT (1658), SAMUGARH (1658), KHAJWA (1659). Killed brothers progressively (Dara executed 1659, Shah Shuja fled + disappeared in Arakan, Murad killed 1661). IMPRISONED Shah Jahan in AGRA FORT (1658-1666); Shah Jahan died there. Crowned at Delhi 1658. INSIGHT — Mughal succession had no fixed primogeniture; 'taqht ya takhta' (throne or coffin). Each major succession was bloody. Aurangzeb's reign — longest of any Mughal (49 years) but seeds of decline planted by his own policies.
cards.option2: Election by the Mughal nobles council here
cards.option3: British East India Company support here

cards.front:
Aurangzeb RE-IMPOSED which tax (abolished by Akbar) on non-Muslims?

(A) Land revenue (basic farm tax)
(B) Jizya (tax on non-Muslims)
(C) Octroi (entry tax in cities)
(D) Salt tax (later by British)
cards.back:
(B) Jizya (tax on non-Muslims)

Mughal Empire — JIZYA — Islamic tax on non-Muslim subjects (in lieu of military service + protection). ABOLISHED by AKBAR in 1564 — sign of his religious tolerance + pluralism. RE-IMPOSED by AURANGZEB in 1679 — alienated Hindu subjects, esp. Rajputs (who had been Mughal allies under Akbar). Triggered Rajput rebellions (Marwar, Mewar). INSIGHT — Aurangzeb is a controversial figure: ORTHODOX ISLAMIC (in contrast to Akbar's pluralism); banned music + paintings at court; demolished some Hindu temples (Vishwanath at Kashi, Keshava Rai at Mathura); imposed sharia. Defenders argue many policies were political (selective application). Re-imposed jizya removed by Bahadur Shah I after his death.

cards.front:
Aurangzeb's main southern adversary, the Maratha leader, was:

(A) Tipu Sultan (much later, in Mysore)
(B) Shivaji and his successors (Sambhaji, Rajaram)
(C) Krishnadeva Raya (long dead by then)
(D) Hyder Ali (later Mysore, 18th c) here
cards.back:
(B) Shivaji and his successors (Sambhaji, Rajaram)

Mughal Empire — MARATHAS — biggest thorn in Aurangzeb's side. SHIVAJI (1630-80) — founded MARATHA EMPIRE; CROWNED CHHATRAPATI 1674 at Raigad. Famous escape from Aurangzeb's Agra (1666 — hidden in fruit baskets). His son SAMBHAJI captured + executed by Aurangzeb (1689) — but Marathas continued under younger son RAJARAM + then Tarabai. Aurangzeb spent his last 25 YEARS (1681-1707) in Deccan, fighting Marathas + Bijapur + Golkonda — depleted treasury, neglected north India → administrative decay. Died at AURANGABAD (1707), buried at KHULDABAD in modest tomb. His Deccan campaign considered a 'WAR OF ATTRITION' that broke the Mughal Empire.

cards.front:
Aurangzeb's MUGHAL EMPIRE reached its GREATEST geographical EXTENT after he annexed:

(A) Kashmir + Afghanistan only here also too
(B) Bijapur (1686) + Golkonda (1687) — Deccan sultanates
(C) Bengal + Burma (eastern part) here also
(D) Sri Lanka + Maldives islands here also
cards.back:
(B) Bijapur (1686) + Golkonda (1687) — Deccan sultanates

Mughal Empire — Aurangzeb annexed BIJAPUR (1686 — defeated Adil Shahi) + GOLKONDA (1687 — defeated Qutb Shahi; Hyderabad area, famous for diamond mines including Kohinoor). Maximum geographical extent of Mughal Empire achieved! From Kabul to Bengal (E-W) + Kashmir to Tamil Nadu's outskirts (N-S) — ~4 million sq km. POPULATION ~150 million (a quarter of world's then). PARADOX: largest empire BUT also weakest financially (constant warfare drained treasury). Started declining BEFORE his death. Successors (BAHADUR SHAH I 1707, JAHANDAR SHAH, FARRUKHSIYAR, MUHAMMAD SHAH) — all weak. By 1748 (Mughal-Persian Battle of Karnal 1739, Nadir Shah looted Delhi, took PEACOCK THRONE + KOHINOOR), Mughal rule was nominal. By 1857, ended with Bahadur Shah Zafar's exile.

cards.front:
Aurangzeb is sometimes called by which title due to his orthodox Islamic stance?

(A) Akbar the Great (his great-grandfather)
(B) Alamgir ('World Conqueror')
(C) Vikramaditya (a Hindu emperor title)
(D) Shahenshah-i-Hind (term for any emperor)
cards.back:
(B) Alamgir ('World Conqueror')

Mughal Empire — ALAMGIR (Persian: 'world-conqueror' or 'world-seizer'). Title taken by Aurangzeb on accession 1658. REFLECTS his ambition + image-projection. Also called: Aurangzeb-i-Alamgir; lived a simple life despite vast empire (sewed caps, copied Quran, ate plain food, no music in court). Earned title 'ZINDA PIR' (living saint) from some, 'destroyer of temples' from others. INSIGHT — Mughal emperors took grand titles: Babur, Humayun, AKBAR ('the Great'), JAHANGIR ('world-seizer'), SHAH JAHAN ('king of the world'), Aurangzeb's ALAMGIR. After his death, successors were too weak for grand titles.

cards.front:
Aurangzeb's MOST CONTROVERSIAL act vis-à-vis Sikhs was:

(A) Inviting them to court diplomatically
(B) Executing Guru Tegh Bahadur (9th Sikh Guru, 1675)
(C) Granting them autonomous status here
(D) Building a temple for the Sikhs here
cards.back:
(B) Executing Guru Tegh Bahadur (9th Sikh Guru, 1675)

Mughal Empire — GURU TEGH BAHADUR (9th Sikh Guru, 1621-75) — refused to convert to Islam + protested Aurangzeb's persecution of Kashmiri Pandits + Hindus. ARRESTED, brought to Delhi, EXECUTED (beheaded) in 1675 at CHANDNI CHOWK (today's GURUDWARA SIS GANJ marks the spot). Title 'HIND-DI-CHADDAR' ('Shield of India') for sacrificing for another faith's freedom. His son GOBIND SINGH (10th + last living Guru) became Guru, founded the KHALSA (1699 at Anandpur Sahib, Punjab — gave Sikhs the 5 Ks, baptismal Pahul, militant identity to defend faith). PYQ FAVOURITE — religious resistance under Aurangzeb. Also: Sambhaji executed 1689 (Maratha leader); Hindus + Sufis also targeted in some areas.
cards.option3: Building a temple for the Sikhs here

Last great Mughal emperor before sustained decline, Aurangzeb died in:

(A) 1605 (Akbar's death year)
(B) 1707 (in Aurangabad, Deccan)
(C) 1857 (Sepoy Mutiny end)
(D) 1947 (Indian independence)
cards.back:
(B) 1707 (in Aurangabad, Deccan)

Mughal Empire — Aurangzeb DIED 3 March 1707 at AURANGABAD (Maharashtra), age ~88. Buried at KHULDABAD (near Aurangabad — close to Ellora Caves) in a SIMPLE TOMB (no mausoleum like Taj or Humayun's; per his wish — followed Islamic austerity). Funded the tomb from the income from his own copying of Quran (also taught religious texts + sewed caps). 1707 marks BEGINNING OF MUGHAL DECLINE — successor wars, Afghan/Persian invasions, Maratha + Sikh + British rises. By 1857, last Mughal Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled to Rangoon (Burma) by British. AURANGABAD city earlier named Khirki, then KHADKI, renamed AURANGABAD by Aurangzeb himself when he was Deccan governor in 1653.

cards.front:
BABUR, founder of the Mughal Empire in India, was descended from:

(A) Genghis Khan only (mother's side)
(B) Timur (paternal) + Genghis Khan (maternal)
(C) Pure Persian Safavid dynasty only
(D) Roman Byzantine line of emperors
cards.back:
(B) Timur (paternal) + Genghis Khan (maternal)

Mughal Empire — BABUR (1483-1530) — born Zahir-ud-din Muhammad in Andijan (Fergana Valley, modern Uzbekistan). Father's lineage: TIMUR / Tamerlane (great-great-great grandfather). Mother's lineage: GENGHIS KHAN (descendant). Hence the name 'MUGHAL' (= Mongol). Started ruling Fergana at age 12 (1494), lost it, conquered Kabul (1504), then turned his eyes to India. Wrote BABURNAMA — autobiography in Chagatai Turkish (one of the world's earliest autobiographies, very candid + observant; on flora, fauna, customs of Hindustan).

cards.front:
Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the FIRST BATTLE OF PANIPAT in:

(A) 1525 (year before founding)
(B) 1526 (start of Mughal era)
(C) 1527 (year after Panipat)
(D) 1530 (Babur's death year)
cards.back:
(B) 1526 (start of Mughal era)

Mughal Empire — FIRST BATTLE OF PANIPAT — 21 April 1526. Babur (~12,000 troops) defeated Ibrahim Lodi (~100,000). Babur's tactical innovations: TULUGHMA (flank attacks); ARABA (cart-mounted CANNONS — first major battlefield use of artillery in India); MATCHLOCK MUSKETS. Won despite huge numerical disadvantage. Founded MUGHAL EMPIRE (lasted 1526-1857, ~331 years). 1527 — BATTLE OF KHANWA (vs Rana Sanga of Mewar — coalition of Rajputs). 1528 — Battle of Chanderi. 1529 — Battle of Ghaghra (vs Afghans). Died 1530 in Agra at 47.

cards.front:
HUMAYUN (Babur's son) was DEFEATED + EXILED by which Afghan ruler?

(A) Daulat Khan Lodi, the Punjab governor
(B) Sher Shah Suri (battles of Chausa + Kannauj)
(C) Adil Shah, who was Hemu's master ruler
(D) Khan-i-Khanan, the senior court general
cards.back:
(B) Sher Shah Suri (battles of Chausa + Kannauj)

Mughal Empire — HUMAYUN (r. 1530-40 + 1555-56) — Babur's son. Inherited unconsolidated empire. SHER SHAH SURI (Farid Khan, an Afghan from Bihar) — defeated Humayun at: BATTLE OF CHAUSA (1539, near Buxar — Humayun barely escaped, swam Ganga); BATTLE OF KANNAUJ (1540 — Humayun fled to Persia). Established SUR DYNASTY (1540-1555). HUMAYUN spent 15 YEARS in exile — Persia (Shah Tahmasp's court), then to Kabul + back. Returned 1555, briefly recaptured Delhi. Died 1556 (fell down stairs in his library). Son AKBAR (13) succeeded him → Mughals.

cards.option2: Adil Shah, who was Hemu's master ruler

SHER SHAH SURI's most enduring administrative reform was:

(A) Abolition of all kinds of property tax
(B) Grand Trunk Road, revenue + currency reforms
(C) Conversion of Hindus to Islam by force
(D) Banning of Hindi as a court language
cards.back:
(B) Grand Trunk Road, revenue + currency reforms

Mughal Empire — SHER SHAH SURI (r. 1540-45) — short reign but enormous influence. Reforms: (1) GRAND TRUNK ROAD — rebuilt + extended ancient road from Sonargaon (Bengal) to Peshawar/Kabul (~2500 km). Sarais (rest houses) every ~25 km. (2) LAND REVENUE — measured land + fixed assessment based on yield (later refined by Akbar's Todar Mal — directly inspired by Sher Shah). (3) CURRENCY — introduced silver RUPEE (~178 grains; basis of modern Rupee) + copper DAM. (4) Improved postal system, taxation, judicial fairness. Died accidentally during siege of Kalinjar (gunpowder explosion). His MAUSOLEUM at Sasaram (Bihar) — magnificent.

(C) Krishnadeva Raya (Vijayanagara king)

(A) First Mughal mausoleum (no garden tomb yet)
(B) Architectural prototype for the Taj Mahal
(C) Plain austere tomb (no decoration)
(D) Underground crypt only (no above-ground)
cards.back:
(B) Architectural prototype for the Taj Mahal

Mughal Empire — HUMAYUN's TOMB (Delhi) — built 1565-72 by his widow HAMIDA BANU BEGUM (Akbar's mother), designed by Persian architect MIRAK MIRZA GHIYAS. UNESCO WORLD HERITAGE SITE (1993). FIRST GARDEN-TOMB on the Indian subcontinent — set the template for Mughal tombs that followed: SIKANDRA (Akbar's), ITIMAD-UD-DAULAH (Nur Jahan's father), AURANGZEB's wife Bibi-ka-Maqbara, + most famously TAJ MAHAL (Shah Jahan, 1632-53). Architectural features: bulbous DOME, garden in CHARBAGH (4-quartered Persian style), red sandstone + white marble. Reverberated through Mughal architecture for 200 years.

(B) Hemu (Vikramaditya, Adil Shah's general)

Mughal Empire — SECOND BATTLE OF PANIPAT (5 Nov 1556) — Akbar's forces (commanded by BAIRAM KHAN) vs HEMU CHANDRA (a Hindu general — born to a poor Brahmin family in Rewari, Haryana; rose through ranks to be Adil Shah Sur's wazir + general). Hemu had recaptured Delhi from Mughals after Humayun's death; declared himself 'VIKRAMADITYA' — a rare instance of a Hindu sovereign in Delhi between Prithviraj Chauhan + Marathas. He was hit by an arrow in the eye; captured + beheaded by Bairam Khan. Re-established Mughal control + ushered in 5 decades of Akbar's rule.

cards.front:
Mughal Emperor JAHANGIR ascended to the throne in which year?

(A) 1605 (after Akbar's death)
(B) 1556 (start of Akbar's reign)
(C) 1627 (year of Jahangir's death)
(D) 1658 (Aurangzeb's accession)
cards.back:
(A) 1605 (after Akbar's death)

Mughal Empire — JAHANGIR (born 1569 as Salim) — became Mughal Emperor in 1605 after AKBAR's death. Original name: NUR-UD-DIN MUHAMMAD SALIM; took regnal title JAHANGIR ('seizer of the world'). REIGN: 1605-1627 (22 years). MUGHAL EMPEROR SEQUENCE — memorize: (1) BABUR (1526-1530, founded Mughal empire after Battle of Panipat). (2) HUMAYUN (1530-1540, exiled by Sher Shah; restored 1555-1556). (3) AKBAR (1556-1605, the Great). (4) JAHANGIR (1605-1627). (5) SHAH JAHAN (1627-1658, built Taj Mahal). (6) AURANGZEB (1658-1707, expanded empire to peak). After Aurangzeb: rapid decline — Bahadur Shah I, Jahandar Shah, Farrukhsiyar, Muhammad Shah, etc. Last Mughal: BAHADUR SHAH ZAFAR (deposed 1858 after 1857 Revolt). KEY EVENTS in JAHANGIR'S REIGN: (1) Marriage to NUR JAHAN (1611) — became co-ruler in practice. (2) GOLDEN CHAIN OF JUSTICE (Zanjir-i-Adl) outside Agra Fort — anyone could pull it to seek redress. (3) Captain Hawkins (1608) and Sir Thomas Roe (1615) — British East India Co. envoys at his court. (4) Annexation of Mewar (1614, Maharana Amar Singh I submitted). (5) Loss of KANDAHAR to Persia (1622). (6) GUSHED rebellion of son SHAH JAHAN (1623-26). PYQ FREQUENCY: Mughal chronology in SSC, UPSC, MPSC — 1-2 per cycle.

cards.front:
JAHANGIR's autobiography is titled:

(A) Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (his memoirs)
(B) Akbarnama (Akbar's chronicle)
(C) Baburnama (Babur's memoirs)
(D) Padshahnama (Shah Jahan's reign)
cards.back:
(A) Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri (his memoirs)

Mughal Empire — TUZUK-I-JAHANGIRI (also JAHANGIRNAMA) — autobiographical memoirs of Emperor Jahangir, written by him in PERSIAN (with Turkish/Hindi blends). COVERAGE: from 1605 to 1622 (he stopped writing as health declined; SECRETARIES continued for last 5 years). CONTENT: keen observations on NATURE, ART, ARCHITECTURE, PEOPLE, animals, religious matters, court politics. Famous for DETAILED ANIMAL/PLANT descriptions (showing scientific curiosity rare for the era). PARALLEL TO BABURNAMA — Babur's memoirs (1483-1530) — also detailed nature observations; Jahangir clearly inherited the family literary tradition. KEY MUGHAL CHRONICLES (memorize): (1) BABURNAMA — Babur's memoirs (in Chagatai Turkic). (2) HUMAYUN-NAMA — by Gulbadan Begum (Humayun's sister), about Humayun. (3) AKBARNAMA — by ABUL FAZL, three volumes about Akbar. (4) AIN-I-AKBARI — third volume of Akbarnama, administrative gazetteer. (5) TUZUK-I-JAHANGIRI — by Jahangir himself. (6) PADSHAHNAMA — by ABDUL HAMID LAHORI, about Shah Jahan's reign. (7) ALAMGIRNAMA — by Mirza Muhammad Kazim, about Aurangzeb's first 10 years. (8) MUNTAKHAB-AT-TAWARIKH — by Badauni (critical/orthodox view of Akbar). PYQ FREQUENCY: Mughal source-author pairings in UPSC, MPSC, NCERT-driven SSC — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Jahangir's powerful queen and effective co-ruler was:

(A) Nur Jahan ('Light of the World')
(B) Mumtaz Mahal (her niece) here
(C) Hamida Banu (Akbar's mother)
(D) Jodha Bai (Akbar's wife)
cards.back:
(A) Nur Jahan ('Light of the World')

Mughal Empire — NUR JAHAN (born MIHR-UN-NISA, 1577-1645) — Jahangir's 20th wife (married 1611), but his FAVOURITE and most influential. ORIGIN: of Persian descent; father MIRZA GHIYAS BEG (later titled ITIMAD-UD-DAULAH, finance minister). FIRST MARRIAGE: to Sher Afkan (a Mughal officer killed in 1607; some accounts allege Jahangir had him killed to claim her). RISE: from 1611 onwards, became 'PADSHAH BEGUM'; coins MINTED in HER NAME (rare for a queen). EFFECTIVELY CO-RULER: dictated court appointments, signed firmans (royal orders), held audiences. NUR JAHAN JUNTA: she + father (Itimad-ud-Daulah) + brother ASAF KHAN + Prince Khurram (Shah Jahan, married Asaf Khan's daughter Mumtaz). KEY MOMENTS: (1) 1620s — power struggle with PRINCE KHURRAM (Shah Jahan); supported a rival prince (Shahryar) for succession — but Khurram won after Jahangir's death (1627). (2) BUILT ITIMAD-UD-DAULAH'S TOMB (1622-28, Agra) — the 'BABY TAJ', precursor of Taj Mahal — finest pietra dura work. (3) Designed gardens — Nur Mahal Sarai (Punjab), Achabal Bagh (Kashmir). NIECE: MUMTAZ MAHAL (Asaf Khan's daughter), Shah Jahan's wife — Taj Mahal built for her. PYQ FREQUENCY: Nur Jahan in UPSC, SSC, NCERT modern — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Jahangir's famous 'CHAIN OF JUSTICE' (Zanjir-i-Adl) was installed at:

(A) Agra Fort (for public petitions)
(B) Red Fort, Delhi (built later)
(C) Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar built it)
(D) Lahore Fort in Punjab area
cards.back:
(A) Agra Fort (for public petitions)

Mughal Empire — ZANJIR-I-ADL (CHAIN OF JUSTICE) — golden chain installed by Jahangir at AGRA FORT, between the FORT WALL and a STONE COLUMN by the YAMUNA RIVER. Anyone with a grievance against an official could PULL THE CHAIN; bells would ring inside the fort, and the case would come directly to the Emperor for redressal. SYMBOLIC: showed Jahangir's commitment to JUSTICE accessible to all (in his words 'so that the oppressed cannot be denied justice'). 60 BELLS connected; chain length supposedly several feet. PRACTICAL USE: actually rang RARELY — most disputes went through normal courts. But the SYMBOL was powerful — captured imagination of poets, chroniclers, even European travellers (Sir Thomas Roe noted it in his memoirs, 1615-19). HISTORICAL: not the FIRST such chain — earlier Persian rulers (Anushirvan the Just, 6th c.) and Indian rulers (Vikramaditya legend) had similar institutions. AGRA FORT: built initially by AKBAR (1565-73), expanded by Jahangir + Shah Jahan. Made of RED SANDSTONE (Akbar) + WHITE MARBLE additions (Shah Jahan). KEY STRUCTURES inside: Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas, Sheesh Mahal, Khas Mahal, Musamman Burj (where Shah Jahan was imprisoned by Aurangzeb). UNESCO HERITAGE 1983. PYQ FREQUENCY: Jahangir's chain in SSC, UPSC, MPSC — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which English ambassador was sent to Jahangir's court by King James I in 1615?

(A) Sir Thomas Roe (East India Co. trade)
(B) Captain William Hawkins (1608, earlier)
(C) Robert Clive (much later, 1750s)
(D) Warren Hastings (Governor 1773-85)
cards.back:
(A) Sir Thomas Roe (East India Co. trade)

Mughal Empire — SIR THOMAS ROE (~1581-1644) — official ambassador of King JAMES I of England to Jahangir's court (1615-1619). PURPOSE: secure trading rights for the BRITISH EAST INDIA COMPANY — particularly to set up factories at Surat and other ports. Earlier, CAPTAIN WILLIAM HAWKINS (1608-11) had been a UNOFFICIAL Mughal envoy — Jahangir gave him a Mughal officer rank but Hawkins was unable to secure formal trading concessions due to PORTUGUESE rivalry. ROE's ACHIEVEMENT: secured a 'Phirman' (royal decree) granting EIC the right to trade and establish a factory at SURAT (1615). KEY OBSERVATIONS in his journals: (1) Mughal court's wealth and ceremonial. (2) Jahangir's love of art, animals (zoo at court), wine. (3) Nur Jahan's quiet but vast power. (4) The competing influence of Portuguese Jesuits. SUBSEQUENT EUROPEANS at Mughal court: PORTUGUESE — first to arrive (Vasco da Gama 1498); maintained influence, supplied artists, missionaries. DUTCH — established VOC (Dutch East India Co.) factories. FRENCH — later, esp. under La Bourdonnais (1740s). LEGACY: Roe's mission INITIATED the SLOW BRITISH PENETRATION of India that culminated in colonial rule by 1757 (Plassey) onwards. PYQ FREQUENCY: Roe's mission in UPSC, SSC, NCERT — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Jahangir's father AKBAR named him SALIM after which Sufi saint who blessed his birth?

(A) Sheikh Salim Chishti of Sikri
(B) Khwaja Moinuddin (Ajmer dargah)
(C) Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi tomb)
(D) Bahauddin Zakaria (Multan saint)
cards.back:
(A) Sheikh Salim Chishti of Sikri

Mughal Empire — SHEIKH SALIM CHISHTI (1478-1572) — Sufi saint of the CHISHTI ORDER. AKBAR was childless for years, lost previous infants. Sheikh Salim Chishti BLESSED him; soon after, prince SALIM (later Jahangir) was born in 1569 — named after the saint in gratitude. AKBAR was so moved that he MOVED HIS CAPITAL to FATEHPUR SIKRI (1571-85), where Sheikh Salim's tomb is located. The TOMB OF SHEIKH SALIM CHISHTI inside Fatehpur Sikri's mosque complex is a famous WHITE MARBLE pavilion with intricate JALI screens. Even today, women tie threads on the screens for blessings. CHISHTI ORDER: founded by KHWAJA MOINUDDIN CHISHTI (~1141-1236) at AJMER — DARGAH of MOINUDDIN draws ~10 lakh pilgrims annually for URS. Other key Chishti saints: NIZAMUDDIN AULIYA (Delhi, ~1238-1325) — disciple AMIR KHUSRAU was his close associate. BAKHTIYAR KAKI (Delhi, ~1173-1235). FARID-UD-DIN GANJSHAKAR (Pakpattan, ~1175-1265). FATEHPUR SIKRI: planned imperial city (1571-85), abandoned after Akbar's reign due to water scarcity; UNESCO World Heritage (1986). KEY STRUCTURES: Buland Darwaza, Diwan-i-Khas, Panch Mahal, Salim Chishti's tomb, Tomb of Akbar's son. PYQ FREQUENCY: Chishti-Akbar-Jahangir links in UPSC, SSC, MPSC — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Jahangir is particularly known as a great patron of which art form?

(A) Mughal miniature painting
(B) Marble inlay architecture
(C) Carnatic music compositions
(D) Bharatanatyam dance forms
cards.back:
(A) Mughal miniature painting

Mughal Empire — JAHANGIR — generally considered the GREATEST PATRON of MUGHAL MINIATURE PAINTING. His personal interest, fine eye for detail, and discriminating commissioning produced the GOLDEN AGE of Mughal art (~1600-1620). KEY ARTISTS in his Atelier: (1) USTAD MANSUR — naturalist painter; depicted exotic birds, flowers, animals (Dodo, Zebra, Turkey, Tulips); titled 'NADIR-UL-ASR' (Wonder of the Age). (2) ABU AL-HASAN — court portraitist; titled 'NADIR-UZ-ZAMAN'. (3) BISHANDAS — portrait specialist. STYLE under Jahangir: shift from BATTLE/COURT SCENES (Akbar era) to more INTIMATE, NATURALISTIC, INDIVIDUAL portraits, animal/bird studies, allegorical subjects. INFLUENCE OF EUROPEAN ART: increased — Jahangir's collection had Albrecht Dürer prints and Italian paintings; cross-cultural fusion visible. PRESERVED IN: Victoria Memorial (Kolkata), Bharat Kala Bhavan (Varanasi), various royal libraries (Tehran, London). FAMOUS MASTERPIECES: 'Squirrels in a Plane Tree' (Mansur), 'Jahangir's Dream of King James I'. JAHANGIR himself is famously quoted: 'I can recognize the work of any of my painters in a single brush-stroke.' RELATED ARTS: he ALSO patronized JEWELLERY, CARPETS, METALWORK, but PAINTING was his clear passion. PYQ FREQUENCY: Mughal art-patron links in UPSC, NCERT, SSC GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Arrange the following BATTLES in correct chronological order. 1. First Battle of Panipat. 2. Battle of Khanwa. 3. Battle of Ghaghra. 4. Battle of Chausa.

(A) 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
(B) 2 → 1 → 3 → 4
(C) 1 → 3 → 2 → 4
(D) 1 → 2 → 4 → 3
cards.back:
(A) 1 → 2 → 3 → 4

Mughal Empire — Panipat-I = 1526 (Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi), Khanwa = 1527 (Babur vs Rana Sanga), Ghaghra = 1529 (Babur vs Afghans + Bengal Sultanate), Chausa = 1539 (Sher Shah Suri vs Humayun). All four touch the early Mughal era. Correct sequence 1526 → 1527 → 1529 → 1539.

cards.front:
Consider the following about AKBAR (1556-1605). 1. He abolished the jizya on non-Muslims in 1564. 2. His 'Din-i-Ilahi' in 1582 was a syncretic spiritual path that did not seek to replace Islam. 3. The Mansabdari system introduced dual ranks: zat (personal rank) and sawar (cavalry rank). 4. The revenue system devised under Raja Todar Mal is known as the 'Zabti' or 'Bandobast' system. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 2 and 3 only
(D) 3 and 4 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Mughal Empire — All four correct. Jizya abolished 1564 (re-imposed by Aurangzeb 1679). Din-i-Ilahi (1582) — a spiritual fraternity, not a state religion, attracted very few followers (Birbal was one). Mansabdari (1571, evolved through Akbar) had zat + sawar. Todar Mal's Zabti (also 'Dahsala') fixed revenue on 10-year averages — the mature stage of the Mughal revenue system.

cards.front:
Match List-I (Mughal emperor) with List-II (architectural masterpiece commissioned during the reign). A. Akbar. B. Jahangir. C. Shah Jahan. D. Aurangzeb. List-II: 1. Bibi Ka Maqbara, Aurangabad. 2. Fatehpur Sikri. 3. Tomb of I'timad-ud-Daulah, Agra. 4. Taj Mahal.

(A) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1
(B) A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1
(C) A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1
(D) A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3
cards.back:
(A) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1

cards.front:
The Buland Darwaza, the imposing 54-m gateway, is part of which complex built by Akbar to commemorate his Gujarat victory (1573)?

(A) Agra Fort
(B) Fatehpur Sikri (Jama Masjid complex)
(C) Red Fort, Delhi
(D) Humayun's Tomb
cards.back:
(B) Fatehpur Sikri (Jama Masjid complex)

Mughal Empire — Buland Darwaza ('high gateway', 54 m) — added 1576 by Akbar to the Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri after his Gujarat victory. Fatehpur Sikri served as Akbar's capital 1571-1585; abandoned probably due to water shortage. Notable structures: Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas (with central pillar 'Akbar's throne'), Panch Mahal (5-storey wind tower), Jodha Bai's palace, Birbal's house, Salim Chishti's tomb (white marble, jali screens — earliest white-marble Mughal tomb). UNESCO 1986. Persian inscription on the Buland Darwaza: 'The world is a bridge, pass over it but build no houses on it' (Quranic). Akbar's syncretic Din-i-Ilahi (1582) was promulgated here.

cards.front:
Pietra dura (Italian for 'hard stone') — extensively used on the Taj Mahal — refers to:

(A) Carving stone in relief
(B) Inlaying cut and polished semi-precious stones into marble to form decorative motifs
(C) Glazed-tile mosaic
(D) Stone-stucco plastering
cards.back:
(B) Inlaying cut and polished semi-precious stones into marble to form decorative motifs

Mughal Empire — Pietra dura — Italian, parchin kari in Persian. Cut + polished semi-precious stones (jasper, jade, lapis lazuli, carnelian, turquoise, malachite, mother-of-pearl) inlaid into marble or hard-stone. Reached its zenith on the Taj Mahal — floral motifs around the cenotaphs and dado panels. Earlier example — Itimad-ud-Daulah's tomb (1622-28). Distinct from PIETRA TENERA (soft-stone) and from KASHIKARI (glazed tilework, used in Lahore Fort). The technique was likely brought from Italy via Mughal contacts but became a distinctive Mughal art form. Other notable techniques in Mughal architecture: jali (perforated stone screens), foliated arches, double dome (introduced at Humayun's Tomb).

cards.front:
The 'charbagh' garden layout, a hallmark of Mughal landscape design, is characterised by:

(A) Random meandering paths
(B) A garden divided into FOUR quadrants by water channels meeting at a central pool — symbolising the four rivers of Paradise
(C) Single rectangular layout without water
(D) Stepped terraces only
cards.back:
(B) A garden divided into FOUR quadrants by water channels meeting at a central pool — symbolising the four rivers of Paradise

Mughal Empire — Charbagh — Persian 'four gardens'. Layout: 4 quadrants divided by intersecting water channels (representing the 4 rivers of Paradise — water, milk, wine, honey — Quranic image). Introduced by Babur (Aram Bagh / Ram Bagh, Agra — earliest). Most famous examples: Humayun's Tomb (the first monumental charbagh tomb in India, ~1572); Taj Mahal (the tomb is offset to the rear edge instead of the centre — unusual); Shalimar Bagh (Kashmir, Jahangir 1619); Pinjore Gardens (Haryana, Aurangzeb's foster brother Fidai Khan). Water flows by gravity through chadar (cascade) and chini-khana (niche where lamps were placed behind falling water).

Humayun's Tomb in Delhi (1572) is historically significant primarily because it:

(A) Was the first Mughal mosque
(B) Introduced the Persian-style double dome and charbagh tomb to India — direct precursor to the Taj Mahal
(C) Was built by Aurangzeb
(D) Is the largest Mughal tomb
cards.back:
(B) Introduced the Persian-style double dome and charbagh tomb to India — direct precursor to the Taj Mahal

Mughal Empire — Humayun's Tomb — commissioned 1565 by Empress Bega Begum (Haji Begum, Humayun's senior widow) ~9 years after his death (he fell down the library stairs of Sher Mandal in Purana Qila in 1556). Architect — Mirak Mirza Ghiyas (Persian). Significance: (1) FIRST garden-tomb on the Indian subcontinent (charbagh); (2) Introduced the double dome — outer is bulbous, inner is shallower; (3) Red sandstone with white marble accents → set the template for the Taj Mahal. UNESCO 1993. Last Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar took refuge here in 1857 → captured by William Hodson.

cards.front:
Mughal painting reached its peak under JAHANGIR. Which feature distinguished his court atelier?

(A) Bold colours; battle and hunt scenes were favoured (as under Akbar)
(B) Refined naturalism — delicate portraits, detailed studies of birds, flowers, and animals (Ustad Mansur was the master nature-painter)
(C) Religious illustrations only
(D) Geometric abstract designs
cards.back:
(B) Refined naturalism — delicate portraits, detailed studies of birds, flowers, and animals (Ustad Mansur was the master nature-painter)

Mughal Empire — Mughal-painting evolution: AKBAR — illustrations of manuscripts (Hamzanama, Akbarnama, Razmnama — Persian Mahabharata); large-scale, narrative; Persian-Indian fusion; Daswanth + Basawan were star painters. JAHANGIR — refined, naturalistic; courtly portraits; flora/fauna studies. USTAD MANSUR (his court painter) — known for the Siberian Crane and Dodo paintings. Abu'l Hasan was titled 'Nadir-uz-Zaman' (wonder of the age) for portraits. SHAH JAHAN — even more refined; Padshahnama; jeweled, formal. AURANGZEB — declined; he disapproved of figural art; many painters dispersed → seeded Rajput/Pahari schools (Kangra, Mewar, Bundi).

cards.front:
A 'jharokha' in Mughal architecture refers to:

(A) An underground water tank
(B) A cantilevered enclosed balcony with stone brackets and jali, typically projecting from an upper-storey wall
(C) A domed pavilion at a corner
(D) A deep recessed entrance arch
cards.back:
(B) A cantilevered enclosed balcony with stone brackets and jali, typically projecting from an upper-storey wall

Mughal Empire — Jharokha — projecting balcony, often supported on stone brackets, with a small dome / chhatri above; often features jali (lattice) screens for purdah viewing. Used widely in Mughal + Rajput architecture (Hawa Mahal, Jaipur, has 953 jharokhas). Akbar instituted 'Jharokha Darshan' — appearing daily to subjects; abolished by Aurangzeb (Islamic puritan). Other elements to know: CHHATRI — domed pavilion / kiosk on roof or corners, signifies royalty; IWAN — vaulted recessed entrance hall; PISHTAQ — large rectangular frame of an iwan (the iconic frame of the Taj's main entrance); CHADAR — sloped water cascade in gardens.
cards.option2: A domed pavilion at a corner

cards.front:
Akbar's new religion, which combined Hindu, Muslim, Zoroastrian and Christian elements, was called:

(A) Sufism
(B) Din-i-Ilahi
(C) Bhakti
(D) Sulh-i-Kul
cards.back:
(B) Din-i-Ilahi

Mughal Empire — Din-i-Ilahi ('Divine Faith') — Akbar proclaimed it in 1582 as a syncretic belief system, though it gained few converts beyond his court. 'Sulh-i-Kul' ('peace with all') was Akbar's broader policy of religious tolerance — not the religion itself. Sufism is Islamic mysticism; Bhakti was a parallel devotional movement within Hinduism. The Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri was the interfaith discussion hall that inspired Din-i-Ilahi.

cards.front:
The 'Mansabdari' system of ranking nobles in the Mughal administration was introduced by:

(A) Babur
(B) Akbar
(C) Shah Jahan
(D) Aurangzeb
cards.back:
(B) Akbar

Mughal Empire — Akbar introduced Mansabdari around 1575 to unify military command, civil administration and revenue. Each 'mansabdar' had two numerical ranks — 'zat' (personal status, salary) and 'sawar' (number of cavalry he had to maintain). The highest rank under Akbar was 7,000. The system gradually decayed in quality under Akbar's successors, contributing to 18th-century decline.

Aurangzeb reimposed which tax on non-Muslims in 1679, reversing Akbar's earlier abolition of it?

(A) Khums
(B) Jizya
(C) Zakat
(D) Kharaj
cards.back:
(B) Jizya

The founder of the Mughal Empire in India, Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur, defeated Ibrahim Lodi in which decisive battle?

(A) Battle of Khanwa (1527)
(B) First Battle of Panipat (1526)
(C) Battle of Chanderi (1528)
(D) Battle of Ghaghra (1529)
cards.back:

Mughal Empire — FIRST BATTLE OF PANIPAT (21 April 1526): Babur's 12,000 troops defeated Ibrahim Lodi's 100,000 with superior artillery (early gunpowder/cannons) and the TULUGHMA battle formation. Ibrahim Lodi was killed — the ONLY Delhi Sultan to die on the battlefield. This founded the Mughal Empire. Later Babur-era battles: KHANWA (1527, defeated Rana Sanga of Mewar), CHANDERI (1528, Medini Rai), GHAGHRA (1529, Afghans + Bengal sultan). Babur wrote Babur-nama (autobiography in Turkish/Chagatai).

(A) Sikandar Lodi
(B) Sher Shah Suri
(C) Mahmud Shah

cards.back:
(B) Sher Shah Suri

Mughal Empire — SHER SHAH SURI (born Farid Khan, 1486–1545) defeated Humayun at the BATTLE OF CHAUSA (1539) and then decisively at the BATTLE OF KANNAUJ / BILGRAM (1540). Humayun fled to Persia (Safavid court of Shah Tahmasp) for 15 years. Sher Shah ruled 1540-45 and founded the SUR DYNASTY. Sher Shah's reforms: Grand Trunk Road extension (Sonargaon to Peshawar), silver RUPIYA coin (basis of modern rupee), postal system, land revenue (zabt system — precursor to Akbar's reforms), sarais. Died in cannon explosion at Kalinjar 1545. Humayun regained Delhi in 1555 but died falling down stairs in 1556 — 'Humayun tumbled through life and tumbled out of it'.

Akbar came to the throne at what age, and who was his regent during the early years?

(A) 13 years; Bairam Khan
(B) 18 years; Todar Mal
(C) 15 years; Abul Fazl
(D) 11 years; Faizi
cards.back:
(A) 13 years; Bairam Khan

Mughal Empire — Akbar (Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar, born 1542, Umarkot) ascended the throne in 1556 at age 13 after Humayun's death. His regent/guardian for the first 4 years was BAIRAM KHAN (Turkoman noble, father of Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan). Akbar's first major victory: SECOND BATTLE OF PANIPAT (5 Nov 1556) — Bairam Khan led Mughal forces against HEMU (the Hindu Suri-era general who had briefly captured Delhi). Bairam's regency ended in 1560 (dismissed by Akbar's foster-mother Maham Anaga). Akbar ruled till 1605 (49 years — longest-reigning Mughal).

cards.front:
The MANSABDARI system — Akbar's military-administrative framework — was based on:

(A) Hereditary territorial chieftainship
(B) DUAL RANKS: zat (personal status) and sawar
(C) Jagirdar assignments only
(D) Fixed cash salaries for all nobles
cards.back:
(B) DUAL RANKS: zat (personal status) and sawar

Mughal Empire — MANSABDARI (Persian 'mansab' = rank) was Akbar's systematic bureaucracy. Each mansabdar had TWO ranks: ZAT (personal status and pay — from 10 to 5000, later up to 10,000 for imperial family) and SAWAR (number of cavalrymen he must maintain — couldn't exceed zat). Rewards were in CASH SALARIES or JAGIRS (revenue assignments — NOT hereditary territorial grants; transferable). Three categories: TROOPED, DUSPA (half on duty), SIHPA. Disadvantages: became corrupt/inefficient over time, led to Mughal decline. Introduced ~1575 following Central Asian precedent. cavalry obligation.
cards.option3: Fixed cash salaries for all nobles

(A) Tansen, Birbal, Todar Mal, Abul Fazl, Faizi, Raja Man Singh, Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, Mullah Do-Piyaza, Fakir Aziao-Din
(B) Tansen, Kalidasa, Varahamihira, Aryabhata (those are Gupta-era gems)
(C) Only Abul Fazl and Birbal

cards.front:
Akbar's new syncretic religion 'DIN-I-ILAHI' was proclaimed in which year?

(A) 1556
(B) 1575 (Ibadat Khana debates began)
(C) 1582
(D) 1605
cards.back:
(C) 1582

Mughal Empire — DIN-I-ILAHI ('Divine Faith') was proclaimed by Akbar in 1582 — a syncretic creed borrowing from Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism, Jainism, Christianity. Prior steps: 1575 IBADAT KHANA (House of Worship) at Fatehpur Sikri for religious debates; 1579 MAZHAR (Infallibility Decree) making Akbar the final arbiter on religious disputes. Din-i-Ilahi had ~19 followers (Birbal being the most prominent) — it died with Akbar. Most orthodox Muslims (including Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi) rejected it. Other Akbar religious policies: abolished JIZYA 1564 (re-imposed by Aurangzeb), PILGRIM TAX abolished 1563, allowed inter-faith marriages (married Rajput princess — later queen mother Mariam-uz-Zamani, Jodha Bai).

cards.front:
The BATTLE OF HALDIGHATI (1576) was fought between the Mughal forces (led by Raja Man Singh) and which Rajput king?

(A) Rana Sanga of Mewar
(B) Maharana Pratap of Mewar
(C) Raja Jai Singh of Amer
(D) Raja Udai Singh
cards.back:
(B) Maharana Pratap of Mewar

Mughal Empire — BATTLE OF HALDIGHATI (18 June 1576, in the Aravalli foothills near Kumbhalgarh, Rajasthan). Mughal forces led by RAJA MAN SINGH (not Akbar personally) vs MAHARANA PRATAP of Mewar (with Afghan general Hakim Khan Sur + Bhil tribal archers). TACTICAL Mughal victory, STRATEGIC stalemate — Rana Pratap escaped on his legendary horse CHETAK (who carried him to safety despite a fatal wound). Rana Pratap continued guerrilla resistance from Aravalli hills, reclaimed most of Mewar by 1585. Rana Pratap's story is a symbol of Rajput resistance; his death 1597. Rana Sanga (different king) had fought Babur at Khanwa 1527.

cards.front:
Akbar shifted his capital FROM Agra TO Fatehpur Sikri in which year, and for what reason?

(A) 1571; to honour Sufi saint Shaikh Salim Chishti who blessed him with a son
(B) 1605; to be closer to the Deccan frontier
(C) 1585; due to plague in Agra
(D) 1562; at Bairam Khan's advice
cards.back:
(A) 1571; to honour Sufi saint Shaikh Salim Chishti who blessed him with a son

Mughal Empire — Akbar shifted his capital to FATEHPUR SIKRI in 1571 to commemorate SHAIKH SALIM CHISHTI's prophecy that he would have a son (who became Jahangir, born 1569). Fatehpur Sikri ('City of Victory') housed the BULAND DARWAZA (1576, commemorating Gujarat conquest — tallest gateway in the world, 54m), the TOMB of Salim Chishti, the DIWAN-I-KHAS (private audience hall), JAMA MASJID, PANCH MAHAL (5-story pleasure palace), IBADAT KHANA. Capital abandoned by 1585 due to water shortage; Akbar moved to Lahore till 1598, then back to Agra. UNESCO WHS since 1986.

cards.front:
The DAHSALA (Ten-Year) land revenue system was introduced under Akbar by which minister?

(A) Abul Fazl
(B) Raja Todar Mal
(C) Birbal
(D) Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan
cards.back:
(B) Raja Todar Mal

Mughal Empire — DAHSALA ZABT system (introduced 1580) — designed by RAJA TODAR MAL, Akbar's finance minister. Method: surveyed cultivated land, categorised by productivity (POLAJ — always cultivated, PARAUTI — left fallow, CHACHAR — 3-4 years fallow, BANJAR — 5+ years fallow), averaged yields of last 10 years, fixed 1/3 of produce as state share (payable in cash or kind based on prevailing prices). Applied in Northern India — Punjab, Allahabad, Awadh, Delhi, Agra, Bihar, Ajmer, Malwa, Lahore, Multan. Todar Mal also conducted comprehensive surveys in BIHAR and BENGAL. Earlier under Sher Shah, he'd served as revenue commissioner. Died 1589. Land revenue system was the single most important administrative innovation — lasted (with modifications) till the British.

cards.front:
Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, built after his death in 1556, was commissioned by:

(A) Akbar
(B) Hamida Banu Begum
(C) Bairam Khan
(D) Shah Jahan, for his ancestor
cards.back:
(B) Hamida Banu Begum

Mughal Empire — HUMAYUN'S TOMB (1565–72), Delhi — commissioned by Humayun's widow HAMIDA BANU BEGUM (a.k.a. Haji Begum). Architect: Mirak Mirza Ghiyath (Persian). It's the FIRST GARDEN-TOMB on the Indian subcontinent and an architectural precursor to the TAJ MAHAL (90 years later, 1632-53, built by Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal). Features: Persian-style CHAR BAGH garden (quadrilateral), double-dome, red sandstone + white marble inlays, axial symmetry. UNESCO WHS since 1993. Humayun's body was originally in Purana Qila; Hamida moved it here. Several later Mughals were also interred here (Dara Shikoh, Rahim Khan-i-Khanan). Library (Sher Mandal) at Purana Qila is where Humayun fell to his death (1556). Humayun's widow, mother of Akbar.

cards.front:
Jahangir (r. 1605-1627) succeeded Akbar. His chief queen, who wielded enormous influence and was the power behind the throne, was:

(A) Nur Jahan
(B) Mumtaz Mahal
(C) Jahanara Begum
(D) Roshanara Begum
cards.back:
(A) Nur Jahan

Mughal Empire — NUR JAHAN (born Mehr-un-Nissa in 1577; married Jahangir in 1611 as his 20th wife) was the ONLY Mughal empress to have coins struck in her name, issue farmans, and effectively co-rule. Formed a 'JUNTA' with her father ITIMAD-UD-DAULAH (Prime Minister), brother ASAF KHAN, and step-son SHAH JAHAN. Her niece ARJUMAND BANU (later MUMTAZ MAHAL) was Shah Jahan's wife — for whom the Taj Mahal was built. Jahangir (Salim) also wrote the 'TUZUK-I-JAHANGIRI' memoir. He was an art patron (Mughal miniature painting peak — Ustad Mansur, Abul Hasan). British East India Company's William Hawkins (1608) and Thomas Roe (1616) visited his court. Tomb: Shahdara Bagh, Lahore.

cards.front:
Shah Jahan built the TAJ MAHAL as a mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. In which years was construction carried out, and who was the CHIEF ARCHITECT?

(A) 1632-1653; Ustad Ahmad Lahauri
(B) 1540-1550; Mirak Mirza Ghiyath
(C) 1628-1640; Ustad Isa Shirazi
(D) 1658-1680; Aurangzeb's royal architect
cards.back:
(A) 1632-1653; Ustad Ahmad Lahauri

Mughal Empire — TAJ MAHAL — commissioned 1632 by SHAH JAHAN (r. 1628-58) for his beloved wife MUMTAZ MAHAL who died during childbirth of their 14th child (1631, Burhanpur). Construction: ~22 years, completed 1653. Chief architect: USTAD AHMAD LAHAURI (some sources credit Mirak Mirza Ghiyath, but Lahauri is more accepted). White Makrana marble. 42-acre complex with char-bagh, mosque (West), jawab (East — mirror-image of mosque but unconsecrated, just for symmetry), gateway, minarets (tilt outward so earthquake doesn't damage the main tomb). UNESCO WHS 1983. Both Shah Jahan and Mumtaz are interred here. Shah Jahan's OTHER architecture: RED FORT DELHI (1648 — with Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas), JAMA MASJID DELHI (1656), MOTI MASJID (Agra), PEACOCK THRONE (Takht-i-Taus).

cards.front:
The War of Succession among Shah Jahan's sons was won by Aurangzeb, who executed his brother Dara Shikoh (the liberal scholar-prince). Dara Shikoh is best known for translating which Hindu texts into Persian?

(A) Ramayana and Mahabharata
(B) The Upanishads
(C) Manusmriti and Arthashastra
(D) Rigveda hymns
cards.back:
(B) The Upanishads

Mughal Empire — DARA SHIKOH (1615-1659), Shah Jahan's eldest son and heir apparent, was a Sufi-leaning scholar who sought syncretism between Islam and Hinduism. His magnum opus: 'SIRR-I-AKBAR' (The Great Secret, 1657) — Persian translation of 52 Upanishads. He also wrote 'MAJMA-UL-BAHRAIN' ('Mingling of Two Oceans') arguing that Islamic Sufism and Hindu Vedanta teach the same truth. This earned him charges of apostasy. The WAR OF SUCCESSION (1657-59): Aurangzeb defeated Dara at the BATTLE OF SAMUGARH (May 1658) near Agra. Dara was captured, paraded in humiliation through Delhi, tried for apostasy, and BEHEADED (1659). His body buried anonymously at Humayun's tomb. Shah Jahan was imprisoned in Agra Fort by Aurangzeb till his death 1666 (buried next to Mumtaz in Taj). titled 'Sirr-i-Akbar' / The Great Secret.

cards.front:
Aurangzeb (r. 1658-1707) reversed several liberal policies of his predecessors. He re-imposed which tax in 1679 that had been abolished by Akbar in 1564?

(A) Zakat
(B) Jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims)
(C) Khums (1/5 war booty)
(D) Kharaj (land tax on non-Muslims)
cards.back:
(B) Jizya (poll tax on non-Muslims)

Mughal Empire — JIZYA — a poll tax on non-Muslim subjects in exchange for protection (dhimmi status) — was abolished by AKBAR in 1564 as part of his Sulh-i-Kul (peace with all) policy. AURANGZEB re-imposed it on 2 April 1679 — a major departure from Mughal syncretism, alienating Rajput and Hindu subjects, contributing to Maratha and Jat uprisings. Jizya was finally abolished by Farrukhsiyar in 1712 (briefly re-imposed, then abolished by Muhammad Shah 1719 permanently). Aurangzeb's other 'orthodox' measures: banned music at court, imposed Sharia law rigorously, demolished several temples (Kashi Vishwanath 1669, Keshava Rai Mathura, Somnath), ordered FATAWA-I-ALAMGIRI compilation (Hanafi fiqh digest). Title: ALAMGIR ('Conqueror of the World').
