cards.front:
Aurangzeb's Deccan campaigns (1681-1707) — fighting the Marathas and Deccan Sultanates — lasted 26 years. Which two Deccan Sultanates did he annex?

(A) Ahmednagar (1636 — during Shah Jahan) and Berar
(B) Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687)
(C) Bidar and Karnataka
(D) Vijayanagara and Mysore
cards.back:
(B) Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687)

Mughal Empire — The five Deccan Sultanates (15th-17th c. successors of the Bahmani): AHMEDNAGAR (conquered by Shah Jahan 1636), BIJAPUR (Adil Shahi — annexed by Aurangzeb 1686), GOLCONDA (Qutb Shahi — annexed by Aurangzeb 1687), BIDAR (absorbed by Bijapur 1619), BERAR (absorbed by Ahmednagar). Thus Aurangzeb completed Mughal unification of the Deccan. But simultaneously, he was fighting MARATHAS under SHIVAJI (d. 1680) and his son SAMBHAJI (captured and executed 1689). Despite imprisoning Shivaji at Agra in 1666 (Shivaji escaped in a basket), he could never break the Marathas. His Deccan stay 1681-1707 drained Mughal resources + alienated nobility. Aurangzeb died at Aurangabad (1707) — buried simply at Khuldabad (Rauza). Empire began crumbling within a decade.

cards.front:
The famous PEACOCK THRONE (Takht-i-Taus) of Shah Jahan — studded with the KOH-I-NOOR diamond — was looted in 1739 by:

(A) Ahmad Shah Abdali (Afghan)
(B) Nadir Shah (Persian)
(C) Robert Clive (British)
(D) Sher Shah Suri
cards.back:
(B) Nadir Shah (Persian)

Mughal Empire — NADIR SHAH of Persia (1688-1747) invaded India in 1739, defeated Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah at the BATTLE OF KARNAL (Feb 1739), and sacked DELHI — massacred ~30,000, looted the Peacock Throne, Koh-i-Noor diamond, Jam-e-Jam, and treasure estimated at 70 crore rupees. He took it all to Persia. Peacock Throne's gold: disassembled, ultimately lost. cards.front:
The last Mughal emperor was Bahadur Shah II 'Zafar' — a poet and symbolic leader. After the 1857 Revolt, what happened to him?

(A) Executed by the British in Delhi
(B) Tried for treason, exiled to Rangoon, Burma, where he died in 1862
(C) Committed suicide at Red Fort
(D) Restored to symbolic throne under British control
cards.back:
(B) Tried for treason, exiled to Rangoon, Burma, where he died in 1862

Mughal Empire — BAHADUR SHAH II 'Zafar' (1775-1862) — the 20th and last Mughal Emperor — was proclaimed 'Emperor of Hindustan' by the 1857 rebel sepoys in Delhi. After the British recapture of Delhi (Sept 1857), he was TRIED for treason (Jan 1858), convicted, and EXILED to Rangoon, Burma (1858), where he died in 1862 aged 87. His wife Zeenat Mahal and remaining family went with him. His sons MIRZA MUGHAL, KHIZR SULTAN, MIRZA ABU BAKR were shot dead by MAJOR WILLIAM HODSON near Khooni Darwaza (Bloody Gate), Delhi — ending the imperial line. Zafar was a prolific Urdu poet ('Na kisi ki aankh ka noor hoon...' famously attributed but actually by Muztar Khairabadi). Tomb: Yangon, Myanmar. The 1857 defeat effectively ENDED Mughal rule (though nominal since 1803) and transferred India to direct British Crown rule via the Government of India Act 1858.

cards.option3: Restored to symbolic throne under British control

cards.front:
Aurangzeb's conflict with the Sikh Gurus led to the execution of which Guru, subsequently called 'Hind di Chadar' (Shield of India)?

(A) Guru Arjan Dev (5th Guru)
(B) Guru Tegh Bahadur (9th Guru)
(C) Guru Gobind Singh (10th Guru)
(D) Guru Hargobind (6th Guru)
cards.back:
(B) Guru Tegh Bahadur (9th Guru)

Mughal Empire — GURU TEGH BAHADUR (9th Sikh Guru, 1621-1675) was executed on 24 November 1675 in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, by order of AURANGZEB. His refusal to convert to Islam AND his defence of Kashmiri Pandits (who came to him for protection against forced conversion) led to his martyrdom. Title: HIND DI CHADAR ('Shield of India'). His son Gobind Rai became the 10th Guru GURU GOBIND SINGH (1666-1708), who later founded the KHALSA at Anandpur on BAISAKHI 1699. Guru Gobind Singh's four sons (sahibzadas) were all martyred: two (elder) killed in battle at Chamkaur (1704); two (younger — Zorawar Singh 9 and Fateh Singh 6) bricked alive in walls at Sirhind on refusal to convert (Dec 1705). Guru Gobind Singh declared the GURU GRANTH SAHIB as the eternal Guru (1708). Earlier: GURU ARJAN DEV (5th) was executed by JAHANGIR in 1606 — first Sikh martyr.

Jahangir's tomb is at Lahore. Whose tomb is located at Sikandra (near Agra)?

(B) Akbar
(C) Shah Jahan
(D) Aurangzeb
cards.back:

cards.front:
SHAH JAHAN built which of the following as his symbol of sovereignty upon shifting his capital from Agra to Delhi in 1648?

(A) Qutb Minar
(B) Red Fort (Lal Qila) + city of Shahjahanabad
(C) Humayun's Tomb
(D) Purana Qila
cards.back:
(B) Red Fort (Lal Qila) + city of Shahjahanabad

Mughal Empire — SHAH JAHAN shifted the Mughal capital from AGRA to DELHI in 1648. He built RED FORT (LAL QILA) — 1638-1648 — and around it, the new capital SHAHJAHANABAD (today's OLD DELHI: Chandni Chowk, Jama Masjid, etc.). Red Fort features: DIWAN-I-AM (Hall of Public Audience, with the famous PIETRA DURA ARCH with original PEACOCK THRONE), DIWAN-I-KHAS (Hall of Private Audience), RANG MAHAL, MOTI MASJID (Pearl Mosque), HAYAT-BAKSH BAGH. UNESCO WHS since 2007. Today, the INDIAN PRIME MINISTER hoists the TRICOLOUR from the LAHORI GATE of the Red Fort every 15 AUGUST. JAMA MASJID (also Shah Jahan, 1656) is India's largest mosque. Qutb Minar was built by Qutbuddin Aibak (1193-1220s) + Iltutmish; Humayun's Tomb by Hamida Banu Begum (1565-72); Purana Qila by Sher Shah + Humayun.

cards.front:
TAJ MAHAL was built by SHAH JAHAN in memory of:

(A) Mumtaz Mahal (his beloved wife)
(B) Nur Jahan (Jahangir's queen)
(C) Jahangir (his own father)
(D) Akbar (his grandfather)
cards.back:
(A) Mumtaz Mahal (his beloved wife)

Mughal Empire — TAJ MAHAL — built 1632-1648 by Shah Jahan in memory of his FAVOURITE WIFE MUMTAZ MAHAL (Arjumand Banu Begum), who died in 1631 giving birth to their 14th child. LOCATION: AGRA, on the banks of YAMUNA. ARCHITECTS: USTAD AHMAD LAHAURI (chief architect); design influenced by Persian, Islamic, Indian styles. WORKERS: ~20,000 craftsmen, 1,000+ elephants for hauling materials. COST estimated at ~32 million rupees of the time (~hundreds of crores in today's money). MATERIALS: WHITE MAKRANA MARBLE from Rajasthan; semi-precious stones inlaid (PIETRA DURA technique) — jasper, jade, sapphire, turquoise, amethyst. UNESCO WORLD HERITAGE 1983; one of NEW SEVEN WONDERS OF THE WORLD (2007 vote). SYMMETRY: perfectly mirrored along central axis; main mausoleum, mosque, jawab (response building), gardens (charbagh). FOUNTAINS, REFLECTING POOL, GARDEN. RECENT (2024): visited by ~7-8 million people/year; major source of foreign exchange for India tourism. TAJ MAHAL TRIVIA: appears to change colour through the day — pinkish at dawn, white at noon, golden at sunset, silvery at moon-light. PRESERVATION: pollution from Mathura refinery, leather tanneries threatened the marble (yellowing); protective measures since 1990s. PYQ FREQUENCY: Taj-Mumtaz link is a 1-mark guarantee in SSC, UPSC, MPSC.

cards.front:
SHAH JAHAN's famous PEACOCK THRONE (Takht-e-Tawus) was looted by which invader?

(A) Nadir Shah of Persia (1739)
(B) Ahmad Shah Abdali (later raids)
(C) Lord Clive (Battle of Plassey)
(D) Aurangzeb (during succession war)
cards.back:
(A) Nadir Shah of Persia (1739)

Mughal Empire — PEACOCK THRONE (Takht-e-Tawus) — golden throne commissioned by Shah Jahan, completed 1635 after 7 years of work; encrusted with thousands of precious stones (including the original KOH-I-NOOR diamond, on the throne in early years). VALUE: estimated at ~1 crore rupees of the time — comparable to TWICE the cost of Taj Mahal. NADIR SHAH — Persian emperor — invaded India in 1739; defeated Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah at the BATTLE OF KARNAL (Feb 1739); LOOTED Delhi for 57 days; carried away the PEACOCK THRONE + KOH-I-NOOR + tons of gold/silver/gems back to Persia. The Mughal treasury was DEPLETED — ~70 crore rupees taken (gigantic for that era). AFTERMATH: Mughal empire NEVER recovered economically; rapid decline post-1739. NADIR SHAH was assassinated 1747; the Peacock Throne was BROKEN UP and parts dispersed across Persia/Afghanistan/India. KOH-I-NOOR ('Mountain of Light') diamond — passed through many hands: Mughals → Nadir Shah (named it 'Koh-i-Noor') → Ahmad Shah Abdali → Punjab's Maharaja Ranjit Singh → seized by British 1849 (Treaty of Lahore) → presented to Queen Victoria 1850. NOW set in Queen Mother's crown (UK Royal Treasury). REPATRIATION DEMANDS: India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran all claim. PYQ FREQUENCY: Nadir Shah-Peacock Throne in SSC, UPSC, MPSC — 1× per cycle.

SHAH JAHAN built which new capital city, including the famous RED FORT?

(A) Shahjahanabad (now Old Delhi)
(B) Fatehpur Sikri (Akbar built it)
(C) Daulatabad (Tughlaq's city)
(D) Dilli (Tughluqabad fort area)
cards.back:
(A) Shahjahanabad (now Old Delhi)

Mughal Empire — SHAHJAHANABAD — capital city established by Shah Jahan in 1648, after he moved his court from Agra to Delhi. Now part of OLD DELHI. KEY STRUCTURES BUILT: (1) RED FORT (Lal Qila) — completed 1648; UNESCO Heritage. Made of red sandstone; key buildings inside: Diwan-i-Aam (Hall of Public Audience), Diwan-i-Khas (Hall of Private Audience — held the Peacock Throne), Naubat Khana, Rang Mahal, Mumtaz Mahal, Khas Mahal. INDEPENDENCE DAY ceremonies: PM addresses nation from Red Fort ramparts each 15 August (since 1947); Republic Day Parade (Jan 26) on Rajpath, ends near India Gate. SHAHJAHANABAD vs NEW DELHI: SHAHJAHANABAD is OLD DELHI; New Delhi was built by British (1911-1931, Lutyens & Baker design) — separate planned city. URBAN SHAHJAHANABAD: ~6 sq km original walls; today merged into massive Delhi metropolis (NCT). PYQ FREQUENCY: Shahjahanabad-Red Fort in SSC, UPSC, MPSC, NCERT 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Shah Jahan's reign is often called the 'GOLDEN AGE' of Mughal:

(A) Architecture (peak of building)
(B) Military conquests in territories
(C) Religious tolerance and unity
(D) Trade with European countries
cards.back:
(A) Architecture (peak of building)

Mughal Empire — SHAH JAHAN's REIGN (1628-1658) — universally regarded as the ARCHITECTURAL ZENITH of the Mughal era. KEY ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) TAJ MAHAL (Agra, 1632-48). (2) RED FORT (Delhi, 1639-48). (3) JAMA MASJID (Delhi, 1650-56). (4) Moti Masjid (Pearl Mosque) at Agra Fort. (5) Sheesh Mahal (Mirror Palace, Lahore). (6) Wazir Khan Mosque (Lahore). (7) Shalimar Gardens (Lahore, Kashmir). (8) Restoration/extension of Akbar's Agra Fort. STYLE: marriage of Persian, Islamic, Indian architecture; emphasis on white MARBLE, intricate INLAY WORK (pietra dura), perfect SYMMETRY, geometrical gardens (charbagh). UNESCO HERITAGE SITES from his era: Taj Mahal (1983), Red Fort (2007), Agra Fort (1983), Lahore Fort (1981 — in Pakistan). MILITARY: also significant — recovery of Kandahar (1638, but lost again 1648), Deccan campaigns, but military expansion was less than father Akbar. RELIGIOUS POLICY: more orthodox than Akbar but not as harsh as Aurangzeb. ECONOMIC: empire's WEALTH at peak; GDP estimates ~25% of world's GDP under Shah Jahan. cards.front:
WHO imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort during the WAR OF SUCCESSION?

(A) Aurangzeb (his third son)
(B) Dara Shikoh (his eldest son)
(C) Murad Bakhsh (fourth son)
(D) Shuja (the second son)
cards.back:
(A) Aurangzeb (his third son)

Mughal Empire — AURANGZEB — Shah Jahan's THIRD son — emerged victorious in the WAR OF SUCCESSION (1657-1658), imprisoned his father, and ascended throne as Mughal Emperor. SHAH JAHAN'S 4 SONS: (1) DARA SHIKOH (eldest, ~1615-1659) — heir-apparent; LIBERAL, scholar, translated Upanishads to Persian (Sirr-e-Akbar); FAVOURED by Shah Jahan. (2) SHAH SHUJA (~1616-1660) — Governor of Bengal; rebellious. (3) AURANGZEB (Mohi-ud-din, 1618-1707) — Governor of Deccan; orthodox, ruthless military strategist. (4) MURAD BAKHSH (~1624-1661) — Governor of Gujarat; weaker. WAR OF SUCCESSION (1657-58) — sparked when Shah Jahan FELL ILL (1657); rumors he was dying. KEY BATTLES: (1) Battle of DHARMAT (April 1658) — Aurangzeb defeated imperial forces. (2) Battle of SAMUGARH (May 1658) — DECISIVE; Aurangzeb crushed Dara Shikoh near Agra. (3) Aurangzeb captured Agra Fort (June 1658), imprisoned Shah Jahan. (4) Aurangzeb crowned himself July 1658 at Shahjahanabad. (5) Pursued and KILLED Dara Shikoh (Aug 1659, Delhi). (6) Eliminated brothers Shuja, Murad. SHAH JAHAN's FATE: imprisoned in Agra Fort (Musamman Burj — view of Taj Mahal); cared for by daughter JAHANARA. Died 1666. AURANGZEB ruled 1658-1707, expanded Mughal empire to greatest extent but seeds of decline. PYQ FREQUENCY: war of succession in SSC, UPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
DARA SHIKOH, Shah Jahan's eldest son, is famous as a:

(A) Scholar who translated Upanishads
(B) Military commander who never lost
(C) Founder of the Maratha empire
(D) Naval admiral on western coast
cards.back:
(A) Scholar who translated Upanishads

Mughal Empire — DARA SHIKOH (1615-1659) — Shah Jahan's eldest son, heir-apparent. PHILOSOPHIC LIBERAL: deeply interested in Hindu philosophy, Sufism, comparative religion. WORKS: (1) MAJMA-UL-BAHRAIN ('Mingling of the Two Oceans') — comparative essay on Hinduism and Islam, finding common ground. (2) SIRR-E-AKBAR ('Great Secret') — Persian translation of 50 UPANISHADS (Hindu philosophical texts); MAJOR cultural milestone — gave Europe access to Hindu philosophy via Persian → Latin (Schopenhauer cited it). (3) Translated YOGA-VASISHTHA, BHAGAVAD GITA into Persian. (4) Wrote SAFINAT-UL-AULIYA on Sufi saints. PHILOSOPHY: believed Hinduism and Islam were SAME core truth in different forms; sought religious harmony — much like his great-grandfather AKBAR. POLITICAL OPPONENTS: orthodox ulema (Muslim clergy) viewed him as HERETIC — fueled their support for AURANGZEB (orthodox). DEATH: defeated at Samugarh (1658), captured 1659, executed by AURANGZEB on charges of HERESY (Aug 1659, Delhi). His tomb is in HUMAYUN'S TOMB COMPLEX. LEGACY: 'WHAT IF DARA HAD WON?' is a famous historical counterfactual; some scholars argue Mughal empire (and India) might have evolved differently — more pluralistic, possibly delayed colonial collapse. RECENT: efforts to rehabilitate Dara Shikoh's image in modern India (street renaming, exhibitions). PYQ FREQUENCY: Dara Shikoh in UPSC History optional, modern history.

cards.front:
Which architect is credited as the chief designer of the TAJ MAHAL?

(A) Ustad Ahmad Lahauri (chief architect)
(B) Mirza Ghiyas Beg (Itimad-ud-Daulah)
(C) Geronimo Veroneo (Italian, debunked)
(D) Vidyadhar (Jaipur architect later)
cards.back:
(A) Ustad Ahmad Lahauri (chief architect)

Mughal Empire — USTAD AHMAD LAHAURI — credited as the CHIEF ARCHITECT of the Taj Mahal. He was an Iranian-origin engineer-architect; led a team of designers including Mir Abd-ul-Karim, Makramat Khan, and others. STYLE INFLUENCES: (1) Persian / Timurid mausoleum tradition (Gur-e-Amir in Samarkand, Humayun's Tomb in Delhi). (2) Islamic geometric symmetry. (3) Indian craftsmanship, jali (latticework). (4) European decorative motifs (introduced through Mughal court). EARLIER MUGHAL ARCHITECT FAMILY: HUMAYUN'S TOMB (built 1565-72 by his widow Hamida Banu, designed by Mirak Mirza Ghiyas) is considered the PROTOTYPE of Taj Mahal architecturally — same charbagh garden, central dome, symmetric layout. ITIMAD-UD-DAULAH'S TOMB (1622-28, Agra) — built for Nur Jahan's father; called 'BABY TAJ' for its pietra dura precursor. THESE EARLIER WORKS led to Taj Mahal's perfection. EUROPEAN MYTH: 17th-century European traveller Manucci speculated GERONIMO VERONEO (Italian) designed Taj — DISCREDITED. Indian and Muslim architects led the design. WORKERS: 20,000+ workers (master craftsmen from across the empire — Bukhara, Persia, Italy for stones), thousands of masons + 1,000 elephants. CONSTRUCTION: 1632-48. UNESCO HERITAGE 1983. PYQ FREQUENCY: Taj Mahal architect in UPSC History optional, NCERT 1× per 2 cycles.

(B) 1628, after the death of his father Jahangir
(C) 1658, succeeding his elder brother Dara Shukoh
(D) 1707, after the death of his son Aurangzeb
cards.back:
(B) 1628, after the death of his father Jahangir

Mughal Empire — Shah Jahan — born 1592 as Khurram, third son of Jahangir. Crowned in Agra on 14 February 1628 after his father Jahangir died (Oct 1627) and a brief succession struggle. Reigned 1628-1658. Distractor 1 = Jahangir's accession (after Akbar). Distractor 3 = Aurangzeb's accession after defeating Dara Shukoh in war. Distractor 4 = post-Aurangzeb period (Bahadur Shah I).

The TAJ MAHAL was commissioned by Shah Jahan in memory of:

(A) Nur Jahan, the famous wife of his father Jahangir
(B) Mumtaz Mahal, his wife who died in childbirth in 1631
(C) Jahanara, his eldest daughter, devoted companion late
(D) Hamida Banu, his great-grandmother in the Mughal line
cards.back:
(B) Mumtaz Mahal, his wife who died in childbirth in 1631

Mughal Empire — Mumtaz Mahal (Arjumand Banu Begum) — Shah Jahan's chief consort. Died on 17 June 1631 in Burhanpur giving birth to her 14th child. Construction of the Taj at Agra started 1632, finished c. 1648-53. Chief architect — Ustad Ahmad Lahauri. UNESCO 1983. Distractor 1 = Jahangir's wife. Distractor 3 = his daughter who survived him; supported him during his last years in captivity. Distractor 4 = Akbar's mother (Humayun's wife).

Shah Jahan moved the Mughal capital from Agra to a newly built city. That new capital was called:

(A) Fatehpur Sikri, also called the abandoned capital
(B) Shahjahanabad, today the Old Delhi area
(C) Akbarabad, named in honour of his grandfather
(D) Lahore, the imperial capital of the Punjab area
cards.back:
(B) Shahjahanabad, today the Old Delhi area

Mughal Empire — Shahjahanabad — new walled capital city built between 1639 and 1648 around the Red Fort (Lal Qila); centred on Chandni Chowk. Today this area is OLD DELHI. Capital shifted from Agra to Shahjahanabad in 1648. Distractor 1 — Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's capital (abandoned ~1585). Distractor 3 — Akbarabad was an alternative name for Agra under the Mughals. Distractor 4 — Lahore was an important provincial capital but not founded by Shah Jahan.

cards.front:
The famous PEACOCK THRONE (Takht-i-Taus), commissioned by Shah Jahan and adorned with the Koh-i-Noor among other gems, was eventually:

(A) Destroyed by fire during a sack of Delhi in 1739
(B) Carried away as plunder by Nadir Shah of Persia in 1739
(C) Sent to England by Aurangzeb as a gift to King Charles
(D) Buried at Akbar's tomb at Sikandra during the 1857 revolt
cards.back:
(B) Carried away as plunder by Nadir Shah of Persia in 1739

Mughal Empire — Peacock Throne — built 1635, took ~7 years; chief jeweller Bebadal Khan. Adorned with Koh-i-Noor, Timur Ruby, Akbar Shah Diamond. Nadir Shah of Persia sacked Delhi (Mar 1739) defeating Muhammad Shah Rangila and carried off the Peacock Throne to Iran. The original throne was later destroyed / disassembled in Persia after his assassination (1747); the Koh-i-Noor passed through Persians, Afghans, Sikhs (Ranjit Singh), and finally to the British (1849, after annexation of Punjab). Distractor 1 — destroyed in transit, not by fire. Distractor 3 — invented. Distractor 4 — invented.

The succession war (1657-58) at the end of Shah Jahan's reign was won by:

(A) Dara Shukoh, the eldest son and Shah Jahan's chosen heir
(B) Aurangzeb, the third son who defeated his three brothers
(C) Shuja, the second son and governor of Bengal
(D) Murad Bakhsh, the fourth son and governor of Gujarat
cards.back:
(B) Aurangzeb, the third son who defeated his three brothers

Mughal Empire — Shah Jahan fell ill in 1657 → triggered succession war among his four sons: DARA SHUKOH (eldest, liberal scholar, Shah Jahan's choice, translator of Upanishads as Sirr-i-Akbar); SHUJA (Bengal); AURANGZEB (Deccan, orthodox); MURAD (Gujarat). Aurangzeb allied tactically with Murad to defeat Dara at Battle of Samugarh (1658), then betrayed Murad. Imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort (he died there 1666, watching the Taj from his window). Aurangzeb crowned 1658, ruled 1658-1707. Distractor 1 — Dara was beheaded by Aurangzeb in 1659.

cards.front:
Shah Jahan spent his last years (1658-1666) confined inside which fort by Aurangzeb?

(A) Red Fort at Delhi, his own newly built capital seat
(B) Agra Fort, with a view of the Taj Mahal across the Yamuna
(C) Lahore Fort, in the western reaches of the empire
(D) Gwalior Fort, traditional Mughal high-security prison
cards.back:
(B) Agra Fort, with a view of the Taj Mahal across the Yamuna

Mughal Empire — Aurangzeb imprisoned his father in the AGRA FORT, not Delhi's Red Fort, in 1658. He spent 8 years there until his death in January 1666. The fort sits on the right bank of the Yamuna, with Taj Mahal a couple of km downstream. The famous Musamman Burj — the small octagonal tower in Agra Fort with a marble lattice screen overlooking the Yamuna — is where Shah Jahan is said to have spent his final hours gazing at the Taj. Tended by his daughter Jahanara, who voluntarily shared his confinement. Buried beside Mumtaz Mahal in the Taj.

cards.option2: Lahore Fort, in the western reaches of the empire
cards.option3: Gwalior Fort, traditional Mughal high-security prison

cards.front:
The BHAKTI MOVEMENT in medieval India emphasised:

(A) Strict ritualism + caste hierarchy
(B) Personal DEVOTION (bhakti) to a single God
(C) Renunciation + monastic life
(D) Animal sacrifice
cards.back:
(B) Personal DEVOTION (bhakti) to a single God

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — BHAKTI MOVEMENT — religious reform movement in India that emphasised DEVOTION (bhakti) to a personal God as the path to salvation, over Vedic ritualism + priestly intermediaries. ORIGINS: South India 7th-12th c. with the ALVARS (Vaishnavite saints devoted to Vishnu, 12 of them) + NAYANARS (Shaivite saints devoted to Shiva, 63 of them) — composed hymns in TAMIL. KEY FEATURES: (1) Direct devotion to God, no need for Brahmin intermediary; (2) rejection of caste discrimination — saints came from low + high castes alike; (3) use of REGIONAL languages (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Punjabi) instead of Sanskrit; (4) composed DEVOTIONAL POETRY accessible to masses; (5) emphasis on unity of God (monotheism or monism). SPREAD TO NORTH INDIA — from 13th-17th c. via saints like Ramananda, Kabir, Nanak, Chaitanya, Meerabai, Tulsidas, Surdas. DIVIDED into SAGUNA (God with form — e.g. Rama, Krishna devotion: Tulsidas, Surdas, Meera) + NIRGUNA (God without form — e.g., Kabir, Nanak). HISTORICAL SIGNIFICANCE: promoted HINDU-MUSLIM synthesis, democratised religion, enriched regional literature, laid foundation for modern Indian vernaculars. CONTEMPORARY SUFI movement in Islam had parallel themes. rejection of elaborate ritual + caste distinctions; use of REGIONAL LANGUAGES.

cards.front:
KABIR (c. 1440-1518) was the disciple of which teacher, and he rejected the distinctions of both Hinduism + Islam?

(A) Shankaracharya
(B) RAMANANDA
(C) Ramanuja
(D) Madhvacharya
cards.back:
(B) RAMANANDA

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — KABIR (c. 1440-1518) — one of the greatest NIRGUNA bhakti saints of N India. BIRTH: said to be born to a Brahmin widow, abandoned + raised by a MUSLIM WEAVER family in Varanasi (hence Kabir — an Arabic name meaning 'the great'). DISCIPLE OF RAMANANDA — the 14th-c. Vaishnavite saint based in Varanasi, himself a disciple-tradition successor of Ramanuja. Ramananda broke caste barriers by teaching bhakti to ALL — his 12 named disciples included Kabir (weaver-Muslim), Ravidas (chamar), Sena (barber), Dhanna (Jat peasant), Pipa (Rajput king), Padmavati (woman), etc. KABIR'S TEACHINGS: (1) ONE formless God (Nirguna); (2) Rejected idolatry, pilgrimage, rituals of BOTH Hindus + Muslims; (3) Criticised caste distinctions (some of the sharpest social critiques in Indian literature — 'If God is in a mosque, whose is the world outside?'); (4) Advocated unity of all religions; (5) used the metaphor of God as the unseen weaver. WORKS: DOHAS (couplets) + SAKHIS; compiled in BIJAK (by his Kabirpanthi followers); 500+ of his verses in the GURU GRANTH SAHIB. DEATH MYTH: died at MAGHAR (near Gorakhpur, UP) — deliberately to reject the superstition that death at Varanasi guarantees moksha; when his followers quarrelled over burial (Muslim) vs cremation (Hindu), his body was said to turn into flowers — divided between the two. Kabirpanthis remain active today. the Vaishnavite saint of Varanasi who opened bhakti to all castes + faiths.

cards.front:
GURU NANAK DEV (1469-1539), founder of Sikhism, was born in:

(A) Amritsar, Punjab
(B) TALWANDI
(C) Delhi
(D) Patna
cards.back:
(B) TALWANDI

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — GURU NANAK DEV JI (1469-1539) — founder of SIKHISM, first of the TEN SIKH GURUS. BIRTH: 15 April 1469, TALWANDI village, now called NANKANA SAHIB in honour of him, in Punjab, Pakistan (~75 km from Lahore). BIRTH ANNIVERSARY ('Gurpurab') celebrated on full moon of Kartik (Nov). TEACHINGS: (1) IK ONKAR — 'One Supreme God'; (2) rejected caste, ritualism, blind faith; (3) equality of men + women; (4) three pillars — NAAM JAPO (meditate on God's name), KIRAT KARO (honest work), VAND CHAKKO (share with others); (5) LANGAR (community kitchen) — free meal for all, regardless of caste/religion. UDASIS: undertook FOUR great travels (udasis) across S Asia, W Asia, Tibet — met Muslim Sufis + Hindu yogis. COMPANION: his Muslim minstrel BHAI MARDANA accompanied him. FOUNDED KARTARPUR: last years at Kartarpur (now in Pak Punjab, visible from Dera Baba Nanak in India — Kartarpur Corridor opened Nov 2019 for pilgrims). SUCCESSOR: named BHAI LEHNA as his successor + renamed him Guru Angad (2nd Sikh Guru). COMPOSITIONS: 974 hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib (JAPJI SAHIB being the most famous — recited daily by Sikhs). Guru Nanak is revered by Hindus, Sikhs, + many Muslims; called 'BABA NANAK' affectionately. now NANKANA SAHIB, in Pakistan's Punjab.

cards.front:
MEERABAI, the Rajput princess-poet devoted to Krishna, belonged to which royal house?

(A) Chittor (Sisodia Rajputs)
(B) MARRIED into MEWAR (Sisodia) house of CHITTOR but was a princess of MERTA (Rathore) branch in Marwar — a grand-daughter of Rao Duda
(C) Amber (Kachwaha)
(D) Marwar (Jodhpur)
cards.back:
(B) MARRIED into MEWAR (Sisodia) house of CHITTOR but was a princess of MERTA (Rathore) branch in Marwar — a grand-daughter of Rao Duda

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — MEERABAI (c. 1498-1547) — greatest WOMAN bhakti saint-poet. BIRTH: MERTA (Rajasthan) in the Rathore clan; grand-daughter of Rao Duda of Merta. MARRIAGE: at ~18 to BHOJRAJ, crown prince of Mewar (Chittor, Sisodia Rajputs); son of RANA SANGA. Bhojraj died young (~1521 from war wounds). WIDOWHOOD: Meera refused to commit Sati, refused to worship family deity Durga (her loyalty was to Krishna alone); faced persecution from in-laws — Rana VIKRAMADITYA (her brother-in-law) tried to poison her (legend: the poison turned to nectar) + sent a serpent in a basket (turned into Krishna's garland). She left Chittor + wandered as a wandering devotee. DEATH: ~1547 at DWARKA (Gujarat), said to merge into the image of Krishna at Dwarkadhish temple. DEVOTION: to KRISHNA, whom she called 'GIRDHAR NAGAR' / 'Giridhar Gopal' — envisioning herself as his eternal wife. BHAJANS: composed in Rajasthani + Braj Bhasha; hundreds survive; themes of divine love, rejection of worldly ties, defiance of patriarchy. Famous bhajans: 'Mere to Giridhar Gopal', 'Paayo ji maine Ram Ratan Dhan Paayo'. ICONIC for CHALLENGING Rajput feudal + patriarchal norms; early 'feminist' voice in Indian literature; revered across N India. Shortcut for memorisation: MEERA = Merta-born, Mewar-married, Krishna-devoted.

cards.front:
TULSIDAS (1532-1623) is known for composing the:

(A) Valmiki Ramayana
(B) RAMCHARITMANAS
(C) Kamba Ramayanam
(D) Bhagavad Gita
cards.back:
(B) RAMCHARITMANAS

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — TULSIDAS (1532-1623) — greatest SAGUNA bhakti poet of North India, devotee of Lord RAMA. MAGNUM OPUS: RAMCHARITMANAS ('The Lake of the Deeds of Rama'), started 1574 at Ayodhya; composed in AWADHI (a dialect of Hindi) — breaking with the Sanskrit norm so that common folk could read + sing it. Still the most-read Hindu religious text in the Hindi belt; basis of Ramleela performances across N India (UNESCO ICH 2005). STRUCTURE: 7 KANDAS (like Valmiki Ramayana) — Bal, Ayodhya, Aranya, Kishkindha, Sundar, Lanka, Uttar. OTHER WORKS: Vinay Patrika, Kavitavali, Hanuman Chalisa (40 verses — most-recited Hindu devotional in India). LIFE: born in Rajapur (Chitrakoot region), UP; guru was Narharidas; lived mostly at Varanasi + Chitrakoot. LEGEND: inspired to retell Ramayana when his wife RATNAVALI chided him for his excessive attachment to her saying 'If you loved Rama as you love me, you'd attain Him' — transformed Tulsidas into a renunciate + poet-saint. CONTRIBUTION: (1) made Rama bhakti central to Hindi-belt Hinduism; (2) literary standard for Awadhi; (3) Hanuman Chalisa — most popular Indian devotional text today; (4) influenced Vaishnava culture + the conception of ideal king (RAMA-RAJYA). Contemporary of Akbar + Abul Fazl. retelling of the Rama story in AWADHI (a dialect of Hindi), making it accessible to non-Sanskrit-reading masses.

cards.front:
SHANKARACHARYA (Adi Shankara, 788-820 CE) propounded the philosophy of:

(A) Vishishtadvaita (qualified non-dualism)
(B) ADVAITA VEDANTA — absolute non-dualism: Brahman is the only reality; the world is Maya (illusion); Atman = Brahman
(C) Dvaita (dualism)
(D) Shuddhadvaita
cards.back:
(B) ADVAITA VEDANTA — absolute non-dualism: Brahman is the only reality; the world is Maya (illusion); Atman = Brahman

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — ADI SHANKARACHARYA (788-820 CE) — philosopher-saint from KALADI (Kerala); FOUNDER of ADVAITA VEDANTA (pure non-dualism). CORE DOCTRINE: BRAHMAN is the only ultimate reality (sat-chit-ananda — existence-consciousness-bliss); the phenomenal world (jagat) is MAYA (appearance); the individual soul (ATMAN) is IDENTICAL with Brahman ('Aham Brahmasmi', 'Tat Tvam Asi'). Liberation (moksha) = realisation of this identity. ACHIEVEMENT: in a short 32-year life, he: (1) travelled all of India debating scholars (DIG-VIJAYA); (2) wrote commentaries (bhashyas) on 10 Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, Brahma Sutras (the 'PRASTHANATRAYI'); (3) authored Vivekachudamani, Bhaja Govindam, Saundaryalahari, etc.; (4) established FOUR MATHAS (monastic seats) in India's four corners: Sringeri (South, Karnataka), Dwarka (West, Gujarat), Jyotirmath/Badrinath (North, UK), Puri (East, Odisha); (5) organised DASHANAMI SANNYASA tradition (10 orders of monks); (6) revived + reformulated Hinduism against Buddhist + Jain ascendancy of his time. CHALLENGER: RAMANUJA (1017-1137) later developed VISHISHTADVAITA ('qualified non-dualism') — Brahman is real + the world + souls are His attributes, not illusion. MADHVACHARYA (1238-1317) went further with DVAITA ('dualism') — God, soul, world are distinct. VALLABHA — Shuddhadvaita. NIMBARKA — Dvaitadvaita.

cards.front:
CHAITANYA MAHAPRABHU (1486-1534), who popularised the worship of Krishna through Sankirtan (congregational chanting), was based primarily in:

(A) Vrindavan, Mathura
(B) NABADWIP (Bengal) + PURI (Odisha)
(C) Ujjain
(D) Kashi (Varanasi)
cards.back:
(B) NABADWIP (Bengal) + PURI (Odisha)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — CHAITANYA MAHAPRABHU (1486-1534) / 'Gauranga' — Bengal's greatest bhakti saint; founder of GAUDIYA VAISHNAVISM. BIRTH: NABADWIP / Navadweep, Nadia district, West Bengal (an ancient centre of Sanskrit learning — sometimes called 'Oxford of Bengal'). Initially a scholar; renounced worldly life at 24 after receiving initiation from Ishwara Puri in Gaya. Spent most of his later years in PURI (Odisha) — at the Jagannath temple. TEACHINGS: (1) Most intense devotion to KRISHNA + RADHA as the supreme couple — 'Krishna-prema'; (2) method = SANKIRTAN / Nama-sankirtan — congregational chanting of God's name, esp. the 16-word MAHA-MANTRA 'Hare Krishna Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna Hare Hare, Hare Rama Hare Rama, Rama Rama Hare Hare'; (3) open to ALL, regardless of caste or creed; (4) emotional devotion (bhava bhakti) as supreme means to moksha. SIX GOSWAMIS: his learned disciples — Rupa, Sanatana, Raghunatha Bhatta, Raghunatha Dasa, Gopala Bhatta, Jiva — systematised his theology + rebuilt Vrindavan's Krishna temples. MODERN IMPACT: ISKCON (International Society for Krishna Consciousness, founded 1966 by A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada) directly descends from Gaudiya Vaishnavism — took 'Hare Krishna' movement worldwide. AUROBINDO + TAGORE were both influenced by Chaitanya's Bengal Vaishnav tradition. DEATH: 1534 in Puri (some say drowned in the sea in a trance; others that he merged with the Jagannath deity). founded the GAUDIYA VAISHNAVISM tradition.

cards.front:
SURDAS, the blind poet-saint, composed his devotional poetry primarily about which deity, and in which language?

(A) Shiva in Sanskrit
(B) BAAL KRISHNA (child Krishna) in BRAJ BHASHA
(C) Rama in Awadhi
(D) Durga in Bengali
cards.back:
(B) BAAL KRISHNA (child Krishna) in BRAJ BHASHA

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — SURDAS (c. 1478-1583 — traditionally) — one of the eight poets of the ASHTACHHAP (founded by VALLABHACHARYA + his son Vitthalnath) at the Shrinathji temple of Govardhan (near Mathura). Devotee of BAAL KRISHNA — the child Krishna in his Vrindavan exploits. LANGUAGE: BRAJ BHASHA (a dialect of Hindi spoken around Mathura/Vrindavan). MAGNUM OPUS: SUR SAGAR ('Ocean of Sur') — 1,00,000 verses traditionally attributed (4,000-5,000 extant); focuses on Krishna's childhood pranks (gopikas' butter theft, Kaliya dance, lifting Govardhan, etc.) + Bhramar-Geet. BLINDNESS: Sur was said to be born blind; yet his poetry describes visual scenes (Krishna's face, Yamuna banks, gopis' expressions) so vividly that poets considered it divine vision; some scholars dispute whether he was literally blind. PHILOSOPHY: belonged to Vallabhacharya's PUSHTI MARGA (Shuddhadvaita / path of Divine Grace) sampradaya. Sur's bhajans are sung daily at Shrinathji Nathdwara (Rajasthan). ASHTACHHAP POETS: Surdas, Kumbhandas, Parmanandadas, Krishnadas (first four disciples of Vallabha) + Govindswami, Chaturbhujdas, Chhitswami, Nanddas (disciples of Vitthalnath). Surdas is celebrated alongside TULSIDAS (Rama) + KABIR (nirguna) + MEERA (Krishna-wife) as the SAGUNA + NIRGUNA twin pillars of N Indian bhakti. his magnum opus is the SUR SAGAR.

cards.front:
Match the Bhakti saint with their region / language of composition: (1) TUKARAM — ? (2) NAMDEV — ? (3) BASAVA — ? (4) NARSINH MEHTA — ?

(A) Gujarati, Tamil, Punjabi, Bengali
(B) MARATHI (Maharashtra); MARATHI (Maharashtra); KANNADA (Karnataka); GUJARATI (Gujarat)
(C) Hindi, Marathi, Telugu, Gujarati
(D) Punjabi, Hindi, Kannada, Marathi
cards.back:
(B) MARATHI (Maharashtra); MARATHI (Maharashtra); KANNADA (Karnataka); GUJARATI (Gujarat)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — BHAKTI SAINTS by REGION + LANGUAGE: (1) TUKARAM (1608-1650) — Maharashtra, MARATHI, devotee of Vithoba (Pandharpur); composed ABHANGAS; contemporary of Shivaji (guru-figure to him); drowned mysteriously at Dehu (disappeared 'taken to heaven by Vishnu', per tradition). (2) NAMDEV (1270-1350) — Maharashtra, MARATHI, also a Vithoba devotee; earlier saint of the Warkari tradition; 61 of his hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib. (3) BASAVA / BASAVANNA (1105-1168) — KARNATAKA, KANNADA; founded LINGAYATISM / VIRASHAIVISM; composed VACHANAS (free-verse sayings); fought caste + championed women's equality; built the Anubhava Mantapa (hall of spiritual experience) at Basavakalyan. (4) NARSINH MEHTA (1414-1481) — GUJARAT, GUJARATI; 'AADI KAVI' (first poet) of Gujarati; composed 'VAISHNAV JAN TO' — Gandhi's favourite bhajan (sung at Sabarmati + every 2 October to date). Devoted to Krishna. OTHER regional saints: (5) JNANESHWAR (1275-1296) — Marathi, wrote Jnaneshwari (Gita commentary); (6) EKNATH — Marathi; (7) ANDAL — Tamil (only female Alvar); (8) LAL DED (Lalleshwari) — Kashmiri, Shaivite; (9) SANKARDEV — Assamese (Ek-Sharana Naam-Dharma); (10) VEMANA — Telugu. Regional diversity of the Bhakti movement made it a pan-Indian phenomenon + enriched all vernaculars.

cards.front:
'VAISHNAV JAN TO TENE KAHIYE' — Mahatma Gandhi's favourite bhajan describing the qualities of a true Vaishnavite — was composed by:

(A) Tulsidas
(B) NARSINH MEHTA, the 15th-century Gujarati bhakti saint + 'Aadi Kavi' of Gujarati literature
(C) Meerabai
(D) Surdas
cards.back:
(B) NARSINH MEHTA, the 15th-century Gujarati bhakti saint + 'Aadi Kavi' of Gujarati literature

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — 'VAISHNAV JAN TO TENE KAHIYE, JE PEED PARAYI JANE RE' ('Call him a Vaishnav who feels the pain of others') — composed by NARSINH MEHTA (1414-1481), the Gujarati bhakti poet-saint of Junagadh. GANDHI'S FAVOURITE BHAJAN: sung every morning at Sabarmati Ashram + at Gandhi's memorial services at Rajghat each 2 October + 30 January. It distils Gandhi's own ethical vision — compassion, absence of ego, detachment, equal treatment of all, service to others. The lyrics list the qualities: (a) feels others' pain; (b) helps the needy without ego; (c) praises none, criticises none; (d) purifies the lineage of 71 generations; (e) faithful in word-thought-deed + worships Rama; (f) treats women as mother; (g) unmoved by greed or lust; (h) forsook false speech; (i) never touched others' wealth; (j) beyond illusions of Maya. NARSINH MEHTA: called the 'AADI KAVI' (first poet) of GUJARATI literature; devotee of KRISHNA; lived in Junagadh, Saurashtra; composed in Gujarati. Popular legends include: God himself filling in Narsinh's debts through miraculous hundis (promissory notes); Krishna dancing as Ras-Leela with him; giving him a HAAR (garland) from Krishna for an exchange of marriage at Dwarka. PM Modi has referenced 'Vaishnav Jan' often — reflects shared Gujarati heritage with Gandhi + Narsinh.

cards.front:
The BHAKTI MOVEMENT in medieval India was a religious-reform movement that emphasised:

(A) Strict caste-based ritual hierarchy
(B) Personal devotion to a chosen God
(C) Conversion to Islamic faith
(D) Memorising Vedic Sanskrit hymns
cards.back:
(B) Personal devotion to a chosen God

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — BHAKTI = devotion (Sanskrit). Bhakti movement (~7th-17th c. CE) emphasised: (1) personal devotion (BHAKTI) to a chosen deity (ISHTA-DEVATA); (2) rejection of caste discrimination + ritual elaborateness; (3) use of VERNACULAR (regional) languages — not Sanskrit; (4) accessibility to all (women, low castes, illiterate); (5) emotional + lyrical worship via songs (BHAJAN, KIRTAN). Started in TAMIL South (Alvars + Nayanars, 6-9th c.), spread north (12-17th c.). Contemporary with Sufi movement in Islam.

KABIR (15th c.), the great Bhakti saint, is associated with which philosophy?

(A) Saguna Bhakti (deity worship with form)
(B) Nirguna Bhakti (formless God; Hindu-Muslim unity)
(C) Vedanta school of Adi Shankara only
(D) Strict Mimamsa school of Vedic philosophy
cards.back:
(B) Nirguna Bhakti (formless God; Hindu-Muslim unity)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — KABIR (~1440-1518 CE) — born in Banaras (Varanasi), weaver-by-trade. Disciple of RAMANANDA. Preached NIRGUNA BHAKTI — devotion to a FORMLESS, attribute-less God. Synthesised Hinduism + Islam: criticised idol worship (against orthodox Hindus), Quranic literalism (against orthodox Muslims), caste, ritualism. Compositions: Dohas (couplets), Sakhis, Padas. Followers: KABIRPANTHIS. His verses in Guru Granth Sahib (Sikh holy book). SAGUNA Bhakti = with form (Tulsi, Surdas, Mira). NIRGUNA = without form (Kabir, Nanak, Dadu, Raidas).

cards.option3: Strict Mimamsa school of Vedic philosophy

TULSIDAS, the Bhakti saint who composed 'Ramcharitmanas', wrote it in which language?

(A) Sanskrit, the classical language
(B) Awadhi, an Eastern Hindi dialect
(C) Persian, the Mughal court language
(D) Tamil, an ancient Dravidian tongue
cards.back:
(B) Awadhi, an Eastern Hindi dialect

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — TULSIDAS (1532-1623 CE) — wrote RAMCHARITMANAS (1574-77, in AWADHI — eastern Hindi dialect spoken in Awadh region around Ayodhya). A retelling of the Ramayana, focused on Rama-bhakti (Saguna). Hugely popular; recited even today across north India (Hanuman Chalisa, Vinaya Patrika are also his). Tulsidas's contribution: brought the Ramayana to common people in their language. Other VERNACULAR Bhakti texts: Bhakta-mala (Hindi), Krishna-bhakti by Surdas (Brajbhasha), Mira's bhajans (Brajbhasha + Rajasthani).

(C) Goddess Kali, the divine mother
(D) Lord Buddha, of the noble path
cards.back:

After husband's early death, devoted herself to KRISHNA — whom she called 'GIRIDHAR' (lifter of Govardhan), 'NAGAR' etc. Composed bhajans + padas in Brajbhasha + Rajasthani — songs of intense devotion. Faced persecution from in-laws (one tried to poison her). Became wandering devotee, eventually merged with Krishna idol at Dwarka per legend. One of the most prominent FEMALE Bhakti saints.

GURU NANAK (founder of Sikhism, 1469-1539) preached:

(C) Strict adherence to Vedic rituals
(D) Only the Buddhist Eight-fold Path
cards.back:

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — GURU NANAK DEV (1469-1539) — founder of SIKHISM, born at Talwandi (Nankana Sahib, Punjab). Preached: 'EK ONKAR' = ONE GOD (formless, eternal); rejected idolatry, caste, ritualism, untouchability; equality of men + women; honest livelihood (KIRAT KARO); sharing with others (VAND CHHAKO); meditation on God's name (NAAM JAPO). Three principles. Travelled across India + west Asia (UDASIS — 4 long journeys). Compositions in 'JAPJI SAHIB'. Initiated 'LANGAR' (community kitchen — eats together, regardless of caste). His teachings + 9 successor Gurus' compiled into GURU GRANTH SAHIB (final Guru, Sikhism).

JNANESHWARI (Bhavartha Dipika) — Marathi commentary on Bhagavad Gita; one of the foundational texts of Marathi literature. Founded the VARKARI sampradaya (devotees of VITHOBA at Pandharpur). Kabir's verses (dohas / sakhis) attack ritualism, idolatry, caste, religious orthodoxy. Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539), founder of Sikhism, was born at:

Travelled extensively — Mecca, Baghdad, Sri Lanka, Tibet — known as 'Udasis'. Settled at Kartarpur (also in Pakistan) in his last years. Died 22 September 1539. Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (1486-1534) — founder of Gaudiya Vaishnavism — preached the 'Hare Krishna' mantra and was born in:

cards.back:

Ramananda (c. 14th century) preached Bhakti in the Ganga valley and was Kabir's guru. Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas.

cards.front:
The Bhakti saint Mirabai is famous for her devotion to:

(A) Lord Shiva
(B) Lord Krishna
(C) Lord Rama
(D) Lord Ganesha
cards.back:
(B) Lord Krishna

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Mirabai (c. 1498-1547) — Rajput princess of Mewar — wrote passionate devotional songs to Krishna and left her palace to wander as a bhakta. She is part of the Nirguna-Saguna Bhakti tradition; her 'Meera Bhajans' are still sung across India. Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas) and Tyagaraja focus on Rama; Basavanna on Shiva (through the Virashaiva movement in Karnataka).

cards.front:
The most influential Sufi order in medieval India, based at the shrine of Khwaja Moinuddin at Ajmer, is the:

(A) Qadri silsila
(B) Chishti silsila
(C) Suhrawardi silsila
(D) Naqshbandi silsila
cards.back:
(B) Chishti silsila

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — The Chishti order was founded in India by Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (d. 1236) at Ajmer. Other great Chishti saints — Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi), Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (Delhi), Baba Farid (Ajodhan/Punjab), Shaikh Salim Chishti (Fatehpur Sikri). Suhrawardi order — centred in Multan. Qadri — popular in the Deccan. Naqshbandi — emphasised orthodoxy; Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani) opposed Din-i-Ilahi.

cards.front:
The Bhakti saint Ramanuja (11th-12th century) is known as the founder of:

(A) Advaita Vedanta
(B) Vishishtadvaita Vedanta
(C) Dvaita Vedanta
(D) Shuddhadvaita Vedanta
cards.back:
(B) Vishishtadvaita Vedanta

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Ramanuja (1017-1137) propagated Vishishtadvaita ('qualified non-dualism') — Brahman is one but qualified by real attributes of souls and matter. Advaita (pure non-dualism) — Adi Shankaracharya (788-820). Dvaita (dualism) — Madhvacharya (13th century). Shuddhadvaita (pure non-dualism with form) — Vallabhacharya (15th-16th century). Ramanuja led the Sri Vaishnava tradition from Srirangam.

cards.front:
Sant Kabir's verses are collected in a work called:

(A) Vinay Patrika
(B) Bijak
(C) Sur Sagar
(D) Padavali
cards.back:
(B) Bijak

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Kabir's dohas and verses are mainly preserved in the 'Bijak' (compiled by his followers). Selected verses also appear in the Guru Granth Sahib. Vinay Patrika is by Tulsidas; Sur Sagar by Surdas; Padavali is the common term for collected songs of several saints (e.g., Vidyapati's Padavali). Kabir rejected ritual, caste, idolatry, and stressed personal experience of one formless God.

cards.front:
Raja Ram Mohan Roy is often called the FATHER OF:

(A) Modern India / Indian Renaissance
(B) Indian Constitution (Ambedkar)
(C) Indian Nation (Gandhi)
(D) Indian Cinema (Dadasaheb Phalke)
cards.back:
(A) Modern India / Indian Renaissance

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — RAJA RAM MOHAN ROY (22 May 1772 - 27 September 1833) — called 'FATHER OF MODERN INDIA' / 'FATHER OF INDIAN RENAISSANCE' / 'FATHER OF BENGAL RENAISSANCE'. KEY ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) Founded BRAHMO SAMAJ (1828) — reformist Hindu monotheistic movement; rejected idol worship, polytheism, caste discrimination, child marriage, sati. (2) CRUSADED AGAINST SATI (widow self-immolation) → Lord William Bentinck's SATI ABOLITION ACT 1829 (XVII of 1829) — landmark social reform. (3) Promoted ENGLISH EDUCATION + Western science alongside Sanskrit + Persian education. (4) Started newspapers + journals: SAMBAD KAUMUDI (Bengali, 1821), MIRAT-UL-AKHBAR (Persian). (5) Translated Upanishads + Vedanta into English. (6) Advocated WIDOW REMARRIAGE, abolition of POLYGAMY, INHERITANCE rights for women. KEY TITLES: (a) 'Father of Modern India' — given by various scholars including S.D. Collet, biographer. (b) Title 'RAJA' was conferred on him by MUGHAL Emperor AKBAR II (1830) — for representing the emperor's case to the British. DEATH: died in BRISTOL, ENGLAND (27 Sept 1833) on a diplomatic mission for the Mughal court; buried in Arno's Vale Cemetery there. His tomb was later erected with funds raised by Brahmo Samaj. UPSC ANGLE: 19TH century social reform — GS-1 modern history; GS-4 ethics (women's rights, social reform). PYQ FREQUENCY: Ram Mohan Roy in UPSC, MPSC, SSC modern history — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
BRAHMO SAMAJ was founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in:

(A) 1828 (originally Brahmo Sabha)
(B) 1875 (Arya Samaj year)
(C) 1885 (Indian Nat Congress)
(D) 1857 (year of revolt)
cards.back:
(A) 1828 (originally Brahmo Sabha)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — BRAHMO SAMAJ (originally BRAHMO SABHA) — founded by Ram Mohan Roy on 20 AUGUST 1828 in CALCUTTA. PHILOSOPHY: monotheistic; worship of formless ONE GOD (Brahman); rejected: (a) Idolatry. (b) Caste discrimination. (c) Religious orthodoxy + meaningless rituals. (d) Sati. (e) Child marriage. (f) Polygamy. ACCEPTED: (a) Universal religion. (b) Reason + science. (c) Education for all. (d) Women's emancipation. KEY LEADERS POST-Ram Mohan: (1) DEBENDRANATH TAGORE (Rabindranath's father) — joined 1843; led organization 1843-1858. (2) KESHAB CHANDRA SEN — radical leader; created BRAHMO SAMAJ OF INDIA (1866 split from Adi Brahmo Samaj). (3) Pratap Chandra Mozoomdar, Rabindranath Tagore (philosophical inheritor). RELATED REFORM ORGANIZATIONS: (1) PRARTHANA SAMAJ (1867) — Maharashtra branch; founder R.G. BHANDARKAR + others; M.G. RANADE active member. (2) ARYA SAMAJ (1875) — by SWAMI DAYANANDA SARASWATI; emphasized Vedas; 'Back to Vedas' movement. (3) RAMAKRISHNA MISSION (1897) — by SWAMI VIVEKANANDA. (4) THEOSOPHICAL SOCIETY (1875) — Madame Blavatsky, Col. Olcott; later Annie Besant. (5) ALIGARH MOVEMENT (1875) — Sir Syed Ahmad Khan. UPSC angle: SOCIO-RELIGIOUS REFORMS in 19th-century India — GS-1; comparative analysis of reform movements. PYQ FREQUENCY: Brahmo Samaj founding year + leaders in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
SATI ABOLITION ACT (1829) was passed by which Governor-General with Ram Mohan Roy's support?

(A) Lord William Bentinck
(B) Lord Cornwallis (3rd Mysore War)
(C) Lord Wellesley (4th Mysore War)
(D) Lord Dalhousie (later, 1848-56)
cards.back:
(A) Lord William Bentinck

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — LORD WILLIAM BENTINCK (1828-35, 1st Governor-General of British India under 1833 Charter Act) — passed SATI ABOLITION REGULATION on 4 DECEMBER 1829 (Regulation XVII of 1829, Bengal Presidency; later extended to Madras + Bombay). KEY: criminalized SATI (or sahamarana — voluntary or forced widow self-immolation on husband's funeral pyre); offenders punishable as murderers. PRECONDITIONS: Ram Mohan Roy's persistent advocacy + petitions + writings + public pressure since ~1818. STATISTICS: ~700-800 sati cases recorded annually in Bengal in early 1800s. POST-ACT: orthodox Hindu groups initially OPPOSED via 'Dharma Sabha' (Calcutta, 1830); appealed to Privy Council in London — Privy Council in 1832 UPHELD the ban. Ram Mohan Roy went to England partly to argue this case. OTHER REFORMS by BENTINCK: (1) Abolition of THUGGEE (organized robber-murderer cult) — under Col. WILLIAM SLEEMAN (1830s). (2) Abolition of FEMALE INFANTICIDE in some communities. (3) ENGLISH as language of higher education + courts (Macaulay's MINUTE 1835 — under Bentinck). (4) Abolition of slavery (later, 1843 by Ellenborough's Act). LATER SATI REGULATIONS: SATI PREVENTION ACT 1987 (after Roop Kanwar incident in Rajasthan, 4 Sept 1987 — last documented sati case); declared sati + glorification of sati as criminal offences. UPSC angle: 19th-century social reform; women's rights timeline. PYQ FREQUENCY: Sati abolition in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Ram Mohan Roy promoted English education in opposition to which group's traditional Sanskrit education?

(A) Orthodox Hindu pandits (orientalists)
(B) Christian missionaries always
(C) Mughal court of Delhi only
(D) Buddhist monastery teachers
cards.back:
(A) Orthodox Hindu pandits (orientalists)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — ORIENTALIST vs ANGLICIST debate (1820s-1830s) was a major colonial education-policy debate: (1) ORIENTALISTS (e.g., H.H. Wilson, Sir William Jones, Henry Princep) — advocated continued use of CLASSICAL SANSKRIT/ARABIC/PERSIAN education for Indians. (2) ANGLICISTS (e.g., Lord Macaulay, William Bentinck, Charles Trevelyan) — argued for ENGLISH-medium education + Western sciences/literature. RAM MOHAN ROY was on the ANGLICIST side: he wrote a letter to Lord Amherst (1823) arguing AGAINST establishing a Sanskrit College for traditional learning, INSTEAD favoring SCIENCE + MATH + WESTERN learning. RATIONALE: (a) Scientific knowledge is in EUROPEAN languages now; modern education needed. (b) Limited resources should fund modern, not antiquated, learning. (c) English would open careers in govt + commerce. KEY MILESTONES: (1) HINDU COLLEGE Calcutta (1817) — co-founded by Ram Mohan Roy + David Hare; English-medium; later became Presidency College + Presidency University. (2) MACAULAY's MINUTE (1835) — settled the debate; English became OFFICIAL medium. (3) WOOD'S DESPATCH (1854) — 'Magna Carta of Indian Education'; established UNIVERSITIES of Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857). (4) RAJA RADHAKANTA DEB (~1838) opposed Roy's reform views — orthodox; founded Dharma Sabha. UPSC angle: education policy in colonial India + role in nationalism. PYQ FREQUENCY: orientalist-anglicist debate in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which BENGALI WEEKLY newspaper was started by Ram Mohan Roy in 1821?

(A) Sambad Kaumudi (Moon of Intelligence)
(B) Hindu Patrika (a different paper)
(C) Kesari (Bal Gangadhar Tilak)
(D) Indian Mirror (a Christian paper)
cards.back:
(A) Sambad Kaumudi (Moon of Intelligence)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — SAMBAD KAUMUDI ('Moon of Intelligence' / 'Moon of News') — Bengali weekly newspaper started by Raja Ram Mohan Roy in 4 DECEMBER 1821 in CALCUTTA. PURPOSE: to disseminate REFORMIST ideas, social-reform debates, modern thought to Bengali public. CONTENT: anti-sati editorials, anti-caste, women's rights, education, science, news. ALSO BY ROY: (1) MIRAT-UL-AKHBAR — Persian-language journal (1822-1823); discontinued after British press regulations (1823) restricted vernacular press. KEY EARLY INDIAN NEWSPAPERS / JOURNALS (memorize): (1) BENGAL GAZETTE (1780) — first Indian newspaper, by JAMES AUGUSTUS HICKY; called 'Hicky's Gazette'. (2) BANGAL DARPAN (1818) — by Ram Mohan + others; Bengali. (3) SAMBAD KAUMUDI (1821) — Bengali. (4) MIRAT-UL-AKHBAR (1822) — Persian. (5) SAMACHAR DARPAN (1818) — by Serampore Baptist Mission; Bengali. (6) BANGADOOT (1829) — by Roy. (7) SOMPRAKASH (1858) — by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar. (8) KESARI + MARATHA (1881) — by BAL GANGADHAR TILAK. (9) HINDU (1878, ENGLISH) — Madras; founded by G. Subramania Iyer + others. (10) AMRITA BAZAR PATRIKA (1868) — Bengal. (11) THE TRIBUNE (1881) — Punjab. PRESS REGULATIONS history: ADAMS REGULATIONS (1823) — restricted vernacular press; METCALFE'S 1835 LIBERATION; LYTTON'S VERNACULAR PRESS ACT 1878 (anti-Indian); REPEALED 1881 by Lord Ripon. UPSC angle: print media + colonial governance. PYQ FREQUENCY: Indian newspaper history in UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Ram Mohan Roy died in 1833 in which country?

(A) England (Bristol)
(B) India (Calcutta) at home
(C) France (Paris) at meeting
(D) America (Washington) abroad
cards.back:
(A) England (Bristol)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — RAM MOHAN ROY DIED on 27 SEPTEMBER 1833 in BRISTOL, England, age 61, of MENINGITIS. He was on an OFFICIAL DIPLOMATIC mission representing AKBAR II (Mughal Emperor) to discuss the EMPEROR'S PENSION + STIPEND with the BRITISH KING WILLIAM IV + East India Company directors. The mission also addressed RIGHTS related to the Mughal household. ARRIVAL IN ENGLAND: April 1831 in LIVERPOOL; received by British political/intellectual circles with great respect. He met King William IV; was the first INDIAN of high rank to visit England in this manner. WHILE IN ENGLAND: (1) Argued against repeal of Sati Abolition Act (Privy Council had upheld it 1832 — Roy's testimony key). (2) Lobbied for the Mughal pension. (3) Met JEREMY BENTHAM, Robert Owen, other British thinkers. (4) Toured England, France. BURIAL: ARNO'S VALE CEMETERY, BRISTOL. Tomb constructed 1843 by Dwarkanath Tagore (Brahmo Samaj patron, Rabindranath's grandfather) using funds raised by Brahmo Samaj. The Tomb is a popular pilgrimage site for Indian visitors to UK. STATUE in Bristol: 1997 BHASKAR ROY built statue near Bristol Council House. POST-INDIA: BRAHMO SAMAJ continued under Debendranath Tagore + Keshab Chandra Sen; eventually contributed to broader Indian Renaissance + nationalism. UPSC angle: ROY's role symbolizes early Indian engagement with WESTERN modernity + diplomacy. PYQ FREQUENCY: Roy's death location in UPSC, MPSC 1× per 2 cycles.

The mission also addressed RIGHTS related to the Mughal household. ARRIVAL IN ENGLAND: April 1831 in LIVERPOOL; received by British political/intellectual circles with great respect. He met King William IV; was the first INDIAN of high rank to visit England in this manner. WHILE IN ENGLAND: (1) Argued against repeal of Sati Abolition Act (Privy Council had upheld it 1832 — Roy's testimony key). (2) Lobbied for the Mughal pension. (3) Met JEREMY BENTHAM, Robert Owen, other British thinkers. (4) Toured England, France. BURIAL: ARNO'S VALE CEMETERY, BRISTOL. Tomb constructed 1843 by Dwarkanath Tagore (Brahmo Samaj patron, Rabindranath's grandfather) using funds raised by Brahmo Samaj. The Tomb is a popular pilgrimage site for Indian visitors to UK. STATUE in Bristol: 1997 BHASKAR ROY built statue near Bristol Council House. POST-INDIA: BRAHMO SAMAJ continued under Debendranath Tagore + Keshab Chandra Sen; eventually contributed to broader Indian Renaissance + nationalism. UPSC angle: ROY's role symbolizes early Indian engagement with WESTERN modernity + diplomacy. PYQ FREQUENCY: Roy's death location in UPSC, MPSC 1× per 2 cycles.

cards.front:
Ram Mohan Roy translated which Sanskrit text into ENGLISH (a key cultural-bridging contribution)?

(A) Upanishads + Vedanta works
(B) Mahabharata epic only here
(C) Ramayana epic in full text
(D) Manusmriti law-code only
cards.back:
(A) Upanishads + Vedanta works

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Ram Mohan Roy translated several UPANISHADS + VEDANTA texts into ENGLISH. KEY WORKS: (1) Translation of KENA, ISHA, KATHA, MUNDAKA UPANISHADS into English (1816-1819). (2) Books expounding UPANISHADIC philosophy + monotheism. (3) 'A Defence of Hindu Theism' — criticized idolatry. (4) 'Tuhfat-ul-Muwahhidin' (1804, in Persian + Arabic) — 'Gift to Monotheists' — early work questioning religious orthodoxy. (5) 'Precepts of Jesus' (1820) — extracted moral teachings of Jesus, set aside miracles + theological claims. PURPOSE: to show that HINDUISM at its philosophical core is MONOTHEISTIC; idolatry is later corruption. INFLUENCE in UK: his English-language scholarship gave WESTERN audiences direct access to Hindu philosophy; influenced TRANSCENDENTALISTS (Emerson, Thoreau in USA) and THEOSOPHISTS (Madame Blavatsky). PARALLEL to DARA SHIKOH (Mughal prince, 1657) who translated Upanishads into PERSIAN — Ram Mohan continued this cross-cultural tradition into English. PROFOUND SCHOLARLY contribution: he was conversant in SANSKRIT, ARABIC, PERSIAN, BENGALI, ENGLISH, HEBREW, GREEK — Renaissance-style polyglot. WORKS IN BENGALI: 'Vedant Grantha' (1815), 'Vedantasara' — popularizing Hindu philosophy. POETRY in Persian. UPSC ANGLE: BENGAL RENAISSANCE figures + their LITERARY contributions; Indian thought + Western interaction. PYQ FREQUENCY: Roy's literary works in UPSC, MPSC History optional, SSC GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
RAJA RAMMOHAN ROY, the 'Father of Modern India' + 'Father of Bengal Renaissance', founded:

(A) Prarthana Samaj
(B) BRAHMO SABHA
(C) Arya Samaj
(D) Ramakrishna Mission
cards.back:
(B) BRAHMO SABHA

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — RAJA RAMMOHAN ROY (1772-1833) — 'FATHER OF MODERN INDIA' + 'FATHER OF INDIAN RENAISSANCE' + 'MAKER OF MODERN INDIA'. Polymath — Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, English, Bengali, Hebrew + Greek. Born Radhanagar, Hooghly (Bengal). Worked for British EIC for a period. FOUNDED: (1) ATMIYA SABHA (1815) — Kolkata discussion group. (2) BRAHMO SABHA (20 Aug 1828) — monotheistic + reformist; later formalised as BRAHMO SAMAJ (1830). Worshipped one impersonal God; rejected idolatry + caste + Vedic infallibility; emphasized reason + humanism. KEY CAMPAIGNS + REFORMS: (1) AGAINST SATI (widow immolation) — campaigned from 1811 (witnessed his sister-in-law's Sati). Got LORD WILLIAM BENTINCK to PASS REGULATION XVII of 1829 (SATI BAN) — effective 4 DEC 1829 in Bengal; extended to all of India by 1830. Orthodox Hindus opposed; Rammohan defended the law + travelled to UK to lobby against repeal. (2) Against CASTE discrimination + untouchability. (3) Against CHILD MARRIAGE + POLYGAMY; for WIDOW REMARRIAGE. (4) For WOMEN's EDUCATION + property rights. (5) For ENGLISH + WESTERN scientific education (influenced Macaulay's Minute 1835 + Wood's Despatch 1854). Supported HINDU COLLEGE Calcutta 1817 (with David Hare + Radhakanta Deb). (6) Against Christian proselytising without reason (wrote 'Precepts of Jesus' 1820 — Jesus as a moral teacher). PUBLICATIONS: (a) 'Tuhfat al-Muwahhidin' (Arabic, 1803-04, 'A Gift to Monotheists') — first major work, against idolatry + superstition. (b) 'SAMBAD KAUMUDI' (Bengali newspaper 1821) + 'MIRAT-UL-AKHBAR' (Persian 1822) — early pioneering journalism; fought Adam's Press Regulations (1823, restrictive). TITLE 'RAJA': given by MUGHAL emperor AKBAR II in 1830; sent to UK on behalf of him to plead for increased pension. Died in BRISTOL, ENGLAND, 27 Sep 1833; buried at Arnos Vale Cemetery (visited by Modi in 2015 + current Indian PMs). First High-Profile Indian to visit UK with public reception. Rammohan = architect of BENGAL RENAISSANCE (19TH C. movement — Vidyasagar, Debendranath + Keshab Chandra Sen, Swami Vivekananda, Bankim Chandra, Tagore all part of it). BRAHMO SAMAJ LATER SPLIT: (1) KESHUB CHANDRA SEN broke off → Brahmo Samaj of India (1866). (2) DEBENDRANATH TAGORE (Rabindranath's father) led ADI BRAHMO SAMAJ — more traditional. (3) Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878) — SHIBNATH SHASTRI. Together contributed to 19th-c. reformism. monotheistic reformist society; campaigned against SATI (1829 ban), caste, child marriage, polygamy; 1828, later BRAHMO SAMAJ.

cards.front:
ISHWAR CHANDRA VIDYASAGAR, Bengal reformer, is most famous for:

(A) Opposition to English
(B) WIDOW REMARRIAGE ACT 1856
(C) Founding Brahmo Samaj
(D) Cow protection movement
cards.back:
(B) WIDOW REMARRIAGE ACT 1856

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — ISHWAR CHANDRA VIDYASAGAR (26 Sep 1820 – 29 Jul 1891) — leading 19th-c. Bengali polymath — scholar, educator, reformer, writer. Born Birsingha village, Midnapore, Bengal (then Bengal Presidency) into a poor Brahmin family. Studied at Sanskrit College Calcutta 1829-41; graduated with distinction in Sanskrit literature + grammar + Vedanta + Samkhya + Nyaya + smriti. Got title 'VIDYASAGAR' ('Ocean of Knowledge') from Sanskrit College for his scholarship. Also learned English independently. SANSKRIT COLLEGE Principal 1851-58. MAJOR REFORMS: (1) HINDU WIDOW REMARRIAGE ACT XV of 1856 — his GREATEST campaign. Conducted systematic research citing Parashara Smriti texts (Manu smriti silent) that supported widow remarriage. Petitioned British Govt with 987 signatures including Rabindranath's grandfather Dwarkanath Tagore. LORD DALHOUSIE + LORD CANNING took it up; Act passed 26 July 1856. LEGAL + GREAT SOCIAL IMPACT on Hindu widows (previously forced into lifelong austerity, tonsure, white saree, fasts, forbidden from festivals). Vidyasagar married his son off to a widow to lead by example. Raised funds for widow remarriages. (2) WOMEN's EDUCATION — helped found 35 GIRLS' SCHOOLS in Bengal (incl. Bethune School 1849 with Drinkwater Bethune; the first secular girls' school in India). Supported Kadambini Ganguly (first female graduate + doctor, 1883). (3) Against POLYGAMY + CHILD MARRIAGE. (4) Opposed POLYGAMY among KULIN Brahmins. LITERARY: (1) 'BARNA PARICHAY' (1855) — BENGALI primer that REVOLUTIONISED Bengali script; used in every Bengali school for 150+ years. (2) 'BETAL PANCHABINGSATI' (translations of Vetala Panchavimshati). (3) 'SHAKUNTALA' (Kalidasa translation). (4) 'SEETAR BANABAS' (1860). (5) 'BRIDDHABIBAHO' (polygamy essay). Vidyasagar's PROSE style shaped modern Bengali. PEDAGOGY: Sanskrit College Principal; opened Sanskrit study to non-Brahmins — radical; modernised curriculum incorporating Western philosophy, logic; English medium for higher learning. BARNAPARICHAY + his 1858 resignation from Sanskrit College (over administration issues) — set him as independent public figure. Also founded several OTHER schools (e.g., METROPOLITAN INSTITUTION, Kolkata, 1864 — now VIDYASAGAR COLLEGE). DEATH: 29 Jul 1891. RABINDRANATH TAGORE wrote VIDYASAGAR Charit — an essay. Ashoka Gupta + others wrote biographies. 200th birth anniversary celebrated 2020. UNION MP RC DEB + PM Modi's frequent tributes. OTHER Bengal reformers: (a) KESHAB CHANDRA SEN — Brahmo leader, Navavidhan; Swami Vivekananda's Ramakrishna association. (b) DEBENDRANATH TAGORE — Adi Brahmo. (c) DAYANANDA SARASWATI — Arya Samaj (Mumbai 1875). (d) SWAMI VIVEKANANDA — Chicago Parliament of Religions 1893; Ramakrishna Mission 1897. secured legalisation of Hindu widow remarriage (ACT XV of 1856); also championed women's education + modernised Bengali primer.

cards.front:
SWAMI DAYANANDA SARASWATI founded which reform movement with the motto 'BACK TO THE VEDAS'?

(A) Brahmo Samaj
(B) ARYA SAMAJ
(C) Ramakrishna Mission
(D) Theosophical Society
cards.back:
(B) ARYA SAMAJ

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — SWAMI DAYANANDA SARASWATI (1824-1883) — Gujarati-born Hindu reformer; founder of ARYA SAMAJ. Born Mool Shankar Tiwari in Tankara, Gujarat, into a Shaiva Brahmin family. As a young boy, during Shivaratri vigil (age 14), he saw mice eating offerings on Shiva lingam — questioned idol worship. Left home at 22; became sannyasi; studied Vedas with SWAMI VIRAJANANDA at Mathura; emerged as reformer. Name 'Dayananda Saraswati' given by Virajananda. FOUNDED ARYA SAMAJ — 10 APRIL 1875 at BOMBAY (later HQ moved to Lahore). PRINCIPLES + 10 tenets: (1) God is sole creator + sustainer + destroyer — formless, eternal, unchangeable; (2) Vedas are INFALLIBLE + sole religious authority ('Back to the Vedas'); (3) Rituals only if rational + for good; (4) No idolatry (murti puja rejected); (5) No caste by birth (emphasis on 'Vedic varna' by qualities); (6) No untouchability; (7) No polygamy, child marriage, Sati, dowry; (8) Women's rights including education + property inheritance + widow remarriage; (9) SHUDDHI (reconversion / purification) of Hindus who had converted to Islam or Christianity — pioneered by Arya Samaj; (10) universal brotherhood. BOOKS: (1) SATYARTH PRAKASH ('Light of Truth', 1875) — MAGNUM OPUS; in Hindi; 14 chapters; comprehensive critique of all religions + Hindu practices; blueprint for reform. (2) RIGVEDADI-BHASHYA-BHUMIKA. (3) BIBLIOGRAPHICAL NOTES on VEDAS. INFLUENCE: INDIA's FIRST SOCIAL REFORM MOVEMENT to spread among WORKING-CLASS + rural areas (vs. Brahmo Samaj's elite Bengali base). Arya Samaj ran SCHOOLS + DAV colleges (Dayanand Anglo-Vedic, first at Lahore 1886 — now 900+ DAV institutions worldwide). EDUCATION + GIRLS' EDUCATION (KANYA MAHAVIDYALAYA, Jalandhar 1896). GURUKUL PATH at Kangri (Haridwar 1902) by Swami Shraddhanand. VEDIC research + publications. MAJOR Arya Samaj influenced leaders: LALA LAJPAT RAI, LALA HANS RAJ, SWAMI SHRADDHANAND (killed 1926 by Muslim fanatic for shuddhi activities), BHAGAT SINGH's uncle Ajit Singh, BHAI PARMANAND, Lala Hardayal (Ghadar Party), Madam Cama, various Punjab + UP political leaders. MOTHER INDIA: the phrase + the term 'Aryavarta' revived. DAYANANDA DIED 1883, AJMER — allegedly POISONED on orders of Jodhpur king's court (disputes). ARYA SAMAJ strongest in Punjab, Haryana, UP, Delhi; ~10 million+ adherents worldwide (diaspora — Surinam, Mauritius, Trinidad, Fiji, South Africa, Kenya, UK, USA). COMPARISON with Brahmo Samaj: both reform, but Brahmo softer (Unitarian flavour) + Arya more assertive + culturally nationalist. DAYANANDA's legacy critical of British rule inspired later nationalism. Bhagat Singh's atheism emerged by questioning Arya Samaj certainty. rejected idolatry + caste; emphasized Vedas as sole authority; Satyarth Prakash (1875); radical social reform + education; 1875, Bombay.

cards.front:
SWAMI VIVEKANANDA's famous address at the WORLD'S PARLIAMENT OF RELIGIONS (Chicago, 1893) began with:

(A) 'Namaste to all'
(B) 'SISTERS AND BROTHERS OF AMERICA'
(C) 'Good morning honourable delegates'
(D) 'Mahatma Gandhi sent me'
cards.back:
(B) 'SISTERS AND BROTHERS OF AMERICA'

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — SWAMI VIVEKANANDA (12 Jan 1863 – 4 Jul 1902) — iconic Indian monk; chief disciple of RAMAKRISHNA PARAMAHAMSA; founder of RAMAKRISHNA MISSION (1897); introduced VEDANTA + YOGA to the WESTERN world. Birth name: NARENDRA NATH DATTA. Born Calcutta, educated at Presidency College + Scottish Church College. Met RAMAKRISHNA (Dakshineswar Kali temple priest) in 1881; became his most devoted disciple. After Ramakrishna's death (1886), led monastic brotherhood at Baranagar + took sannyas name 'Vivekananda'. CHICAGO 1893 — PARLIAMENT OF RELIGIONS (first of its kind globally; 11-27 Sep 1893; part of World's Columbian Exposition). Vivekananda arrived with no invitation + no organisational backing; introduced by Prof. J.H. Wright of Harvard (who famously wrote: 'To ask for your credentials is like asking the sun to state its right to shine'). 11 SEPTEMBER 1893 — HIS DEBUT ADDRESS began with 'SISTERS AND BROTHERS OF AMERICA' — got a 2-MINUTE STANDING OVATION from 7,000 audience members (none had greeted them thus — typical 'Ladies + Gentlemen'). Spoke about religious tolerance + Hinduism's universal acceptance. 11 Sep 1893 known as 'VIVEKANANDA's DAY'; India's NATIONAL YOUTH DAY (12 Jan, his birthday). SUBSEQUENT: toured USA + UK for 4 YEARS; founded VEDANTA SOCIETY in NYC (1894); returned to India 1897 to hero's welcome; founded RAMAKRISHNA MISSION on 1 MAY 1897 at Belur Math, Howrah (HQ, near Kolkata; now a world-headquartered order with 225+ branches). Ramakrishna Math (monastic) + Ramakrishna Mission (service) + Belur Math. TEACHINGS: (1) 'SHIVA JNANE JIVA SEVA' — 'service to man is service to God'; every human has divine spark; serve humanity = serve God. (2) 'Arise, awake + stop not till the goal is reached' (from Katha Upanishad). (3) Muscular spirituality; emphasised strength, self-confidence, positive thinking. (4) Promoted Vedanta (non-dualistic Advaita) globally. (5) Defended Hinduism vs Christian missionary + colonial critique. (6) Supported women's education + empowerment (influenced Sister Nivedita / Margaret Noble — Irish disciple). (7) Rejected caste. WORKS: (1) KARMA YOGA + BHAKTI YOGA + JNANA YOGA + RAJA YOGA — 4 paths of yoga lectures in USA (1896). (2) 'Colombo to Almora Lectures'. (3) Speeches compiled in multiple volumes. (4) SONGS to Kali. DIED 4 July 1902, Belur Math (age 39, Mahasamadhi). LEGACY: (a) India's first global 'cultural ambassador'; (b) inspired RAMAKRISHNA VIVEKANANDA VEDANTA MOVEMENT worldwide; (c) Swami Tejomayananda + current Swami Gautamananda; (d) Tagore, Gandhi, Subhas Bose, Rolland, Aurobindo + later India's leaders drew inspiration. Vivekananda Rock Memorial at Kanyakumari (1970). Ramakrishna Mission runs ~140+ hospitals, schools, relief work globally. received 2-minute standing ovation; became global face of Hindu spirituality + yoga.

After Ramakrishna's death (1886), led monastic brotherhood at Baranagar + took sannyas name 'Vivekananda'. CHICAGO 1893 — PARLIAMENT OF RELIGIONS (first of its kind globally; 11-27 Sep 1893; part of World's Columbian Exposition). Vivekananda arrived with no invitation + no organisational backing; introduced by Prof. J.H. Wright of Harvard (who famously wrote: 'To ask for your credentials is like asking the sun to state its right to shine'). 11 SEPTEMBER 1893 — HIS DEBUT ADDRESS began with 'SISTERS AND BROTHERS OF AMERICA' — got a 2-MINUTE STANDING OVATION from 7,000 audience members (none had greeted them thus — typical 'Ladies + Gentlemen'). Spoke about religious tolerance + Hinduism's universal acceptance. 11 Sep 1893 known as 'VIVEKANANDA's DAY'; India's NATIONAL YOUTH DAY (12 Jan, his birthday). SUBSEQUENT: toured USA + UK for 4 YEARS; founded VEDANTA SOCIETY in NYC (1894); returned to India 1897 to hero's welcome; founded RAMAKRISHNA MISSION on 1 MAY 1897 at Belur Math, Howrah (HQ, near Kolkata; now a world-headquartered order with 225+ branches). Ramakrishna Math (monastic) + Ramakrishna Mission (service) + Belur Math. TEACHINGS: (1) 'SHIVA JNANE JIVA SEVA' — 'service to man is service to God'; every human has divine spark; serve humanity = serve God. (2) 'Arise, awake + stop not till the goal is reached' (from Katha Upanishad). (3) Muscular spirituality; emphasised strength, self-confidence, positive thinking. (4) Promoted Vedanta (non-dualistic Advaita) globally. (5) Defended Hinduism vs Christian missionary + colonial critique. (6) Supported women's education + empowerment (influenced Sister Nivedita / Margaret Noble — Irish disciple). (7) Rejected caste. WORKS: (1) KARMA YOGA + BHAKTI YOGA + JNANA YOGA + RAJA YOGA — 4 paths of yoga lectures in USA (1896). (2) 'Colombo to Almora Lectures'. (3) Speeches compiled in multiple volumes. (4) SONGS to Kali. DIED 4 July 1902, Belur Math (age 39, Mahasamadhi). LEGACY: (a) India's first global 'cultural ambassador'; (b) inspired RAMAKRISHNA VIVEKANANDA VEDANTA MOVEMENT worldwide; (c) Swami Tejomayananda + current Swami Gautamananda; (d) Tagore, Gandhi, Subhas Bose, Rolland, Aurobindo + later India's leaders drew inspiration. Vivekananda Rock Memorial at Kanyakumari (1970). Ramakrishna Mission runs ~140+ hospitals, schools, relief work globally. received 2-minute standing ovation; became global face of Hindu spirituality + yoga.

cards.front:
JYOTIRAO (JYOTIBA) PHULE + his wife SAVITRIBAI PHULE were PIONEERS of:

(A) Banking reform
(B) WOMEN's + LOWER-CASTE EDUCATION in Maharashtra
(C) Military reform
(D) Cricket in India
cards.back:
(B) WOMEN's + LOWER-CASTE EDUCATION in Maharashtra

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — JYOTIRAO GOVINDRAO PHULE (11 Apr 1827 – 28 Nov 1890) + his wife SAVITRIBAI PHULE (3 Jan 1831 – 10 Mar 1897) — 19th-c. social reformers in Maharashtra; revolutionary against CASTE OPPRESSION + for WOMEN's + LOWER-CASTE EDUCATION. Jyotiba's Mali caste (gardener/cultivator) was classified 'Shudra' — oppressed. REFORMS: (1) JANUARY 1848 — opened INDIA's FIRST GIRLS' SCHOOL at Bhide Wada, Pune — Savitribai taught the 8 students. She thus became INDIA'S FIRST WOMAN TEACHER. Opposed by orthodox Hindus (Savitribai faced abuse — cow dung + stones thrown at her en route; wore extra sari to change before teaching). Phules later opened ~17-18 schools for girls, untouchables, widows. (2) 1851 — Phules opened a GIRLS' SCHOOL specifically for UNTOUCHABLE (Dalit) children. (3) 1863 — established an HOME FOR CHILD-BEARING WIDOWS + ORPHANS (Balhatya Pratibandhak Griha) — rescued pregnant Brahmin widows from infanticide; adopted a Brahmin widow's son Yashwant Rao. (4) Campaigned against CHILD MARRIAGE, SATI, caste restrictions, enforced WIDOWHOOD. (5) Opened first DRINKING WATER well in Pune for 'untouchable' use (common well was denied to them). (6) Named their movement 'TRUTH SEEKERS' SOCIETY' — SATYASHODHAK SAMAJ founded 24 SEPTEMBER 1873 by Jyotiba — rejected caste, Brahmin priesthood, demanded rationality + social justice. Non-Brahmin priests for rituals. BOOKS by JYOTIBA: (1) 'GULAMGIRI' ('Slavery', 1873) — landmark; dedicated to American abolitionists — parallel between American slavery + Indian caste oppression. Direct critique of Brahmin supremacy. (2) 'SHETKARYACHA ASUD' ('Cultivator's Whipcord', 1881) — on farmer exploitation. (3) 'Sarvajanik Satya Dharma Pustak' (1891, posthumous). POETRY by SAVITRIBAI — 'Kavya Phule' (1854) + 'Bavan Kashi Subodh Ratnakar' (1892); first female Marathi poet of modern era. DIED: Jyotiba 1890; Savitribai 10 March 1897 NURSING PLAGUE PATIENTS during Pune bubonic plague (1896-97 Pune) — caught plague, died. 'Mahatma' title given to Jyotiba on 11 May 1888 by Mumbai public function. LEGACY: (1) PHULES' work inspired BR AMBEDKAR (who cited Phule as one of his gurus — with Buddha + Kabir); (2) laid foundation of ANTI-CASTE + DALIT rights movement; (3) BAHUJAN (majority low-caste) movement; (4) MAHARASHTRA's strong reform tradition. Savitribai's birth anniversary 3 JAN = MAHARASHTRA GIRL EDUCATION DAY since 2015. Pune University renamed SAVITRIBAI PHULE PUNE UNIVERSITY (2014). Phule-Shahu-Ambedkar trinity of Maharashtra reform. SHAHUJI MAHARAJ of Kolhapur — princely reformer + ally of the Phules + influence on Ambedkar; introduced RESERVATION for non-Brahmins in Kolhapur state 1902 (50% — FIRST reservation policy in India).

cards.front:
Dr B.R. AMBEDKAR is known as the 'ARCHITECT OF THE INDIAN CONSTITUTION' + champion of Dalit rights. He converted along with ~5 lakh followers to:

(A) Christianity
(B) BUDDHISM
(C) Islam
(D) Sikhism
cards.back:
(B) BUDDHISM

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Dr. BHIMRAO RAMJI AMBEDKAR (14 Apr 1891 – 6 Dec 1956) — Indian jurist, economist, politician, social reformer; first LAW Minister of India; architect + Chairman of DRAFTING COMMITTEE of the CONSTITUTION of INDIA; principal champion of DALIT RIGHTS. Born Mhow, MP, into MAHAR family (Dalit caste, then 'untouchable') — extensive experience of caste discrimination from childhood. EDUCATION: Elphinstone College Mumbai BA 1912; Columbia University (USA) MA 1915 + PhD 1927 (economics; 'The Evolution of Provincial Finance in British India'); LSE MSc 1921 + DSc 1923; Gray's Inn Bar-at-Law 1923. First ASIAN with a PhD in Economics. ACTIVISM: (1) 1924 — BAHISHKRIT HITAKARINI SABHA founded in Bombay for Dalit welfare. (2) 1927 — MAHAD SATYAGRAHA (Chowdar Tank) — Dalits claimed right to drink public water; burned Manusmriti copy (25 Dec 1927). (3) 1930s — founded political parties; Dalit rights advocacy. (4) 1930-32 — ROUND TABLE CONFERENCES in London (sole Dalit spokesperson); demanded separate electorates for Depressed Classes — granted by Communal Award 1932 but Gandhi opposed; POONA PACT 24 Sep 1932 — joint electorates with reserved seats. (5) 1936 — 'Annihilation of Caste' (his greatest treatise, undelivered speech). (6) 1942-46 — Labour Member, Viceroy's Executive Council. (7) CONSTITUTION: (1946-49) — Constituent Assembly member from Bombay; CHAIRMAN OF DRAFTING COMMITTEE from 29 Aug 1947. Drafted CONSTITUTION in collaboration with advisor B.N. RAO + members (Munshi, Ayyar, Madhava Rao, Saadullah, Khaitan, Mitter, Gopalaswami Ayyangar). 'FATHER OF CONSTITUTION' title. Championed (a) secular republic; (b) FRs + DPSPs; (c) RESERVATIONS for SC/ST in legislatures + education + govt jobs; (d) abolition of untouchability (Art 17); (e) equality + rule of law. (8) POST-independence: LAW MINISTER in Nehru's cabinet 1947-51. PIONEERED HINDU CODE BILL (sought to codify + reform Hindu personal law — women's rights to property, divorce, polygamy ban). OPPOSED by conservatives; partially implemented only post-1955; Ambedkar RESIGNED Sept 1951 over stalled progress. (9) 14 OCTOBER 1956, DEEKSHABHOOMI, NAGPUR — CONVERTED TO BUDDHISM along with ~3.8 LAKH followers (largest religious conversion ceremony in modern history). Took 22 vows rejecting Hinduism. Founded NAVAYANA BUDDHISM (modern egalitarian Buddhism). DIED 6 Dec 1956 at Delhi (just 2 months later), age 65. 6 DEC = MAHAPARINIRVAN DIWAS. BHARAT RATNA posthumous 1990 (belated). LEGACY: 'DALIT MESSIAH', 'Bodhisattva', father of Indian Constitution. 14 APRIL = AMBEDKAR JAYANTI (national holiday since 2016). Statue at Parliament + Ambedkar Memorial Delhi. Books: 'Who were the Shudras?', 'The Untouchables: Who Were They?', 'Buddha and his Dhamma', 'Thoughts on Pakistan'. 4 books on Indian currency. Bhim Jayanti, Dr B.R. AMBEDKAR Open University. 14 Oct 1956 at Nagpur (Deekshabhoomi); mass conversion ceremony; revived Navayana Buddhism; died 6 Dec 1956 (just 2 months later).
