cards.front:
PERIYAR (E.V. Ramasamy), leader of the DRAVIDIAN Self-Respect Movement in Tamil Nadu, is most associated with:

(A) Hindi promotion
(B) DRAVIDAR KAZHAGAM (1944)
(C) Sanskrit revival
(D) Cow protection
cards.back:
(B) DRAVIDAR KAZHAGAM (1944)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — E.V. RAMASAMY 'PERIYAR' (17 Sep 1879 – 24 Dec 1973) — Tamil social reformer + politician; leader of the SELF-RESPECT MOVEMENT + the DRAVIDIAN MOVEMENT. 'PERIYAR' = 'RESPECTED ONE' / 'GRAND OLD MAN'; title conferred 1938 by 9th Tamil Nadu Women's Conference. Born Erode, TN to a Kannada-speaking Balija Naidu family (ironic given his later Dravidian militancy). EARLY LIFE: merchant; joined Indian National Congress 1919 at Gandhi's Champaran call; active in Vaikom Satyagraha 1924 (fought for Dalit right to walk temple roads in Travancore; called 'Vaikom Veeran' — hero of Vaikom; jailed). Disillusioned with Congress 1925 over caste discrimination issues — left party 1925. FOUNDED: (1) SELF-RESPECT MOVEMENT (1925, Kudi Arasu newspaper) — rationalist + anti-caste + anti-religion + anti-hindutva. Promoted 'Self-Respect Marriages' (no priest + no religious rituals + no astrology). (2) JUSTICE PARTY membership 1935 (earlier founded 1916 by Pitti Tyagaraya Chetty + Natesa Mudaliar + T.M. Nair — first non-Brahmin party challenging Brahmin domination in Madras Presidency). (3) 1938 — Anti-Hindi Agitation in Madras Presidency when CM Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) made Hindi compulsory — violent protests; 2 deaths (Thalamuthu + Natarajan); Hindi order withdrawn 1940. Solidified Tamil linguistic nationalism. (4) 1944 — Renamed Justice Party as 'DRAVIDAR KAZHAGAM' (DK); demanded SEPARATE DRAVIDA NADU (for Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam peoples) — later dropped the separation demand. (5) 1949 — His protégé C.N. ANNADURAI broke off DK → founded DRAVIDA MUNNETRA KAZHAGAM (DMK); Periyar stayed with DK. (6) 1967 — DMK swept TN assembly elections; Annadurai = CM; end of Congress era in TN; Tamil politics became Dravidian-dominated ever since (DMK + later AIADMK split 1972 by MGR). IDEOLOGY: (1) RATIONALISM — atheist; rejected all religions; burned Manusmriti + Ramayana copies ('RAVANA is the HERO' — reversed reading of Ramayana); saw Brahmanism as tool of North Indian / Aryan domination of South Indian / Dravidian people. (2) ANTI-BRAHMIN + anti-caste; advocated self-respect + human dignity. (3) WOMEN'S RIGHTS — contraception, widow remarriage, property rights, against child marriage; radical for 1920s. (4) Anti-Hindi; pro-Tamil identity. (5) Rejected 'India' as a construct + 'Hindi-Hindu-Hindustan' slogan. (6) Called 'SOCRATES OF SOUTH ASIA' by UNESCO 1970. DIED 24 Dec 1973; statue at Vaikom Kerala. IMPACT: Tamil Nadu remains DRAVIDIAN political stronghold (DMK — MK Stalin CM 2021-present; AIADMK); non-Brahmin reservation policy + social justice benchmark in TN. PERIYAR NAIDU CENTER + Memorial at Erode. fought Brahmin supremacy + Hindi imposition; advocated separate Dravida Nadu briefly; championed women's + Dalit rights.

cards.front:
Which reformer is called the 'GRAND OLD MAN OF INDIA' + wrote 'POVERTY + UN-BRITISH RULE IN INDIA' proving the DRAIN of wealth from India?

(A) Gopal Krishna Gokhale
(B) DADABHAI NAOROJI (1825-1917)
(C) Firoz Shah Mehta
(D) Surendranath Banerjee
cards.back:
(B) DADABHAI NAOROJI (1825-1917)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — DADABHAI NAOROJI (4 Sep 1825 – 30 Jun 1917) — 'GRAND OLD MAN OF INDIA'; 'PITAMAHA OF INDIAN NATIONALISM'; 'UNOFFICIAL AMBASSADOR OF INDIA'. Born in Bombay Parsi family. Studied Elphinstone Institution — first Indian to be Professor (Maths + Natural Philosophy, 1855). ACHIEVEMENTS: (1) FIRST ASIAN to become a BRITISH MP — elected 1892 from FINSBURY CENTRAL (London) as Liberal Party candidate, serving 1892-95. Won by just 5 votes. Salisbury had earlier remarked 'a black man cannot be elected to the British Parliament' — Naoroji proved him wrong. Later Mancherjee Bhownagree (1895-1906, Conservative) + Shapurji Saklatvala (1922-1929, Communist) became 2nd + 3rd Indian MPs. (2) THRICE PRESIDENT of INDIAN NATIONAL CONGRESS — (a) 1886 Calcutta (2nd session); (b) 1893 Lahore; (c) 1906 Calcutta (Swaraj session). (3) 1906 CONGRESS — FIRST to explicitly demand 'SELF-GOVERNMENT' / 'SWARAJ' as a goal. (4) Founded the EAST INDIA ASSOCIATION (1866, London) — to present Indian grievances to British public + Parliament; precursor of Congress. DRAIN THEORY: Naoroji's MAJOR intellectual + political contribution. Thesis: BRITISH drained Indian wealth out of the country via salaries + pensions of British officials in India, home charges, ship transport, exports under-priced, imports over-priced, interest on public debt. Developed through years of ECONOMIC study + lectures 1860s-1900s. (a) 'ENGLAND'S DEBT TO INDIA' (1867 lecture, London). (b) 'POVERTY OF INDIA' (1876, pamphlet). (c) 'POVERTY + UN-BRITISH RULE IN INDIA' (1901 — seminal book; estimated DRAIN at ~£30 million per year, equivalent to 20-30% of India's annual revenue; per-capita income of India ₹20/year in 1867-68 — LESS THAN cost of a decent meal). Showed India's economic backwardness was MADE, not inherent. His drain theory armed later nationalists — GOKHALE (his protégé), TILAK, RANADE, R.C. DUTT (author of 'Economic History of India' 1902-04). INSPIRED GANDHI (who called him 'Dada', father-figure; Gandhi's South Africa work supported by him). Influenced Nehru's economic views (mixed economy, planning). MEMORIALS: Dadabhai Naoroji Road in most Indian cities; at Flora Fountain in Mumbai. Bharatiya Arts + Culture Award. Early 20TH c INC 'Moderates' — Naoroji, Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee, Pherozeshah Mehta, Dinshaw Wacha, Dutt, Phirojshah (leader of Bombay triumvirate + Congress), W.C. Bonnerjee (first INC President 1885 Bombay). Approach: CONSTITUTIONAL agitation, petitions, prayers, appealing to British sense of justice. Replaced by EXTREMISTS (Tilak + Lajpat + Pal) post-1905 Bengal Partition. first Asian British MP (Liberal Party, Finsbury 1892-95); 3-time INC President; first to quantify COLONIAL DRAIN.

DUTT (author of 'Economic History of India' 1902-04). INSPIRED GANDHI (who called him 'Dada', father-figure; Gandhi's South Africa work supported by him). Influenced Nehru's economic views (mixed economy, planning). MEMORIALS: Dadabhai Naoroji Road in most Indian cities; at Flora Fountain in Mumbai. Bharatiya Arts + Culture Award. Early 20TH c INC 'Moderates' — Naoroji, Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee, Pherozeshah Mehta, Dinshaw Wacha, Dutt, Phirojshah (leader of Bombay triumvirate + Congress), W.C. Bonnerjee (first INC President 1885 Bombay). Approach: CONSTITUTIONAL agitation, petitions, prayers, appealing to British sense of justice. Replaced by EXTREMISTS (Tilak + Lajpat + Pal) post-1905 Bengal Partition. first Asian British MP (Liberal Party, Finsbury 1892-95); 3-time INC President; first to quantify COLONIAL DRAIN.

cards.front:
The THEOSOPHICAL SOCIETY in India was associated with:

(A) Swami Vivekananda
(B) ANNIE BESANT + Col. OLCOTT + Madame Blavatsky
(C) Dayananda Saraswati
(D) Bhagat Singh
cards.back:
(B) ANNIE BESANT + Col. OLCOTT + Madame Blavatsky

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — THEOSOPHICAL SOCIETY — spiritualist + reformist organisation. FOUNDED: 17 NOV 1875 in NEW YORK CITY by HELENA PETROVNA BLAVATSKY (Madame Blavatsky, Russian-born) + Col. HENRY STEEL OLCOTT (American) + William Quan Judge. HEADQUARTERS moved to ADYAR, CHENNAI (then Madras) in 1882. Adyar HQ since 1886 became international centre. OBJECTIVES ('3 OBJECTS'): (1) To form a nucleus of the UNIVERSAL BROTHERHOOD of Humanity; (2) To encourage the study of comparative RELIGION, PHILOSOPHY + SCIENCE; (3) To investigate unexplained laws of Nature + the powers LATENT in man. Emphasis on UNIVERSAL SPIRITUAL WISDOM ('Theosophy' = divine wisdom); syncretic; drew from Hindu + Buddhist + Egyptian + Christian mysticism, Kabbalah + Western occult. ANNIE BESANT (1 Oct 1847 – 20 Sep 1933) — British-born socialist, women's rights activist, freethinker, orator; joined Theosophical Society 1889; MOVED to INDIA 1893; succeeded Olcott as PRESIDENT of Theosophical Society 1907. Stayed in India till death. CONTRIBUTIONS: (1) CHAMPIONED Hindu revival + reform — edited 'The Commonweal' + 'New India' newspapers. (2) Founded CENTRAL HINDU COLLEGE, Banaras (1898) with MADAN MOHAN MALAVIYA — nucleus of BANARAS HINDU UNIVERSITY (BHU, 1916). (3) Opened girls' school in Varanasi. (4) HOME RULE MOVEMENT — founded INDIAN HOME RULE LEAGUE in 1916 (Tilak founded a parallel one in Maharashtra same year; both coordinated). Demanded SELF-GOVERNMENT within British Empire (Dominion Status like Canada/Australia). Led massive civil agitation. Arrested 1917 by Madras govt; agitation intensified; released. Chosen as CONGRESS PRESIDENT in CALCUTTA SESSION 1917 — FIRST WOMAN President of INC. (5) Discovered + popularised J. KRISHNAMURTI (1895-1986) at Adyar — believing him a future 'World Teacher' / Maitreya; groomed him as the head of 'Order of the Star in the East'; Krishnamurti later DISSOLVED the Order (1929) + rejected all authority-based spirituality; became an iconic independent philosopher. (6) WORKS: 'Why I Became A Theosophist' (1889), 'Ancient Wisdom', 'Esoteric Christianity', 'India: A Nation' (1915). Translated BHAGAVAD GITA. OTHER NOTABLES of Theosophical Society: (a) CHARLES LEADBEATER — clairvoyant author. (b) GEORGE ARUNDALE — later president. (c) NEHRU as young man attended Theosophy lectures. (d) Gandhi first READ GITA (in English translation) at Theosophical Society meetings in London (1890s). INFLUENCE: brought Hindu-Buddhist ideas to Western audiences; countered missionary discrediting of Hinduism; fed Indian cultural + national confidence; bridge between East + West. DECLINE after 1920s as freedom struggle focused elsewhere; ATTENDANCE still at Adyar (one of the most beautiful HQ campuses). Adyar Library — valuable collection of Sanskrit manuscripts. founded 1875 New York; HQ Adyar Chennai from 1882; championed Hindu revival + Indian home rule (1916).

cards.front:
Which Muslim reformer founded MUHAMMADAN ANGLO-ORIENTAL COLLEGE at ALIGARH in 1875, which became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920?

(A) Sir Muhammad Iqbal
(B) SIR SYED AHMAD KHAN
(C) Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
(D) Muhammad Ali Jinnah
cards.back:
(B) SIR SYED AHMAD KHAN

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — SIR SYED AHMAD KHAN (17 Oct 1817 – 27 Mar 1898) — 19th-c. Indian Muslim reformer + educationist + founder of the ALIGARH MOVEMENT. Born Delhi to noble Mughal-era family; educated at home in Arabic + Persian + Islamic studies + mathematics. Joined EIC judicial service 1838; loyal servant of the British throughout. KEY CONTRIBUTIONS: (1) SAVED many British lives during 1857 REVOLT at Bijnor (where he was Sadr Amin); stayed loyal. (2) Wrote 'ASBAB-E-BAGHAWAT-E-HIND' ('Causes of the Indian Revolt', 1859) — analytical account; criticised British mistakes that caused revolt (denied government of Indians by Indians, missionary arrogance, cow-cartridges, etc.) but also criticised Muslim backwardness + urged modernisation. Published 1873 in English. (3) Visited LONDON 1869-70; impressed by Cambridge + Oxford; decided to build similar institution for Muslims. (4) FOUNDED 'MUHAMMADAN ANGLO-ORIENTAL COLLEGE' (MAO COLLEGE) at ALIGARH, UP on 24 MAY 1875 — patterned on Cambridge; offered MODERN ENGLISH + SCIENTIFIC education along with Islamic studies. Elevated to ALIGARH MUSLIM UNIVERSITY in 1920 (by Indian Legislative Council Act). (5) Founded SCIENTIFIC SOCIETY (1864, Aligarh) to translate Western scientific + literary works into Urdu. (6) Edited 'TAHZIB-UL-AKHLAQ' ('Social Reformer', 1870s magazine) — reformist writings. (7) Introduced MODERN INTERPRETATION of Quran compatible with science + rationality; emphasised ALLEGORICAL reading of supernatural elements (jinn, miracles). Wrote 'TAFSIR-UL-QURAN'. (8) Opposed PURDAH + polygamy; advocated women's education later in life. (9) Opposed INC (Indian National Congress 1885) — feared it dominated by Hindu majority; instead called for Muslim political separation from INC. TWO-NATION precursor views. Started ALL-INDIA MUHAMMADAN EDUCATIONAL CONFERENCE 1886 — politically informed Muslim League (1906 Dacca). HONOURS: knighted 1888 (KCSI); DCL by Edinburgh 1889. LEGACY: (a) BELOVED founder-figure of AMU; Strachey HALL + SYED HALL buildings. (b) 'FATHER OF MUSLIM MODERNISM in INDIA'; (c) Aligarh Movement produced generations of Muslim leaders — Mohsin-ul-Mulk, Viqar-ul-Mulk, Maulana Muhammad Ali (Khilafat), Shibli Nomani, Hasrat Mohani, Zakir Hussain (later President of India), many Pakistani leaders (Liaqat Ali Khan, Ayub Khan connections via AMU), + many Indian leaders. (d) Aligarh vs Darul Uloom DEOBAND (1867, Shah Waliullah's traditionalist school — Mohammad Qasim Nanotvi + Rashid Ahmad Gangohi) — Aligarh modernist + pro-British; Deoband Traditional + anti-British + pro-INC (Jamiat Ulama-e-Hind 1919 closely with Congress). Ratna Bharat Ratna did not receive. (e) Negative legacy: some historians trace seeds of Muslim separatism + Partition to Aligarh's communal politics. OTHER Muslim social reformers: (a) BADRUDDIN TYABJI — Bombay, 3rd INC President (1887). (b) MAULANA ABUL KALAM AZAD — scholar, Congress President (2 terms), education minister independent India. Aligarh Movement; advocated modern English + scientific education for Muslims; loyalty to British; opposed 1857 revolt.

cards.front:
The founder of the Brahmo Samaj (1828), who campaigned against Sati, was:

(A) Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
(B) Raja Ram Mohan Roy
(C) Dayananda Saraswati
(D) Swami Vivekananda
cards.back:
(B) Raja Ram Mohan Roy

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772-1833) — often called the 'Father of Modern India'/'Father of the Indian Renaissance' — founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828 (renamed Brahmo Samaj). His campaigning led to Lord William Bentinck's 1829 Regulation abolishing Sati. He died in Bristol, England. Vidyasagar led the widow-remarriage campaign. Dayananda Saraswati founded Arya Samaj in 1875. Vivekananda spoke at the Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, 1893.

cards.front:
The Widow Remarriage Act, 1856, was the direct result of the untiring efforts of:

(A) Raja Ram Mohan Roy
(B) Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
(C) Swami Dayananda Saraswati
(D) M. G. Ranade
cards.back:
(B) Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Vidyasagar (1820-91) — scholar, educator, polymath — petitioned the government with supporting scriptural evidence; the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856 followed. He also promoted girls' education and founded the Metropolitan Institution (now Vidyasagar College). Ram Mohan Roy had earlier focused on Sati abolition (1829). Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj. Ranade co-founded the Prarthana Samaj in Maharashtra (1867).

cards.front:
Jyotirao Phule and his wife Savitribai Phule are most celebrated for their work on:

(A) Abolition of the zamindari system
(B) Women's education and rights of lower castes
(C) Freedom of the press
(D) Temperance / anti-liquor movement
cards.back:
(B) Women's education and rights of lower castes

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Jyotirao Phule (1827-90) — with his wife Savitribai Phule (1831-97) — founded India's first school for girls in Pune in 1848. He formed the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873) to oppose caste and promote the rights of Shudras and untouchables. His book 'Gulamgiri' (1873) analyses caste oppression and is dedicated to the abolition of slavery in the US. Savitribai is regarded as India's first woman teacher.

cards.front:
The 'Arya Samaj' was founded in 1875 by:

(A) Ram Mohan Roy
(B) Dayananda Saraswati
(C) Vivekananda
(D) Keshub Chandra Sen
cards.back:
(B) Dayananda Saraswati

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Dayananda Saraswati (1824-83) — founded Arya Samaj at Bombay in 1875 with the motto 'Back to the Vedas'. He opposed idolatry, polytheism, caste hierarchy and child marriage; supported Shuddhi (reconversion) and widow remarriage. His Satyartha Prakash ('Light of Truth') is the key text. Keshub Chandra Sen led a breakaway Brahmo Samaj of India after 1866. Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.

cards.front:
Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired which important committee of the Constituent Assembly?

(A) Union Constitution Committee
(B) Drafting Committee
(C) Rules of Procedure Committee
(D) States Committee
cards.back:
(B) Drafting Committee

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Dr B. R. Ambedkar (1891-1956) chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly (appointed 29 Aug 1947). He is widely considered the 'Father of the Indian Constitution'. Earlier work — the Hindu Code Bill (which he resigned over), the Mahad Satyagraha (1927), the Kalaram Temple entry (1930). He embraced Buddhism along with thousands of followers on 14 October 1956. Bharat Ratna posthumously in 1990.

cards.front:
Sati (the practice of a widow being burned on her husband's funeral pyre) was legally abolished in British India by a Regulation passed in 1829 by Governor-General:

(A) Lord Curzon
(B) Lord William Bentinck
(C) Lord Dalhousie
(D) Lord Ripon
cards.back:
(B) Lord William Bentinck

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — Lord William Bentinck (Governor-General 1828-35) passed Regulation XVII of 1829 declaring Sati illegal in the Bengal Presidency; it was extended to Madras and Bombay in 1830. The Regulation followed a long campaign by Raja Ram Mohan Roy. Other Bentinck reforms — use of English as medium of instruction (1835, on Macaulay's Minute), suppression of the Thugs. Lord Dalhousie annexed states via the Doctrine of Lapse; Lord Ripon introduced local self-government (1882).

'DRAIN THEORY' — critiquing the systematic transfer of wealth from India to Britain — was propounded by:

cards.front:
SUFISM in India was primarily organised into SILSILAS (orders). The most popular silsila in medieval India was the:

(A) Suhrawardi
(B) CHISHTI
(C) Naqshbandi
(D) Qadiri
cards.back:
(B) CHISHTI

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — SUFISM — mystical Islamic tradition emphasising LOVE of God (ishq), inner purification (tasawwuf), self-annihilation in God (fana), + union with the Divine (baqa). Entered India via Central Asia in the 12th-13th c. Organised into SILSILAS — mystical orders traced via a CHAIN (silsila) of spiritual transmission from the founder back to Prophet Muhammad. FOUR MAIN silsilas in medieval India: (1) CHISHTI — founded in Herat by Abu Ishaq Shami; brought to India by KHWAJA MOINUDDIN CHISHTI (1141-1236), who settled at AJMER (~1195); most POPULAR order; accepted poverty, sama (musical assembly), open-door policy for Hindus + low-castes + women. Famous saints: Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (Delhi), Baba Farid (Pakpattan, Punjab), NIZAMUDDIN AULIYA (Delhi), AMIR KHUSRAU (disciple of Nizamuddin, father of Qawwali), Nasiruddin Chirag-e-Dilli, Shaikh Salim Chishti (Fatehpur Sikri). (2) SUHRAWARDI — brought by Bahauddin Zakariya to Multan; accepted state patronage; more aligned with orthodoxy. (3) QADIRI — later entry (15th-16th c., Dara Shikoh's order). (4) NAQSHBANDI — orthodox order; entered via Baqi Billah in 16th c.; Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani) was a Naqshbandi who opposed Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi. CHISHTI SHRINES are still the MOST VISITED — Ajmer attracts millions. founded by Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer; embraced poverty, music (sama), and openness to all faiths.

cards.front:
KHWAJA MOINUDDIN CHISHTI, founder of the Chishti order in India, is buried at the famous dargah in:

(A) Delhi
(B) AJMER SHARIF (Rajasthan)
(C) Fatehpur Sikri
(D) Multan
cards.back:
(B) AJMER SHARIF (Rajasthan)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — KHWAJA MOINUDDIN CHISHTI (1141-1236), also called 'GHARIB NAWAZ' ('Benefactor of the Poor'). BIRTH in Sistan (modern Iran/Afghanistan); migrated to India in late 12th c., settled in AJMER (~1195, during Prithviraj Chauhan's rule; some accounts differ). Preached love-based Islam, mystical union, rejection of worldly attachments. Died 1236 at Ajmer, age 97. TOMB — AJMER SHARIF DARGAH — built in 1240s; continuously patronised by Mughal emperors: (a) AKBAR walked BAREFOOT from Agra to Ajmer (Nov 1570, a 14-day pilgrimage) to offer thanks for the birth of Salim (later Jahangir); (b) BUILT a cauldron (Kalan Deg) in the dargah for communal meals; (c) Jahangir's wife Nur Jahan also visited. URS: 6-day annual festival on the anniversary of his death (Rajab month) — up to 4-6 lakh pilgrims. Interfaith character: the dargah welcomes people of all faiths; Hindu-Muslim composite culture icon. PM + CM often send chadars (offerings) to Ajmer. DARGAH HIERARCHY of CHISHTI saints + shrines: (1) Ajmer (Moinuddin); (2) Delhi — Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki (Mehrauli, near Qutb Minar); (3) Pakpattan (now in Pakistan) — Baba Farid; (4) Delhi — NIZAMUDDIN AULIYA (largest shrine complex in Delhi, also where Amir Khusrau + Mirza Ghalib are buried); (5) Fatehpur Sikri — Salim Chishti (white marble tomb inside Buland Darwaza complex). one of the most visited shrines in India; pilgrimage (ziyarat) attracts millions, Muslims + Hindus alike.

cards.front:
AMIR KHUSRAU (1253-1325), the 'PARROT OF INDIA' (Tuti-e-Hind), was a disciple of which Sufi saint?

(A) Moinuddin Chishti
(B) NIZAMUDDIN AULIYA
(C) Baba Farid
(D) Shaikh Salim Chishti
cards.back:
(B) NIZAMUDDIN AULIYA

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — AMIR KHUSRAU (1253-1325) — the most celebrated multilingual Indo-Persian poet-musician of medieval India. BIRTH: Patiyali, UP (father was a Turkic noble, mother an Indian Muslim). Served in the courts of 7 SULTANS (from Balban to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq) — longest court career of any poet. DISCIPLE of NIZAMUDDIN AULIYA (~1238-1325) — the great Chishti saint of Delhi; Khusrau's devotion to his pir was legendary. Both died within 6 months of each other in 1325; Khusrau is buried at the same DARGAH COMPLEX of Nizamuddin in Delhi (his tomb adjacent to the master's). LITERARY CONTRIBUTIONS: (1) 'TUTI-E-HIND' (Parrot of India) — title for his unmatched Persian + Hindavi poetry; (2) pioneered HINDAVI (early Urdu/Hindi) literature; earliest known 'Pahelis' (riddles) + 'Mukarniyan' (poetic games) + 'Dohas' in Hindavi. (3) Wrote 8 books including Khamsa-i-Khusrau (5 romances incl. Shirin Khusrau, Laila Majnun), Miftah-ul-Futuh, Nuh Sipihr, Tughlaqnama. MUSICAL CONTRIBUTIONS: (1) Invented QAWWALI — devotional Sufi music (Allah-hoo; his most famous is 'Man Kunto Maula'). (2) Credited with inventing several ragas (Yaman, Sarparda, Zilaph) + the SITAR + TABLA (debated — instruments actually evolved later but in his tradition). FAMOUS LINES: 'Agar firdaus bar roo-e-zameen ast / hameen asto, hameen asto, hameen ast' ('If there is heaven on earth — it is here, it is here, it is here') — about KASHMIR. the celebrated Chishti saint of Delhi; Khusrau's tomb lies beside Nizamuddin's dargah.

cards.front:
The concept of WAHDAT-UL-WUJUD (Unity of Being) in Sufi philosophy means:

(A) Multiple deities
(B) ALL existence is ONE
(C) Rejection of God
(D) Strict ritual observance
cards.back:
(B) ALL existence is ONE

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — WAHDAT-UL-WUJUD ('Unity of Being') — a central metaphysical doctrine in Islamic mysticism, propounded most systematically by the Andalusian Sufi IBN ARABI (1165-1240). CORE IDEA: there is only ONE REAL EXISTENCE — GOD; everything else is a MANIFESTATION / 'self-disclosure' (tajalli) of that divine reality. The phenomenal world is God's mirror; the mystic's goal is to realise this unity by extinguishing his ego in God (FANA FIL ALLAH). STRIKING parallel to Advaita Vedanta's 'Brahman alone is real; the world is Maya' + 'Tat Tvam Asi' — a major reason Sufism + Bhakti movement had fruitful dialogues in medieval India. Dara Shikoh (Shah Jahan's eldest son, executed by Aurangzeb in 1659) wrote MAJMA-UL-BAHRAIN ('Confluence of Two Oceans') comparing Sufi + Vedantic ideas, + translated UPANISHADS into Persian (SIRR-I-AKBAR, 1657 — this Persian version reached Europe and influenced Schopenhauer). COMPETING DOCTRINE: WAHDAT-USH-SHUHUD ('Unity of Witness') — proposed by Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani, 16th-17th c.); held that the unity is PERCEPTUAL (the mystic SEES only God everywhere) but creator-creature distinction REMAINS. This was Orthodox Naqshbandi Sufis' corrective against Wahdat-ul-wujud, which orthodox ulema found heretical. AURANGZEB's religious orthodoxy was influenced by Sirhindi's school; DARA SHIKOH's syncretism by Ibn Arabi's. there is no being other than God; the phenomenal world is a manifestation of the Divine.

cards.front:
The SUFI practice of 'SAMA' refers to:

(A) Fasting
(B) Listening to MUSIC + devotional song as a means of attaining ecstatic union with God; central to Chishti practice; origin of QAWWALI
(C) Pilgrimage to Mecca
(D) Daily prayers
cards.back:
(B) Listening to MUSIC + devotional song as a means of attaining ecstatic union with God; central to Chishti practice; origin of QAWWALI

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — SAMA (Arabic 'listening') — the Sufi spiritual practice of listening to devotional POETRY + MUSIC as a means to attain HAAL (ecstatic state) + WAJD (religious ecstasy) + ultimately FANA (annihilation of self in God). Essential to the CHISHTI order; its presence distinguished Chishtis from more orthodox orders. Condemned by strict ulema (who argued music is haram). EVOLVED into QAWWALI — the distinctive genre of Sufi devotional music in India, pioneered by AMIR KHUSRAU at the dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya. QAWWALI ELEMENTS: (1) group of singers called a qawwal party led by the main qawwal; (2) harmonium + tabla + dholak + hand-clapping; (3) call-and-response structure; (4) builds to ecstatic intensity; (5) Hamd (praise of Allah) → Naat (praise of Prophet) → Manqabat (praise of saints/Imams) → Ghazal (love themes, often with spiritual allegory) → Tarana (vocal acrobatics). FAMOUS QAWWALS: Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan (died 1997), Sabri Brothers (Ghulam Farid + Maqbool Ahmed — 'Bhar Do Jholi'), Rahat Fateh Ali Khan, Warsi Brothers, Wadali Brothers, Kailash Kher (fusion). Famous qawwalis: 'Man Kunto Maula', 'Allah Hoo', 'Chaap Tilak', 'Aaj Rang Hai', 'Damadam Mast Qalandar' (about Lal Shahbaz Qalandar of Sehwan Sharif). Bollywood adaptation: 'Kun Faya Kun' (Rockstar 2011); 'Piya Haji Ali'. CHISHTI SHRINES in India, esp. Ajmer + Nizamuddin Delhi, have weekly sama sessions — pilgrims gather to listen + enter mystical states.

cards.front:
SHAIKH SALIM CHISHTI, to whose blessings Akbar attributed the birth of his son Jahangir (Salim), had his shrine located at:

(A) Ajmer
(B) FATEHPUR SIKRI
(C) Agra
(D) Sikandra
cards.back:
(B) FATEHPUR SIKRI

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — SHAIKH SALIM CHISHTI (1478-1572) — a 16th-century Chishti Sufi saint of Sikri (a village near Agra). REGAL CONNECTION: Emperor AKBAR (1556-1605), childless despite multiple queens, visited Salim Chishti in 1569 seeking blessings for an heir. The Shaikh's blessings were believed to have resulted in the birth of JAHANGIR (born 30 August 1569 in Sikri) — NAMED SALIM after the saint. In gratitude, AKBAR MOVED HIS CAPITAL from Agra to Sikri, and renamed it FATEHPUR SIKRI ('City of Victory') — served as capital 1571-85 (abandoned due to water scarcity). TOMB of Salim Chishti — built 1581 during Akbar's reign, initially of red sandstone; later REBUILT in pure white marble by Jahangir (one of the earliest Mughal white-marble tombs, a precursor to the Taj Mahal). EXQUISITELY CARVED JAALIS (stone lattices) — widely celebrated. PILGRIMAGE: childless couples visit + tie SACRED THREADS on the jaalis praying for offspring. Located inside FATEHPUR SIKRI's JAMA MASJID complex; access through BULAND DARWAZA ('Lofty Gate', built 1575 by Akbar after his Gujarat conquest — at 54m tall, one of the highest gateways in the world, bears Quranic inscription referring to Jesus). UNESCO World Heritage Site (Fatehpur Sikri, 1986). Other Fatehpur Sikri buildings: Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Khas (with the central pillar), Jodha Bai's palace, Ibadat Khana (religious debate hall). the white marble tomb inside the Jama Masjid complex; one of Mughal architecture's earliest white-marble masterpieces.

cards.front:
Which Sufi saint's teachings strongly influenced GURU NANAK, with 134 of his verses appearing in the GURU GRANTH SAHIB?

(A) Moinuddin Chishti
(B) BABA FARID
(C) Nizamuddin Auliya
(D) Bulleh Shah
cards.back:
(B) BABA FARID

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — BABA FARID — FARIDUDDIN MASUD GANJSHAKAR (c. 1173-1266) — one of the first Punjabi SUFI POETS + a major Chishti saint. DISCIPLE of Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki; in turn Nizamuddin Auliya's spiritual GRANDMASTER + Baba Farid chose Nizamuddin as his successor. BASED at Pakpattan (then Ajodhan) in Punjab (now Pakistan). HIS 134 VERSES (SHLOKAS / SALOKS) — composed in early PUNJABI — are included in the GURU GRANTH SAHIB (the Sikh holy scripture) by Guru Arjan in 1604. This is the LARGEST non-Sikh-Guru contribution to the Granth — showing how deeply Baba Farid influenced early Sikhism through Guru Nanak's devotion. HIS PUNJABI poetry laid the foundation of Punjabi literature. THEMES: the transience of life, poverty, humility, love of God. FAMOUS line: 'Nanga aya nanga chalega' ('You came naked and will leave naked'). NAME 'GANJSHAKAR' ('treasure of sugar') — per legend, in his extreme fasting his mouth would even taste salt as sugar due to his sweetness of devotion. FARIDKOT city in Punjab named after him. His URS is a major event in Pakpattan (Oct-Nov). BULLEH SHAH (1680-1757), Waris Shah (Heer Ranjha), + Shah Hussain are later Punjabi Sufi poets influenced by Baba Farid's tradition. Pakistani Coke Studio features many Baba Farid kalams. 12th-13th-c. Chishti saint of Pakpattan, Punjab; whose compositions form the largest non-Sikh Guru section of Guru Granth Sahib; Sheikh Fariduddin Ganjshakar.

Match the Sufi order with its chief Indian centre: (1) CHISHTI; (2) SUHRAWARDI; (3) NAQSHBANDI; (4) QADIRI.

(A) Delhi; Agra; Multan; Bengal
(B) AJMER + Delhi; MULTAN; SIRHIND; Uch Sharif + Lahore
(C) Karnataka; Rajasthan; UP; Bengal
(D) Kashmir only; Lahore only; Delhi; Bihar
cards.back:
(B) AJMER + Delhi; MULTAN; SIRHIND; Uch Sharif + Lahore

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — FOUR MAJOR SUFI SILSILAS in medieval India, with chief centres: (1) CHISHTIYA — Introduced by KHWAJA MOINUDDIN CHISHTI (Ajmer, 1190s). Key centres: AJMER (Moinuddin), DELHI (Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Nizamuddin Auliya, Chirag-e-Dilli), PAKPATTAN (Baba Farid), Fatehpur Sikri (Salim). Characteristic: poverty, sama (music), open to all, rejected state patronage. (2) SUHRAWARDIYA — Introduced by BAHAUDDIN ZAKARIYA (d.1262) at MULTAN; orthodoxy-friendly; accepted state patronage + wealth. Other centre: Uch Sharif; Makhdoom Jahanian Jahangasht. (3) NAQSHBANDIYA — introduced by KHWAJA BAQI BILLAH (1564-1603) at Delhi; later centred at SIRHIND under SHAIKH AHMAD SIRHINDI ('Mujaddid Alf-i-Sani' / 'Revivalist of the Second Millennium', 1564-1624), who opposed Akbar's Din-i-Ilahi + advocated strict sharia; criticised wahdat-ul-wujud in favour of wahdat-ush-shuhud. Influential on Aurangzeb. (4) QADIRIYA — founded globally by Abdul Qadir Jilani (Baghdad, 12th c.); in India brought to UCH SHARIF + LAHORE by Sayyid Muhammad Ghaus + Sayyid Bandagi (15-16th c.); later centre in AURANGABAD. DARA SHIKOH (Shah Jahan's son) was a Qadiri Sufi — wrote Sakinat-ul-Auliya, Safinat-ul-Auliya. OTHER smaller silsilas: SHATTARI (popularised by Muhammad Ghaus in Gwalior; Mian Tansen of Akbar's court was a Shattari). later Aurangabad.

cards.front:
'DIN-I-ILAHI' ('Divine Faith'), a syncretic religious movement combining elements of Islam, Hinduism, Jainism, Zoroastrianism + Christianity, was founded by:

(A) Aurangzeb
(B) AKBAR
(C) Jahangir
(D) Babur
cards.back:
(B) AKBAR

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — DIN-I-ILAHI ('Religion of God') — a syncretic religious movement propounded by AKBAR in 1582 CE. CONTEXT: Akbar, greatly influenced by Sufi thought (Chishti) + Hindu + Jain + Parsi + Christian ideas, held inter-religious debates at the IBADAT KHANA ('House of Worship') built at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575. Scholars from different faiths were invited — Portuguese Jesuits (Monserrate, Aquaviva), Parsi priests (Meherji Rana), Jain monks (Hiravijaya), Hindu Brahmins (Purushottama), Sufi mystics, Sunni + Shia ulema. Out of these debates Akbar issued the 'Mahzar' declaration (1579) making himself the Mujtahid (supreme interpreter). In 1582 he promulgated DIN-I-ILAHI. FEATURES: strict MONOTHEISM (TAWHID); rejected caste; preached ethical life (no meat; no marriage with aged/child; respect for animals; sun salutations; evening-prayer to light); membership voluntary, open to all; Akbar himself was 'spiritual guide'. NOT imposed. FOLLOWERS: barely 18-19 courtiers — RAJA BIRBAL (the most prominent), Abul Fazl, Faizi. DECLINE: died out soon after Akbar's death (1605); never had mass appeal; not a proper 'religion' but more a philosophical order. BACKLASH: (a) SHAIKH AHMAD SIRHINDI (Naqshbandi) emerged as sharp critic, rallying orthodoxy; (b) Badauni, Akbar's historian, was privately hostile (read Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh). AKBAR ALSO abolished jizya (1564) + pilgrimage tax (1563); married Rajput princesses (Jodha Bai / Hira Kunwari from Amber); promoted Rajputs to highest offices. SULH-I-KUL ('universal peace') was Akbar's broader doctrine. in 1582, at Fatehpur Sikri's Ibadat Khana.

cards.front:
The NIZAMUDDIN DARGAH complex in Delhi (13th-century Chishti shrine) contains the tombs of several famous persons. Which of these is NOT buried there?

(A) Amir Khusrau
(B) Mirza Ghalib
(C) Jahanara Begum (Shah Jahan's eldest daughter)
(D) DARA SHIKOH
cards.back:
(D) DARA SHIKOH

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — NIZAMUDDIN DARGAH COMPLEX (Nizamuddin West, Delhi) — the shrine of Hazrat Nizamuddin Auliya (1238-1325), 4th great Chishti saint. DESIGNED by medieval Chishti architecture; shrine built 1562 during Humayun's reign. NOTABLE GRAVES in the complex: (1) HAZRAT NIZAMUDDIN AULIYA — saint's grave (under white marble + red sandstone chattri). (2) AMIR KHUSRAU — closest disciple of Nizamuddin; buried a few metres from his master per his own wish. (3) JAHANARA BEGUM (1614-1681) — Shah Jahan's eldest daughter, herself a Sufi (Qadiriyya) — buried adjacent to her master Nizamuddin Auliya's tomb per her will ('no marble, only grass be my shroud'). (4) MIRZA GHALIB (1797-1869) — Urdu + Persian poet; his tomb is in the Ghalib Qabristan, a separate enclosed compound just to the south of the dargah (not in the main shrine premises, but within the complex). (5) Atgah Khan (Akbar's foster father, murdered by Adham Khan). (6) Muhammad Shah Rangeela (Mughal emperor 1719-48). (7) Inayat Khan (jewel merchant). DARA SHIKOH (1615-1659), Shah Jahan's eldest son, was EXECUTED by Aurangzeb in 1659; his body was buried in HUMAYUN'S TOMB complex in an unmarked grave (some historians say Grave 14 there; others say unidentified). Was himself a Qadiri Sufi + scholar (translated Upanishads as Sirr-i-Akbar). MODI GOVT in 2020 set up committee to identify Dara Shikoh's grave — unresolved. ANNUAL URS at Nizamuddin = huge gathering; QAWWALI every Thursday evening in the courtyard. actually buried in HUMAYUN'S TOMB (some sources say just a marker; site remains unidentified).

cards.front:
Swami VIVEKANANDA delivered his FAMOUS SPEECH at the World's Parliament of Religions in:

(A) Chicago, USA in 1893
(B) London, UK in 1900 here
(C) Bombay (Mumbai) in 1897
(D) Calcutta (Kolkata) in 1893
cards.back:
(A) Chicago, USA in 1893

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — SWAMI VIVEKANANDA delivered his FAMOUS SPEECH on 11 SEPTEMBER 1893 at the WORLD'S PARLIAMENT OF RELIGIONS, held at the Art Institute of Chicago, USA, as part of the World's Columbian Exposition. OPENING: 'Sisters and Brothers of America!' — drew an immediate 2-MINUTE STANDING OVATION from ~7,000 people (he had not even started his speech yet!). KEY POINTS in his ADDRESS: (1) Introduced HINDUISM + Vedantic philosophy to the WEST. (2) Urged TOLERANCE + ACCEPTANCE of all religions; quoted from BHAGAVAD GITA, Upanishads. (3) Spoke of UNITY in DIVERSITY of religions. (4) Made INDIA shine on world stage. AFTERMATH: lecture tours across USA + UK (~3-4 years); founded VEDANTA SOCIETY of NEW YORK (1894), London (1895), and others. Returned to INDIA 1897 to massive public welcomes. RAMAKRISHNA MISSION founded by him on 1 MAY 1897 (Belur Math area). BIRTH: 12 JANUARY 1863 (Calcutta) — celebrated as NATIONAL YOUTH DAY in India since 1985. ORIGINAL NAME: NARENDRA NATH DATTA. DEATH: 4 JULY 1902 (Belur Math, age 39 — short life but immense impact). FAMOUS QUOTES: 'Arise, Awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.' 'You cannot believe in God until you believe in yourself.' UPSC angle: Indian Renaissance + 19th-century reform. PYQ FREQUENCY: Vivekananda's Chicago speech in UPSC, MPSC, SSC modern history 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Swami Vivekananda was the most prominent disciple of:

(A) Ramakrishna Paramahamsa (Bengal saint)
(B) Adi Shankaracharya (8th century)
(C) Dayananda Saraswati (Arya Samaj)
(D) Raja Ram Mohan Roy (Brahmo)
cards.back:
(A) Ramakrishna Paramahamsa (Bengal saint)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — RAMAKRISHNA PARAMAHAMSA (1836-1886) — Bengali mystic + saint; Vivekananda's GURU. Lived at DAKSHINESWAR KALI TEMPLE (Calcutta), priest there. Practiced + experienced multiple religious paths (Hindu sects, Islam, Christianity) and concluded: 'YATA MAT, TATA PATH' ('As many faiths, so many paths to God') — championed UNIVERSAL RELIGIOUS HARMONY. Met young NARENDRA NATH DATTA (later VIVEKANANDA) in 1881 — became spiritual mentor. RAMAKRISHNA's wife: SARADA DEVI ('Holy Mother') — also revered. RAMAKRISHNA's TEACHINGS: simple, profound; emphasized DIRECT EXPERIENCE of GOD over dogma; UNIVERSAL TRUTH in all religions; serve mankind = serve God. KEY DISCIPLES: (1) VIVEKANANDA — most famous; carried teachings worldwide. (2) Brahmananda — first president of Ramakrishna Math. (3) Saradananda. (4) Other 'direct disciples'. RAMAKRISHNA MISSION (1897, founded by Vivekananda after Ramakrishna's death) — based on RK's teachings; emphasizes service to humanity ('Daridra Narayana' — service to poor as service to God). CONTRAST to other 19th-century reformers: (a) Ram Mohan Roy — Brahmo Samaj (monotheism, anti-idolatry; rationalist). (b) Dayananda Saraswati — Arya Samaj (back to Vedas; militant Hindu reform). (c) RAMAKRISHNA-VIVEKANANDA — emphasized UNIVERSALITY of religious experience; less iconoclastic, more synthetic. UPSC angle: BENGAL RENAISSANCE + comparative reform movements. PYQ FREQUENCY: Ramakrishna-Vivekananda link in UPSC, SSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
RAMAKRISHNA MISSION was founded by Vivekananda in:

(A) 1897 (at Belur Math, near Calcutta)
(B) 1885 (Indian National Congress)
(C) 1893 (Chicago speech year)
(D) 1875 (Arya Samaj founding)
cards.back:
(A) 1897 (at Belur Math, near Calcutta)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — RAMAKRISHNA MISSION — founded by SWAMI VIVEKANANDA on 1 MAY 1897 at BELUR (near Calcutta). HEADQUARTERS: BELUR MATH (West Bengal) — sprawling complex on banks of Hooghly river; main temple opened 1938. ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE: (1) RAMAKRISHNA MATH — monastic order (sanyasis). (2) RAMAKRISHNA MISSION — service organization; legally registered. KEY FIGURES: (a) RAMAKRISHNA — founder-inspiration. (b) VIVEKANANDA — formal founder, 1st president. (c) BRAHMANANDA — first elected president (1901-1922). (d) Many subsequent presidents. PHILOSOPHY: 'ATMANO MOKSHARTHAM JAGAD HITAYA CHA' — 'For one's own salvation + welfare of the world'. ACTIVITIES: (1) RELIEF WORK — disaster relief (floods, famines, earthquakes). (2) HOSPITALS + dispensaries (~25). (3) SCHOOLS + colleges (~200+). (4) Vocational training centers. (5) Spiritual + cultural events. (6) PUBLISHING — 'Prabuddha Bharata', 'Vedanta Kesari', 'Udbodhan'. SIZE today: ~250 centres globally; 1000s of monks. INDIAN STATE STATUS: in Bengal, RK Mission has CULTURAL+EDUCATIONAL significance — RAMAKRISHNA MISSION VIDYAMANDIRA (Belur), RAMAKRISHNA MISSION VIVEKANANDA UNIVERSITY (deemed univ., 2005). RAMAKRISHNA MISSION INSTITUTE OF CULTURE (Gol Park, Kolkata) — major library + cultural center. UPSC angle: socio-religious organizations + their educational impact. PYQ FREQUENCY: RK Mission founding in UPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Swami Vivekananda's BIRTHDAY (12 January) is celebrated as:

(A) National Youth Day (since 1985)
(B) National Teachers Day (Sept 5)
(C) National Science Day (Feb 28)
(D) National Education Day (Nov 11)
cards.back:
(A) National Youth Day (since 1985)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — NATIONAL YOUTH DAY — observed on 12 JANUARY (Vivekananda's birth anniversary) since 1985, declared by GOVT OF INDIA (Rajiv Gandhi era). PURPOSE: inspire INDIAN YOUTH with Vivekananda's vision of: (a) Spiritual awakening + character building. (b) Service to society. (c) Self-reliance. (d) Patriotism. EVENTS: speeches, debates, youth-empowerment programs across India. INDIA's MAJOR NATIONAL OBSERVANCES (memorize for SSC, UPSC, GA): (1) NATIONAL YOUTH DAY — 12 January (Vivekananda). (2) ARMY DAY — 15 January (KM Cariappa, 1st Indian C-in-C). (3) REPUBLIC DAY — 26 January (Constitution adopted 1950). (4) INTERNATIONAL WOMEN's DAY — 8 March. (5) NATIONAL SCIENCE DAY — 28 February (Raman Effect 1928). (6) NATIONAL VOTERS DAY — 25 January (ECI's foundation 1950). (7) NATIONAL POSTAL DAY — 10 October. (8) NATIONAL EDUCATION DAY — 11 November (Maulana Azad's birthday). (9) NATIONAL UNITY DAY — 31 October (Sardar Patel — 'Statue of Unity'). (10) NATIONAL TEACHERS DAY — 5 September (Dr. S. Radhakrishnan's birthday). (11) NATIONAL ENGINEERS DAY — 15 September (M. Visvesvaraya's birthday). (12) NATIONAL DOCTORS DAY — 1 July (BC Roy). (13) GANDHI JAYANTI — 2 October. (14) AMBEDKAR JAYANTI — 14 April. (15) NATIONAL FARMERS DAY — 23 December (Choudhary Charan Singh). UPSC angle: ACOR (Awareness of National Observances) is GA-essential. PYQ FREQUENCY: Vivekananda-Youth Day in UPSC, SSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
ROCK MEMORIAL dedicated to Vivekananda is located at:

(A) Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu, southern tip)
(B) Belur Math, West Bengal (HQ)
(C) Chicago (where he spoke 1893)
(D) Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh here
cards.back:
(A) Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu, southern tip)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — VIVEKANANDA ROCK MEMORIAL — located on a small ROCKY ISLAND off the coast of KANYAKUMARI, TAMIL NADU (the southernmost tip of mainland India). LEGEND: in DECEMBER 1892, young Vivekananda swam from mainland Kanyakumari to this island; meditated for 3 days/nights on the rock, contemplating India's spiritual + social condition. This 'COSMIC VISION' shaped his future mission. MEMORIAL CONSTRUCTION (1963-1970): EKNATH RANADE (RSS leader, founder Vivekananda Kendra) led the FUNDRAISING + construction effort. Inaugurated 2 SEPTEMBER 1970 by President V.V. Giri. STRUCTURE: combines rocks, mandapam, dhyana mandapam (meditation hall); ~7-foot statue of Vivekananda. OBSERVATIONS: clear view of where 3 oceans MEET — ARABIAN SEA, BAY OF BENGAL, INDIAN OCEAN. Small ferry takes visitors from mainland (~10 mins). NEAR: another rock has 133-foot statue of TIRUVALLUVAR (Tamil poet, 1st century BC, author of THIRUKKURAL) — built 2000. KANYAKUMARI is named after KUMARI AMMAN (Goddess Devi). FAMOUS DESTINATIONS at Kanyakumari: (1) Vivekananda Rock Memorial. (2) Tiruvalluvar Statue. (3) Bhagavathy Amman Temple. (4) Sunset point. (5) Triple-ocean confluence (Triveni Sangam — different from Allahabad's). UPSC angle: cultural-tourism + Indian heritage. PYQ FREQUENCY: Kanyakumari memorial in SSC GA, UPSC, NDA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Vivekananda's PRE-MONASTIC name was:

(A) Narendra Nath Datta
(B) Surendra Nath Bose here
(C) Mohandas Karamchand here
(D) Subhash Chandra Bose only
cards.back:
(A) Narendra Nath Datta

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — NARENDRA NATH DATTA (Narendra, 'Naren' to friends) — Vivekananda's birth name. Born 12 JANUARY 1863 in CALCUTTA into KAYASTHA family. FATHER: VISHWANATH DATTA — successful attorney at Calcutta High Court. MOTHER: BHUVANESHWARI DEVI — pious Hindu housewife. EDUCATION: Presidency College + Scottish Church College, Calcutta — BA in 1884. Studied PHILOSOPHY (Western: Hume, Spencer, Mill; Indian: Vedanta). KEY MOMENTS: (1) AS A STUDENT — questioned existence of God; visited various religious leaders without satisfaction. (2) MET RAMAKRISHNA at DAKSHINESWAR (1881-82); RK eventually convinced young Naren of God's reality + true spirituality. (3) Death of FATHER (1884) plunged family into POVERTY; Naren took up monastic vows formally after Ramakrishna's death (1886). (4) Adopted name 'VIVEKANANDA' before Chicago trip (1893): 'VIVEKA' (discrimination/wisdom) + 'ANANDA' (bliss). MONASTIC NAME suggested by Maharaja of Khetri (Rajasthan, who patronized his US trip). KEY WORKS by Vivekananda: (1) RAJA YOGA — practical yoga based on Patanjali's sutras. (2) JNANA YOGA — path of knowledge. (3) BHAKTI YOGA — devotion. (4) KARMA YOGA — selfless action. (5) Lectures published as 'Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda' (9 volumes). PYQ FREQUENCY: Naren-Vivekananda identity in UPSC, MPSC History 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The BELUR MATH (Ramakrishna Mission HQ) is located in which state?

(A) West Bengal (Howrah district)
(B) Bihar (Buddhist circuit only)
(C) Maharashtra (RK had little there)
(D) Tamil Nadu (Kanyakumari only)
cards.back:
(A) West Bengal (Howrah district)

Bhakti, Sufi & Social Reform — BELUR MATH — HEADQUARTERS of RAMAKRISHNA MATH and RAMAKRISHNA MISSION; located on the WEST BANK of HOOGHLY RIVER in BELUR town, HOWRAH district, WEST BENGAL (across the river from Calcutta/Kolkata). FOUNDED: 1898; main temple completed 1938. UNIQUE ARCHITECTURE: deliberate FUSION of Hindu, Christian, Islamic + Buddhist motifs — symbolizing UNIVERSAL RELIGION concept. Designed by SWAMI VIJNANANANDA (architect-monk, RK's direct disciple). KEY STRUCTURES: (1) MAIN TEMPLE — houses SHRINE of RAMAKRISHNA. (2) Holy Mother's TEMPLE (Sarada Devi). (3) SWAMI VIVEKANANDA's TEMPLE — built on his cremation site (he was cremated here 1902). (4) BRAHMANANDA's TEMPLE. (5) Old monastery building. (6) NEW dispensary, hospital, library. SIZE: ~40 acres along river. ATTRACTIONS for visitors: meditation halls, gardens, museum, bookstore. PILGRIMAGE: lakhs visit annually; major events on Vivekananda Jayanti (12 Jan), Buddha Purnima, Christmas, Ramakrishna Jayanti, Sarada Devi Jayanti. NEAR Belur Math: DAKSHINESWAR KALI TEMPLE (across Hooghly, where Ramakrishna lived as priest) — also major pilgrimage. CONNECTION: VIVEKANANDA SETU (bridge) connects Belur to Dakshineswar (built later, 1990s). UPSC angle: cultural heritage + religious tourism. PYQ FREQUENCY: Belur Math location in UPSC PT, SSC GA 1× per 2 cycles. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests state-religious-site mapping.

cards.front:
Vasco da Gama landed at which Indian port in May 1498, establishing the first direct sea route from Europe to India?

(A) Cochin (Kochi)
(B) Calicut (Kozhikode)
(C) Goa
(D) Surat
cards.back:
(B) Calicut (Kozhikode)

Maratha & Later Rulers — Vasco da Gama reached CALICUT on 20 May 1498 and was received by the local ruler Zamorin (Samoothiri Raja). Calicut was the preeminent Malabar spice-trade port at the time. Cochin became a later Portuguese stronghold (after Zamorin's hostility drove them south in 1500). Goa was captured much later (1510) under Albuquerque. Surat became a Mughal port the Portuguese — and later the English — used in the 17th century. The 1498 Calicut landfall is the canonical date that opens modern European–Indian history.

cards.front:
Who among the following is credited with formulating the 'Blue Water Policy' (Cartaze system) that aimed at establishing Portuguese control of the Indian Ocean through a passport-permit regime for non-Portuguese ships?

(A) Vasco da Gama
(B) Francisco de Almeida
(C) Afonso de Albuquerque
(D) Nino da Cunha
cards.back:
(B) Francisco de Almeida

Maratha & Later Rulers — Francisco de Almeida (Viceroy 1505-09) articulated the 'Blue Water Policy' (Portuguese: 'Política do Mar Azul') — Portugal's strength lay in sea-power, not in holding territory on land; command of the sea would let them monopolise the spice trade. The complementary Cartaze system required non-Portuguese merchant ships to buy Portuguese-issued permits to trade in the Indian Ocean. Albuquerque, his successor (1509-15), pivoted to 'blue-water-plus-strategic-land-bases' — capturing Goa (1510), Malacca (1511), Hormuz (1515). Vasco da Gama was the navigator, not an administrator. Nino da Cunha moved the Portuguese capital from Cochin to Goa (1530).

cards.front:
Arrange the following European trading companies in India in the correct CHRONOLOGICAL order of their FOUNDING (not of their arrival in India):
(i) French East India Company (La Compagnie des Indes orientales)
(ii) English East India Company
(iii) Dutch East India Company (VOC)
(iv) Portuguese Estado da Índia

(A) (iv) → (ii) → (iii) → (i)
(B) (iv) → (iii) → (ii) → (i)
(C) (ii) → (iii) → (iv) → (i)
(D) (iii) → (ii) → (iv) → (i)
cards.back:
(A) (iv) → (ii) → (iii) → (i)

Maratha & Later Rulers — Correct order: (iv) Portuguese Estado da Índia — 1505 (Almeida appointed first Viceroy); (ii) English East India Company — 31 Dec 1600 (Queen Elizabeth I's charter); (iii) Dutch East India Company (VOC) — 20 Mar 1602 (Dutch States-General charter, only 15 months after the English); (i) French East India Company — 1664 (under Jean-Baptiste Colbert, Louis XIV's finance minister). Despite Dutch and English founding dates being only ~15 months apart, English is first. The Portuguese didn't have a joint-stock company structure — the 'Estado da Índia' was a royal government apparatus.

cards.front:
Sir Thomas Roe's diplomatic mission (1615-18) to secure trading rights for the English East India Company was sent to the court of which Mughal Emperor?

(A) Akbar
(B) Jahangir
(C) Shah Jahan
(D) Aurangzeb
cards.back:
(B) Jahangir

Maratha & Later Rulers — Sir Thomas Roe was dispatched by James I of England to the court of JAHANGIR (r. 1605-27) at Ajmer and later Agra. Roe secured a royal firman permitting English factories at Surat and other Mughal ports — a diplomatic coup. His memoirs (published as 'The Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe to India') remain a primary source for Jahangir's court. Akbar died in 1605, before the mission; Shah Jahan reigned 1628-58; Aurangzeb 1658-1707 — Roe met neither. (An EARLIER English envoy, William Hawkins, had been at Jahangir's court 1609-11 without securing firm concessions.)

cards.front:
The three Carnatic Wars (1744-48, 1749-54, 1758-63) decided the colonial fate of South India. Which war effectively settled the Anglo-French struggle in India, with the decisive Battle of Wandiwash?

(A) First Carnatic War (1744-48), ended by the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle
(B) Second Carnatic War (1749-54), ended by the Treaty of Pondicherry
(C) Third Carnatic War (1758-63), ended by the Treaty of Paris
(D) A fourth war fought separately in 1780-84
cards.back:
(C) Third Carnatic War (1758-63), ended by the Treaty of Paris

Maratha & Later Rulers — The THIRD Carnatic War (1758-63) — a sideshow to the global Seven Years' War — was the decisive British victory. At Wandiwash (22 Jan 1760) Eyre Coote crushed the French under Comte de Lally. The subsequent Treaty of Paris (1763) restored French factories to France but STRIPPED them of the right to fortify — thereby ending French ambitions to compete as a political power in India. The First Carnatic War saw French gains (capture of Madras) later returned via the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle; the Second was inconclusive. Option D refers to the Second Mysore War (1780-84) — different theatre.

cards.option2: Second Carnatic War (1749-54), ended by the Treaty of Pondicherry
cards.option3: A fourth war fought separately in 1780-84

cards.front:
The Battle of Plassey (23 June 1757) was fought between the forces of Robert Clive and:

(A) Shuja-ud-Daula, Nawab of Awadh
(B) Siraj-ud-Daula, Nawab of Bengal
(C) Mir Qasim, Nawab of Bengal
(D) Haider Ali of Mysore
cards.back:
(B) Siraj-ud-Daula, Nawab of Bengal

Maratha & Later Rulers — Plassey (Palashi in Bengali) pitted Clive against SIRAJ-ud-DAULA, Nawab of Bengal (who had captured Calcutta from the British in 1756, causing the 'Black Hole' incident). Clive's victory — aided by Mir Jafar's betrayal of Siraj — was the foundational moment of British territorial power in India. Mir Qasim was a later Nawab (installed then deposed by the British) — he lost the Battle of Buxar in 1764. Shuja-ud-Daula was Awadh's Nawab, also defeated at Buxar. Haider Ali of Mysore was an entirely different theatre (Mysore Wars 1767-1799).

cards.front:
The Treaty of Allahabad (1765), signed between Robert Clive and the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, transferred which crucial right to the British East India Company?

(A) The office of Nizamat (criminal administration) of Bengal
(B) The Diwani (revenue collection rights) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa
(C) Ownership of the city of Delhi
(D) Permission to mint coins in the name of the British Crown
cards.back:
(B) The Diwani (revenue collection rights) of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa

Maratha & Later Rulers — The Treaty of Allahabad (signed after British victory at Buxar 1764) granted the Company the DIWANI of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa — the right to collect land revenue — in exchange for an annual payment of 26 lakh rupees to the emperor. This marked the TRANSITION of the Company from 'traders' to a 'territorial power' with a steady revenue source (₹30+ million annually by the 1770s). The Nizamat (criminal and police administration) was initially left with the Nawab of Bengal but became a puppet office — Warren Hastings formally combined Diwani + Nizamat under Company control in 1772. Options C and D describe events that never happened under this treaty.

cards.option2: Ownership of the city of Delhi
cards.option3: Permission to mint coins in the name of the British Crown

cards.front:
Which of the following European powers established its first Indian factory at TRANQUEBAR (on the Coromandel coast) in 1620 and later sold all its Indian possessions to the British in 1845?

(A) Dutch
(B) Danish
(C) Swedish
(D) French
cards.back:
(B) Danish

Maratha & Later Rulers — The DANISH East India Company (Dansk Ostindisk Kompagni, 1616) operated from Tranquebar (Tharangambadi, Tamil Nadu) and Serampore (West Bengal). Denmark's Indian presence was always modest — never a major political force — and after financial troubles, Denmark sold Tranquebar and Serampore to the British in 1845. The Dutch had factories further south (Nagapattinam, Pulicat) and dominated Cochin — they lost most holdings to the British by the 1780s-90s. The Swedish East India Company (1731) traded with Canton but didn't establish lasting Indian factories. The French had Pondicherry, Chandernagore, Mahé, Karaikal, Yanam — all retained until 1954 (de facto).

cards.front:
Joseph François Dupleix — who famously envisioned a French empire in India through intervention in local succession disputes — served as the Governor-General of which French Indian enclave?

(A) Chandernagore (Bengal)
(B) Pondicherry
(C) Mahé (Kerala coast)
(D) Surat
cards.back:
(B) Pondicherry

Maratha & Later Rulers — Joseph François Dupleix was Governor-General of French India (1742-54), based at PONDICHERRY (Puducherry). He pioneered the strategy of training sepoys on European lines and backing local claimants to the Nawabi of Carnatic and the Nizamate of Hyderabad — a tactic Robert Clive later turned against him. Dupleix was eventually recalled to France in 1754 and died in 1763 in poverty and disgrace, ironic given his Indian ambitions. Chandernagore was a French factory but never their capital. Mahé was a minor French enclave. Surat was a Mughal/English port — never French.

cards.front:
The Battle of Colachel (1741) — a rare and decisive DEFEAT of a European colonial power by an Indian kingdom — was won by Maharaja Marthanda Varma of Travancore against which European power?

(A) Portuguese
(B) Dutch
(C) French
(D) British
cards.back:
(B) Dutch

Maratha & Later Rulers — Colachel (31 July 1741) was fought between Travancore and the DUTCH East India Company. Marthanda Varma's forces captured Dutch commander Captain Eustachius De Lannoy (who subsequently served as Travancore's military chief — 'Valiya Kapitaan' — and modernised its army). This battle is often highlighted in UPSC/state-PSC answer keys as the 'first European defeat by an Indian kingdom' — though Portuguese defeats by local Zamorin forces had occurred earlier in the 16th century. After Colachel, Dutch power in the Malabar never recovered; by 1795 their last holdings fell to the British.

cards.front:
Bombay was transferred to the English East India Company in 1668 by which English monarch, having received the islands as part of the dowry of his Portuguese queen?

(A) Queen Elizabeth I
(B) King James I
(C) King Charles II
(D) King George III
cards.back:
(C) King Charles II

Maratha & Later Rulers — When Charles II of England married Catherine of Braganza (daughter of King John IV of Portugal) in 1661, the Portuguese dowry included Bombay (7 small islands). Charles II, finding the islands hard to administer, leased them to the EIC in 1668 for a nominal rent of £10 per year. The EIC rapidly developed Bombay as a fortified port, and by the late 17th century it had eclipsed Surat as the Company's western headquarters. Elizabeth I died in 1603 — before the dowry event. James I was on the throne when Sir Thomas Roe went to Jahangir's court but died in 1625. George III came much later (r. 1760-1820).

cards.front:
Which of the following is the CORRECT chronological order of the establishment of EIC 'Presidency' headquarters in India?
(i) Madras  (ii) Bombay  (iii) Calcutta  (iv) Surat

(A) (iv) → (i) → (ii) → (iii)
(B) (i) → (ii) → (iii) → (iv)
(C) (iv) → (ii) → (i) → (iii)
(D) (i) → (iv) → (ii) → (iii)
cards.back:
(A) (iv) → (i) → (ii) → (iii)

Maratha & Later Rulers — Correct order: (iv) SURAT was the first EIC factory (1613, after Thomas Best's 1612 Swally battle) — served as the western headquarters initially. (i) MADRAS was founded 1639-40 when Francis Day obtained Madrasapatnam from the Vijayanagara viceroy — Fort St. George built there. (ii) BOMBAY was leased to EIC in 1668 (dowry from Charles II's Portuguese marriage), displacing Surat as the western headquarters by 1687. (iii) CALCUTTA (Fort William) was established 1690 by Job Charnock. So: Surat → Madras → Bombay → Calcutta. Knowing the decade of each presidency is a high-ROI memorisation.

cards.front:
Who was appointed as the FIRST Governor of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773, and subsequently became the first Governor-General of Bengal (with supervisory authority over Madras and Bombay)?

(A) Robert Clive
(B) Warren Hastings
(C) Lord Cornwallis
(D) Lord Wellesley
cards.back:
(B) Warren Hastings

Maratha & Later Rulers — Warren Hastings was already Governor of Bengal when the Regulating Act 1773 elevated the Bengal governorship to 'Governor-General of Bengal' — with authority to oversee (but not directly govern) Madras and Bombay presidencies. The post carried a 4-member council (initially hostile to him under Philip Francis). Hastings served 1773-85. Clive's role was earlier — he was Governor of Bengal twice (1757-60, 1765-67) but predated the Regulating Act and never held the 'Governor-General' title. Cornwallis (1786-93) succeeded Hastings and pushed the Permanent Settlement. Wellesley (1798-1805) pushed Subsidiary Alliances.

cards.front:
Afonso de Albuquerque — often called the 'founder of the Portuguese empire in the East' — captured which three strategic cities during his governorship (1509-15)?

(A) Goa, Calicut, Colombo
(B) Goa, Malacca, Hormuz
(C) Bombay, Malacca, Macau
(D) Cochin, Hormuz, Aden
cards.back:
(B) Goa, Malacca, Hormuz

Maratha & Later Rulers — Albuquerque's strategic trifecta: GOA (1510, from Bijapur — made Portugal's Asian capital), MALACCA (1511, from the Malay Sultanate — controlling the Strait and spice route east), HORMUZ (1515, controlling the Persian Gulf trade). He tried and failed at Aden. Calicut was never conquered — only unsuccessfully besieged. Macau was acquired in 1557, decades after his death. Colombo came to Portuguese control later through negotiation with Kotte. Knowing GOA-MALACCA-HORMUZ as Albuquerque's signature conquests is the canonical answer.

cards.front:
The Pitt's India Act of 1784 established the Board of Control to oversee the EIC in London. This Board was chaired by which official of the British Government?

(A) The Prime Minister of Britain
(B) A Cabinet Minister
(C) The King personally
(D) The Archbishop of Canterbury
cards.back:
(B) A Cabinet Minister

Maratha & Later Rulers — Pitt's India Act (1784) created a DUAL system: the EIC retained commercial control, but political/military decisions came under a Board of Control composed of 6 Cabinet members, headed by a 'President of the Board of Control' — a Cabinet-rank minister. This post, reorganised by the Government of India Act 1858 after the 1857 Revolt, became the 'Secretary of State for India' reporting to Parliament. So answer B is correct. The PM did NOT directly chair the Board; the King had a ceremonial role but not operational chairmanship. The Archbishop has no role here — pure distractor. later the Secretary of State for India.

cards.front:
MAHARANA PRATAP fought the famous BATTLE OF HALDIGHATI in:

(A) 1576 (against Akbar's forces)
(B) 1556 (Akbar's accession year)
(C) 1605 (Akbar's death year)
(D) 1526 (Babur's first Panipat)
cards.back:
(A) 1576 (against Akbar's forces)

Maratha & Later Rulers — BATTLE OF HALDIGHATI — fought on 18 JUNE 1576 between MAHARANA PRATAP of Mewar and Mughal forces commanded by RAJA MAN SINGH I of Amber (acting for Akbar). LOCATION: HALDIGHATI PASS — between Khamnor and Balicha villages in Aravalli range, near Udaipur, Rajasthan. NAME: 'Haldighati' = 'turmeric pass' (yellow soil resembles turmeric powder). BACKGROUND: Akbar had subdued most Rajput states via marriage alliances + diplomacy. Pratap REFUSED to bow to Mughals; Akbar sent armies. OUTCOME: TACTICAL Mughal victory but MEWAR's resistance continued. Pratap escaped on his beloved horse CHETAK; the horse died after the battle from injuries (carrying Pratap to safety). BATTLE FORCES: Mughal ~80,000-100,000; Mewar ~20,000-22,000 (greatly outnumbered). KEY FIGURES on Mewar side: HAKIM KHAN SUR (Pathan Muslim general loyal to Pratap — symbolic of Pratap's secular leadership), JHALA MAN. ON MUGHAL SIDE: Man Singh I, Asaf Khan IV. MEWAR PROVERB: 'Padharo Mhare Des' welcoming visitors but RESIST invaders. AFTERMATH: Pratap continued GUERRILLA WARFARE for 20+ years from forest hideouts (Chittor was permanently lost; capital moved to KUMBHALGARH then CHAVAND). Eventually recovered most of Mewar's territories. PYQ FREQUENCY: Battle of Haldighati in SSC, UPSC, MPSC, RPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
MAHARANA PRATAP was the ruler of which kingdom?

(A) Mewar (capital Chittor/Udaipur)
(B) Marwar (capital Jodhpur, distinct)
(C) Amber (capital Jaipur, Mughal allies)
(D) Bundi (Hadoti area, Rajasthan)
cards.back:
(A) Mewar (capital Chittor/Udaipur)

Maratha & Later Rulers — MEWAR — kingdom in southern RAJASTHAN; ruling dynasty: SISODIA RAJPUTS (still extant; current Maharana of Mewar lives at City Palace, Udaipur). KEY MEWAR CAPITALS over time: (1) NAGDA — early. (2) CHITTOR / CHITTORGARH — main historic capital (lost to Akbar 1568). (3) UDAIPUR — founded by Maharana UDAI SINGH II (Pratap's father) in 1559 as new safer capital. (4) KUMBHALGARH — refuge fort. KEY MEWAR RULERS: BAPPA RAWAL (~8th c., legendary founder), RANA HAMMIR (~14th c.), RANA KUMBHA (~1433-68, built Kumbhalgarh fort with 36-km wall — 2nd longest after Great Wall of China), RANA SANGA (1509-1528, defeated by Babur at Khanwa 1527), UDAI SINGH II, MAHARANA PRATAP (1572-97). RAJPUTANA STATES (memorize for SSC, UPSC, RPSC): (1) MEWAR — Sisodia (Udaipur). (2) MARWAR — Rathore (Jodhpur). (3) AMBER → JAIPUR — Kachhwaha (founded by Sawai Jai Singh II 1727). (4) BIKANER — Rathore. (5) JAISALMER — Bhati. (6) BUNDI + KOTA — Hada Chauhan (Hadoti region). (7) ALWAR — Naruka. (8) TONK, BHARATPUR (Jat), DHOLPUR. UPSC angle: Rajputana history is GS-1 medieval; particularly Akbar's diplomacy with Rajputs. PYQ FREQUENCY: Mewar-Pratap link in SSC, UPSC, MPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Maharana Pratap's faithful HORSE, who saved his life at Haldighati, was named:

(A) Chetak (legendary blue horse)
(B) Bucephalus (Alexander's horse)
(C) Marengo (Napoleon's horse)
(D) Tarini (mythological horse)
cards.back:
(A) Chetak (legendary blue horse)

Maratha & Later Rulers — CHETAK — Maharana Pratap's beloved blue-grey stallion; immortalized in Rajasthan folklore. SIZE: ~14.2 hands; described as remarkably loyal + intelligent. ROLE AT HALDIGHATI: when Pratap was surrounded by Mughal forces, Chetak gallop carried him to safety despite suffering severe injury (one leg cut off by an enemy elephant's blade). Legend: Chetak made a 22-foot leap across a stream/ravine while wounded, then collapsed and died. PRATAP himself was wounded but survived. CHETAK'S CHHATRI (memorial pavilion): in HALDIGHATI area, near the battlefield — popular pilgrimage site. POETIC TRIBUTE: SHYAM NARAYAN PANDEY's poem 'CHETAK' is taught in Hindi/Rajasthani schools — 'Chetak ban kar Chetak doudaa, Pratap ne pukara — koi nahin'. WORLD-FAMOUS HORSES (parallel mention): (1) BUCEPHALUS — Alexander the Great's horse (~356-326 BCE). (2) MARENGO — Napoleon's horse at Waterloo. (3) BLACK BESS — Dick Turpin's horse (legendary highwayman). (4) TURPIN's STAGECOACH HORSES. INDIAN connections — RANI LAKSHMIBAI's horse BADAL/RAJBHASHA — died in 1857 revolt; SHIVAJI MAHARAJ's horse KRISHNA was famous. STATUES of CHETAK + Pratap: (1) Pratap Smarak, Udaipur. (2) Connaught Place, Delhi. (3) Mumbai's Pratap statue. PYQ FREQUENCY: Chetak-Pratap in SSC, UPSC, RPSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Maharana Pratap belonged to which Rajput clan?

(A) Sisodia (of Mewar dynasty)
(B) Rathore (Marwar dynasty)
(C) Kachhwaha (Amber dynasty)
(D) Chauhan (Delhi-area dynasty)
cards.back:
(A) Sisodia (of Mewar dynasty)

Maratha & Later Rulers — SISODIA RAJPUTS — branch of GUHILA dynasty; ruled MEWAR since 8th century. CLAIMED LINEAGE: from RAGHUVANSHA (Lord Rama's lineage); 'SISODIA' name from village SESODA. KEY DATES: founded by BAPPA RAWAL (~728 CE); continuous rule 8th-21st century. CURRENT TITULAR HEAD: Maharana ARVIND SINGH MEWAR (HRH the Maharana of Udaipur; head of Mewar Foundation). MAJOR RAJPUT CLANS (memorize for UPSC): (1) GUHILOT/SISODIA — Mewar, Udaipur. (2) RATHORE — Marwar, Jodhpur, Bikaner. (3) KACHHWAHA — Amber/Jaipur, Alwar. (4) CHAUHAN — Ajmer (Prithviraj), Bundi (Hadoti). (5) BHATI — Jaisalmer. (6) PARMAR/PARAMARA — Malwa. (7) PRATIHARA — Kannauj (8-11th c.). (8) SOLANKI/CHAULUKYA — Gujarat. (9) HADA — branch of Chauhans, Bundi-Kota. ORIGIN MYTHOLOGY: AGNIKULA theory — 4 Rajput clans (Pratihara, Solanki, Chauhan, Parmar) emerged from sacred fire-ritual at Mt Abu (mythological). MODERN view: Rajput identity emerged ~7-9th century from various sources. KEY POLITICAL: only MEWAR (Pratap) DEFIANTLY refused to ally with Mughals via marriage; OTHER RAJPUT clans (Amber, Bikaner, Jodhpur, etc.) accepted Akbar's matrimonial alliances → became 'Rajputana Mughal allies' contributing top military officers. UPSC History optional has substantial Rajput content. PYQ FREQUENCY: Sisodia-Mewar link in SSC, UPSC, RPSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
After Haldighati, where did Maharana Pratap retreat to continue resistance?

(A) Aravalli forests + Kumbhalgarh fort
(B) Surrendered to Akbar at Agra
(C) Fled to Persia for safe haven
(D) Returned to Chittor immediately
cards.back:
(A) Aravalli forests + Kumbhalgarh fort

Maratha & Later Rulers — After HALDIGHATI defeat (1576), Pratap RETREATED INTO ARAVALLI FORESTS and used HILL-FORTS like KUMBHALGARH and CHAVAND as bases. Mughal forces could not penetrate the rugged terrain effectively. GUERRILLA WARFARE: Pratap launched repeated raids on Mughal positions, gradually recovering territories. Akbar sent multiple expeditions (1577, 1578, 1579, 1582) — all failed to capture Pratap. KEY ALLY: BHIL TRIBES of Aravalli forests — provided crucial intelligence, food, fighters; BHIL LOYALTY to Mewar continues today. PRATAP's HARDSHIPS during forest years: (1) Family ate ROTI made from grass (legend). (2) Daughter's bread snatched by a wild cat — Pratap weeping over child's hunger. (3) BHAMASHAH — wealthy Jain merchant — donated his ENTIRE FORTUNE to fund Pratap's army; saved the resistance. KEY VICTORIES post-Haldighati: (1) BATTLE OF DEWAIR (1582) — DECISIVE Mewar victory; Pratap recovered most lost territories. (2) Recapture of CHAVAND (declared new capital, 1585). (3) By 1597 (death), Pratap had recovered ALL of Mewar EXCEPT CHITTOR + AJMER + MANDALGARH. AKBAR's response: gave up direct campaigns; focused on Deccan + Northwest. CHAVAND TODAY: small village in Udaipur district; archaeological remains. RAJASTHAN's PRATAP-MEMORIAL: lots — Pratap Smarak Udaipur, Haldighati battlefield museum, etc. PYQ FREQUENCY: Pratap's resistance in UPSC, MPSC, RPSC 1× per cycle.
cards.option2: Fled to Persia for safe haven

cards.front:
Who funded Maharana Pratap's war by donating his entire fortune?

(A) Bhama Shah (Jain merchant + minister)
(B) Tansen (Akbar's musician here)
(C) Birbal (an Akbar courtier)
(D) Tulsidas (poet of Ramcharitmanas)
cards.back:
(A) Bhama Shah (Jain merchant + minister)

Maratha & Later Rulers — BHAMA SHAH KAVADIA (~1547-1600) — JAIN MERCHANT + senior minister of Mewar; donated his ENTIRE FORTUNE to Pratap when latter was destitute in Aravalli forests. AMOUNT: reportedly enough to fund 25,000 soldiers for 12 years. SIGNIFICANCE: Bhama Shah's contribution was DECISIVE in turning the tide — Pratap launched the BATTLE of DEWAIR (1582) using these funds, recovering large territories. ROLE: Bhama Shah served as PRATAP's PRIME MINISTER + WAZIR + treasurer; later succeeded by his brother Tarachand as Pratap's chief revenue officer. STATURE in Indian history: Bhama Shah is celebrated as a SYMBOL of patriotism + selfless service to the nation. RAJASTHAN GOVT: 'BHAMASHAH YOJANA' (now 'Mukhyamantri Chiranjeevi Yojana' under different governments) — major welfare scheme named after him. RECOGNITION: 'BHAMASHAH' as a generic title for great Indian PHILANTHROPISTS. UPSC angle: communal harmony in Indian history (Pratap, a Hindu Rajput, had Muslim general HAKIM KHAN SUR + Jain treasurer BHAMA SHAH — diversity in his army was a strength); secular historiography. ALSO key generals of Pratap: Hakim Khan Sur (Pathan), JHALA MAN (Jhala clan, sacrificed by wearing Pratap's crown to misdirect enemy at Haldighati). PYQ FREQUENCY: Bhama Shah in UPSC History, RPSC 1× per 2 cycles. EXAMINER MINDSET — UPSC-level: tests beyond textbook generals — to broader societal contributors.

cards.front:
MAHARANA PRATAP died in:

(A) 1597 at Chavand (his last capital)
(B) 1576 at Haldighati battle (option here)
(C) 1605 (year Akbar died) (option here)
(D) 1582 at Battle of Dewair (option here)
cards.back:
(A) 1597 at Chavand (his last capital)

Maratha & Later Rulers — MAHARANA PRATAP died on 19 JANUARY 1597 at CHAVAND (his then-capital after Mewar's recovery), age ~57. CAUSE: hunting injury (fell off horse, sustained internal injuries). DEATH-SCENE LEGEND: even on his deathbed, Pratap made his son AMAR SINGH I swear to NEVER ALLY with Mughals; to recover CHITTOR. SUCCESSION: AMAR SINGH I (1597-1620) honoured the oath for years; eventually had to make peace with Jahangir (1615 — Jahangir agreed Mewar wouldn't have to attend Mughal court; Mewar formally accepted Mughal SUZERAINTY but largely autonomous). MEWAR THEREAFTER: continued under Sisodia Maharanas; British East India Co. signed treaty 1818 (Subsidiary Alliance under Lord Hastings); Mewar was a PRINCELY STATE under British Crown 1858-1947; merged into Indian Union 1949. AKBAR DEATH: 1605 — 8 years after Pratap. AKBAR REPORTEDLY WEPT on hearing of Pratap's death — recognized Pratap as a worthy adversary. POEM by ABDUL RAHIM (Rahim, in Akbar's court) commemorating Pratap's death — testifies to Mughal-court respect. CHAVAND TODAY: small village; some excavated structures; moderately developed for tourists. UDAIPUR: city palace, Pratap Smarak, Bhamashah Park — major Pratap-related sites; also annual MAHARANA PRATAP JAYANTI (9 May) celebration in Rajasthan. UPSC angle: Mewar-Mughal relations — case study of resistance vs accommodation. PYQ FREQUENCY: Pratap death year + successor in UPSC, RPSC 1× per cycle.

MEWAR THEREAFTER: continued under Sisodia Maharanas; British East India Co. signed treaty 1818 (Subsidiary Alliance under Lord Hastings); Mewar was a PRINCELY STATE under British Crown 1858-1947; merged into Indian Union 1949. AKBAR DEATH: 1605 — 8 years after Pratap. AKBAR REPORTEDLY WEPT on hearing of Pratap's death — recognized Pratap as a worthy adversary. POEM by ABDUL RAHIM (Rahim, in Akbar's court) commemorating Pratap's death — testifies to Mughal-court respect. CHAVAND TODAY: small village; some excavated structures; moderately developed for tourists. UDAIPUR: city palace, Pratap Smarak, Bhamashah Park — major Pratap-related sites; also annual MAHARANA PRATAP JAYANTI (9 May) celebration in Rajasthan. UPSC angle: Mewar-Mughal relations — case study of resistance vs accommodation. PYQ FREQUENCY: Pratap death year + successor in UPSC, RPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Who was the FOUNDER of the Maratha Empire, crowned 'Chhatrapati' in 1674?

(A) Shahaji Bhonsle
(B) Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj (1630-1680)
(C) Sambhaji Maharaj
(D) Baji Rao I
cards.back:
(B) Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj (1630-1680)

Maratha & Later Rulers — SHIVAJI BHONSLE (1630-1680) — founded the Maratha Empire from his base in the Deccan. Born at SHIVNERI FORT (Maharashtra) to Shahaji Bhonsle + JIJABAI (a formidable influence on his upbringing). Began by capturing Torna Fort at age 17 (1646). Expanded by 'ganimi kava' (guerrilla warfare). KEY EVENTS: (1) 1659 — killed Afzal Khan (Adil Shahi general) with WAGHNAKH ('tiger claws') at Pratapgad; (2) 1666 — imprisoned by Aurangzeb at Agra, escaped in fruit baskets; (3) 1674 — CROWNED CHHATRAPATI at RAIGAD FORT in a grand Vedic ceremony performed by Gaga Bhatt of Kashi, on 6 June 1674 (SHIV RAJYABHISHEK). Established EIGHT MINISTERS (ASHTAPRADHAN) council — Peshwa (PM), Amatya (Finance), Mantri (Interior), Senapati (Commander), Sachiv (Correspondence), Sumant (Foreign Affairs), Nyayadhish (Chief Justice), Panditrao (Religious Affairs). Forts: RAIGAD (capital), SINHAGAD, PURANDAR, PRATAPGAD, RAJGAD. Died 3 April 1680. Succeeded by son SAMBHAJI (captured + tortured + executed by Aurangzeb 1689).

cards.front:
The TREATY OF PURANDAR (1665) was signed between Shivaji and which Mughal general?

(A) Afzal Khan
(B) Raja Jai Singh I of Amber
(C) Shaista Khan
(D) Aurangzeb personally
cards.back:
(B) Raja Jai Singh I of Amber

Maratha & Later Rulers — TREATY OF PURANDAR (June 1665) — signed between SHIVAJI + RAJA JAI SINGH I OF AMBER (Amer/Jaipur, Rajput general under Aurangzeb). Jai Singh's Mughal force besieged Purandar Fort; after heavy fighting, Shivaji accepted terms: (1) Surrendered 23 of his 35 forts to Mughals; (2) Agreed to serve as a mansabdar of 5000 with his son Sambhaji; (3) Paid tribute + kept only 12 forts (collective revenue 1 lakh huns); (4) Assisted Mughals against Bijapur. As part of this, Shivaji visited Agra in 1666 where he was insulted by Aurangzeb (placed in a lower rank). Imprisoned — famously ESCAPED on 19 August 1666, hidden in fruit/sweet baskets with his son. EARLIER generals Aurangzeb sent: SHAISTA KHAN (Shivaji's maternal uncle by marriage, infamous raid on Lal Mahal Pune 1663 — Shivaji chopped off his fingers in a night raid); AFZAL KHAN (Adil Shahi, killed at Pratapgad 1659). LATER: Pronounced war 1670 onwards, Shivaji sacked SURAT TWICE (1664, 1670) — richest Mughal port.

cards.front:
After Shivaji + Sambhaji's deaths, the Maratha polity was transformed into a CONFEDERACY under the PESHWAS. The most powerful Peshwa (1720-1740) who established Maratha supremacy in northern India was:

(A) Balaji Vishwanath (1st Peshwa, 1713-20)
(B) BAJI RAO I (1720-1740) — never lost a battle in his 20-year career
(C) Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb, 1740-61)
(D) Madhav Rao I (1761-72)
cards.back:
(B) BAJI RAO I (1720-1740) — never lost a battle in his 20-year career

Maratha & Later Rulers — BAJI RAO I (Bajirao Ballal, 1700-1740) — 7th Peshwa (first among the Chitpavan Brahmin Peshwas to wield full power). Ruled 1720-1740. Expanded Maratha power from Deccan to Delhi. Famous for: (1) Guerrilla warfare mastery — UNDEFEATED in 41 battles; (2) Strategy: 'Strike at the trunk of the withering tree (Mughals); the branches will fall off themselves'; (3) Military campaigns: defeated Nizam-ul-Mulk of Hyderabad at PALKHED (1728); raided Delhi (1737, reached Red Fort); took Malwa + Bundelkhand + Gujarat; fought the BATTLE OF BHOPAL (1737) vs combined Nizam forces — Maratha victory. (4) Personal life: Married Kashibai + later MASTANI (Muslim/half-Muslim princess, scandalous at the time, immortalised in Bhansali's 2015 film 'Bajirao Mastani'). Died young (1740, age 39) of heatstroke/sudden illness at Raver camp. Succeeded by son BALAJI BAJI RAO (Nana Saheb, 1740-1761). Marathas reached zenith under him but then PANIPAT III DISASTER (14 Jan 1761) vs Ahmad Shah Abdali — broke the expansion.

cards.front:
The THIRD BATTLE OF PANIPAT (14 January 1761) was fought between the MARATHAS and:

(A) The Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb
(B) Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani) of Afghanistan + Rohilla + Awadh allies
(C) The East India Company
(D) The Sikh Confederacy
cards.back:
(B) Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani) of Afghanistan + Rohilla + Awadh allies

Maratha & Later Rulers — THIRD BATTLE OF PANIPAT — 14 January 1761, at Panipat (Haryana). MARATHAS under SADASHIV RAO BHAU (Peshwa's cousin) + VISHWAS RAO (young heir apparent) + MALHAR RAO HOLKAR, MAHADJI SCINDIA, etc. vs AHMAD SHAH ABDALI (DURRANI) from Afghanistan + Indian allies: NAJIB-UD-DAULA (Rohilla), SHUJA-UD-DAULA (Nawab of Awadh). Maratha force ~45,000 soldiers + massive refugee camp. Outcome: MARATHAS DEVASTATED — ~40,000 killed in battle + 40,000 captives later massacred. Both Sadashiv Rao Bhau + Vishwas Rao killed. Peshwa Nana Saheb died of shock 6 months later. SIGNIFICANCE: Ended Maratha dream of replacing Mughals as paramount power; created vacuum for British East India Company expansion (started 4 years later at Battle of Buxar 1764). Abdali's victory didn't translate to lasting rule in India — he retreated. Sadashiv Rao Bhau's body never found — legend he survived (multiple imposter claims). Maratha historian Govind Sakharam Sardesai called this battle 'the saddest day in the history of India'.
