cards.front:
The MARATHA CONFEDERACY post-Panipat was a loose federation of autonomous chiefs. Which of the following was NOT a major Maratha chieftain family?

(A) Scindias of Gwalior
(B) Holkars of Indore
(C) Gaekwads of Baroda
(D) Deccan Nizams of Hyderabad
cards.back:
(D) Deccan Nizams of Hyderabad

Maratha & Later Rulers — MARATHA CONFEDERACY (post-Panipat) — five major chieftainships ('Panchayatana'): (1) PESHWAS of PUNE — nominal overall leaders (Bhatt family, Chitpavan Brahmins); (2) SCINDIAS of GWALIOR (Madhya Pradesh) — founded by Ranoji Scindia; famous descendant Mahadji Scindia; (3) HOLKARS of INDORE (MP) — founded by Malhar Rao Holkar; famous AHILYABAI HOLKAR (queen-regent 1767-95 — great patron of temples, built ghats + temples at Varanasi, Somnath, Haridwar, Dwarka, etc.); (4) GAEKWADS of BARODA (Gujarat) — still continues as Baroda royal family (titular); (5) BHONSLES of NAGPUR (Maharashtra — different from Shivaji's Bhonsle line). The NIZAM of HYDERABAD was NOT Maratha — he was a Mughal-descended ruler (Asaf Jahi dynasty, independent from 1724 under Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I). Marathas extracted CHAUTH (1/4 revenue) + SARDESHMUKHI (1/10 revenue) from rulers who wanted protection / non-invasion. By early 19th c., weakened by internal conflicts + Anglo-Maratha wars (1775-82, 1803-05, 1817-18), British annexed them one by one.

cards.front:
The THREE ANGLO-MARATHA WARS (1775-82, 1803-05, 1817-18) culminated in the complete defeat of the Marathas. The LAST Peshwa, BAJI RAO II, surrendered after which war + retired where?

(A) 1st Anglo-Maratha War; retired to Satara
(B) 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1818); exiled to BITHUR (near Kanpur, UP) on pension
(C) Battle of Panipat; retired to Gwalior
(D) Battle of Plassey
cards.back:
(B) 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1818); exiled to BITHUR (near Kanpur, UP) on pension

Maratha & Later Rulers — BAJI RAO II — the LAST (13th) Peshwa (r. 1795-1818). Signed the TREATY OF BASSEIN (1802) with British — a Subsidiary Alliance, ceding authority — which triggered 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Defeated in 1st Anglo-Maratha War (partial). Defeated + exiled after 3rd ANGLO-MARATHA WAR (1817-18 — actually the Peshwa-led 'war' ended 1818). Signed Treaty of Poona (1817) surrendering power. The PESHWAI was formally ABOLISHED in 1818 by Lord Hastings. Baji Rao II was exiled to BITHUR (near Kanpur, UP) on a pension of ₹8 lakh/year. He lived there till his death in 1851. His adopted son NANA SAHEB (Dhondu Pant) was denied the pension continuation by Dalhousie — a key grievance that made Nana a leader of the 1857 Revolt. LATER Marathas: SATARA annexed 1848 (Doctrine of Lapse); NAGPUR 1854; JHANSI 1853. Saw themselves as successors to Shivaji via the Bhonsle line. Maharashtra's identity post-Shivaji became powerfully anti-imperial.
cards.option2: Battle of Panipat; retired to Gwalior

cards.front:
SHIVAJI's famous title 'CHHATRAPATI' means:

(A) Chief of the sea
(B) Lord of the umbrella / Supreme sovereign
(C) Fortress commander
(D) Warrior priest
cards.back:
(B) Lord of the umbrella / Supreme sovereign

Maratha & Later Rulers — CHHATRAPATI = 'Chhatra' (umbrella / royal canopy) + 'Pati' (master/lord) = 'Lord of the Umbrella' — a symbol of sovereign kingship in Indian tradition (the umbrella is an ancient Sanskrit royal insignia, going back to Vedic times). Hence CHHATRAPATI = Supreme Sovereign / Paramount Ruler. The title put Shivaji on par with (or superior to) Mughal Padshah + Adil Shah + Nizam — asserting Maratha independence. The coronation ceremony on 6 June 1674 at Raigad was performed by GAGA BHATT (Pandit Vishwanath Bhatt of Banaras), who after initial objections (Marathas not being ritualistic Kshatriyas) agreed to perform a Vedic RajyaAbhishek. A second Tantric Abhishek was also done later. Shivaji adopted new regnal insignia: his own coinage (HOH / HONS / SHIVRAI), royal seal in Sanskrit, titles like HAINDAVA-DHARMODDHAARAKA (Defender of Hindu Dharma), MARATHA MAHAMARATHA. Modern Indian railway stations + international airport in Mumbai named after him (CSMT — Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus, 1996 renaming; CSMIA airport). Hon'd with national importance post-independence. umbrella-bearer, symbol of kingship.

cards.front:
The first PESHWA of the Maratha empire who held the office as a hereditary office was:

(A) Balaji Vishwanath Bhat (1713-1720)
(B) Bajirao I, the celebrated military commander
(C) Balaji Bajirao (also called Nanasaheb)
(D) Madhavrao I, the youngest of the Peshwas
cards.back:
(A) Balaji Vishwanath Bhat (1713-1720)

Maratha & Later Rulers — Balaji Vishwanath — the FIRST hereditary Peshwa, appointed by Shahu Chhatrapati in 1713. Before him, the Peshwa office existed under Shivaji and his successors but was not hereditary. Balaji secured the Maratha 'sardeshmukhi' rights from the Mughals and laid the foundation of confederate Maratha rule. His son Bajirao I (1720-40) was the great expansionist. Grandson Balaji Bajirao / Nanasaheb (1740-61) expanded but lost at Panipat-3. Madhavrao I (1761-72) revived Maratha power after Panipat.

cards.front:
Bajirao I (Peshwa, 1720-40) is most remembered for:

(A) Concluding peace with the Nizam of Hyderabad
(B) Rapidly extending Maratha rule deep into north India
(C) Capturing the Bahamani sultanate of Bijapur
(D) Forming a permanent alliance with the British EIC
cards.back:
(B) Rapidly extending Maratha rule deep into north India

Maratha & Later Rulers — Bajirao I — perhaps the greatest Maratha military commander; never lost a battle. Took Maratha cavalry as far as Delhi (1737), defeated the Nizam at Palkhed (1728) and Bhopal (1737-38). Rapidly extended Maratha rule beyond the Narmada into Malwa, Bundelkhand, Gujarat. Distractor 1 — Bajirao DEFEATED the Nizam, did not make peace. Distractor 3 — Bijapur was a Mughal province by then. Distractor 4 — anachronistic; the EIC was still consolidating coastal trade. Bajirao died young at 39 of fever in 1740.

cards.front:
The THIRD BATTLE OF PANIPAT (14 January 1761) was fought between:

(A) Babur and the last Lodi sultan Ibrahim
(B) The Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan
(C) Akbar's general Bairam Khan and Hemu
(D) The British East India Company and Sirajuddaula
cards.back:
(B) The Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan

Maratha & Later Rulers — Third Panipat (14 Jan 1761) — Marathas (commanded by Sadashivrao Bhau, with Vishwasrao the heir-apparent) vs Ahmad Shah Abdali / Durrani of Afghanistan (allied with Najib-ud-Daula and Shuja-ud-Daulah). Decisive Maratha defeat — ~50-70,000 Maratha casualties. Halted Maratha northward expansion at the worst possible moment for them. Distractor 1 = First Panipat (1526). Distractor 3 = Second Panipat (1556, Akbar vs Hemu). Distractor 4 = Battle of Plassey (1757).

cards.front:
After Panipat-3 (1761), Maratha power was revived under which young Peshwa?

(A) Bajirao II (the last Peshwa, surrendered to British)
(B) Madhavrao I (Peshwa 1761-72, revived the empire)
(C) Narayanrao (Peshwa briefly, assassinated 1773)
(D) Sawai Madhavrao (boy Peshwa under Nana Phadnavis)
cards.back:
(B) Madhavrao I (Peshwa 1761-72, revived the empire)

Maratha & Later Rulers — Madhavrao I — became Peshwa at age 16 in 1761, when the empire seemed broken after Panipat. In just 11 years he restored Maratha hegemony in the north (re-established suzerainty over Mughal emperor Shah Alam II in 1772), defeated the Nizam, suppressed Mysore raids. Died of TB at age 27 (1772). Often called the 'last great Peshwa'. After him decline set in. Distractor 1 — Bajirao II's tenure ended in surrender to the British in 1818. Distractor 3 — Narayanrao was murdered in 1773 by his uncle Raghunathrao's guards. Distractor 4 — Sawai Madhavrao reigned briefly as a child under Nana Phadnavis's regency.

cards.front:
The Maratha CONFEDERACY in the late 18th century included five major chiefs (sardars). Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

(A) Holkar — Indore; Scindia — Gwalior; Bhonsle — Nagpur
(B) Holkar — Pune; Gaekwad — Indore; Bhonsle — Mysore
(C) Scindia — Pune; Holkar — Tanjore; Gaekwad — Lucknow
(D) Bhonsle — Bijapur; Scindia — Mysore; Holkar — Cuttack
cards.back:
(A) Holkar — Indore; Scindia — Gwalior; Bhonsle — Nagpur

Maratha & Later Rulers — Maratha confederacy seats (after consolidation): PESHWA — Pune (titular head). HOLKAR — Indore. SCINDIA / SHINDE — Gwalior (and Ujjain). BHONSLE — Nagpur (a different branch from Shivaji's family who ruled in Maharashtra and Tanjore). GAEKWAD — Baroda (Vadodara, Gujarat). Each chief was largely autonomous; only loosely answered to the Peshwa. This decentralisation was a strategic strength but a coordination weakness in the Anglo-Maratha wars.

cards.front:
The Treaty of Bassein (December 1802), which placed the Peshwa under British 'subsidiary alliance', triggered the:

(A) First Anglo-Maratha War (Salbai treaty, 1782)
(B) Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05, Wellesley)
(C) Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-18, Hastings)
(D) First Anglo-Sikh War (1845-46, Hardinge)
cards.back:
(B) Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05, Wellesley)

Maratha & Later Rulers — Treaty of Bassein (Dec 1802) — Bajirao II, after losing to Holkar, fled to British protection and signed this treaty accepting subsidiary alliance and a British force at Pune. The other Maratha sardars (Scindia, Bhonsle, Holkar) saw this as betrayal and the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) followed under Lord Wellesley → Battles of Assaye (Arthur Wellesley, future Duke of Wellington), Argaon, Laswari. Treaty of Salbai (1782) ended the First war. Third war (1817-18) under Lord Hastings ended the Maratha confederacy entirely.

cards.front:
The LAST Peshwa, who was defeated by the British in 1818 and exiled to Bithur near Kanpur, was:

(A) Madhavrao Narayan, the boy Peshwa of Pune
(B) Bajirao II, son of Raghunathrao 'Raghoba'
(C) Balaji Bajirao, defeated earlier at Panipat
(D) Bajirao I, the great expansionist of the north
cards.back:
(B) Bajirao II, son of Raghunathrao 'Raghoba'

Maratha & Later Rulers — Bajirao II — the last Peshwa. Surrendered after the Third Anglo-Maratha War (June 1818, Battle of Koregaon-Bhima earlier in Jan 1818). Accepted a pension of ₹8 lakh/year and was exiled to Bithur (near Kanpur). His adopted son was NANA SAHIB — leader of the 1857 revolt at Kanpur. Distractor 1 — Madhavrao Narayan died young in 1795. Distractor 3 — Balaji Bajirao (Nanasaheb) died of grief shortly after Panipat-3. Distractor 4 — Bajirao I died in 1740.

cards.front:
The Portuguese explorer who reached the port of Calicut on India's Malabar coast on 20 May 1498 was:

(A) Pedro Álvares Cabral
(B) Vasco da Gama
(C) Bartolomeu Dias
(D) Afonso de Albuquerque
cards.back:
(B) Vasco da Gama

Maratha & Later Rulers — Vasco da Gama — landed at Kappad near Calicut on 20 May 1498, ending centuries-old Arab monopoly on the Indo-European spice trade route. Welcomed by Zamorin of Calicut. Made three voyages; died at Cochin (1524) on the third. Cabral followed in 1500 (also discovered Brazil en route). Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope (1488) but never reached India. Albuquerque was the second governor (1509-15) who captured Goa in 1510.

cards.front:
Goa was captured by the Portuguese in 1510 from:

(A) Mughals
(B) Bijapur Sultanate (Yusuf Adil Shah)
(C) Vijayanagar Empire
(D) Marathas
cards.back:
(B) Bijapur Sultanate (Yusuf Adil Shah)

Maratha & Later Rulers — Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the Bijapur Sultanate (ruled by Yusuf Adil Shah) on 25 November 1510. Goa became the capital of Portuguese India. Notable Portuguese policy — 'Estado da Índia' (the State of India) ruled from Goa over Portuguese settlements stretching from East Africa to Macau. Goa Inquisition was established 1560 by Francis Xavier's request. Goa remained Portuguese until Operation Vijay liberated it on 19 December 1961, ending 451 years of Portuguese rule.

cards.front:
The French East India Company was established by Jean-Baptiste Colbert during the reign of Louis XIV in:

(A) 1600
(B) 1664
(C) 1700
(D) 1614
cards.back:
(B) 1664

Maratha & Later Rulers — Compagnie française des Indes orientales — founded 1664 by Colbert, Louis XIV's finance minister, much later than English (1600), Dutch (1602) or Danish (1616) companies. Headquarters at Surat (1668), then Pondicherry (1674). Other settlements — Chandernagore (1690), Mahe (1721), Yanam (1731), Karikal (1739). All five were transferred to India between 1949-54 (de jure 1962). The company was dissolved 1769 after losing the Carnatic wars.

cards.front:
The decisive Battle of Wandiwash (22 January 1760), which broke French power in India, was fought between:

(A) Robert Clive vs Dupleix
(B) Sir Eyre Coote (English) vs Comte de Lally (French)
(C) Cornwallis vs Tipu Sultan
(D) Hastings vs Mahadji Scindia
cards.back:
(B) Sir Eyre Coote (English) vs Comte de Lally (French)

Maratha & Later Rulers — Battle of Wandiwash (Vandavasi, modern Tamil Nadu) — fought during the Third Carnatic War (1756-63) — Anglo-French rivalry. Sir Eyre Coote led the English; Comte de Lally the French. English victory was decisive; Pondicherry fell in 1761. Treaty of Paris (1763) restored Pondicherry to France but stripped it of military / political power — became merely a commercial outpost. Marks the 'end of French ambitions' in India. Robert Clive had earlier won Plassey 1757; Dupleix recalled to France 1754.

cards.front:
The Portuguese policy of 'Cartaz' was best described as:

(A) Religious conversion drive in Goa
(B) A licence/pass system requiring all Asian ships to buy Portuguese permits to trade in Indian Ocean
(C) A naval treaty with Mughals
(D) A spice price-control mechanism
cards.back:
(B) A licence/pass system requiring all Asian ships to buy Portuguese permits to trade in Indian Ocean

Maratha & Later Rulers — Cartaz (Portuguese for 'pass / placard') — Portuguese ships intercepted any Asian merchant vessel without one. Without a Cartaz, ships were considered hostile and could be sunk or seized. This monopolised the Indian Ocean trade — until the Dutch and English broke it in the 17th century. The system was the precursor to later European 'navicert' practices. Other Portuguese institutions in India — Estado da Índia (the colonial admin), the Goa Inquisition (religious court), Cidade Velha de Goa.

cards.front:
Goa, Daman and Diu were liberated from Portuguese rule by Indian armed action — codenamed 'Operation Vijay' — in:

(A) August 1947
(B) December 1961
(C) January 1950
(D) March 1956
cards.back:
(B) December 1961

Maratha & Later Rulers — Operation Vijay (17-19 December 1961) — Indian forces under Maj Gen K.P. Candeth liberated Goa, Daman and Diu after years of failed diplomacy with Portugal under António Salazar. PM Nehru took the decision after the Portuguese refused all UN appeals. Casualties were minimal. Goa, Daman and Diu became a Union Territory in 1962. Goa attained statehood on 30 May 1987 (became 25th state). Daman & Diu merged with Dadra & Nagar Haveli in 2020 to form a single UT.

cards.front:
Joseph François Dupleix, the French Governor-General who built up French ambitions in South India in the 1740s, was based at:

(A) Chandernagore
(B) Pondicherry
(C) Mahe
(D) Karikal
cards.back:
(B) Pondicherry

Maratha & Later Rulers — Joseph François Dupleix (Gov-Gen of French India 1742-54) operated from Pondicherry. He pioneered the use of European-trained Indian sepoys and the strategy of intervening in Indian princely politics — both later perfected by the British. He won the First Carnatic War (1746-48), but was overstretched in the Second (1748-54). Recalled to France in disgrace; died bankrupt 1763. The other 4 French settlements were smaller — Chandernagore (Bengal), Mahe (Malabar), Yanam (Andhra), Karikal (Tamil coast).

cards.front:
When was CHHATRAPATI SHIVAJI MAHARAJ formally crowned at Raigad?

(A) 6 June 1674 — Raigad coronation
(B) 1656 at Pune fort alone alone
(C) 1680 at Pratapgarh fort alone
(D) 1672 at Sinhagad fort alone
cards.back:
(A) 6 June 1674 — Raigad coronation

Maratha & Later Rulers — CHHATRAPATI SHIVAJI MAHARAJ was crowned on 6 JUNE 1674 (Jyeshta Shukla Trayodashi 1596 Shaka) at RAIGAD FORT — establishing the MARATHA EMPIRE as an independent Hindu sovereignty. CORONATION CEREMONY: officiated by Pandit GAGA BHATT of Varanasi (a top Sanskrit scholar) who declared Shivaji a 'Kshatriya' (some priests had questioned his caste). EXPENDITURE: ~50 lakh huns (gold coins) — astronomical for the time. SIGNIFICANCE: First Hindu king crowned in India after centuries of Mughal/Sultanate dominance; established 'Hindavi Swarajya' (self-rule for Indians). MARATHA NEW CALENDAR: started the Rajyabhishek Shaka era. SHIVAJI'S BIRTH: 19 February 1630 (some scholars say 1627) at Shivneri Fort, near Junnar. PARENTS: Shahaji Bhosale (Bijapur general) and Jijabai (educator-mother). DEATH: 3 April 1680 at Raigad, age 50. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'Shivaji's coronation' is a UPSC, SSC, MPSC top-history fact — 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests precise dates of foundational events.

cards.front:
What was Shivaji's SIGNATURE MILITARY TACTIC against Mughal armies?

(A) Guerrilla warfare from hill forts
(B) Massive cavalry charges alone
(C) Naval blockades only alone
(D) Long-range cannon bombardment.
cards.back:
(A) Guerrilla warfare from hill forts

Maratha & Later Rulers — SHIVAJI's brilliance lay in GANIMI KAVA (guerrilla warfare) — small mobile units hitting larger Mughal armies and disappearing into the rugged Sahyadri hills. KEY ELEMENTS: (1) SUDDEN AMBUSHES on troop columns. (2) Use of ~250+ HILL FORTS as bases — Raigad, Pratapgarh, Sinhagad, Torna, Rajgad, Shivneri. (3) Lightning-fast strikes; never engaged in pitched battle against superior numbers. (4) Local Konkani/Maratha troops who knew the terrain intimately. FAMOUS TACTICAL BRILLIANCES: (a) AFZAL KHAN ENCOUNTER (1659) — Shivaji used WAGHNAKHA (tiger-claws) hidden in his fist to disembowel Khan during a 'peace meeting' at Pratapgarh. (b) SHAISTA KHAN RAID (1663) — Shivaji's commandos snuck into Pune red-fort, severed Khan's fingers, escaped (a personal humiliation for Aurangzeb's uncle). (c) SURAT SACK (1664) — Shivaji's army looted the Mughal-financed Surat port for ~1 crore rupees of treasure. NAVY: Shivaji established the FIRST INDIAN NAVY (~400 vessels) — earned title 'Father of Indian Navy'. PYQ ANGLE: tactical innovations frequently asked.

cards.front:
Shivaji's council of EIGHT MINISTERS was called:

(A) Ashtapradhan (eight chief ministers)
(B) Mansabdar council alone alone
(C) Diwan-i-Khas alone alone alone
(D) Gupta council alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Ashtapradhan (eight chief ministers)

Maratha & Later Rulers — ASHTAPRADHAN (literally 'eight chiefs') — Shivaji's PRIME COUNCIL of MINISTERS for administering the Maratha state. THE EIGHT POSITIONS: (1) PESHWA — Prime Minister (later became hereditary; Bajirao I etc. famous Peshwas). (2) AMATYA / MAJUMDAR — Finance Minister. (3) MANTRI / WAQENAVIS — Records Officer (chronicler). (4) SACHIV / SHURUNAVIS — Royal Correspondence Secretary. (5) SUMANT / DABIR — Foreign Affairs Minister. (6) SENAPATI / SAR-I-NAUBAT — Commander-in-chief of military. (7) PANDITRAO — Religious Affairs / Charitable Endowments. (8) NYAYADHISH — Chief Justice. STRUCTURAL INNOVATION: Shivaji broke the Mughal/Bijapur tradition of granting hereditary jagirs (land assignments) — instead his ministers were SALARIED, REVOCABLE, and rotated periodically — preventing power consolidation. ROUTINE: Ashtapradhan met daily; major decisions required council deliberation. INFLUENCE ON LATER EMPIRES: post-Shivaji, Peshwa Baji Rao I (1720-40) effectively became the de-facto head; the Maratha Confederacy emerged. PYQ FREQUENCY: Ashtapradhan structure tested in UPSC, MPSC every 2 cycles. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests Maratha-administration knowledge.

INFLUENCE ON LATER EMPIRES: post-Shivaji, Peshwa Baji Rao I (1720-40) effectively became the de-facto head; the Maratha Confederacy emerged. PYQ FREQUENCY: Ashtapradhan structure tested in UPSC, MPSC every 2 cycles. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests Maratha-administration knowledge.

cards.front:
Which Mughal Emperor invited Shivaji to AGRA in 1666, leading to a famous escape?

(A) Aurangzeb (the sixth Mughal Emperor)
(B) Shah Jahan, who was deposed.
(C) Akbar I, who died 1605. (option here)
(D) Bahadur Shah, who was Aurangzeb's son.
cards.back:
(A) Aurangzeb (the sixth Mughal Emperor)

Maratha & Later Rulers — AURANGZEB (r. 1658-1707) invited Shivaji to Agra in 1666 to receive him at his 50th-birthday darbar — but humiliated him by seating him among lower-ranked nobles. Furious, Shivaji demonstrated displeasure and was placed under HOUSE ARREST. THE ESCAPE — 17 AUGUST 1666: in one of history's most legendary escapes, Shivaji had himself + son Sambhaji smuggled out of Agra in BIG FRUIT BASKETS (mithai/sweets baskets, prepared 'as offerings to Brahmins'). They reached Mathura, then Vrindavan, then Banaras, finally Raigad in October 1666 — disguised at various points. CONSEQUENCES: Aurangzeb was livid; Shivaji intensified his anti-Mughal campaigns. The PURANDAR TREATY (1665, with Raja Jai Singh of Amber on Aurangzeb's behalf) had earlier ceded 23 forts to Mughals — Shivaji recovered most by 1670. CULTURAL ICON: this escape is dramatized in countless plays, films, comics. The 'fruit-basket escape' is part of every Indian schoolchild's history syllabus. PYQ ANGLE: Shivaji-Aurangzeb interactions are perennial UPSC, SSC, MPSC content. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests dates + key historical events recall.
cards.option3: Bahadur Shah, who was Aurangzeb's son.

cards.front:
Who was the first PESHWA (chief minister) of the Maratha Empire under Shivaji?

(A) Moropant Trimbak Pingle
(B) Balaji Vishwanath Bhat alone.
(C) Baji Rao I of Pune alone.
(D) Madhav Rao I as young.
cards.back:
(A) Moropant Trimbak Pingle

Maratha & Later Rulers — MOROPANT TRIMBAK PINGLE was the FIRST PESHWA appointed by Shivaji in 1674 (at Raigad coronation). He served as the head of the Ashtapradhan administrative council. PESHWA EVOLUTION: under Shivaji, the post was a SALARIED OFFICE — not hereditary. After Shivaji's son SAMBHAJI (1680-1689) and grandson SHAHU (after 1707, post-Mughal release), the Peshwa role became progressively more powerful. From BALAJI VISHWANATH BHAT (1713-1720), the Peshwa's office became HEREDITARY in the BHAT FAMILY — known as the BHAT (Brahmin) PESHWAS. FAMOUS HEREDITARY PESHWAS: Balaji Vishwanath (1713-20), Bajirao I (1720-40, the 'unconquered general'), Balaji Bajirao 'Nanasaheb' (1740-61, lost at Panipat 1761), Madhav Rao I (1761-72, restored Maratha glory), Bajirao II (1796-1818, last Peshwa, defeated at Battle of Bhima Koregaon 1818 ending Maratha rule). FACT: by 18th century, Peshwa effectively ran the Maratha Confederacy; the Chhatrapati at Satara was nominal. PYQ ANGLE: Peshwa chronology is a perennial MPSC, UPSC, SSC topic.
cards.option2: Baji Rao I of Pune alone.

cards.front:
Shivaji's two main land-revenue taxes on conquered Mughal/Bijapur territories were:

(A) Chauth and Sardeshmukhi
(B) Jizya and Khums alone alone
(C) Zakat and Ushr alone alone
(D) Mahsul and Kharaj alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Chauth and Sardeshmukhi

Maratha & Later Rulers — CHAUTH = 1/4 (25%) of land revenue — collected from non-Maratha territories in exchange for not raiding them. SARDESHMUKHI = an additional 10% — claimed as the 'hereditary right' of the Maratha Sardeshmukh (chief). TOGETHER: 35% of revenue — Marathas collected this from Mughal and other states starting from Aurangzeb's later years and into the 18th century. STRATEGIC USE: chauth-sardeshmukhi funded the Maratha military expansion across India — northwards to Lahore, eastwards to Bengal, southwards to Tanjore. By the 1750s, Marathas had become the de-facto ruling power in the north (Pindari raids fed by chauth). HISTORICAL CONTRAST: Marathas didn't generally CONQUER and ADMINISTER all these territories — they extracted revenue while allowing local rulers to remain. This 'tribute system' eventually weakened them; lacking a unified bureaucracy they were vulnerable to British divide-and-rule. AURANGZEB'S DECCAN CAMPAIGN (1681-1707) was driven by his frustration at chauth-collection by Marathas — he died in Deccan, exhausted. PYQ ANGLE: chauth-sardeshmukhi is top-5 medieval-history MCQ.

cards.front:
Shivaji's tutor and chief mentor in his early years (military strategy, ethics, administration) was:

(A) Dadoji Konddev (his Pune mentor)
(B) Samarth Ramdas, the spiritual guru
(C) Tukaram, bhakti poet alone alone
(D) Eknath, philosopher-saint alone
cards.back:
(A) Dadoji Konddev (his Pune mentor)

Maratha & Later Rulers — DADOJI KONDDEV was Shivaji's tutor and JAGIR ADMINISTRATOR for the Pune jagir during his minority. Appointed by his father Shahaji Bhosale, Dadoji trained young Shivaji in: (1) Military strategy and weapons (sword, lance, archery, horseback). (2) Reading, writing, Sanskrit, Persian. (3) Statecraft and administration. (4) Mavla guerrilla traditions of the Sahyadri hills. He died ~1647 when Shivaji was ~17 — Shivaji thereafter independently ran Pune affairs. SAMARTH RAMDAS (1608-1681) was Shivaji's SPIRITUAL GURU later in life — author of the 'Dasbodh', a treatise on ethics, statecraft, and devotion. Shivaji deeply respected Ramdas; some legends say he offered his entire kingdom in symbolic 'bhiksha' (alms) to Ramdas, who blessed it back to him. JIJABAI (mother) was an enormous moral influence — she narrated Mahabharata-Ramayana stories, instilling values of justice and bravery. PYQ FREQUENCY: Shivaji's biographical figures (mentors, generals, family) appear in 1-2 MPSC, UPSC questions per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests detailed biographical knowledge of Shivaji's formative years.

cards.front:
Haidar Ali was the de-facto ruler of which kingdom in the late 18th century?

(A) The Maratha confederacy with seat at Pune
(B) The Mysore kingdom in southern Karnataka
(C) The Hyderabad state of the Asaf Jahi Nizams
(D) The Travancore state on the Malabar coast
cards.back:
(B) The Mysore kingdom in southern Karnataka

Maratha & Later Rulers — Haidar Ali (1721-82) — rose from soldier to commander to ruler of Mysore (1761), nominally serving the Wodeyar dynasty as 'Sarvadhikari'. Built up a modern infantry-artillery army with French help. Engaged the British in the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69, Treaty of Madras restoring status quo). Died during the Second Anglo-Mysore War (1782); succeeded by his son TIPU SULTAN. Distractor 1 = Marathas (Peshwas at Pune). Distractor 3 = Asaf Jahis. Distractor 4 = Travancore was ruled by its own dynasty.
cards.option1: The Maratha confederacy with seat at Pune
cards.option2: The Hyderabad state of the Asaf Jahi Nizams
cards.option3: The Travancore state on the Malabar coast

cards.front:
Tipu Sultan, often called the 'Tiger of Mysore', died in 1799 defending which fortress against the British?

(A) Bidar fort, in northern Karnataka region
(B) Srirangapatna, on the Cauvery river
(C) Bhondsi fort, in Maharashtra Deccan
(D) Bekal fort, in northern Kerala coast
cards.back:
(B) Srirangapatna, on the Cauvery river

Maratha & Later Rulers — Srirangapatna (Seringapatam) — Tipu's island capital, on the Cauvery near Mysore. Fell on 4 May 1799 to British under Lord Wellesley + Arthur Wellesley (later Duke of Wellington); Tipu died in the breach. End of FOURTH Anglo-Mysore War (1798-99). Mysore territory split — restored to a child Wodeyar (Krishnaraja Wodeyar III) under British subsidiary alliance, plus annexations to British and to Hyderabad. Tipu's family imprisoned at Vellore Fort — site of 1806 Vellore Mutiny. Distractor 1, 3, 4 are real forts but not associated with Tipu's death.
cards.option1: Bidar fort, in northern Karnataka region
cards.option3: Bekal fort, in northern Kerala coast

cards.front:
Tipu Sultan was a pioneer in the military use of:

(A) Submarines for naval warfare on the western coast
(B) Iron-cased rockets, technology adopted later by the British
(C) Hot-air balloons used for surveying enemy formations
(D) Steam-powered warships in the Bay of Bengal area
cards.back:
(B) Iron-cased rockets, technology adopted later by the British

Maratha & Later Rulers — MYSOREAN ROCKETS — iron-tube-encased gunpowder rockets, range up to ~2 km. Used effectively at Pollilur (1780) by Haidar Ali against East India Company. The British captured many at Srirangapatna (1799); Sir William Congreve studied them at the Royal Arsenal, Woolwich → developed CONGREVE ROCKETS used by British in Napoleonic Wars + War of 1812 (the 'rockets' red glare' line in the US national anthem). Tipu's rockets thus had a direct line to modern artillery rockets. APJ Abdul Kalam (former Indian President + ISRO scientist) cited Mysorean rockets as inspiration.

cards.option2: Hot-air balloons used for surveying enemy formations
cards.option3: Steam-powered warships in the Bay of Bengal area

cards.front:
Which TREATY ended the Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84)?

(A) Treaty of Salbai with the Marathas in 1782
(B) Treaty of Mangalore between Tipu and the British in 1784
(C) Treaty of Seringapatam after the third war in 1792
(D) Treaty of Bassein with the Peshwa Bajirao II in 1802
cards.back:
(B) Treaty of Mangalore between Tipu and the British in 1784

Maratha & Later Rulers — Treaty of Mangalore — March 1784. Tipu and the British. Restored prisoners and conquests to status quo ante. Notable as the LAST treaty between an Indian ruler and the British that was negotiated on equal terms (Tipu held the British weaker position then). Distractor 1 — Salbai ended the FIRST Anglo-Maratha War. Distractor 3 — Treaty of Seringapatam ended the THIRD Anglo-Mysore War (1790-92), forcing Tipu to cede half his territory + send two sons as hostages. Distractor 4 — Treaty of Bassein triggered the SECOND Anglo-Maratha War.

cards.option2: Treaty of Seringapatam after the third war in 1792
cards.option3: Treaty of Bassein with the Peshwa Bajirao II in 1802

cards.front:
How many ANGLO-MYSORE WARS were fought between the British East India Company and the Mysore kingdom?

(A) Two wars, in 1767-69 and in 1798-99
(B) Four wars, between 1767 and 1799
(C) Six wars, similar to the Anglo-Maratha sequence
(D) Three wars, all of which Tipu Sultan led
cards.back:
(B) Four wars, between 1767 and 1799

Maratha & Later Rulers — Four Anglo-Mysore Wars: 1ST (1767-69) — Treaty of Madras (Haidar against EIC + Hyderabad + Marathas). 2ND (1780-84) — Treaty of Mangalore (Haidar early, Tipu finished). 3RD (1790-92) — Treaty of Seringapatam (Tipu lost half territory, two sons as hostages). 4TH (1798-99) — Tipu killed at Srirangapatna; Mysore largely annexed/restored to Wodeyars under subsidiary alliance. Distractor 1 misses 2 of the 4. Distractor 3 = Anglo-Maratha sequence (3 wars in fact, not 6). Distractor 4 — Tipu led only 2nd (partly), 3rd, 4th (his father led the 1st).
cards.option2: Six wars, similar to the Anglo-Maratha sequence
cards.option3: Three wars, all of which Tipu Sultan led

cards.front:
Tipu Sultan's foreign policy was distinctive in seeking diplomatic ties with which European power against the British?

(A) Portugal, then losing influence in Asian trade routes
(B) Revolutionary / Napoleonic France, particularly after 1789
(C) Russia, the rising European empire from the north
(D) Spain, with bases in the Philippines and far-east Asia
cards.back:
(B) Revolutionary / Napoleonic France, particularly after 1789

Maratha & Later Rulers — Tipu corresponded with Revolutionary France: planted a 'Liberty Tree' at Srirangapatna (1797), styled himself 'Citoyen Tipu' (Citizen Tipu) in Jacobin fashion, sought Napoleonic alliance after Bonaparte's Egyptian expedition (1798). The Treaty of Hyderabad (1798) — British forced Hyderabad's Nizam to dismiss French officers, isolating Tipu. The Fourth Anglo-Mysore War followed, leading to Tipu's death. Distractor 1 — Portugal had no significant influence by then. Distractor 3 — Russian engagement in S Asia came later. Distractor 4 — Spain was waning.

cards.option2: Russia, the rising European empire from the north
cards.option3: Spain, with bases in the Philippines and far-east Asia

cards.front:
Tipu Sultan introduced an administrative + revenue innovation that significantly increased state revenue. He:

(A) Sold all the state's land directly to private buyers
(B) Eliminated middlemen zamindars and collected revenue directly
(C) Reduced agricultural taxes to one-tenth of normal levels
(D) Banned all foreign trade through coastal Mysore ports
cards.back:
(B) Eliminated middlemen zamindars and collected revenue directly

Maratha & Later Rulers — Tipu abolished the intermediary zamindari/poligar system in much of Mysore — assessed and collected land revenue DIRECTLY by state officials (similar to Sher Shah Suri's earlier reforms). Increased state revenue, undermined the local landed aristocracy. Also encouraged commerce: established trading depots at foreign ports (Muscat, Pegu, Aden, China), built a state navy, established sericulture (silk industry — ~21 silk production centres), introduced new tax systems. Distractor 1 — false. Distractor 3 — taxes were not slashed dramatically. Distractor 4 — opposite of true; he encouraged trade.

cards.option2: Reduced agricultural taxes to one-tenth of normal levels
cards.option3: Banned all foreign trade through coastal Mysore ports

cards.front:
TIPU SULTAN, the 'Tiger of Mysore', was killed in which battle?

(A) Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (Srirangapatna 1799)
(B) Second Anglo-Mysore War (Mangalore)
(C) Battle of Plassey (Bengal 1757)
(D) Battle of Buxar (1764, Bengal)
cards.back:
(A) Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (Srirangapatna 1799)

Maratha & Later Rulers — TIPU SULTAN was killed on 4 MAY 1799 during the FOURTH ANGLO-MYSORE WAR at the SIEGE OF SERINGAPATAM (SRIRANGAPATNA), his capital. British forces under LORD CORNWALLIS's earlier setup, completed by GENERAL HARRIS, broke through the fort walls; Tipu fought hand-to-hand and was killed. He was 48. KEY BATTLES — ANGLO-MYSORE WARS: (1) FIRST (1767-69) — Hyder Ali (Tipu's father) FORCED British to TREATY OF MADRAS. (2) SECOND (1780-84) — Hyder Ali died (1782); Tipu continued; ended with TREATY OF MANGALORE — generally favourable to Mysore. (3) THIRD (1789-92) — vs Cornwallis; ended with TREATY OF SERINGAPATAM — Tipu lost half his territory + paid 3 crore indemnity + sent 2 sons as hostages. (4) FOURTH (1799) — vs Wellesley; Tipu killed; Mysore split among allies. AFTERMATH: WODEYAR DYNASTY restored to throne under British paramountcy. TIPU's SWORD + WAR ROCKETS captured by British, displayed in London/Edinburgh; some recovered post-2000 by Indian collectors. TIPU'S TIGER (toy organ depicting tiger mauling British soldier) is in the Victoria & Albert Museum, London. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'death of Tipu' is a top SSC, UPSC, MPSC fact — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
TIPU SULTAN's CAPITAL was:

(A) Srirangapatna (in Karnataka)
(B) Bangalore in southern Karnataka
(C) Hyderabad of Nizam family rule
(D) Mangalore on the western coast
cards.back:
(A) Srirangapatna (in Karnataka)

Maratha & Later Rulers — SRIRANGAPATNA (or SERINGAPATAM, Anglicized) — Tipu Sultan's capital, on an ISLAND in the KAVERI river, ~15 km north of present-day MYSURU (Mysore). KEY FEATURES: massive FORT, RANGANATHASWAMY temple, MASJID-E-ALA (mosque), DARIA DAULAT BAGH (summer palace), GUMBAZ (mausoleum of Hyder Ali, Tipu, and Tipu's mother). BACKGROUND: Sri Ranganathaswamy temple is one of the PANCHA-RANGAS (5 sacred Vishnu temples on Kaveri) — Adi Ranga at Srirangapatna; Madhya Ranga at Shivanasamudra; Antya Ranga at Srirangam (Tamil Nadu). HYDER ALI (Tipu's father) — ascended to power as commander of Wodeyar Mysore army; effectively took over Mysore in 1761. Tipu took over fully in 1782 after Hyder's death. CAPITAL CHOICE: Srirangapatna is naturally fortified by river; strategic location to control southern Karnataka and access to Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra. TODAY: a town of ~25,000; UNESCO Tentative World Heritage List (since 2014, jointly with Hyder Ali sites). VISIT: Daria Daulat Bagh is famous for murals depicting battles, including Tipu's victory over British forces. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'capital of Tipu' is a 1× per cycle SSC, UPSC, MPSC fact.

cards.front:
Tipu Sultan is credited as a PIONEER of which military innovation?

(A) Iron-cased war rockets
(B) Naval steam-powered warships
(C) First gunpowder use ever
(D) Hot-air balloon reconnaissance
cards.back:
(A) Iron-cased war rockets

Maratha & Later Rulers — TIPU SULTAN — pioneered the WORLD's first IRON-CASED WAR ROCKETS (Mysorean rockets). DESIGN: iron tubes (vs. earlier bamboo/cardboard); range up to 1.5-2 km; effective against cavalry and dense formations. MASS PRODUCTION: ~5,000 rocketeers in Tipu's army. KEY USE: BATTLE OF POLLILUR (1780) — Mysorean rockets devastated British East India Company forces, contributing to the British defeat. The rockets struck a British ammunition cart, causing a catastrophic explosion. INTERNATIONAL IMPACT: after Tipu's defeat (1799), captured rockets were sent to BRITAIN's Royal Arsenal in Woolwich. Sir WILLIAM CONGREVE studied them, leading to the 'Congreve rockets' — used in Napoleonic Wars and the War of 1812 (Bombardment of Fort McHenry, 1814 — inspiring 'rockets' red glare' in the US national anthem!). RECENT: Indian space scientist VIKRAM SARABHAI cited Mysorean rockets as inspiration; APJ Abdul Kalam noted them in his autobiography 'Wings of Fire'. ROCKET PARK at Pataluru (Tamil Nadu) — commemorates Tipu's rocket warfare. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'Tipu's rocket innovation' is a top UPSC, SSC, MPSC fact — 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests military-technology history.

cards.front:
Tipu Sultan's father, who founded Mysore's military power, was:

(A) Hyder Ali (commander turned ruler)
(B) Aurangzeb (a Mughal Emperor)
(C) Krishnaraja Wodeyar III only
(D) Nader Shah of Persia ruler
cards.back:
(A) Hyder Ali (commander turned ruler)

Maratha & Later Rulers — HYDER ALI (1722-1782) — Tipu Sultan's father. Born in BUDIKOTE (near Kolar, Karnataka) to a humble military family. Joined the WODEYAR Mysore army; rose through ranks via military genius. By 1761, he was de-facto ruler of Mysore (the Wodeyar king Krishnaraja Wodeyar II was reduced to figurehead). EXPANSION: Hyder conquered Bednur, Sondh, Sera, parts of Malabar, Coorg. CONFLICT WITH BRITISH: First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69) — Hyder forced the British to seek peace; SECOND ANGLO-MYSORE WAR (1780-84) — fought brilliantly; allied with Marathas, Nizam, French; British struggled. Hyder died of cancer in 1782 mid-war; Tipu took over. KEY MILITARY INNOVATIONS: (1) Modernized army with FRENCH advisors. (2) Used cavalry effectively. (3) Pioneered the rocket corps (which Tipu expanded). DIPLOMATIC: maintained correspondence with Ottomans, French, even Napoleon. MODERN VIEW: Hyder is hailed in Karnataka as a regional hero; portraits in state legislative buildings. CONTRASTING NARRATIVE: some communities accuse him of religious persecution during Malabar campaigns (debated by historians). PYQ FREQUENCY: 'Tipu's father' is a 1-mark guaranteed SSC, UPSC, MPSC MCQ.

cards.front:
Tipu Sultan formally ALLIED with which European power against the British?

(A) France (under Napoleon's plans)
(B) Portugal (which controlled Goa)
(C) The Netherlands (East Indies)
(D) Spain (had Philippines empire)
cards.back:
(A) France (under Napoleon's plans)

Maratha & Later Rulers — TIPU SULTAN cultivated a strong DIPLOMATIC ALLIANCE with FRANCE — the British East India Company's biggest European rival. He sent EMBASSIES to Paris (1788) and corresponded with NAPOLEON BONAPARTE. Tipu wrote Napoleon expressing alliance interest; Napoleon WROTE BACK from Cairo (1798) during his Egyptian campaign — reportedly saying he was looking forward to liberating India from British hands by joining with Tipu. KEY MOVES: (1) Stationed ~300 FRENCH OFFICERS in his army (training, weapons). (2) Planted a 'TREE OF LIBERTY' in his capital after the French Revolution — declared himself 'Citizen Tipu'. (3) Joined the JACOBIN Club of Mysore (a French Revolution inspired political club). BRITISH PARANOIA: French + Tipu alliance was the British strategic NIGHTMARE — fueled the urgency of Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance system. The 4TH ANGLO-MYSORE WAR (1799) was triggered by RICHARD WELLESLEY's anxiety about Tipu's French connections (after Napoleon invaded Egypt 1798). NAPOLEON'S Egyptian campaign was partly aimed at threatening British India; defeated by British naval power (Nelson at Battle of Nile, 1798). PYQ FREQUENCY: Tipu-France alliance is a top UPSC, SSC, MPSC fact — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which Governor-General of British India led the FOURTH ANGLO-MYSORE WAR against Tipu?

(A) Lord Wellesley (Richard Wellesley)
(B) Warren Hastings (first GG India)
(C) Lord Cornwallis (3rd War only)
(D) Lord Dalhousie (much later GG)
cards.back:
(A) Lord Wellesley (Richard Wellesley)

Maratha & Later Rulers — LORD RICHARD WELLESLEY (Governor-General 1798-1805) — initiated the FOURTH ANGLO-MYSORE WAR (1799) against Tipu Sultan. STRATEGIC AIM: eliminate Tipu (a French ally) before Napoleon could reach India. WELLESLEY's KEY INNOVATIONS — SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE SYSTEM: Indian rulers were forced to accept British 'protection' in exchange for ceding territory and accepting British military stationing. First applied to Hyderabad (1798); after Tipu's fall, expanded to Mysore (Wodeyar restored), Awadh, Marathas, etc. WELLESLEY'S BROTHER — Arthur Wellesley (later DUKE OF WELLINGTON) — was a major commander in the 1799 Mysore campaign and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War; later defeated Napoleon at WATERLOO (1815). EARLIER GOVERNOR-GENERALS — sequence: (1) Warren Hastings (1773-85) — first under Regulating Act 1773. (2) Lord Cornwallis (1786-93) — won 3rd Anglo-Mysore War; introduced PERMANENT SETTLEMENT in Bengal (1793). (3) Sir John Shore (1793-98). (4) Lord Wellesley (1798-1805). LATER: Lord Cornwallis returned for a brief 2nd term (1805); Lord Minto, Lord Hastings, etc. KEY PYQ ANGLE: Wellesley = 4th Mysore War; Cornwallis = 3rd; Hastings = 1st & 2nd planning. SSC, UPSC, MPSC routinely test this.

cards.front:
Tipu Sultan kept his TIGER throne in which form?

(A) A jeweled throne with tiger motifs
(B) Plain wooden throne with no design
(C) Marble throne (like Mughal rulers)
(D) Throne shaped like an elephant only
cards.back:
(A) A jeweled throne with tiger motifs

Maratha & Later Rulers — TIGER (HUMA) THRONE — Tipu Sultan's GOLDEN-JEWELED OCTAGONAL THRONE, with eight tiger heads supporting it; surmounted by a HUMA bird (mythical Persian bird associated with sovereignty). BUILT: ~1787, ~10 feet wide, weighed many maunds, encrusted with diamonds, rubies, emeralds, pearls. SYMBOLISM: Tipu chose tiger imagery — his personal emblem ('I would rather live one day as a tiger than 100 years as a sheep') — and the 'BUBRI' (tiger-stripe) pattern adorned his court banners, weapons, even uniforms. POST-1799: After Tipu's death, the British looted Srirangapatna for THREE WEEKS (despite Wellesley's orders); the throne was DISMANTLED and parts dispersed. The HUMA bird is in WINDSOR CASTLE (gifted to King George III); other gold tiger heads ended up in the British royal collection, V&A Museum, and private collections. TIPU'S TIGER (toy organ depicting tiger mauling British soldier) — captured at Srirangapatna; now in V&A Museum, London. RECENT: in 2009, Tipu's GOLDEN BIRD (one of the eight) sold at SOTHEBY'S for ~£400,000. INDIA's CULTURAL DIPLOMACY: ongoing efforts to repatriate looted artifacts (like Kohinoor diamond, also from Punjab via Wodeyars in 1799). PYQ FREQUENCY: cultural-history MCQs in UPSC, KAS optional 1× per cycle.

cards.option3: Throne shaped like an elephant only

cards.front:
The FIRST Governor-General of British India (Bengal Presidency) was:

(A) Lord Cornwallis, who later codified land revenue
(B) Warren Hastings, appointed under the 1773 Regulating Act
(C) Lord Wellesley, who started subsidiary alliances
(D) Lord Dalhousie, of Doctrine of Lapse fame
cards.back:
(B) Warren Hastings, appointed under the 1773 Regulating Act

British India — Warren Hastings (1772-1785) — first Governor-General of Bengal, appointed under the Regulating Act of 1773. Reorganised judiciary; founded Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784, with Sir William Jones); patronised Sanskrit + Persian studies. Famous trial in Britain (1787-95, acquitted) — accused of corruption + atrocities (Pitt's Bill). LORD CORNWALLIS (1786-93) — Permanent Settlement of Bengal (1793). LORD WELLESLEY (1798-1805) — Subsidiary Alliance system; defeated Tipu (1799). LORD DALHOUSIE (1848-56) — Doctrine of Lapse; first railway 1853.

cards.option2: Lord Wellesley, who started subsidiary alliances
cards.option3: Lord Dalhousie, of Doctrine of Lapse fame

cards.front:
The PERMANENT SETTLEMENT (Zamindari system) of Bengal in 1793 was introduced by:

(A) Warren Hastings, the first Governor-General
(B) Lord Cornwallis, the Governor-General then
(C) Lord Curzon, much later in the early 1900s
(D) Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of India
cards.back:
(B) Lord Cornwallis, the Governor-General then

British India — Permanent Settlement of Bengal — introduced by LORD CORNWALLIS in 1793. Made zamindars (intermediaries) the legal owners of land in exchange for fixed revenue (~9/10 to British, 1/10 to zamindar). Long-term consequences: rural impoverishment, rise of absentee landlordism, fall of village community. Other Cornwallis reforms: separated revenue + judicial administration; introduced civil service exams. Distractor 3 — Curzon partitioned Bengal (1905). Distractor 4 — Mountbatten oversaw partition (1947).
cards.option2: Lord Curzon, much later in the early 1900s
cards.option3: Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of India

cards.front:
The DOCTRINE OF LAPSE — annexing princely states without male heirs — was associated with:

(A) Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General 1848-1856
(B) Lord William Bentinck, the abolitionist of sati
(C) Lord Curzon, who partitioned Bengal in 1905
(D) Lord Hardinge, of the second Sikh war fame
cards.back:
(A) Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General 1848-1856

British India — Doctrine of Lapse — Lord Dalhousie (1848-56). If a ruler died without a NATURAL male heir, the state would 'lapse' to the Company. Annexed: Satara (1848), Jaipur + Sambalpur (1849), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853 — leading to 1857 revolt by Rani Lakshmibai), Nagpur (1854), Awadh (1856 — annexed on 'misrule' grounds, not lapse). Also abolished titles + pensions of ex-Mughal/Maratha figures (Nana Sahib's grievance). Major contributor to 1857 anger. Lord Canning (1856-62) repudiated the doctrine after the revolt.

cards.option2: Lord Curzon, who partitioned Bengal in 1905
cards.option3: Lord Hardinge, of the second Sikh war fame

cards.front:
The PARTITION OF BENGAL (1905), which sparked nationalist protests, was decreed by:

(A) Lord Curzon, Viceroy of India 1899-1905
(B) Lord Hardinge, Viceroy of India 1910-1916
(C) Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General 1848-56
(D) Lord Wellesley, Governor-General 1798-1805
cards.back:
(A) Lord Curzon, Viceroy of India 1899-1905

British India — Lord Curzon (1899-1905) — partitioned Bengal (October 1905) along religious lines, ostensibly for administrative efficiency, actually to weaken Bengali nationalism. Sparked SWADESHI Movement, boycott of British goods. Annulled in 1911 by Lord Hardinge — and capital shifted from Calcutta to DELHI same year. Curzon's other acts: Universities Act (1904), founded Archaeological Survey reforms, Younghusband expedition to Tibet (1903-04). Resigned 1905 over conflict with C-in-C Kitchener.

Sati was officially ABOLISHED in British India in 1829 under the Governor-General:

(A) Lord William Bentinck, with Raja Rammohun Roy's support
(B) Lord Cornwallis, of Permanent Settlement fame
(C) Lord Wellesley, the architect of subsidiary alliance
(D) Lord Auckland, of the First Anglo-Afghan War
cards.back:
(A) Lord William Bentinck, with Raja Rammohun Roy's support

British India — Lord William Bentinck (1828-1835) — Governor-General of India. ABOLISHED SATI by Regulation XVII of December 1829 (Bengal Presidency; extended to other regions later). Strongly supported by RAJA RAMMOHUN ROY (founder of Brahmo Samaj, 1828). Other Bentinck reforms: suppressed Thuggee (Col. Sleeman); promoted ENGLISH-MEDIUM education following Macaulay's Minute (1835); ended ritual female infanticide. Often called 'the most liberal' of British governors.

cards.front:
The REGULATING ACT of 1773 was the FIRST step taken by the British Parliament to regulate the affairs of the East India Company. It:

(A) Abolished the East India Company
(B) Established the OFFICE OF GOVERNOR-GENERAL of Bengal + a Supreme Court at Calcutta; first = WARREN HASTINGS
(C) Created direct Crown rule over India
(D) Gave voting rights to Indians
cards.back:
(B) Established the OFFICE OF GOVERNOR-GENERAL of Bengal + a Supreme Court at Calcutta; first = WARREN HASTINGS

British India — REGULATING ACT OF 1773 — passed by the British Parliament under PM Frederick North to address the corruption + mismanagement of the EIC (East India Company) after the Bengal famine of 1770 + Company's near-bankruptcy. PROVISIONS: (1) Created office of GOVERNOR-GENERAL OF BENGAL (first was WARREN HASTINGS, 1773-1785) with an Executive Council of 4. (2) Governors of Bombay + Madras made SUBORDINATE to GG of Bengal. (3) Established a SUPREME COURT at Calcutta (1774) with a Chief Justice + 3 judges appointed by the Crown — first CJ = Sir Elijah Impey. (4) Prohibited Company servants from private trade or accepting 'presents'. (5) Required Court of Directors to report revenue, civil, military matters to British Govt. LIMITATIONS: (a) GG could be overruled by 3-majority Council; (b) Supreme Court jurisdiction unclear vs Company courts — clashes; (c) PITT's INDIA ACT 1784 (passed by William Pitt the Younger) fixed many of these — established dual control: Court of Directors (commerce) + BOARD OF CONTROL (political affairs, under Crown); GG's council reduced to 3 with decisive vote for GG. SUBSEQUENT Charter Acts (renewing EIC's charter): (1) 1793 — Cornwallis + permanent settlement era. (4) 1853 — open competitive examinations for ICS (separated legislative + executive); first ICS exam at London 1855, Indians only from 1864 (Satyendranath Tagore). cards.front:
The MORLEY-MINTO REFORMS of 1909 introduced:

(A) Universal adult franchise
(B) SEPARATE ELECTORATES for MUSLIMS
(C) Full provincial autonomy
(D) End of British rule
cards.back:
(B) SEPARATE ELECTORATES for MUSLIMS

British India — INDIAN COUNCILS ACT 1909 / MORLEY-MINTO REFORMS — named after the Secretary of State for India (JOHN MORLEY) + Viceroy (LORD MINTO II). BACKGROUND: Partition of Bengal (1905) + Swadeshi agitation + rising Extremist demands. Aims: pacify Moderates, undermine Extremists, divide Hindus + Muslims. KEY PROVISIONS: (1) Enlarged Imperial + Provincial Legislative Councils — INDIANS ADMITTED (limited) for FIRST TIME to ELECTED membership (indirect election via local bodies, landowners, universities). (2) SEPARATE ELECTORATES for MUSLIMS — 'communal' electorates where only Muslims could vote for Muslim candidates; originated from Simla Deputation (1906) by Aga Khan III — led to founding of Muslim League (Dec 1906, Dhaka). (3) SATYENDRA P. SINHA became first INDIAN member of Viceroy's Executive Council; S.P. SINHA + LORD KRISHNA GUPTA also nominated. (4) Indian members could ASK questions + discuss budget — but VOTING power remained advisory. (5) Expanded functions of Legislative Councils — could debate matters of public interest. CRITICISM: (1) Separate electorates = seeds of communalism + eventual Partition; (2) Franchise extremely limited (~1% of population); (3) No transfer of real power; (4) Gokhale welcomed as step; Tilak + Extremists rejected. LALA LAJPAT RAI called Muslim League as 'convenient baby of Minto + Morley'. BEST KNOWN for COMMUNAL ELECTORATES — BAD legacy. Rescinded in part only by Govt of India Act 1935 (joint electorates with reservations). Poll was through Presidency, indirect, with property qualifications. INDIAN COUNCILS ACT 1861 was EARLIER important Act (3 Indians as ADVISORY members only). THE NEXT BIG act was GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms). sowing seeds of future communal politics + two-nation theory.

cards.front:
The GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1919 introduced the system of:

(A) Communal awards
(B) DIARCHY (dual government) in PROVINCES
(C) Complete independence
(D) Universal franchise
cards.back:
(B) DIARCHY (dual government) in PROVINCES

British India — GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1919 / MONTAGU-CHELMSFORD (Montford) REFORMS — named after Secretary of State EDWIN MONTAGU + Viceroy LORD CHELMSFORD. Introduced following Montagu's DECLARATION of 20 August 1917 — 'gradual development of self-governing institutions + responsible government' was the ULTIMATE aim. KEY FEATURES: (1) DIARCHY in PROVINCES — 'diarchy' = rule by TWO authorities. Provincial subjects SPLIT into: (a) TRANSFERRED (education, public health, agriculture, local govt, industries, etc.) — handled by Indian ministers responsible to Legislative Council; (b) RESERVED (finance, home, law + order, land revenue) — remained with British Governor. Failed experiment — ministers had responsibility without financial power. (2) BICAMERAL CENTRAL Legislature — (a) Council of State (Upper House, 60 members, some elected); (b) Legislative Assembly (Lower House, 145 members, 104 elected). First elected Speaker = Vithalbhai Patel (1925). No real power over Executive though. (3) CENTRAL subject-list + PROVINCIAL list formalised — forerunner to federal structure. (4) SEPARATE ELECTORATES extended to SIKHS, INDIAN CHRISTIANS, ANGLO-INDIANS, EUROPEANS (not just Muslims). (5) Limited franchise based on tax + property; ~7 million voters (out of 300 million population). (6) HIGH COMMISSIONER of INDIA in London established. (7) A STATUTORY commission to report after 10 years — became the SIMON COMMISSION (1927). EVALUATION: (a) Some scope for Indian participation but CORE power retained by British; (b) Congress called it 'inadequate, unsatisfactory + disappointing' (1919 Amritsar session post-Jallianwala); (c) Rowlatt Act + Jallianwala in same year 1919 (April) MADE IT A FARCE in Indian eyes. NEXT Act = Government of India Act 1935 (provincial autonomy, federation), followed by Indian Independence Act 1947. subjects divided into 'TRANSFERRED' (to Indian ministers) + 'RESERVED' (kept with British Governor).

cards.front:
The GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1935 abolished provincial DIARCHY and introduced it at the CENTRE; its PROVINCIAL AUTONOMY feature was enacted but which feature of the Act was never put into force?

(A) Provincial autonomy
(B) ALL-INDIA FEDERATION
(C) Bicameral Central Legislature
(D) Direct elections
cards.back:
(B) ALL-INDIA FEDERATION

British India — GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1935 — longest British statute enacted on India (451 clauses + 15 Schedules); largely based on (a) Simon Commission Report 1930; (b) Round Table Conferences (1930-32); (c) White Paper 1933 + Joint Select Committee. KEY FEATURES: (1) PROVINCIAL AUTONOMY — provincial diarchy ABOLISHED; entire provincial sphere transferred to elected Indian ministers responsible to Legislative Assembly. Governor remained titular head with 'special responsibilities'. 11 PROVINCES held elections in 1937; Congress formed governments in 7+ provinces; resigned 1939 over WWII without consultation. (2) CENTRAL DIARCHY — introduced at Centre (reverse of 1919 Act provincial diarchy): Executive Council split — DEFENCE, EXTERNAL AFFAIRS, RELIGIOUS AFFAIRS, TRIBES = reserved to Governor-General; rest = transferred to Indian ministers responsible to Federal Legislature. NEVER implemented. (3) ALL-INDIA FEDERATION — envisaged uniting British Provinces + 562 Princely States under one federation. PRINCES had to VOLUNTARILY accede (Instrument of Accession). REFUSED by most Princes (they wanted more power); WWII broke out in Sep 1939 before required number acceded (need 50% of Princely states by population); part never brought into force. (4) BICAMERAL CENTRAL LEGISLATURE (Federal Assembly + Council of States). (5) Separate electorates PRESERVED + EXTENDED (Depressed Classes, women, labour). Poona Pact (1932) compromise on depressed classes. (6) RESERVE BANK OF INDIA (RBI) established 1935 under this Act's powers. (7) FEDERAL COURT (1937) — precursor to Supreme Court; first CJ = Sir Maurice Gwyer. (8) Franchise extended to ~14% (~30 million voters). (9) BURMA separated (1937). SIGNIFICANCE: MOST PROVISIONS of the 1935 Act were ADOPTED into the 1950 INDIAN CONSTITUTION — 'Ambedkar's constitution is essentially a federation modelled on the 1935 Act' — notable inspirations include: federal division of powers, Concurrent List, emergency provisions, public service commissions, federal court structure. never became operational because princes did not accede by 1939/WWII; envisaged joining princely states with British provinces.

cards.front:
The INDIAN INDEPENDENCE ACT 1947 was PASSED by the British Parliament on:

(A) 15 August 1947
(B) 18 JULY 1947
(C) 26 January 1950
(D) 14 August 1947
cards.back:
(B) 18 JULY 1947

British India — INDIAN INDEPENDENCE ACT 1947 — passed by British Parliament on 18 JULY 1947 (Royal Assent); implemented based on MOUNTBATTEN PLAN (3 June 1947). PROVISIONS: (1) Partition of BRITISH INDIA into two DOMINIONS — INDIA + PAKISTAN, effective 15 August 1947 (midnight of 14/15). Dominion Status = sovereign + self-governing under British Crown (similar to Canada + Australia). (2) Ended British sovereignty over Indian Princely States — each to accede to either India or Pakistan or remain independent (most acceded via Instruments of Accession; Hyderabad, Junagadh, Jammu + Kashmir were controversial). (3) Office of Secretary of State for India abolished. (4) Britain's MONARCH ceased to use the title 'Emperor of India' (George VI, effective 22 June 1948). (5) Constituent Assemblies of both Dominions to draft new constitutions (Indian CA already existed since Dec 1946). Sir Cyril Radcliffe was given 5 weeks (July-Aug 1947) to demarcate BOUNDARIES between India + Pakistan (West = Punjab; East = Bengal) — RADCLIFFE LINE; published 17 Aug 1947 (2 days after independence); caused massive displacement + ~15 million refugees + estimated 1-2 million deaths in Partition violence. LEADING UP TO IT: (a) CRIPPS MISSION (1942) — rejected (offered dominion status + constitution-making body after war); (b) QUIT INDIA (Aug 1942); (c) WAVELL PLAN / SIMLA CONF (1945) — failed over Muslim League's demand for exclusive Muslim representation; (d) CABINET MISSION (1946) — rejected; (e) DIRECT ACTION DAY (16 Aug 1946, Jinnah) → Great Calcutta Killings; (f) Mountbatten appointed March 1947; (g) 3 June Plan announced partition. JINNAH became Pakistan's 1st Governor-General (Aug 1947 - Sep 1948 died); Mountbatten was India's 1st Governor-General (till June 1948, succeeded by C. Rajagopalachari — only + last Indian GG). Nehru became 1st PM; Constitution came into force 26 Jan 1950 — making India a REPUBLIC. received Royal Assent; partitioned British India into DOMINIONS of India + Pakistan on 15 August 1947.

cards.front:
'DIVIDE + RULE' policy was deepened by the COMMUNAL AWARD (1932) announced by British PM:

(A) Winston Churchill
(B) RAMSAY MacDONALD
(C) Clement Attlee
(D) David Lloyd George
cards.back:
(B) RAMSAY MacDONALD

British India — COMMUNAL AWARD — announced on 16 August 1932 by British PM RAMSAY MacDONALD (Labour Party, National Government) to resolve the communal representation question at the 2nd Round Table Conference in London where Indian parties had failed to agree. PROVISIONS: SEPARATE ELECTORATES for (a) Muslims (expanded since 1909); (b) Sikhs; (c) Indian Christians; (d) Anglo-Indians; (e) Europeans; AND additionally now for (f) DEPRESSED CLASSES (SCs/Dalits); (g) Women. B.R. AMBEDKAR (at the RTC) had argued for separate electorates for Dalits to ensure their political representation independent of caste-Hindus. GANDHI bitterly opposed — believed separate Dalit electorate would permanently divide Hindu society + postpone social reform. GANDHI'S FAST-UNTO-DEATH (20 September 1932) at YERAVADA JAIL, Pune — where he was imprisoned during Civil Disobedience. Gandhi's death fear sparked nationwide agitation. POONA PACT (24 September 1932, signed by Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya on behalf of Hindus + AMBEDKAR for the depressed classes) — compromise: (a) SINGLE general electorate for Hindus (no separate Dalit electorate); (b) but RESERVED SEATS for Dalits — 148 (up from 78 in the Communal Award) within general constituencies; (c) primary election among Dalits to select 4 candidates, then general electorate chose 1; (d) LOCAL bodies + govt services promises for Dalits. INDIAN Constitution (1950) preserved the spirit — joint electorates + reserved seats for SC + ST in Lok Sabha + State Assemblies (originally 10-year sunset, renewed every 10 years, latest 104th CAA 2020 extended to 2030). Separate electorates for religious minorities were ABOLISHED in Constitution. Ambedkar's legacy: Constitution's architect; Father of Indian Constitution; Bharat Ratna (posthumous 1990). extended separate electorates to 'DEPRESSED CLASSES' (Dalits); Gandhi opposed with fast-unto-death; POONA PACT (1932) with Ambedkar compromised.

cards.front:
Which Viceroy is associated with the introduction of 'LOCAL SELF-GOVERNMENT' in India (1882) and is called the 'FATHER OF LOCAL SELF-GOVERNMENT'?

(A) Lord Curzon
(B) LORD RIPON (1880-84)
(C) Lord Lytton
(D) Lord Mayo
cards.back:
(B) LORD RIPON (1880-84)

British India — LORD RIPON (George Frederick Samuel Robinson; Viceroy 1880-1884) — reformist Liberal Viceroy appointed by Gladstone's government. Known as 'FATHER OF LOCAL SELF-GOVERNMENT IN INDIA'. KEY REFORMS: (1) RIPON'S RESOLUTION of 18 MAY 1882 — on 'Local Self-Government' — decentralisation of municipal administration; majority of members to be ELECTED NON-OFFICIALS; limited governmental control; local institutions = 'political + popular education'. Led to creation of elected municipal bodies, district boards, local funds in various provinces. (2) HUNTER COMMISSION on EDUCATION (1882) — first major review after Wood's Despatch 1854; recommended primary education in mother-tongue, expansion of govt-aided schools, promotion of women's + vocational education. (3) REPEAL of VERNACULAR PRESS ACT (1882) — Lord Lytton had passed the repressive Act 1878 targeting Indian-language press; Ripon repealed it restoring press freedom. (4) ILBERT BILL (1883) — proposed by law-member Courtenay Ilbert — would allow INDIAN judges to try EUROPEANS in mofussil courts (no racial distinction). CAUSED UPROAR among British residents + press ('white revolt') against it; forced Ripon to DILUTE it (1884) — final compromise: Indian judges could try Europeans only with a jury of Europeans (majority). The episode exposed RACIAL ARROGANCE of British in India + taught Indians power of organised political agitation — influenced the founding of INC in 1885. (5) FACTORIES ACT 1881 (enacted, Ripon oversaw implementation) — first factory legislation, restricted child labour. LEGACY: Ripon remains probably the ONLY Viceroy genuinely LIKED by Indians. Ripon Club in Bombay, Ripon College in Kolkata (now Surendranath College) named after him. Nationalists gave him a hero's farewell when he left India. OPPOSITE to him — LORD LYTTON (Viceroy 1876-80): Vernacular Press Act 1878, Arms Act 1878, Delhi Durbar 1877 (proclaimed Queen Victoria as Empress of India), stoked second Afghan War, Great Famine 1876-78 (5M deaths). liberal Viceroy; Ripon's Resolution 1882 introduced elected municipal bodies, laid foundation for modern local self-government.

cards.front:
The SIMON COMMISSION (1927-1930), which came to India to review the 1919 Act, was boycotted because:

(A) It was too radical
(B) It had NO INDIAN MEMBERS
(C) It proposed independence
(D) It had only Muslim members
cards.back:
(B) It had NO INDIAN MEMBERS

British India — SIMON COMMISSION — 7-member STATUTORY Commission appointed in Nov 1927 (3 years early, because Tory Conservative govt wanted to pre-empt incoming Labour from appointing liberal Indian members). OFFICIAL TITLE: Indian Statutory Commission. CHAIR: SIR JOHN SIMON. Purpose: review the working of the Government of India Act 1919 + recommend constitutional reforms. ALL-WHITE composition (7 British MPs including CLEMENT ATTLEE — future PM who granted Indian independence 1947) → SEEN AS AN INSULT to Indian aspirations. NATIONWIDE BOYCOTT: (1) CONGRESS (Madras Session Dec 1927, Ansari) resolved to boycott. (2) Muslim League (Jinnah) boycotted. (3) ARRIVED IN BOMBAY on 3 FEBRUARY 1928 — massive protests. Black flags + slogan 'SIMON GO BACK'. (4) LAHORE protest on 30 OCTOBER 1928 — LALA LAJPAT RAI ('Lion of Punjab') led 'Simon Go Back' procession. Superintendent JAMES SCOTT ordered lathi charge; Lajpat Rai severely injured + died on 17 NOV 1928 (apparently from injuries + heart attack). His last words: 'every blow inflicted on me is a nail in the coffin of the British Empire'. REVENGE: HSRA (Bhagat Singh + Rajguru + Chandra Shekhar Azad) killed (by mistake) ASP J.P. SAUNDERS on 17 Dec 1928 (mistaken for Scott). Saunders murder → Lahore Conspiracy Case → Bhagat Singh + Sukhdev + Rajguru hanged 23 March 1931. NEHRU REPORT (1928) — response by All Parties Conference, drafted by MOTILAL NEHRU — India's first attempt at constitutional self-drafting; demanded DOMINION STATUS, joint electorates, fundamental rights; rejected by Jinnah (who submitted 14-point demand including separate electorates). SIMON REPORT (May 1930, 2 vols) — recommended abolition of diarchy, provincial autonomy, federation, continued communal electorates — basis for Govt of India Act 1935. Meanwhile Round Table Conferences (1930-32) ran in parallel. Attlee's exposure to India during this Commission likely influenced his 1947 decision to grant independence. all 7 British members; greeted with 'SIMON GO BACK' protests; Lala Lajpat Rai died after lathi-charge (Nov 1928).

cards.front:
The PERMANENT SETTLEMENT of BENGAL (1793), fixing land revenue in PERPETUITY with Zamindars, was introduced by Governor-General:

(A) Warren Hastings
(B) LORD CORNWALLIS
(C) Lord Wellesley
(D) Lord Dalhousie
cards.back:
(B) LORD CORNWALLIS

British India — LORD CORNWALLIS — Governor-General of Bengal 1786-1793 (returned briefly 1805 + died). Before India, he was the British general who SURRENDERED to George Washington at YORKTOWN (1781) ending the American Revolutionary War — a post-Yorktown 'rehabilitation' posting in India. KEY REFORMS: (1) PERMANENT SETTLEMENT of Bengal (1793) — fixed land revenue demand in PERPETUITY from ZAMINDARS (landlords, mainly Hindu); revenue = 10/11 of rental; zamindars could keep 1/11. Created private PROPERTY in land; zamindars became owners. Applied in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, parts of Madras + UP (~19% of British India). RYOTWARI SYSTEM (direct revenue from cultivators, no intermediary) elsewhere — introduced by Munro in Madras 1820 + later Bombay. MAHALWARI system — village-level revenue. CORNWALLIS CODE 1793 = 48 regulations — established fundamentals of civil + criminal admin. (2) FATHER of CIVIL SERVICE IN INDIA — separated revenue + judicial services; created COVENANTED Service (higher ranks, British only); reformed police + judiciary; abolished Nizamat Adalats. Introduced hierarchy of courts — munsiff, district court, provincial court, Sadar Diwani Adalat, Sadar Nizamat Adalat. Brought district collectors + magistrates. (3) POLICING reforms — district superintendents, thanas, officers' accountability. ASSESSMENT: (1) Permanent settlement BENEFITED zamindars hugely + gave stable revenue to British; BUT failed cultivators (rents passed on + exploited) + led to SUB-INFEUDATION + absentee landlordism; (2) reduced opportunity cost for British administrators + made governance professional; (3) 1793 code was a foundation of Indian jurisprudence. Cornwallis died at GHAZIPUR (UP, 1805) on a second stint + is buried there. SUCCESSOR: LORD WELLESLEY (GG 1798-1805) — SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE system, Mysore wars (defeated Tipu 1799), Maratha wars. introduced Zamindari system in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha; FATHER of CIVIL SERVICE IN INDIA; GG 1786-93, 1805.

cards.front:
The WOOD'S DESPATCH of 1854 is known as the 'MAGNA CARTA' of:

(A) Indian Labour law
(B) INDIAN EDUCATION
(C) Land reforms
(D) Military reorganisation
cards.back:
(B) INDIAN EDUCATION

British India — WOOD'S DESPATCH of 1854 — drafted by SIR CHARLES WOOD, President of Board of Control of EIC — sent to Governor-General Lord DALHOUSIE as a policy directive on Education. Hence 'DESPATCH'. Known as 'MAGNA CARTA of English Education in India' or 'MAGNA CARTA of INDIAN EDUCATION'. KEY PROVISIONS: (1) COMPREHENSIVE education system — from primary (vernacular-medium) → high school (Anglo-vernacular) → UNIVERSITY (English-medium) — three-tier pyramid. (2) Establishment of UNIVERSITIES at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras — founded 1857 on the University of London model (examining, not teaching — affiliated colleges, central examinations). (3) Creation of DEPARTMENTS OF PUBLIC INSTRUCTION in 5 provinces (Bengal, NWFP, Bombay, Madras, Punjab); designated Director of Public Instruction. (4) GRANTS-IN-AID system for private schools + colleges; fostered Christian missionary + Indian educational enterprise. (5) STRESS on Women's education — 'Girls' schools need encouragement'. (6) Promoted VERNACULAR languages (mother-tongue) for mass education (unusual for colonial Britain — but practical). (7) VOCATIONAL + TECHNICAL education encouraged — engineering colleges (Roorkee 1847), law colleges. EARLIER ORIENTALIST vs ANGLICIST DEBATE (1820s-30s): (a) Orientalists (H.H. Wilson etc.) — promote Sanskrit, Arabic, Persian education; (b) ANGLICISTS (T.B. MACAULAY, Minute on Indian Education 1835) — 'English at the apex' → produce a 'class Indian in blood + colour, English in tastes + opinions, intellect + morals'. MACAULAY'S MINUTE (1835) won; Bentinck's Resolution March 1835 adopted ENGLISH as medium of higher education + GOV language. INSTITUTIONS: (1) Fort William College (1800, for Company servants). (2) Hindu College Calcutta 1817 (first modern Indian college, founded by Raja Rammohan Roy + David Hare). (3) ELPHINSTONE COLLEGE Bombay 1834. (4) Calcutta Medical College 1835, Grant Medical College Bombay 1845. OTHER education commissions: HUNTER 1882 (Ripon); RALEIGH 1902 (Curzon); SADLER 1917; HARTOG 1929; WARDHA 1937 (Gandhi-Zakir Hussain basic education scheme). Post-independence: RADHAKRISHNAN 1948 (universities); KOTHARI 1964-66 (comprehensive); NEP 1968, 1986, 2020. laid framework for modern Indian education system; established universities at Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857).

cards.front:
The 'Zabti' (or 'Dahsala') system of Mughal land revenue — based on measured area and a 10-year price average — is credited to:

(A) Sher Shah Suri
(B) Raja Todar Mal
(C) Abul Fazl
(D) Man Singh
cards.back:
(B) Raja Todar Mal

British India — Todar Mal, Akbar's revenue minister (Diwan-i-Ashraf / Diwan-i-Kul), introduced the Dahsala system in 1580. Land was surveyed, classified into four types — Polaj (always cultivated), Parauti (fallow one year), Chachar (fallow 3-4 years), Banjar (fallow >5 years). A 10-year average of produce and prices was fixed; revenue = 1/3 of the average. Sher Shah had earlier made the measurement-based assessments that Todar Mal refined.

cards.front:
The Permanent Settlement of 1793 in Bengal was introduced by:

(A) Warren Hastings
(B) Lord Cornwallis
(C) Lord Wellesley
(D) Lord Hastings
cards.back:
(B) Lord Cornwallis

British India — Lord Cornwallis (Governor-General 1786-93) introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa in 1793. Zamindars became owners of land; revenue was fixed in perpetuity. The drafters were John Shore and James Grant. The 'sunset clause' said zamindars who failed to pay by sunset on the due date lost their estates. Criticism — fixed revenue benefited zamindars (prices rose, peasants suffered); led to mass transfer of land to city-based moneylenders.

cards.front:
The Ryotwari system — assessing revenue directly from the cultivator — was introduced primarily in Madras and Bombay Presidencies by:

(A) Holt Mackenzie
(B) Thomas Munro and Alexander Read
(C) Cornwallis and Shore
(D) William Bentinck
cards.back:
(B) Thomas Munro and Alexander Read

British India — The Ryotwari system (ryot = peasant) eliminated middlemen — direct link between the state and the cultivator. Alexander Read piloted it in the Baramahal (1792) and Thomas Munro extended it across Madras Presidency after becoming Governor (1820). Also adopted by Bombay under Elphinstone and in parts of Assam. Revenue was usually 45-55% of the produce; re-assessed every 20-30 years. Peasant retained ownership but bore all risk.

cards.front:
The Mahalwari system — where revenue was assessed on a 'mahal' (village / estate group) collectively — was introduced in:

(A) Bengal and Bihar
(B) North-Western Provinces, Punjab and parts of Central India
(C) Madras and Bombay
(D) Hyderabad and Mysore
cards.back:
(B) North-Western Provinces, Punjab and parts of Central India

British India — Mahalwari — formalised by Holt Mackenzie's 1822 Regulation VII and revised by R.M. Bird's 1833 settlement — covered the North-Western Provinces (modern UP), Punjab (after 1849 annexation), parts of the Central Provinces (modern MP). Revenue fixed on the entire mahal; the village headman (lambardar) collected from cultivators and paid the state. Revision every 20-30 years. Combined features of both Zamindari and Ryotwari.

cards.front:
Under the Permanent Settlement, the share of revenue demanded from the zamindar was approximately:

(A) 1/11 of total collection
(B) 10/11 of total collection
(C) 1/3 of the produce
(D) 1/2 of the produce
cards.back:
(B) 10/11 of total collection

British India — Zamindar paid 10/11 to the Company; kept 1/11 as remuneration. Revenue was fixed in 1793 at a very high level (on inflated 1789 prices) — in the next decade, two-fifths of Bengal's zamindars defaulted and their estates were auctioned. Buyers were often Calcutta merchants / officials — creating a new class of absentee landlords. The 'famous' (or infamous) Sunset Law drove the auction process.

cards.front:
The 'Jagirdari' and 'Mansabdari' systems of Mughal administration were closely linked because:

(A) Mansabdars received land in lieu of salary
(B) Jagirs were reserved only for the royal family
(C) Mansab ranks were purchased, not assigned
(D) Jagirdars were exempt from military service
cards.back:
(A) Mansabdars received land in lieu of salary

British India — A mansabdar held a 'mansab' (rank) with two numbers — zat (personal rank) and sawar (cavalry he maintained). Salary could be paid in cash (naqdi) or by assignment of a jagir — the right to collect revenue from a specified area. Most mansabdars were jagirdars. Jagirs were transferable and non-hereditary — part of Akbar's centralising design. Highest zat was reserved for princes; nobles went up to 7,000/7,000.

cards.option2: Mansab ranks were purchased, not assigned

cards.front:
By the time of independence in 1947, the approximate share of Indian territory under each British revenue system was:

(A) Zamindari ~19%, Ryotwari ~51%, Mahalwari ~30%
(B) Zamindari ~57%, Ryotwari ~38%, Mahalwari ~5%
(C) Zamindari ~30%, Ryotwari ~30%, Mahalwari ~40%
(D) Zamindari ~10%, Ryotwari ~70%, Mahalwari ~20%
cards.back:
(B) Zamindari ~57%, Ryotwari ~38%, Mahalwari ~5%

British India — By 1947, Zamindari (Permanent Settlement + temporary zamindari variants) covered ~57% of cultivated land — chiefly Bengal, Bihar, eastern UP, parts of Madras and Central Provinces. Ryotwari was ~38% — Madras, Bombay, Assam, Berar. Mahalwari was ~5% — parts of UP, Punjab, Central India. Post-1947 Zamindari Abolition Acts (1950 onwards) dismantled intermediaries; state-level tenancy reforms followed.

cards.front:
The Revolt of 1857 began at which cantonment on which date, over the issue of greased cartridges?

(A) Barrackpore, Bengal — 29 March 1857 (Mangal Pandey)
(B) MEERUT, 10 May 1857 — later reached Delhi 11 May
(C) Kanpur — June 1857
(D) Lucknow — July 1857
cards.back:
(B) MEERUT, 10 May 1857 — later reached Delhi 11 May

British India — THE FULL-SCALE REVOLT began at MEERUT on 10 MAY 1857 — 85 sepoys of the 3rd Light Cavalry who refused to use the new cartridges on 24 April were court-martialled and sentenced to 10 years' hard labour. On 9 May, they were publicly humiliated (stripped of uniforms). On 10 May, fellow sepoys mutinied, released them, killed British officers + civilians. The next day (11 May), mutineers reached DELHI and proclaimed BAHADUR SHAH II ZAFAR (the last Mughal emperor) as Emperor of Hindustan. MANGAL PANDEY (34th Bengal Native Infantry) had attacked a British officer at BARRACKPORE on 29 March 1857 — he was hanged 8 April 1857. Though not the start of the revolt, he is considered its first martyr. The CARTRIDGE ISSUE: the new Enfield rifles required biting paper cartridges greased with BEEF (offending Hindus) + PORK (offending Muslims) — though other causes were deeper.

Match the 1857 Revolt centre to its leader:

(A) Delhi — Bakht Khan; Kanpur — Nana Saheb + Tantia Tope; Jhansi — Rani Lakshmibai; Lucknow — Begum Hazrat Mahal; Bihar — Kunwar Singh
(B) Delhi — Rani Lakshmibai; Kanpur — Bahadur Shah
(C) All centres led by Tantia Tope
(D) All led by civilian leaders only
cards.back:
(A) Delhi — Bakht Khan; Kanpur — Nana Saheb + Tantia Tope; Jhansi — Rani Lakshmibai; Lucknow — Begum Hazrat Mahal; Bihar — Kunwar Singh

ONLY Nana Saheb's fate remains unknown — possibly escaped to Nepal.

cards.front:
The 1857 Revolt's IMMEDIATE trigger — the ENFIELD RIFLE cartridge issue — offended sepoys because:

(A) Cartridges were made of cow's leather only
(B) Cartridges were greased with COW + PIG fat, offending Hindus + Muslims respectively, requiring sepoys to BITE THE CARTRIDGE before loading
(C) Cartridges were too expensive
(D) New rifles were inaccurate
cards.back:
(B) Cartridges were greased with COW + PIG fat, offending Hindus + Muslims respectively, requiring sepoys to BITE THE CARTRIDGE before loading

British India — ENFIELD RIFLE issued in 1853-56 required the user to BITE off the top of the paper cartridge before loading. The paper was greased to be water-resistant; rumour spread (likely true in some batches) that the grease was TALLOW (COW fat — offensive to Hindus, sacred cow) + LARD (PIG fat — haram for Muslims). This triggered sepoy refusal. While the cartridge issue was the IMMEDIATE trigger, DEEPER CAUSES included: (1) POLITICAL — Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie — annexed Jhansi, Nagpur, Satara, Awadh, etc. without heir), Subsidiary Alliance, annexation of Awadh 1856, pension cut-off to Nana Saheb; (2) ECONOMIC — Permanent Settlement caused zamindar-peasant distress; Indian artisans destroyed by British imports; heavy taxation; (3) SOCIAL/RELIGIOUS — abolition of sati (1829), widow remarriage (1856) seen as interference; missionary activity; (4) MILITARY — sepoy discrimination in pay, promotion, overseas postings (General Service Enlistment Act 1856 required overseas deployment, violating caste).
