The paper was greased to be water-resistant; rumour spread (likely true in some batches) that the grease was TALLOW (COW fat — offensive to Hindus, sacred cow) + LARD (PIG fat — haram for Muslims). This triggered sepoy refusal. While the cartridge issue was the IMMEDIATE trigger, DEEPER CAUSES included: (1) POLITICAL — Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie — annexed Jhansi, Nagpur, Satara, Awadh, etc. without heir), Subsidiary Alliance, annexation of Awadh 1856, pension cut-off to Nana Saheb; (2) ECONOMIC — Permanent Settlement caused zamindar-peasant distress; Indian artisans destroyed by British imports; heavy taxation; (3) SOCIAL/RELIGIOUS — abolition of sati (1829), widow remarriage (1856) seen as interference; missionary activity; (4) MILITARY — sepoy discrimination in pay, promotion, overseas postings (General Service Enlistment Act 1856 required overseas deployment, violating caste).

cards.front:
After the defeat of the 1857 Revolt, the BRITISH CROWN took DIRECT control from the East India Company via:

(A) Charter Act 1813
(B) Government of India Act 1858
(C) Indian Councils Act 1861
(D) Government of India Act 1935
cards.back:
(B) Government of India Act 1858

British India — GOVERNMENT OF INDIA ACT 1858: passed 2 August 1858 — formally ended East India Company rule; transferred all territories to the BRITISH CROWN. KEY CHANGES: (1) The office of GOVERNOR-GENERAL was retitled VICEROY (Lord Canning became first Viceroy, 1 Nov 1858); (2) Created the SECRETARY OF STATE FOR INDIA (first: Lord Stanley) — a UK cabinet minister responsible for India, assisted by a 15-member Council of India; (3) ABOLISHED Board of Control + Court of Directors (East India Company dissolved). QUEEN'S PROCLAMATION (1 November 1858, Allahabad, read by Canning) — Queen Victoria's declaration: (a) Promise of religious tolerance; (b) Respect for princely states' rights; (c) NO MORE annexations via Doctrine of Lapse; (d) Equal rights for all subjects, no racial discrimination (promised but rarely delivered); (e) Amnesty for most rebels. Queen Victoria took the title EMPRESS OF INDIA via ROYAL TITLES ACT 1876 (during Lord Lytton's viceroyalty). 1857 is sometimes called INDIA'S FIRST WAR OF INDEPENDENCE (V.D. Savarkar's 1909 book popularised this view, though many British historians call it 'Sepoy Mutiny'). + Queen's Proclamation, 1 Nov 1858.

cards.front:
'DOCTRINE OF LAPSE' — a major cause of 1857 Revolt — was a policy by which British Governor-General?

(A) Lord Bentinck
(B) Lord Dalhousie
(C) Lord Cornwallis
(D) Lord Hastings
cards.back:
(B) Lord Dalhousie

British India — DOCTRINE OF LAPSE (1848) — introduced by LORD DALHOUSIE (Governor-General 1848-56). POLICY: if an Indian ruler died without a BIOLOGICAL MALE HEIR, his kingdom would LAPSE to (be annexed by) the British EIC. Traditional Indian practice of adopting an heir was disallowed. States annexed under this doctrine: SATARA (1848 — first, Maratha), JAITPUR (1849), SAMBALPUR (1849), BAGHAT (1850), UDAIPUR (1852), JHANSI (1853 — Rani Lakshmibai's adopted son Damodar Rao denied inheritance), NAGPUR (1854 — Bhonsles). AWADH annexed in 1856 NOT under Doctrine of Lapse but on grounds of 'MISGOVERNANCE' (even more resented since Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was a British ally). The Doctrine was FORMALLY REVOKED via the Queen's Proclamation 1858. Dalhousie's other actions: Railways 1853 (Bombay-Thana), Telegraph 1853 (Calcutta-Agra), Postal Service 1854, Wood's Despatch on Education 1854, Widow Remarriage Act 1856. Governor-General 1848-1856.

cards.front:
RANI LAKSHMIBAI of Jhansi — iconic heroine of 1857 — died in battle on which date at which location?

(A) 1 January 1858; Jhansi Fort
(B) 17/18 June 1858; Kotah-ki-Sarai, Gwalior
(C) 10 May 1857; Meerut
(D) 15 August 1857; Delhi
cards.back:
(B) 17/18 June 1858; Kotah-ki-Sarai, Gwalior

British India — RANI LAKSHMIBAI (born 19 Nov 1828 Varanasi as MANIKARNIKA 'Manu' Tambe) — married Raja Gangadhar Rao of Jhansi 1842, renamed Lakshmi Bai. Husband died 1853; adopted son Damodar Rao's succession was REJECTED by British under Doctrine of Lapse → Jhansi annexed 1854. Rani took charge during 1857 Revolt — held Jhansi fort against Sir Hugh Rose's siege (March-April 1858) — fell after bombardment. Fled with adopted son + small force → reached Kalpi → met TANTIA TOPE + NANA SAHEB's brother Rao Saheb → captured GWALIOR FORT (June 1858, ousted Scindia ruler who was pro-British). British (under Sir Hugh Rose + Sir Robert Hamilton) counter-attacked Gwalior. Rani died in battle on 17-18 JUNE 1858 at KOTAH-KI-SARAI near Gwalior — cut down fighting in male disguise, her body burnt by her own soldiers to prevent British desecration. Age 29. HUGH ROSE called her 'the best and bravest of rebel leaders'. MEMORIAL: Jhansi Fort today. Subhadra Kumari Chauhan's famous poem: 'Khoob Lari Mardani Wo To Jhansi Wali Rani Thi' ('She fought valiantly, she was the Rani of Jhansi').

cards.front:
Which of the following regions/groups did NOT participate actively in the 1857 Revolt?

(A) Awadh (Oudh) — one of the major centres
(B) Delhi — nominal leader Bahadur Shah Zafar
(C) Rohilkhand + Bundelkhand
(D) Punjab (Sikhs), South India, most Princely States — largely LOYAL to British
cards.back:
(D) Punjab (Sikhs), South India, most Princely States — largely LOYAL to British

British India — GEOGRAPHIC LIMIT of 1857 REVOLT: CONFINED largely to NORTH + CENTRAL India. Affected areas: UP (Awadh = most intense), Delhi, Bihar, parts of MP, Rajasthan. NOT AFFECTED / LOYAL TO BRITISH: (1) PUNJAB — recently conquered (1849); Sikh soldiers actually helped British retake Delhi (memories of Mughal persecution of Gurus). (2) BENGAL PROPER — civilian areas remained largely calm. (3) SOUTH INDIA — Madras + Bombay Presidencies showed no significant rebellion. (4) MOST PRINCELY STATES — remained LOYAL: Gwalior's Scindia, Hyderabad's Nizam, Travancore, Mysore, Kashmir, Nepal (Jung Bahadur's Gurkhas HELPED British). Canning called these princes the 'BREAKWATERS IN THE STORM'. (5) MOST EDUCATED INDIANS (new middle class) — saw British as modernisers. This limited scope made the revolt defeatable. By mid-1858, British had crushed most centres. Only Tantia Tope lingered as a guerrilla till his capture + execution in April 1859.

cards.front:
The Revolt of 1857 began on 10 May 1857 at:

(A) Delhi
(B) Meerut (Bengal Army sepoys mutinied; marched to Delhi the next day)
(C) Lucknow
(D) Kanpur
cards.back:
(B) Meerut (Bengal Army sepoys mutinied; marched to Delhi the next day)

British India — 10 May 1857 — sepoys of the Bengal Army's 3rd Light Cavalry refused to use the new Enfield rifle cartridges (rumoured to be greased with cow + pig fat). 85 imprisoned sepoys had been court-martialled the previous day. Massive mutiny on 10 May; sepoys + civilians attacked British officers in Meerut, then marched ~70 km south to Delhi overnight, declaring Bahadur Shah Zafar (the last Mughal) as Emperor of Hindustan on 11 May. Mangal Pandey's earlier incident at Barrackpore (29 March 1857) is sometimes called the proximate trigger.

(C) Indian Independence Act 1947
(D) Charter Act 1853
cards.back:

British India — Government of India Act 1858 — abolished East India Company. Power transferred to Crown. New post: Secretary of State for India + 15-member Council of India to assist. Governor-General became 'Viceroy' as well — Lord Canning, the first. Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled to Rangoon, died 1862. Mughal Empire formally ended.

cards.front:
Mangal Pandey — sepoy whose actions on 29 March 1857 are considered a precursor to the Revolt — was executed at:

(A) Meerut
(B) Barrackpore (modern WB) on 8 April 1857
(C) Calcutta
(D) Delhi
cards.back:
(B) Barrackpore (modern WB) on 8 April 1857

British India — Mangal Pandey — 34th Bengal Native Infantry sepoy at Barrackpore. On 29 March 1857, attacked Lt Baugh + Sgt Hewson over the Enfield cartridge issue + general resentment. Was overpowered, court-martialled, hanged on 8 April 1857 — 10 days earlier than scheduled, fearing public unrest. His unit (34th BNI) was disbanded. The reverberations contributed to the May 1857 Meerut incident. Often hailed as 'first martyr of Indian independence struggle'. Hindi film 'Mangal Pandey: The Rising' (Aamir Khan, 2005). Birthday celebrated as 'Shaheed Diwas' in his hometown Nagwa, UP.

cards.front:
The principal cause of immediate sepoy outrage was the introduction of the Enfield rifle. The greased cartridges were rumoured to contain:

(A) Lard from horses only
(B) Tallow from cow (offending Hindus) and pig fat (offending Muslims)
(C) Iron filings
(D) Salt
cards.back:
(B) Tallow from cow (offending Hindus) and pig fat (offending Muslims)

British India — Enfield Pattern 1853 rifle — required biting open paper cartridge before loading; cartridge was greased with animal fat. Rumour spread that the grease was a mix of cow tallow + pig fat — abhorrent to Hindus (cow sacred) AND Muslims (pig haram). The Company tried to mitigate (use unsalted/tallow-free, use teeth alternative — bite less etc) but rumour had spread. Larger underlying causes: economic distress, Doctrine of Lapse annexations (Awadh 1856), missionary activity, treatment of Indian soldiers. The cartridge was the spark, not the cause.

V.D. Savarkar's 1909 book 'The Indian War of Independence — 1857' was significant because it:

(C) Documented British casualties only

cards.back:
(B) Recast the 1857 events as a planned 'first war of independence' rather than a sepoy 'mutiny'

British India — Savarkar's 'The Indian War of Independence — 1857' — written in Marathi 1908; published in English 1909 from London (where he was a law student); banned by British. Recast 1857 as the first organised, premeditated nationalist uprising against British rule (a major shift from the British framing of 'sepoy mutiny'). Influenced later nationalists. Other major historians of 1857: R.C. Majumdar (cautious — argued events were diverse, not centrally coordinated), S.N. Sen (1857), Eric Stokes, Tapti Roy, Rudrangshu Mukherjee. Surendra Nath Sen's centenary government work (1957) is balanced.

cards.front:
Who was the first VICEROY of India, after the Crown took direct control in 1858?

(A) Lord Dalhousie
(B) Lord Canning
(C) Lord Mayo
(D) Lord Lytton
cards.back:
(B) Lord Canning

British India — LORD CANNING (1856-62) was both: (a) the LAST Governor-General of India under the Company (1856-58), and (b) the FIRST VICEROY of India when the Queen's Proclamation of 1 November 1858 (Government of India Act 1858) transferred power from the East India Company to the British Crown. Known as 'Clemency Canning' for his comparatively restrained handling of post-1857 reprisals. Ended Doctrine of Lapse. Restored princely states' rights via Queen's Proclamation. Lord Dalhousie (1848-56) was the GG BEFORE Canning. Lord Mayo (1869-72) — financial decentralisation, first census 1872, assassinated at Port Blair (only Viceroy killed in office). Lord Lytton (1876-80) — Vernacular Press Act 1878, Arms Act 1878, Royal Titles Act 1876 (Queen Victoria became 'Empress of India').

Which Viceroy is associated with the Partition of Bengal (1905), its reversal (1911), and the Delhi Darbar?

(A) Lord Curzon ordered partition; Lord Hardinge II reversed it
(B) Lord Minto ordered partition; Lord Curzon reversed it
(C) Lord Lytton ordered partition; Lord Ripon reversed it
(D) Lord Mayo ordered partition; Lord Elgin reversed it
cards.back:

British India — LORD CURZON (1899-1905) ordered the PARTITION OF BENGAL (October 1905), ostensibly for administrative convenience but actually to divide Hindu-majority West & Muslim-majority East — sparking the Swadeshi Movement. Also: founded ASI under John Marshall, Indian Universities Act 1904, Police Commission 1902, Railway Board 1905. LORD HARDINGE II (1910-16) — ANNULLED the Bengal partition at the DELHI DARBAR of 12 Dec 1911 (where King George V & Queen Mary were present; also shifted capital from Calcutta to Delhi). Survived a bomb attack 1912 by revolutionaries (Chandni Chowk bombing). Lord Minto II (1905-10) = Morley-Minto Reforms 1909 (separate electorates for Muslims, sowing seeds of two-nation theory).

The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) took place during the tenure of which Viceroy?

(A) Lord Hardinge II
(B) Lord Chelmsford
(C) Lord Reading
(D) Lord Irwin
cards.back:
(B) Lord Chelmsford

British India — LORD CHELMSFORD (1916-21) was Viceroy during the Jallianwala Bagh massacre (Baisakhi day, 13 April 1919) at Amritsar — Brig-Gen Reginald Dyer ordered firing on unarmed crowd protesting the Rowlatt Act (passed March 1919). 379+ killed (official), ~1000+ (unofficial). Hunter Commission (1920) denounced Dyer. Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest. Chelmsford's tenure also saw: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms 1919 (Dyarchy in provinces, Govt of India Act 1919), Rowlatt Act 1919, Non-Cooperation Movement launched Aug 1920. Lord Reading (1921-26) followed — Chauri Chaura 1922 and Non-Coop suspension. Lord Irwin (1926-31) — Simon Commission, Nehru Report, Dandi March, Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931.

Lord Dufferin (1884-88) followed — INC founded 1885 during his tenure. Lord Mayo (1869-72) — financial decentralisation, assassinated Port Blair.

(C) 10 days; 100 km; broke the Rowlatt Act

DISTANCE: 240 MILES (~386 km). 78 initial marchers; tens of thousands joined en route. At Dandi, Gandhi picked up a handful of salt-encrusted mud on the beach and symbolically violated the SALT ACT 1882 (which gave the British govt a monopoly on salt production + taxed salt — a burden on the poor). Sparked the full CIVIL DISOBEDIENCE MOVEMENT (1930-34). Salt-making spread across India. Accompanying events: Abbas Tyabji + Sarojini Naidu led the Dharasana Salt March (May 1930, after Gandhi's arrest — British brutally beat unarmed satyagrahis; global press coverage by Webb Miller). Gandhi jailed 5 May 1930. RELEASED via GANDHI-IRWIN PACT (5 March 1931). Dandi's original name 'Dandi Kutir' memorialised Salt Satyagraha site today. which gave British monopoly on salt production + imposed salt tax.

cards.front:
The POONA PACT (24 Sept 1932) was signed between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar to resolve the issue of:

(A) Partition of India
(B) Separate electorates for Depressed Classes (Dalits)
(C) Salt tax
(D) Permission for Gandhi to meet Viceroy
cards.back:
(B) Separate electorates for Depressed Classes (Dalits)

Freedom Movement — POONA PACT (Yerwada Jail, Pune — 24 September 1932) — between Gandhi + Ambedkar. Background: Ramsay MacDonald's COMMUNAL AWARD (16 Aug 1932) granted SEPARATE ELECTORATES to Depressed Classes (Dalits). Gandhi vehemently opposed — saying it would divide Hindu society permanently — began his 'fast unto death' (20 Sept 1932) at Yerwada jail where he was imprisoned. After 6 days of national tension, Dr. AMBEDKAR agreed to withdraw separate electorates in exchange for: (1) RESERVED SEATS (148 instead of original 71) for Depressed Classes within the JOINT ELECTORATE; (2) Primary electorate (by Dalits) → 4 candidates → final election by all. Became the foundation of caste-based reservations in post-Independence India. Ambedkar later expressed ambivalence about this compromise (felt pressured). The pact was ratified by British PM. Gandhi's concept of 'SATYAGRAHA' (non-violent resistance) was first developed during his 21-year stay in:

(A) India
(B) South Africa (1893-1914)
(C) England

Freedom Movement — GANDHI'S SOUTH AFRICA years (1893-1914, age 24-45) — 21 years spent here, where he developed SATYAGRAHA (from satya = truth, agraha = insistence). Key moments: (1) 1893 — thrown off Pietermaritzburg train for being in first class despite ticket → politicised him. (2) 1906 — Johannesburg: 'Asiatic Law Amendment Ordinance' required Indians to register fingerprints — Gandhi launched first SATYAGRAHA; called 'passive resistance' then. Advised by GOPAL KRISHNA GOKHALE ('political guru') to travel India before jumping into politics. Early influences: Tolstoy, Ruskin ('Unto This Last'), Thoreau's civil disobedience, Jain + Hindu + Christian teachings. Gandhi's South African autobiography 'SATYAGRAHA IN SOUTH AFRICA' (1928).

cards.front:
The CHAMPARAN SATYAGRAHA (1917) — Gandhi's first satyagraha in INDIA — was against:

(A) Salt Tax
(B) The oppressive TINKATHIA system imposed on indigo cultivators in Bihar
(C) Rowlatt Act
(D) Cow slaughter
cards.back:
(B) The oppressive TINKATHIA system imposed on indigo cultivators in Bihar

Freedom Movement — CHAMPARAN SATYAGRAHA (April 1917, Champaran district, Bihar). Gandhi, barely 2 years back from SA, was summoned by RAJ KUMAR SHUKLA — a local peasant leader — to investigate the plight of INDIGO CULTIVATORS. British planters forced farmers to grow INDIGO on 3/20 (TINKATHIA SYSTEM) of their land and sell it at fixed low prices. When synthetic dyes made indigo uneconomic (~1890s), planters pressed farmers harder + demanded 'tavan' compensation. Gandhi conducted survey, was ordered to leave Champaran — REFUSED — was arrested → local mass support → British backed down. Outcome: CHAMPARAN AGRARIAN ACT (1918) abolished Tinkathia + refunded a portion of illegal exactions. Gandhi's colleagues: RAJENDRA PRASAD (later 1st President of India!), J.B. Kripalani, Brajkishore Prasad, Mahadev Desai, Anugrah Narayan Sinha. This was Gandhi's FIRST ALL-INDIA political triumph using Satyagraha. Later satyagrahas: KHEDA (1918, against high land revenue during bad crops, Gujarat), AHMEDABAD MILL WORKERS (1918, wage strike).

cards.front:
Gandhi's KHILAFAT MOVEMENT alliance (1919-1924) aligned the Indian National Congress with Muslim leaders to protest:

(A) British rule in India
(B) The British dismantling of the Ottoman Caliphate after World War I
(C) Partition of Bengal
(D) Rowlatt Act only
cards.back:
(B) The British dismantling of the Ottoman Caliphate after World War I

Freedom Movement — KHILAFAT MOVEMENT (1919-1924) — a pan-Islamic movement by Indian Muslims to protest the British proposal (after WWI) to dismember the OTTOMAN EMPIRE + reduce the status of the Caliph (Khalifa — the spiritual head of Sunni Islam, historically the Ottoman Sultan). Led by the ALI BROTHERS (Muhammad Ali + Shaukat Ali), Maulana Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Hasrat Mohani. GANDHI supported it strongly — saw it as opportunity for HINDU-MUSLIM UNITY — merged Khilafat with the NON-COOPERATION MOVEMENT (1920). Khilafat Committee + Congress joint campaign. The movement COLLAPSED when: (1) Chauri Chaura led Gandhi to suspend NCM in 1922; (2) TURKEY itself (Mustafa Kemal Atatürk) ABOLISHED the Caliphate in 1924, ending the movement's raison d'être. Aftermath: communal riots, Moplah uprising (Kerala, 1921, peasant + Khilafat), eventual break in Hindu-Muslim political unity. Some argue this alliance indirectly strengthened pan-Islamic identity, contributing to later demand for Pakistan.

(B) 1885 (founding of INC) too
(C) 1857 (Sepoy Mutiny year)
(D) 1891 (return from England)
cards.back:

Freedom Movement — Mohandas Karamchand GANDHI — born 2 October 1869 at PORBANDAR, GUJARAT (a princely state in Kathiawar; coastal town). Father Karamchand = diwan (PM) of Porbandar; mother Putlibai = devout Vaishnav Hindu (heavy influence on Gandhi's vegetarianism, fasting, simple living). Married KASTURBA at 13 (child marriage common then). Studied LAW in LONDON (Inner Temple, 1888-91) — in his autobiography, Gandhi confesses early struggles to fit in (clothes, food). After law degree, returned to India 1891; tried law practice (unsuccessful in Bombay + Rajkot). 1893: went to SOUTH AFRICA on a 1-year contract for Indian merchant Dada Abdulla — turned into 21 years there, transformed him into 'Mahatma'. Birthday = INTERNATIONAL DAY OF NON-VIOLENCE (UN, 2007).

cards.back:

Freedom Movement — SATYAGRAHA — Sanskrit 'satya' (truth) + 'agraha' (insistence / firmness) = 'truth-force' / 'soul-force'. Coined by Gandhi (1906, after a competition; suggested by his cousin) to describe his non-violent civil disobedience. Roots: Tolstoy (Christian non-resistance), Thoreau (Civil Disobedience), Gita (selfless action), Jainism (ahimsa). FIRST SATYAGRAHA: 1906, JOHANNESBURG, against COMPULSORY REGISTRATION of Indians (Black Act). Famous TRAIN INCIDENT — June 1893, Pietermaritzburg: Gandhi thrown out of FIRST-CLASS coach despite valid ticket — defining moment of his political awakening. Later led: protests against £3 tax on Indians, the Indian Relief Act 1914 (Gandhi-Smuts agreement). Returned to INDIA Jan 1915 (Bombay reception). PHOENIX (1904) + TOLSTOY FARM (1910) — his ashrams in S Africa.

GOKHALE (advised him to spend 1 year travelling India to understand it before politicising). FIRST SATYAGRAHAS in India: (1) CHAMPARAN (Bihar, 1917) — exploitation of indigo planters by British; (2) KHEDA (Gujarat, 1918) — peasants' tax relief during drought; (3) AHMEDABAD MILL strike (1918, textile workers vs owners). Freedom Movement — 'MY EXPERIMENTS WITH TRUTH' (1925-29; serialised in his journal NAVAJIVAN). Originally written in GUJARATI ('Satyana Prayogo athwa Atmakatha'); translated to English by his secretary Mahadev Desai. Covers his life from birth to ~1921 (didn't continue to later years). FRANK + SELF-CRITICAL — discusses his shyness, brief meat-eating phase as boy, sexual desires, struggles. 'EXPERIMENTS' reflects his views: every choice = an experiment in truthful living. CHIEF source for studying his thought.

The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 at Bombay. Who was the Scottish-born British civil servant who played the key role in its founding?

(B) Allan Octavian Hume
(C) George Yule
(D) Henry Cotton
cards.back:
(B) Allan Octavian Hume

Acted as its first General Secretary. Wedderburn, Yule, Cotton were all sympathetic British who served as INC presidents — the only Britons to preside: George YULE (1888, first non-Indian president), William WEDDERBURN (1889 & 1910), Alfred WEBB (1894), Henry COTTON (1904), Annie BESANT (Irish-born, 1917 — first woman). Dadabhai Naoroji's 1886 presidential address established INC as a national body. INC had 3 phases: MODERATE (1885-1905) → EXTREMIST (1905-1917) → GANDHIAN (1917-1947).

Tilak's 'Swaraj is my birthright' slogan came in 1916 during the Home Rule Movement.

cards.front:
The famous 'Surat Split' of the INC in 1907 was a formal division between which two factions?

(A) Hindus vs Muslims
(B) Moderates (Gokhale, Mehta) vs Extremists
(C) Gandhians vs Revolutionaries
(D) Swarajists vs No-changers
cards.back:
(B) Moderates (Gokhale, Mehta) vs Extremists

Freedom Movement — The SURAT SPLIT (Dec 1907 at Surat, Gujarat) formally divided the Congress into two factions: MODERATES led by Gopal Krishna GOKHALE + Pherozeshah MEHTA + Dadabhai Naoroji — favouring prayer-petition-protest, gradual reforms; EXTREMISTS led by the TRIO 'LAL-BAL-PAL' (Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal) + Aurobindo Ghosh — wanting militancy, boycott, swadeshi, Swaraj. Trigger: Surat session presidency choice — Moderates wanted Rashbehari Ghose; Extremists wanted Tilak. Reunion at LUCKNOW 1916 session (under Ambika Charan Mazumdar), which ALSO saw the HC Pact with the Muslim League. The 1905 Bengal Partition had catalysed Extremist rise; Moderates faded post-1916. Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal — 'Lal-Bal-Pal'.

Gopal Krishna Gokhale founded which society in 1905, aimed at training Indians to serve the motherland in a self-less manner?

(A) Servants of India Society
(B) Hindu Mahasabha
(C) Ramakrishna Mission
(D) Arya Samaj
cards.back:
(A) Servants of India Society

Freedom Movement — Gopal Krishna GOKHALE (1866-1915) — called Mahatma Gandhi's 'POLITICAL GURU' — founded the SERVANTS OF INDIA SOCIETY in 1905 in Pune. Aim: to train national missionaries for the service of India and to promote the interests of the Indian people by constitutional means. Gokhale presided over the 1905 Benares session of INC. Also: Gokhale drafted the ELEMENTARY EDUCATION BILL 1911 (defeated in Council). Other similar societies: Ramakrishna Mission (Swami Vivekananda, 1897), Arya Samaj (Dayanand Saraswati, 1875), Theosophical Society (Blavatsky/Olcott, 1875 US; Annie Besant brought it to prominence in India), Prarthana Samaj (Atmaram Pandurang, 1867 Bombay — Ranade, Bhandarkar active), Brahmo Samaj (Raja Rammohan Roy, 1828), Hindu Mahasabha (Madan Mohan Malaviya, 1915).

cards.front:
Bal Gangadhar Tilak popularised the slogan 'Swaraj is my birthright, and I shall have it'. During which movement/occasion was this famously declared?

(A) Non-Cooperation Movement (1920)
(B) Home Rule Movement (1916)
(C) Civil Disobedience Movement (1930)
(D) Quit India Movement (1942)
cards.back:
(B) Home Rule Movement (1916)

Freedom Movement — Bal Gangadhar TILAK (1856-1920, 'Lokmanya') coined 'SWARAJYA MAZHA JANMA SIDDHA HAKKA AHE ANI TO MI MILAVANARACH' (Marathi) — 'Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it' — during the Home Rule Movement (1916), which he launched from Pune in April 1916. Annie Besant launched a parallel Home Rule League from Madras in Sept 1916. Both Leagues merged with the INC effectively by 1918. Tilak started the newspapers KESARI (Marathi) and MAHRATTA (English) in 1881. Promoted GANESH UTSAV (1893) and SHIVAJI UTSAV (1895) as mass mobilisation tools. Jailed multiple times; wrote 'Gita Rahasya' (1915) in Mandalay prison. Died on 1 August 1920 — the day Non-Cooperation was formally launched.

cards.front:
The historic 1929 LAHORE session of the INC, where 'PURNA SWARAJ' (Complete Independence) was declared as the goal, was presided by:

(A) Mahatma Gandhi
(B) Jawaharlal Nehru
(C) Motilal Nehru
(D) Subhas Chandra Bose
cards.back:
(B) Jawaharlal Nehru

Freedom Movement — JAWAHARLAL NEHRU (1889-1964), aged 40, became the YOUNGEST INC President at the LAHORE session (December 1929). At midnight of 31 December 1929, the TRICOLOUR was unfurled on the banks of the Ravi river, and the Purna Swaraj resolution was passed — declaring COMPLETE INDEPENDENCE as the ultimate goal. 26 JANUARY 1930 was observed as the first INDEPENDENCE DAY nationwide (celebrated annually till 1947 as 'Purna Swaraj Day'). Upon independence, 26 Jan 1950 was deliberately chosen as REPUBLIC DAY (when Constitution came into force) to honour this legacy. MOTILAL NEHRU (JLN's father) had presided INC in 1919 and 1928 (when the Nehru Report was finalised). SC Bose presided in 1938 Haripura and 1939 Tripuri (led to his split with Gandhi).

cards.front:
The INDIAN INDEPENDENCE ACT, 1947 was passed by which legislature?

(A) The Indian Constituent Assembly meeting at Delhi
(B) The British Parliament at Westminster, London
(C) The Imperial Legislative Council in colonial Delhi
(D) The All India Congress Committee at Bombay
cards.back:
(B) The British Parliament at Westminster, London

Freedom Movement — Indian Independence Act 1947 — passed by the British Parliament; received Royal Assent on 18 July 1947. Provided for the partition of British India into two independent dominions (India + Pakistan) on 15 August 1947. Both dominions free to write their own constitutions. The Act ended British paramountcy over princely states (~565 of them), giving them choice to accede to either dominion or remain independent. Distractor 1 — Constituent Assembly drafted India's Constitution (Jan 1950), not the 1947 Act. Distractor 3 — Imperial Legislative Council was abolished by then. Distractor 4 — AICC is a Congress body, not a legislature.

(B) Partition of British India into two new dominions with princely choice
(C) Direct annexation of all the princely states by Britain itself
(D) A federal Indian dominion functioning under the British Crown only

Announced partition of British India into India + Pakistan; PRINCELY STATES given choice to join either dominion or remain independent (subsequently nearly all integrated, with exceptions: Hyderabad — annexed via Operation Polo 1948; Junagadh — plebiscite + accession 1948; Jammu & Kashmir — accession after Pakistani tribal incursion, October 1947). cards.front:
The boundary between India and Pakistan was drawn by a commission headed by:

(A) Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of India
(B) Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had not visited India
(C) Stafford Cripps, the leader of the Cripps Mission
(D) Pethick Lawrence, head of the Cabinet Mission
cards.back:
(B) Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had not visited India

Freedom Movement — RADCLIFFE LINE — drawn by Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer with no prior knowledge of India, in just 5 weeks (June-Aug 1947). He chaired two boundary commissions (one for Bengal, one for Punjab), each with 4 members (2 Congress + 2 ML). He resolved deadlocks alone. The boundary was announced on 17 August 1947 (TWO DAYS AFTER independence), causing massive last-minute uncertainty + violence. Resulted in one of the largest mass migrations in history (~14-18 million displaced) and the deaths of ~1-2 million in communal violence. Radcliffe never visited India again; said he'd 'never do it again'.

The integration of princely states into the Indian Union was masterminded by:

(A) Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister
(B) Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, with V.P. Menon as Secretary
(C) Maulana Azad, the first Education Minister
(D) Dr B.R. Ambedkar, the chief drafter of the Constitution

Freedom Movement — Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel — Home Minister + States Department head; nicknamed the 'Iron Man of India'. With V.P. The CABINET MISSION (1946) — which preceded independence — proposed an arrangement that did NOT include:

(A) A three-tiered union of British India and princely states
(B) Immediate full partition of India into India and Pakistan
(C) A grouping system for provinces along religious-majority lines
(D) A constituent assembly to draft a constitution for united India
cards.back:
(B) Immediate full partition of India into India and Pakistan

Freedom Movement — Cabinet Mission (March-June 1946) — sent by the Attlee Labour government; consisted of Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, A.V. Alexander. PROPOSED: a UNITED India with three GROUPS of provinces (A = Hindu majority, B = Muslim-majority west, C = Muslim-majority east); a weak federal centre handling defence, foreign affairs, communications; provinces could opt out after 10 years. Did NOT propose partition. Initially accepted by Congress + ML but ML withdrew over interpretation. Direct Action Day (16 Aug 1946) — Calcutta riots → confirmed partition unavoidable. Cabinet Mission is the LAST significant unification attempt.

Pakistan was founded on the basis of the TWO-NATION THEORY, propounded principally by:

(A) Mahatma Gandhi during the early Civil Disobedience movement
(B) Muhammad Ali Jinnah, leader of the All-India Muslim League
(C) Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, founder of Aligarh Muslim University

Freedom Movement — Two-nation theory — Hindus and Muslims constitute two distinct nations. Earliest articulated by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (late 19th century, Aligarh Movement) and refined by Allama Iqbal (Allahabad Address, 1930). Distractor 3 — Sir Syed FORESHADOWED but didn't politically demand partition. Distractor 4 — Iqbal articulated the idea poetically but Jinnah converted it into political reality.

cards.front:
The slogan 'SWARAJ IS MY BIRTHRIGHT, AND I SHALL HAVE IT' was given by:

(A) Mahatma Gandhi
(B) BAL GANGADHAR TILAK
(C) Subhas Chandra Bose
(D) Gopal Krishna Gokhale
cards.back:
(B) BAL GANGADHAR TILAK

Freedom Movement — BAL GANGADHAR TILAK (1856-1920) — ‘LOKMANYA' ('accepted by the people'); leader of the EXTREMIST / RADICAL faction of the Indian National Congress (INC) + icon of early militant nationalism. FAMOUS SLOGAN: 'SWARAJ IS MY BIRTHRIGHT AND I SHALL HAVE IT' — uttered during his 1908 sedition trial in Bombay HC. BOOKS: 'GITA RAHASYA' (written in Mandalay prison 1908-14 on Bhagavad Gita's karma yoga), 'The Arctic Home in the Vedas', 'The Orion'. NEWSPAPERS: KESARI (Marathi, 1881) + MAHRATTA (English) — sharp anti-British journalism. MASS MOBILISATION: revived GANAPATI FESTIVAL (1893) + SHIVAJI JAYANTI (1895) as public, anti-colonial mobilisation tools — making festivals community-wide instead of private. LAL-BAL-PAL TRIO: TILAK (Maharashtra) + Lala LAJPAT RAI (Punjab) + BIPIN CHANDRA PAL (Bengal) = Extremist trinity. Advocated boycott of British goods, Swadeshi, National Education. SURAT SPLIT (1907) — Congress split between MODERATES (Gokhale, Phirozeshah Mehta) + EXTREMISTS (Tilak, Lajpat, Pal) over the 'four resolutions' (Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education, Self-government). Reunited at LUCKNOW SESSION 1916 (also signed Lucknow Pact between INC + Muslim League). IMPRISONMENT: 1908-14 — 6 years in MANDALAY prison (Burma) for sedition (published articles critical of British). HOMERULE LEAGUE: founded 1916 with Annie Besant — demanded Home Rule for India within Empire (like Canada, Australia). DEATH: 1 August 1920 (same year Gandhi's Non-Cooperation Movement began). Called 'Father of Indian Unrest' by V.B. Fielding. leader of the Extremists + called 'LOKMANYA' ('accepted by the people').

cards.front:
The SURAT SPLIT of 1907 divided the Indian National Congress into:

(A) Hindus vs Muslims
(B) MODERATES (Gokhale, Mehta, S.N. Banerjee) vs EXTREMISTS
(C) Congress vs Muslim League
(D) North vs South
cards.back:
(B) MODERATES (Gokhale, Mehta, S.N. Banerjee) vs EXTREMISTS

Freedom Movement — SURAT SPLIT (26 December 1907) — the famous rift at the Surat Congress Session over differences in METHODS + STRATEGY. MODERATES: Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjee, Dadabhai Naoroji, Dinshaw Wacha, R.C. Dutt — believed in constitutional agitation, petitions, prayers, cooperation with British, gradual reforms. EXTREMISTS: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal ('Lal-Bal-Pal'), Aurobindo Ghosh — believed in direct action, boycott of British goods, passive resistance, Swadeshi, National Education, swaraj. IMMEDIATE CAUSE: (1) Moderates wanted to hold the session at Nagpur (Tilak's stronghold) — shifted to SURAT under pressure. (2) Moderates opposed Rash Behari Ghose (then Nagpur president-elect moderate) being nominated again. (3) Key 4 Surat resolutions on Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education, Self-Government were proposed by Extremists; Moderates wanted watered-down versions. CHAOS: scuffle in the pandal; Tilak thumped by a shoe (thrown at Surendranath Banerjee, hit Tilak); session suspended. RESULT: Extremists WALKED OUT + were EXPELLED from Congress. Congress remained moderate-led till 1916. CONGRESS REUNIFIED at LUCKNOW SESSION 1916 (after Tilak's return from Mandalay); this year also saw LUCKNOW PACT between Congress + Muslim League (Jinnah's famous negotiation). IMPACT: Surat split set back nationalist movement — until Gandhi's 1915 return from South Africa + 1917 emergence (Champaran). PARTITION OF BENGAL (1905, Curzon) was the spark that radicalised the movement + produced the Swadeshi + Boycott movement. REVOKED Partition in 1911 + shifted capital from Calcutta to Delhi. over methods + Swadeshi-boycott; Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Pal, Aurobindo.

cards.front:
The PARTITION OF BENGAL (1905) was carried out by Viceroy ______, ostensibly for administrative efficiency.

(A) Lord Dalhousie
(B) LORD CURZON (1899-1905)
(C) Lord Ripon
(D) Lord Mountbatten
cards.back:
(B) LORD CURZON (1899-1905)

Freedom Movement — PARTITION OF BENGAL — announced 19 July 1905, effective 16 OCTOBER 1905, by Viceroy LORD CURZON (Viceroy 1899-1905). DIVIDED Bengal Presidency into: (1) BENGAL (with Bihar + Orissa) — Hindu-majority, ~4.2 crore population; (2) EASTERN BENGAL + ASSAM — Muslim-majority, ~3.1 crore, new province with Dacca as capital. OFFICIAL REASON: administrative convenience (Bengal was too large + unwieldy). REAL REASON (widely condemned by Indian historians): DIVIDE + RULE — weaken the strong Bengali-led nationalist movement (Bengal was then the main centre of INC, Swadeshi, anti-British agitation) by splitting Hindus + Muslims. RESPONSE: MASS PROTESTS all over India. (1) 16 October 1905 = 'day of mourning' (rakhi-bandhan between Hindus + Muslims led by Tagore). (2) SWADESHI MOVEMENT — boycott of British goods, promotion of Indian-made (inaugurated 7 Aug 1905 at Calcutta Town Hall); burning of British textiles at Parel. (3) BOYCOTT of British institutions, courts, schools — NATIONAL EDUCATION movement (founding of Bengal National College; Aurobindo Ghosh's principalship). (4) SAMITIS (volunteer corps) formed. (5) Revolutionary violence rose (Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar, Muzaffarpur bombing 1908 by Khudiram Bose + Prafulla Chaki). TAGORE composed 'AMAR SONAR BANGLA' as protest anthem (later Bangladesh's national anthem). REVERSAL: British ANNULLED the partition in DECEMBER 1911 at Delhi Durbar (King George V), also shifting capital from CALCUTTA to DELHI the same year. But OUTCOMES persisted: (a) gave massive fillip to Swadeshi + nationalist movement; (b) birth of Muslim League 1906 (All India Muslim League in Dhaka — to safeguard Muslim interests during the Eastern Bengal province's popularity). Partition's communalising effect lingered + contributed to 1947 Partition. cited administrative convenience; real aim was to divide Hindu-majority + Muslim-majority areas + weaken Bengali nationalism.

cards.front:
AUROBINDO GHOSH, before his spiritual turn, was associated with which extremist revolutionary organisation?

(A) Hindustan Republican Association
(B) ANUSHILAN SAMITI (Bengal)
(C) Ghadar Party
(D) Azad Hind Fauj
cards.back:
(B) ANUSHILAN SAMITI (Bengal)

Freedom Movement — AUROBINDO GHOSH (1872-1950, later 'Sri Aurobindo') — pre-1910 EXTREMIST revolutionary; post-1910 spiritual PHILOSOPHER. EARLY LIFE: born Calcutta; educated in England (age 7-21) at ICSE + St. Paul's + King's College Cambridge (classics). Worked in Baroda State (1893-1906). NATIONALIST PHASE (1906-1910): returned to Bengal after Partition (1905); became editor of newspapers 'BANDE MATARAM' + 'KARMAYOGIN'; Principal of Bengal National College. Articulated 'spiritual nationalism' — India's freedom as divine mission. REVOLUTIONARY INVOLVEMENT: ANUSHILAN SAMITI founded 1902 by Promotha Nath Mitra; Aurobindo + his brother Barindra Kumar Ghosh were its key ideologues + organisers. JUGANTAR — the militant extremist wing of Anushilan — Barindra led it. MUZAFFARPUR BOMBING 1908 — KHUDIRAM BOSE (18) + PRAFULLA CHAKI threw a bomb at the carriage of Magistrate KINGSFORD (who gave harsh sentences to nationalists); killed Mrs + Miss KENNEDY (British ladies) instead. Khudiram was HANGED (11 Aug 1908, YOUNGEST martyr at 18); Chaki shot himself. ALIPORE CONSPIRACY CASE (1908-09) — Aurobindo ARRESTED + TRIED for sedition + conspiracy; 38 accused; defended by CHITTARANJAN DAS in a legendary year-long trial ending in Aurobindo's ACQUITTAL. SPIRITUAL TURN: while in jail, Aurobindo had mystical experiences reading the Gita; on release 1909, gradually withdrew from politics. 1910 — moved to PONDICHERRY (French India, safe from British) + devoted himself to integral yoga. AUROBINDO ASHRAM founded; along with THE MOTHER (Mirra Alfassa) in 1920s-30s developed INTEGRAL YOGA philosophy. Writings: 'The Life Divine', 'The Synthesis of Yoga', 'Savitri' (epic poem). AUROVILLE founded 1968 near Pondicherry by the Mother — international township experiment. Aurobindo's birthday 15 August coincided with India's Independence Day — auspicious symbolism. led ideologically by Aurobindo + his brother Barindra; involved in Muzaffarpur bombing + Alipore Conspiracy case (1908-09).

MUZAFFARPUR BOMBING 1908 — KHUDIRAM BOSE (18) + PRAFULLA CHAKI threw a bomb at the carriage of Magistrate KINGSFORD (who gave harsh sentences to nationalists); killed Mrs + Miss KENNEDY (British ladies) instead. Khudiram was HANGED (11 Aug 1908, YOUNGEST martyr at 18); Chaki shot himself. ALIPORE CONSPIRACY CASE (1908-09) — Aurobindo ARRESTED + TRIED for sedition + conspiracy; 38 accused; defended by CHITTARANJAN DAS in a legendary year-long trial ending in Aurobindo's ACQUITTAL. SPIRITUAL TURN: while in jail, Aurobindo had mystical experiences reading the Gita; on release 1909, gradually withdrew from politics. 1910 — moved to PONDICHERRY (French India, safe from British) + devoted himself to integral yoga. AUROBINDO ASHRAM founded; along with THE MOTHER (Mirra Alfassa) in 1920s-30s developed INTEGRAL YOGA philosophy. Writings: 'The Life Divine', 'The Synthesis of Yoga', 'Savitri' (epic poem). AUROVILLE founded 1968 near Pondicherry by the Mother — international township experiment. Aurobindo's birthday 15 August coincided with India's Independence Day — auspicious symbolism. led ideologically by Aurobindo + his brother Barindra; involved in Muzaffarpur bombing + Alipore Conspiracy case (1908-09).

cards.front:
The KAKORI TRAIN ROBBERY (9 August 1925) was carried out by:

(A) Congress socialists
(B) HRA — Hindustan Republican Association (later HSRA) — led by RAMPRASAD BISMIL, CHANDRA SHEKHAR AZAD, ASHFAQULLAH KHAN, ROSHAN SINGH, RAJENDRA LAHIRI + others
(C) Indian National Army
(D) Ghadar Party
cards.back:
(B) HRA — Hindustan Republican Association (later HSRA) — led by RAMPRASAD BISMIL, CHANDRA SHEKHAR AZAD, ASHFAQULLAH KHAN, ROSHAN SINGH, RAJENDRA LAHIRI + others

Freedom Movement — KAKORI TRAIN ROBBERY / KAKORI CONSPIRACY — 9 August 1925, at KAKORI village (near Lucknow, UP). HRA (HINDUSTAN REPUBLICAN ASSOCIATION) — revolutionary organisation founded 1924 at Kanpur by Sachindra Nath Sanyal; aimed at armed overthrow of British rule + federal republic. EXECUTORS: RAM PRASAD BISMIL (leader, also poet — 'Sarfaroshi ki tamanna...' credited widely to him, actually by Bismil Azimabadi — Bismil adopted it as HRA anthem), ASHFAQULLAH KHAN (Muslim revolutionary, Bismil's best friend — symbol of Hindu-Muslim revolutionary unity), ROSHAN SINGH, RAJENDRA LAHIRI, CHANDRASHEKHAR AZAD (escaped), Banwari Lal, Sachindra Bakshi, Manmath Nath Gupta + others — totally 10 revolutionaries. OPERATION: stopped the 8-Down Saharanpur-Lucknow train at Kakori by pulling the alarm chain; looted a government treasury of ~₹8,000 (some sources ₹4,600) to fund arms purchases + activities; a passenger (AHMED ALI) was killed by accidental firing (only casualty). BRITISH CRACKDOWN: massive manhunt; 40+ arrested; KAKORI CONSPIRACY CASE lasted 18 months. OUTCOMES: (1) BISMIL, ASHFAQULLAH, ROSHAN SINGH, LAHIRI — HANGED in Dec 1927 (at Gorakhpur, Faizabad, Allahabad, Gonda jails respectively). (2) Sanyal + others — deportation to Andamans + long sentences. (3) CHANDRASHEKHAR AZAD EVADED arrest, reorganised HRA as HSRA (Hindustan Socialist Republican Association, 1928 at Ferozeshah Kotla Delhi — socialist added) along with BHAGAT SINGH, SUKHDEV, RAJGURU, BATUKESHWAR DUTT. AZAD died on 27 Feb 1931 at Alfred Park Allahabad (Chandrashekhar Azad Park today), shooting himself with last bullet to remain 'AZAD' (free) — aged 24. HSRA carried out assembly bombing (1929 Bhagat Singh-Batukeshwar Dutt), Saunders murder (1928).

cards.front:
BHAGAT SINGH, SUKHDEV + RAJGURU were HANGED on:

(A) 13 April 1919
(B) 23 MARCH 1931 at Lahore Central Jail
(C) 30 January 1948
(D) 15 August 1947
cards.back:
(B) 23 MARCH 1931 at Lahore Central Jail

Freedom Movement — BHAGAT SINGH (1907-1931) — SHAHEED-E-AZAM (Supreme Martyr); SUKHDEV THAPAR, SHIVARAM RAJGURU — HANGED together at LAHORE CENTRAL JAIL on 23 MARCH 1931 (evening, BEFORE scheduled 6 AM the next day — to avoid mass rioting). Ages at death: Bhagat 23, Sukhdev 23, Rajguru 22. 23 MARCH now observed as SHAHEED DIWAS (Martyrs' Day). CHARGES: LAHORE CONSPIRACY CASE — murder of Asst Superintendent of Police JOHN SAUNDERS (17 Dec 1928). BACKGROUND: (a) SIMON COMMISSION (1927, all-white, no Indian members) faced 'SIMON GO BACK' protests; (b) at LAHORE on 30 Oct 1928, LALA LAJPAT RAI was lathi-charged by Supt JAMES SCOTT, grievously injured; died 17 Nov 1928. (c) HSRA vowed vengeance. On 17 Dec 1928 outside Lahore Police HQ, Bhagat + Rajguru shot SAUNDERS (mistaken for Scott); Chandrashekhar Azad covered their escape. 8 APRIL 1929 — ASSEMBLY BOMB: Bhagat Singh + BATUKESHWAR DUTT threw 2 non-lethal BOMBS in Central Legislative Assembly (Delhi) + 'INQUILAB ZINDABAD!' slogan + leaflets ('to make the deaf hear'), protesting against the Public Safety Bill + Trade Disputes Bill. SURRENDERED voluntarily to be tried + use trial as propaganda platform. LAHORE CONSPIRACY TRIAL (May 1930 – Oct 1930): found guilty; sentenced to hang. HUNGER STRIKE in jail (116 days by Jatin Das, who died) — demanding political-prisoner status. GANDHI-IRWIN PACT (5 Mar 1931) — Congress didn't insist on commuting death sentences (controversial historical debate). Bhagat + 2 comrades were CREMATED at HUSSAINIWALA (Ferozepur bank of Sutlej, Pakistan border) by British before news spread. MOTHER Vidyavati, BROTHER Kulbir + Kultar; ROLE MODEL: Kartar Singh Sarabha (Ghadar martyr). WRITINGS: 'Why I Am an Atheist' (1931 prison essay). Bhagat Singh remains India's most popular revolutionary icon. for the Lahore Conspiracy case (Saunders murder Dec 1928); 23 March now SHAHEED DIWAS.

cards.front:
The GHADAR PARTY was founded in 1913 in:

(A) London
(B) SAN FRANCISCO, USA
(C) Lahore
(D) Rangoon
cards.back:
(B) SAN FRANCISCO, USA

Freedom Movement — GHADAR PARTY / GHADR PARTY ('Revolt Party') — founded 1 November 1913 in SAN FRANCISCO, California, by Indian emigrants (predominantly PUNJABI SIKHS, also Hindus + some Muslims) working as farmers + labourers on the Pacific Coast (USA, Canada). PRESIDENT: SOHAN SINGH BHAKNA. SECRETARY + intellectual leader: LALA HAR DAYAL (Oxford-educated radical, anarchist influenced; later exiled, died 1939 in US). PUBLICATION: 'GHADAR' newspaper (multilingual — Urdu, Punjabi, Gujarati, Hindi) distributed among Indian expats globally. IDEOLOGY: armed revolution to overthrow British Raj; republican + secular; 'India for the Indians'. OPPORTUNITY: outbreak of WWI in AUG 1914 — Ghadar leaders saw Britain's distraction as chance to spark uprising. PLAN: thousands of Ghadarites returned to Punjab by sea (via Hong Kong, Singapore, Shanghai) aiming to incite mutiny in British Indian Army + general revolt. FAILURE: British intelligence infiltrated the movement; informant network caught plans; mass arrests on arrival. KOMAGATA MARU INCIDENT (1914) — Japanese ship chartered by Gurdit Singh carrying 376 Punjabi passengers (mostly Sikh) denied entry to Canada (Vancouver) on racist exclusion laws; forced back; on return to Budge Budge near Calcutta (Sep 1914), police fired on them — 19 killed. Radicalised many who joined Ghadar. LAHORE CONSPIRACY CASE (1915) — main Ghadar-linked trial; 42 hanged, 114 transported to Andamans; notables hanged: KARTAR SINGH SARABHA (age 19, Bhagat Singh's hero), VISHNU GANESH PINGLE. FIRST LAHORE CONSPIRACY CASE was this 1915 one (second was Bhagat Singh's 1929). LEGACY: (1) Inspired subsequent revolutionaries (Bhagat Singh held Sarabha's photo close to heart); (2) Canada's Komagata Maru apology (2016 by PM Trudeau); (3) Ghadar Memorial in San Francisco + Jalandhar (Deshbhagat Yadgar Hall). by Indian emigrants (Punjabi Sikhs + Hindus) led by LALA HAR DAYAL + Sohan Singh Bhakna; aimed at armed overthrow of British Raj via expat uprising.

cards.front:
The JALLIANWALA BAGH MASSACRE took place on:

(A) 30 January 1948
(B) 13 APRIL 1919 (Baisakhi day) at Amritsar
(C) 15 August 1947
(D) 2 October 1919
cards.back:
(B) 13 APRIL 1919 (Baisakhi day) at Amritsar

Freedom Movement — JALLIANWALA BAGH MASSACRE — 13 APRIL 1919 (BAISAKHI Day), at Jallianwala Bagh, AMRITSAR, Punjab. CONTEXT: (1) ROWLATT ACT (March 1919) — allowed arrest + indefinite detention without trial; opposed as 'no appeal, no plea, no dalil'; Gandhi called it 'Black Act' + launched ROWLATT SATYAGRAHA (his first nationwide movement, April 1919). (2) In Punjab, arrests of popular local leaders DR SATYAPAL + DR SAIFUDDIN KITCHLEW on 10 April 1919 triggered protests; police fired + killed 2-3, mob then killed 5 British in retaliation (Marcia Sherwood assault, bank employees killed). (3) Punjab Lt-Governor Michael O'Dwyer + General REGINALD DYER imposed martial law, banned gatherings. (4) 13 April, Baisakhi + annual Amritsar fair — ~20,000 people (many unaware of ban) gathered at Jallianwala Bagh (a walled enclosure with single narrow entrance) to peacefully protest + celebrate Baisakhi. (5) GENERAL DYER arrived with ~90 Gurkha + Baluchi soldiers + blocked the entrance; WITHOUT WARNING ordered 10 MINUTES of continuous rifle fire (1,650 rounds); pit ceased only when ammunition ran out. (6) Many jumped into the well to escape bullets (120 bodies retrieved from it, still preserved as memorial). DEATHS: Official British tally = 379 dead + 1,100 injured; Indian INC estimate = 1,000+ dead. AFTERMATH: (1) HUNTER COMMITTEE (1919-20) — inquiry: criticised Dyer for 'serious error of judgment' but didn't prosecute him; House of Lords supported him; British public raised £26,000 fund for 'The Saviour of Punjab'. (2) Rabindranath TAGORE RENOUNCED KNIGHTHOOD (31 May 1919). (3) Gandhi returned his Kaiser-i-Hind Medal; launched NON-COOPERATION MOVEMENT (1920-22). (4) UDHAM SINGH — Amritsar resident present at massacre, AVENGED the atrocity on 13 March 1940 by shooting Michael O'Dwyer at Caxton Hall, London; Udham Singh hanged 31 July 1940 at Pentonville Prison. (5) Dyer retired 1920; died 1927. British PM David Cameron (2013) + UK govt have repeatedly refused a formal apology (deepest 'regret' offered). General REGINALD DYER opened fire on a peaceful crowd; ~400-1000+ killed.

cards.front:
The INDIAN NATIONAL ARMY (INA / Azad Hind Fauj) was founded in 1942 in ______ by Captain Mohan Singh, later REVIVED + led by Subhas Chandra Bose.

(A) Berlin
(B) SINGAPORE
(C) Rangoon
(D) Tokyo
cards.back:
(B) SINGAPORE

Freedom Movement — INDIAN NATIONAL ARMY (INA) / AZAD HIND FAUJ — formed to liberate India from British rule with Axis (Japanese) military support during WWII. PHASES: (1) FIRST INA (1942) — founded 17 FEBRUARY 1942 in SINGAPORE by Captain MOHAN SINGH (Indian Army officer captured by Japanese in Malaya); initial strength ~40,000 from Indian POWs surrendered after Japan's lightning victories in Malaya + Singapore. RASH BEHARI BOSE (earlier revolutionary, fled to Japan in 1915) — gave political leadership. First INA disbanded Dec 1942 due to Japanese-INA disputes (Japanese treated INA as subordinate); Mohan Singh arrested by Japanese. (2) SECOND INA (1943) — SUBHAS CHANDRA BOSE reached Japan via dramatic escape: (a) Jan 1941 — escaped house arrest in Calcutta, via Afghanistan to Berlin; (b) Met Hitler (May 1942) — coined title 'NETAJI' (Leader), received by Indian soldiers as Indische Legion; (c) Feb 1943 — submarine voyage from Kiel to Madagascar to Japanese submarine, to Tokyo (July 1943); (d) 4 July 1943 in SINGAPORE — Bose took command of INA. (e) 21 OCTOBER 1943 — Declared AZAD HIND GOVERNMENT (Provisional Government of Free India) in Singapore; Bose was 'Head of State + Prime Minister + Minister of War'. Recognised by 9 Axis + neutral countries (Japan, Germany, Italy, Burma, Thailand, Nanking China, Manchukuo, Philippines, Croatia). (f) Women's regiment — RANI OF JHANSI REGIMENT, led by CAPTAIN LAKSHMI SAHGAL (first all-women combat unit in modern Asia). (g) Slogans: 'Dilli Chalo!', 'Jai Hind!', 'Tum mujhe khoon do, main tumhe azadi dunga'. (h) Battles: INA's Bahadur brigade fought alongside Japanese in IMPHAL-KOHIMA OFFENSIVE (Mar-Jul 1944) — failed due to monsoon + Allied resistance; Japanese defeat; INA lost ~50% to disease, starvation, fighting. (i) NETAJI's DEATH: officially in air crash at TAIHOKU (Taipei), TAIWAN, 18 AUGUST 1945 — some dispute it, multiple commissions; Shah Nawaz (1956), Khosla (1974), Mukherjee (2005) differ. (3) POST-WAR: RED FORT TRIALS (Nov 1945 – Jan 1946) of 3 INA officers — PK Sahgal (Hindu), Shah Nawaz Khan (Muslim), Gurbaksh Singh Dhillon (Sikh) — symbolic communal unity; defended by Bhulabhai Desai, Asaf Ali, Nehru, Tej Bahadur Sapru; massive public sympathy + demos + Naval Mutiny (Feb 1946) forced British to commute sentences + speeded up Independence. initially formed in 1942 from Indian POWs of the Japanese; REVIVED + inspired by Subhas Bose in July 1943.

cards.front:
Which revolutionary is known for the slogan 'INQUILAB ZINDABAD' + its assembly-bombing association?

(A) Subhas Chandra Bose
(B) BHAGAT SINGH + BATUKESHWAR DUTT
(C) Chandrasekhar Azad
(D) Lala Lajpat Rai
cards.back:
(B) BHAGAT SINGH + BATUKESHWAR DUTT

Freedom Movement — 'INQUILAB ZINDABAD' (Urdu/Hindi: 'Long Live Revolution') — slogan popularised by BHAGAT SINGH + BATUKESHWAR DUTT during the CENTRAL LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY BOMBING (8 April 1929). ORIGIN of slogan: first used by poet MAULANA HASRAT MOHANI (a Muslim League Communist freedom fighter, from Mohan, UP — also coined 'Complete Independence' for INC + championed it at the 1921 Ahmedabad Session before Nehru formalised it at Lahore 1929). EVENT: on 8 April 1929 at Central Legislative Assembly (then in New Delhi, now Parliament complex), Bhagat Singh + Batukeshwar Dutt tossed TWO non-lethal bombs + red pamphlets from the visitors' gallery as the Assembly was debating the PUBLIC SAFETY BILL + TRADE DISPUTES BILL (oppressive measures). PURPOSE: (a) political theatre — not to kill (deliberately low-explosive bombs; no injuries reported); (b) 'TO MAKE THE DEAF HEAR' — to wake up the government + public to oppression; (c) use the trial as a propaganda platform. They SURRENDERED ON THE SPOT instead of escaping, shouting 'Inquilab Zindabad!' + 'Samrajyavaad ka nash ho!' ('Down with imperialism!'). TRIAL 1929-30: Bhagat was simultaneously linked via fingerprints to the earlier SAUNDERS murder (Dec 1928); LAHORE CONSPIRACY CASE added. Defended trial as political. Wrote extensively from jail — 'Why I Am an Atheist' (1931), manifestos for HSRA's socialist republic. EXECUTION 23 March 1931 alongside Sukhdev + Rajguru. BATUKESHWAR DUTT survived — sentenced to life in Andamans; released 1938; continued struggle; died 1965 in poverty (ironic — forgotten by govt till late). INQUILAB ZINDABAD became THE defining slogan of Indian revolutionary movement + continues to resonate in progressive politics across South Asia. on 8 April 1929 threw non-lethal bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly (Delhi) shouting 'Inquilab Zindabad!'.

Wrote extensively from jail — 'Why I Am an Atheist' (1931), manifestos for HSRA's socialist republic. EXECUTION 23 March 1931 alongside Sukhdev + Rajguru. BATUKESHWAR DUTT survived — sentenced to life in Andamans; released 1938; continued struggle; died 1965 in poverty (ironic — forgotten by govt till late). INQUILAB ZINDABAD became THE defining slogan of Indian revolutionary movement + continues to resonate in progressive politics across South Asia. on 8 April 1929 threw non-lethal bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly (Delhi) shouting 'Inquilab Zindabad!'.

The Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22) was launched under the leadership of:

(A) B.G. Tilak
(B) Mahatma Gandhi
(C) Gopal Krishna Gokhale
(D) Subhash Chandra Bose
cards.back:
(B) Mahatma Gandhi

Freedom Movement — Non-Cooperation Movement (NCM) — Gandhi's first nationwide mass movement. Approved at the special Calcutta session of INC (Sep 1920) and ratified at Nagpur session (Dec 1920). Tilak — passed away on 1 Aug 1920, the very day NCM was launched (also Khilafat Day). Gokhale — Gandhi's political mentor, died 1915. Bose — emerged later, in the 1930s. Programme: surrender titles, boycott of councils, courts, schools, foreign cloth; promote khadi, swadeshi, national education (Jamia Millia Islamia, Kashi Vidyapith, Gujarat Vidyapith founded), Hindu-Muslim unity, removal of untouchability.

cards.front:
Two events that triggered Gandhi's call for the Non-Cooperation Movement were:

(A) Quit India Resolution and Cripps Mission
(B) Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) and the Khilafat issue (post-Treaty of Sèvres)
(C) Partition of Bengal and Swadeshi Movement
(D) Battle of Plassey and Permanent Settlement
cards.back:
(B) Jallianwala Bagh massacre (1919) and the Khilafat issue (post-Treaty of Sèvres)

Freedom Movement — Triggers: (1) Jallianwala Bagh (13 April 1919) under General Dyer at Amritsar — followed by the Hunter Committee report (1920) which Gandhi found unsatisfactory. Tagore renounced his knighthood in protest. (2) Khilafat issue — the Allies' harsh post-WW1 treatment of the Ottoman Caliph (Treaty of Sèvres, 1920) angered Indian Muslims. Khilafat Committee (Ali brothers — Maulana Mohammad Ali + Shaukat Ali) and INC joined hands → Hindu-Muslim unity. (3) The Rowlatt Act (1919) — Gandhi's first satyagraha was against this. The Khilafat issue collapsed in 1924 when Mustafa Kemal Atatürk himself abolished the Caliphate in Turkey.

cards.front:
The Non-Cooperation Movement was abruptly WITHDRAWN by Gandhi in February 1922 after the:

(A) Surat Split
(B) Chauri Chaura incident (5 Feb 1922) — a mob set fire to a police station killing 22 policemen
(C) Lucknow Pact
(D) Cabinet Mission failure
cards.back:
(B) Chauri Chaura incident (5 Feb 1922) — a mob set fire to a police station killing 22 policemen

Freedom Movement — Chauri Chaura — Gorakhpur district, UP. On 5 Feb 1922, a peaceful procession of nationalists turned violent after police fired; the agitated crowd set fire to the police station, killing 22 policemen. Gandhi was deeply disturbed by the violence — withdrew the NCM on 12 Feb 1922 (Bardoli Resolution). Many leaders (Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, Subhash Bose) opposed the withdrawal — felt it killed momentum at its peak. Gandhi was arrested on 10 March 1922, tried by Justice Broomfield, sentenced to 6 years (the 'Great Trial'). The withdrawal led to the formation of the Swaraj Party (Jan 1923) by C.R. Das + Motilal Nehru — they wanted to enter the councils to wreck them from within.

cards.front:
The Tilak Swaraj Fund — the financial backbone of the Non-Cooperation Movement — collected approximately how much?

(A) ₹10 lakh
(B) ₹1 crore (within six months — a remarkable feat in 1921)
(C) ₹100 crore
(D) ₹50 lakh
cards.back:
(B) ₹1 crore (within six months — a remarkable feat in 1921)

Freedom Movement — Tilak Swaraj Fund — set up at the Nagpur session (Dec 1920) in memory of Tilak. Target ₹1 crore in 6 months, attained promptly — symbolised mass financial support for the movement. Used for funding khadi work, national schools, swadeshi industries, propaganda. The Nagpur session also reorganised the Congress — pradesh committees by linguistic states (a forerunner of linguistic states reorganisation later in 1956), Hindi as a major Congress language, lower membership fee to mass-enrol peasants/workers. Membership rose from ~60,000 to ~20 lakh.

cards.front:
Which leader famously renounced his British KNIGHTHOOD in protest after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, foreshadowing the Non-Cooperation spirit?

(A) Mahatma Gandhi
(B) Rabindranath Tagore
(C) C. Rajagopalachari
(D) Lala Lajpat Rai
cards.back:
(B) Rabindranath Tagore

Freedom Movement — Rabindranath Tagore — renounced his Knighthood (Sir, conferred 1915) on 31 May 1919 in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, in a letter to Viceroy Chelmsford ('the time has come when badges of honour make our shame glaring in their incongruous context of humiliation'). Gandhi later returned the Kaiser-i-Hind medal (1920) when launching NCM. Tagore — Nobel Literature 1913 (first non-European Nobel laureate); composed Jana Gana Mana (India) and Amar Shonar Bangla (Bangladesh); founded Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan. Lala Lajpat Rai — 'Sher-e-Punjab', injured in lathi-charge at Lahore against Simon Commission (1928), died shortly thereafter.

cards.front:
Of the following national universities/educational institutions founded during the Non-Cooperation Movement era, which one was established in DELHI?

(A) Kashi Vidyapith
(B) Jamia Millia Islamia (founded 1920 at Aligarh, shifted to Delhi in 1925)
(C) Gujarat Vidyapith
(D) Visva-Bharati
cards.back:
(B) Jamia Millia Islamia (founded 1920 at Aligarh, shifted to Delhi in 1925)

Freedom Movement — Jamia Millia Islamia ('national Muslim university') — founded 22 Oct 1920 at Aligarh by Mohammad Ali Jauhar, Hakim Ajmal Khan, Dr Mukhtar Ahmad Ansari, Dr Zakir Husain (later President of India 1967-69), and Maulana Mahmud Hasan, in response to the Non-Cooperation call to boycott colonial education. Shifted to Karol Bagh, Delhi (1925), then Okhla, New Delhi (1935); central university status 1988. Other NCM-era national institutions — Kashi Vidyapith (Varanasi, 1921, Bhagwan Das), Gujarat Vidyapith (Ahmedabad, 1920, Gandhi himself), Bihar Vidyapith (1921), Tilak Maharashtra Vidyapeeth (Pune, 1921). Visva-Bharati was founded earlier by Tagore in 1921, but its philosophical roots go back to 1901 Santiniketan ashram.

cards.front:
Which Tribal / Peasant uprising in the Madras Presidency (1922-24), led by Alluri Sitarama Raju, took inspiration from the Non-Cooperation Movement but eventually turned to armed methods?

(A) Mappila rebellion (Malabar)
(B) Rampa Rebellion (Andhra agency tracts)
(C) Tana Bhagat movement
(D) Chenchu rebellion
cards.back:
(B) Rampa Rebellion (Andhra agency tracts)

Freedom Movement — Rampa Rebellion (1922-24) — led by Alluri Sitarama Raju ('Manyam Veerudu' — hero of the jungle) in the Visakhapatnam-Godavari agency tracts of Madras Presidency. Tribal grievances: forest laws restricting podu (shifting cultivation), forced labour. Initially inspired by Gandhi's NCM but turned to armed raids on police stations after NCM's withdrawal. Alluri was captured and shot on 7 May 1924. The Mappila Rebellion (Malabar, 1921) — coincided with NCM in Kerala; began as Khilafat-inspired but turned communal. Tana Bhagat (Jharkhand, Oraon tribals, Jatra Bhagat) — also drew on NCM ideas. These uprisings showed the deeper rural reach of nationalist politics during 1920-22.

cards.front:
The 'Quit India' movement was launched by Mahatma Gandhi on:

(A) 8 April 1942
(B) 8 August 1942
(C) 15 August 1947
(D) 26 January 1950
cards.back:
(B) 8 August 1942

Freedom Movement — On 8 August 1942, the AICC at Gowalia Tank Maidan (Mumbai) passed the Quit India Resolution; Gandhi gave the 'Karo ya Maro' (Do or Die) call. The next day, 9 August, top Congress leaders (Gandhi, Nehru, Patel, Azad) were arrested; the movement went underground with Jayaprakash Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali (hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank), Ram Manohar Lohia, Usha Mehta (Congress Radio) leading it.

cards.front:
The Cripps Mission came to India in 1942 with an offer of:

(A) Complete independence immediately
(B) Dominion status after the Second World War
(C) A 10-year plan for self-rule
(D) Direct British rule for 30 more years
cards.back:
(B) Dominion status after the Second World War

Freedom Movement — Stafford Cripps (March-April 1942) offered Dominion Status after the war + the right of provinces / princely states to opt out of the Indian Union (a non-accession clause). Congress rejected the offer as a 'post-dated cheque on a failing bank' (attributed to Gandhi). The Muslim League also rejected it because it did not concede Pakistan outright. The failure of the Cripps Mission led directly to Quit India.

The Cabinet Mission of 1946 — which proposed a federation of three groups of provinces — had as one of its members:

(A) Stafford Cripps
(B) Lord Mountbatten
(C) Lord Irwin
(D) Lord Curzon
cards.back:
(A) Stafford Cripps

Freedom Movement — The Cabinet Mission (1946) consisted of Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A. V. Alexander. It proposed a three-tier federal union with three groupings of provinces and rejected Pakistan. Its plan was initially accepted by Congress and the Muslim League but quickly broke down. Mountbatten — Last Viceroy, 1947. Irwin — famous for the Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931). Curzon — Viceroy 1899-1905, known for the Partition of Bengal 1905.

cards.front:
The Indian Independence Act 1947 was passed by the Parliament of:

(A) India
(B) The United Kingdom
(C) Pakistan
(D) The Commonwealth
cards.back:
(B) The United Kingdom

Freedom Movement — The Indian Independence Act — passed by the British Parliament on 18 July 1947 — legally created the two Dominions of India and Pakistan on 15 August 1947. Royal assent was given the same day. India was granted full legislative sovereignty on that date. Our own Constituent Assembly (elected 1946) began sitting from 9 December 1946 and completed drafting the Constitution on 26 November 1949 (adopted; brought into force on 26 January 1950).

The Radcliffe Line that divided India and Pakistan in 1947 was drawn by:

(A) Lord Mountbatten
(B) Sir Cyril Radcliffe
(C) Stafford Cripps
(D) Jinnah
cards.back:
(B) Sir Cyril Radcliffe

Freedom Movement — Sir Cyril Radcliffe chaired the Boundary Commission that drew the India-Pakistan border between July and August 1947 — despite having never visited India before. The line was made public on 17 August 1947 — two days AFTER independence.

Mahatma Gandhi attended only the Second Round Table Conference (Sep-Dec 1931). He went as the sole representative of:

(A) All-India Muslim League
(B) Indian National Congress
(C) Hindu Mahasabha
(D) Princely States
cards.back:
(B) Indian National Congress

The 'Communal Award' announced in 1932 by British PM Ramsay MacDonald provided separate electorates for:

(A) Only Muslims and Sikhs

cards.front:
India's first full-length silent feature film, released in 1913, was:

(A) Alam Ara
(B) Raja Harishchandra
(C) Mother India
(D) Pundalik
cards.back:
(B) Raja Harishchandra

Art, Culture & Post-Independence — Raja Harishchandra (1913) — directed, produced and shot by Dadasaheb Phalke (Dhundiraj Govind Phalke). Released 3 May 1913 at Coronation Cinema, Bombay. Silent, 40 minutes, with all-male cast (women considered unrespectable on screen — the female lead Taramati was played by male actor Anna Salunke). Pundalik (1912) preceded it but was a recorded play, not a true motion picture. Phalke is honoured by the Dadasaheb Phalke Award — India's highest cinema honour, instituted 1969.

India's first 'talkie' (sound film), released in 1931, was:

(A) Achhut Kanya
(B) Alam Ara
(C) Devdas
(D) Sant Tukaram
cards.back:
(B) Alam Ara

Art, Culture & Post-Independence — Alam Ara (Hindi-Urdu) — directed by Ardeshir Irani, released 14 March 1931 at Majestic Cinema, Bombay. Used Tanar single-system camera. The same year saw the first Bengali talkie (Jamai Sasthi) and first Tamil/Telugu talkies (Kalidas).

The first Indian film officially nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film was:

(A) Pather Panchali
(B) Mother India (1957)
(C) Salaam Bombay
(D) Lagaan
cards.back:

cards.front:
Satyajit Ray was awarded an honorary Academy Award (Lifetime Achievement Oscar) in:

(A) 1985
(B) 1992 — just weeks before his death
(C) 1979
(D) 2000
cards.back:
(B) 1992 — just weeks before his death

Art, Culture & Post-Independence — Satyajit Ray received an honorary Oscar on 16 March 1992 — the only Indian filmmaker to do so. He was bedridden in a Calcutta hospital and accepted via video message. Died 23 April 1992 (about 5 weeks later). His Apu Trilogy (Pather Panchali 1955, Aparajito 1956, Apur Sansar 1959) is widely regarded among the finest film trilogies in world cinema. Bharat Ratna also conferred 1992. Ray won 32 National Film Awards over his career.

cards.front:
India's first PRIME MINISTER + his tenure was:

(A) Sardar Patel (1947-50)
(B) JAWAHARLAL NEHRU
(C) Lal Bahadur Shastri
(D) Rajendra Prasad
cards.back:
(B) JAWAHARLAL NEHRU

Art, Culture & Post-Independence — JAWAHARLAL NEHRU (14 Nov 1889 – 27 May 1964) — FIRST PRIME MINISTER of INDIA (15 Aug 1947 – 27 May 1964); LONGEST-serving Indian PM (16 years 286 days). Born Allahabad; Harrow + Trinity College Cambridge + Inner Temple London; lawyer; INC leader; 9-year jailed under British. ICONIC speeches: 'TRYST WITH DESTINY' (midnight 14-15 Aug 1947, Parliament address) — 'At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life + freedom...' KEY NEHRU POLICIES: (1) PARLIAMENTARY DEMOCRACY — set strong precedents; SECULAR STATE; (2) PLANNED MIXED ECONOMY — 5-Year Plans; PSUs (IIT, IIM, AIIMS, Bhilai/Rourkela/Durgapur steel plants, dams Bhakra-Nangal 'temples of modern India', Hirakud, HEC, BHEL, ONGC, HAL). (3) NON-ALIGNMENT / NAM — co-founded 1961 Belgrade with Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia), Nkrumah (Ghana). (4) PANCHSHEEL — 5 Principles of Peaceful Coexistence with China (1954, Nehru-Zhou). (5) Promoted Science + Technology — DAE (Homi Bhabha 1954), ISRO predecessor INCOSPAR (Sarabhai 1962), CSIR labs. FAILURES: (1) 1962 SINO-INDIAN WAR — India humiliated militarily (Aksai Chin lost); 'Hindi-Chini Bhai Bhai' betrayed; Nehru's health declined. (2) KASHMIR — took to UN 1948, stalemate. (3) BABU-ism + red tape in PSUs. SUCCESSION: died 27 May 1964 of heart attack; LAL BAHADUR SHASTRI became PM (9 Jun 1964 – 11 Jan 1966). GULZARILAL NANDA — acting PM for 13 days (Nehru's death → Shastri). SHASTRI: 'JAI JAWAN JAI KISAN' slogan; led India through 1965 Indo-Pak War (PAKISTAN's Operation Grand Slam + India's Lahore push); Tashkent Agreement 10 Jan 1966; DIED mysteriously next day (11 Jan 1966, Tashkent) — officially heart attack. Ganda acted again 11-24 Jan 1966. INDIRA GANDHI won Congress Parliamentary Party election + became 3rd PM 24 Jan 1966. FULL LIST of PMs: (1) Nehru; (2) Shastri; (3) Indira Gandhi (1966-77, 1980-84); (4) Morarji Desai (1977-79, Janata — first non-Congress PM); (5) Charan Singh (1979-80, never faced Parliament); (6) Rajiv Gandhi (1984-89, youngest at 40); (7) V.P. Singh (1989-90, Janata Dal); (8) Chandra Shekhar (1990-91); (9) P.V. Narasimha Rao (1991-96, first South Indian PM, first minority-govt 5-year term, LPG reforms); (10) A.B. Vajpayee (3 stints — 1996 13 days, 1998-99, 1999-2004); (11) H.D. Deve Gowda (1996-97); (12) I.K. Gujral (1997-98); (13) Manmohan Singh (2004-14, UPA-I/II, first Sikh PM); (14) Narendra Modi (26 May 2014 onwards, 3rd term from 9 June 2024 — only 2nd PM after Nehru to return for a 3rd full term). 15 Aug 1947 to 27 May 1964 (died in office); 3 consecutive general election wins (1952, 1957, 1962); India's longest-serving PM (16 yrs 286 days).

cards.front:
The EMERGENCY (declared 25 June 1975 by PRESIDENT Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed on PM INDIRA GANDHI's advice) lasted for:

(A) 3 months
(B) 21 MONTHS
(C) 5 years
(D) 10 days
cards.back:
(B) 21 MONTHS

Art, Culture & Post-Independence — EMERGENCY (1975-77) — 21 MONTHS (25 June 1975 – 21 March 1977) — the darkest period of Indian democracy. DECLARED by PRESIDENT FAKHRUDDIN ALI AHMED on advice of PM INDIRA GANDHI on 25 June 1975, night. BACKGROUND: (1) 12 JUNE 1975 — ALLAHABAD HC (Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha) in RAJ NARAIN v INDIRA GANDHI ruled Indira GUILTY of election MALPRACTICES (using state resources for her 1971 Rae Bareli campaign); set aside her election + banned her from office for 6 years. (2) JAYAPRAKASH NARAYAN (JP) had launched 'SAMPURNA KRANTI' / TOTAL REVOLUTION movement 1974 from Bihar — calling for resignation; massive anti-govt rallies; even exhorting police + army to disobey unconstitutional orders. (3) OPPOSITION demanded Indira's resignation. To stay in power, she advised Emergency on grounds of 'INTERNAL DISTURBANCE' — signed by Ahmed that very night; Cabinet informed only next morning (violated conventions). FEATURES OF EMERGENCY: (1) PRESS CENSORSHIP — newspapers pre-censored; electricity cut to Bahadur Shah Zafar Marg press quarter; Kuldip Nayar, Lok Sabha Speaker prohibited; many journalists jailed (Kuldip Nayar, Rajmohan Gandhi). (2) ARRESTS of opposition — JP + Vajpayee + Advani + Morarji Desai + Charan Singh + Chandra Shekhar + Raj Narain + over 100,000 others under MISA (Maintenance of Internal Security Act); detention without trial. (3) FORCED STERILISATION campaigns under Sanjay Gandhi (Indira's younger son, informal power) — 6.2 million sterilisations 1975-77; mostly poor Muslims + Dalits; 2,000+ deaths; massive social resentment. (4) DELHI SLUM DEMOLITIONS — TURKMAN GATE shooting April 1976; ~150 killed; Muslim-majority slums razed (Sanjay Gandhi's '5-point programme' drives). (5) 42nd CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT (1976) — 'MINI CONSTITUTION' — 59 changes; added 'SECULAR SOCIALIST' to Preamble; Fundamental Duties (Part IVA); centralised powers; curtailed judicial review. (6) POSTPONEMENT of 1976 general elections; LS extended. POSITIVES (debated): Some economy / strikes discipline. 21 MARCH 1977 — Emergency LIFTED; elections held. CONGRESS CRUSHINGLY DEFEATED: 154 seats (from 352); JANATA PARTY won 298/542 (merged from Jana Sangh, Congress-O, BLD, SP, Socialist, Scholar Party — heterogeneous). MORARJI DESAI became PM (March 1977 — first non-Congress PM). INDIRA + SANJAY lost their own Rae Bareli + Amethi seats. Charan Singh = Home Minister briefly put Indira in jail (Oct 1977 release). Janata collapsed 1979 over Dual Membership issue (RSS). Indira returned 1980 with Congress(I). 44TH CAA (1978, Janata) — reversed Emergency excesses; 'internal disturbance' replaced with 'armed rebellion' in Art 352; Art 20 + 21 non-suspendable; PM's advice = Cabinet's recommendation binding; restored judicial review. INDIA'S DEMOCRACY emerged STRONGER post-Emergency. 25 June 1975 to 21 March 1977; longest in Indian history; elections called + Congress lost; Janata Party won.

cards.front:
The 1971 INDO-PAKISTAN WAR led to the:

(A) Annexation of Kashmir by India
(B) BIRTH OF BANGLADESH
(C) Merging of India + Pakistan
(D) Return of Goa
cards.back:
(B) BIRTH OF BANGLADESH

Art, Culture & Post-Independence — 1971 INDO-PAKISTAN WAR — 'BANGLADESH LIBERATION WAR'. 13-day military campaign (3 DEC – 16 DEC 1971); INDIA's most decisive military victory; led to CREATION of BANGLADESH. BACKGROUND: (1) Pakistan's 1970 general elections — SHEIKH MUJIBUR RAHMAN's AWAMI LEAGUE won 160/162 East Pakistan seats + overall majority (167/300). But WEST Pakistani elite (Zulfikar Bhutto's PPP + Yahya Khan military) REFUSED to transfer power. (2) Mujib launched civil disobedience; YAHYA KHAN launched 'OPERATION SEARCHLIGHT' 25-26 MARCH 1971 — brutal military crackdown on Bengalis; estimated 3 MILLION KILLED, 400,000 women raped (per Bangladeshi accounts); 10 MILLION refugees fled to India (Calcutta + Tripura). GENOCIDE recognised by many historians + some UN bodies. (3) MUKTI BAHINI (Freedom Fighters) — Bengali resistance; trained + armed with covert Indian support (R&AW, BSF) from April 1971. (4) INDIA hosted govt-in-exile + refugees; economy strained. (5) PM INDIRA GANDHI's diplomacy 1971 — Treaty of Friendship with USSR (Aug 1971) for deterrence vs USA/China; went to Washington + European capitals to brief. USA (Nixon-Kissinger) sided with Pakistan; sent USS Enterprise carrier group to Bay of Bengal (signal); USSR sent its fleet in support of India. (6) 3 DEC 1971 — Pakistan LAUNCHED PRE-EMPTIVE air strikes on Indian airfields (Operation Chengiz Khan — mirrored Israel's 1967 strike); India formally entered war. INDIAN FORCES: Army's EASTERN COMMAND under Lt. General JAGJIT SINGH AURORA; Navy's Eastern Fleet; IAF; assisted by MUKTI BAHINI. CAMPAIGN: multi-pronged thrusts from Tripura, Meghalaya, W Bengal, Assam; encircled Dhaka in 2 weeks. WESTERN FRONT: defensive; Chhamb, Longewala (Brigadier KULDIP SINGH CHANDPURI + 120 men held 2,000+ Pak troops + 45 tanks — later film 'Border' 1997 immortalised); PAF attacks on Jaisalmer, Bhuj, Amritsar; counter-attacks at Chhamb, Shakargarh, Sindh captured. NAVAL: INS VIKRANT launched air strikes on Chittagong + Cox's Bazar; INS Nipat + Nirghat missile boats attacked Karachi harbour 4+8 Dec (OPERATION TRIDENT + OPERATION PYTHON) — sank Pakistani destroyers + oil depots — NAVY DAY 4 DEC commemorates. 16 DECEMBER 1971 — PAKISTAN'S LT. GEN. A.A.K. NIAZI SURRENDERED at DHAKA Ramna Race Course to Lt Gen. JAGJIT SINGH AURORA (joint Indian-Mukti Bahini accepting). ~93,000 POW (LARGEST surrender since WWII) — repatriated after SIMLA AGREEMENT (28 Jun-2 Jul 1972, signed by Indira + Bhutto). BANGLADESH formally constituted 16 Dec 1971. 1971 WAR HEROES: Capt M.N. Mulla (INS Khukri, PVC posthumous), Flying Officer N.S. Sekhon (PVC, only IAF), Maj Hoshiar Singh (PVC), 2nd Lt Arun Khetarpal (PVC, age 21 — Battle of Basantar); Sam Manekshaw (Chief of Army Staff — FIRST Field Marshal). FIELD MARSHALS OF India: SAM MANEKSHAW (1973), K.M. CARIAPPA (1986). VIJAY DIWAS / VICTORY DAY = 16 DEC annually. East Pakistan separated after India's 13-day military campaign; Pakistan's General Niazi surrendered 16 Dec 1971 (Dhaka).

cards.front:
The ECONOMIC REFORMS of 1991 (LPG — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation) were launched by:

(A) PM Rajiv Gandhi + FM Pranab Mukherjee
(B) PM P.V. NARASIMHA RAO + FM MANMOHAN SINGH
(C) PM Vajpayee + FM Yashwant Sinha
(D) PM Manmohan Singh + FM Chidambaram (UPA-I)
cards.back:
(B) PM P.V. NARASIMHA RAO + FM MANMOHAN SINGH

Art, Culture & Post-Independence — 1991 ECONOMIC REFORMS / LPG — LIBERALISATION, PRIVATISATION, GLOBALISATION. Most consequential policy shift in Indian economy post-independence. ARCHITECTS: (1) PM P.V. NARASIMHA RAO (9th PM, June 1991 – May 1996, Congress) — political backing. (2) FM Dr. MANMOHAN SINGH (former RBI Governor 1982-85; 'accidental FM' as economist brought in; later PM 2004-14) — technocratic architect. PRECIPITATING CRISIS: (1) 1990s BoP CRISIS — forex reserves collapsed to ~$1.2 BILLION (2 weeks of imports); Chandra Shekhar govt pledged 67 TONNES of GOLD to Bank of England + Union Bank of Switzerland (May-July 1991) to raise ~$400 million. (2) Post-Gulf War oil prices spike; remittances dropped; NRI bank runs. (3) Credit rating downgraded; loans from commercial banks dried up. IMF BAILOUT: India sought ~$2 billion from IMF; conditions = structural reforms. REFORMS: (1) NEW INDUSTRIAL POLICY 1991 (24 JULY, same day as Manmohan's first Budget Speech) — abolished INDUSTRIAL LICENSING for most industries (keep only 18 strategic sectors — reduced later); removed MRTP Act restrictions for large firms; opened more sectors to private capital. (2) DEVALUATION of rupee — 18-19% in two tranches July 1991 (₹21 → ₹26 per USD). (3) Trade liberalisation — customs duties reduced (from avg 85% to ~25% over years); Replenishment License → EXIM Scrip → transferable; PL-480 imports; foreign trade convertibility. (4) FDI policies — allowed up to 51% in many sectors (automatic route); Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) set up; mostly dismantled later (2017) as sectors liberalised via automatic route. (5) RUPEE CONVERTIBILITY — 1992 LERMS (Liberalised Exchange Rate Mgmt System, partial convertibility); 1993-94 FULL convertibility on CURRENT ACCOUNT (not capital; Tarapore 1997 + 2006 roadmaps). (6) Disinvestment of PSUs started 1992 (minority stakes; accelerated under NDA 1998). (7) TAX REFORMS — Chelliah Committee + Raja Chelliah; lower direct tax rates; VAT began (→ GST 2017). (8) Capital markets — SEBI statutory 1992; dematerialisation; FII entry; Bombay Stock Exchange vs NSE competition. (9) BANKING reforms — Narasimham Committee I (1991) II (1998); new private banks (ICICI, HDFC, Axis, IndusInd 1993-94); new foreign banks. (10) TELECOM reforms — NTP 1994 + 1999 (AB Vajpayee); revenue-sharing; enabling Sunil Mittal (Airtel) + others. IMPACT: growth accelerated (4-5% 1980s → 6-7% 1990s → 8-9% 2000s); poverty declined from ~45% in 1993-94 to 22% in 2011-12 (Tendulkar line); IT-BPO boom; middle class doubled. CRITIQUES: inequality rose; jobless growth; agriculture neglected. MANMOHAN's 1991 BUDGET SPEECH famous line — 'No power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come' (Victor Hugo paraphrase; ending line: 'Let this be the beginning'). Rao quoted similarly about India on world stage. LPG = 'MANMOHAN-RAO CONSENSUS'. Later enhanced by VAJPAYEE (NHDP highway network, PMGSY, Golden Quadrilateral, disinvestment, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan). in response to 1991 BoP crisis; dismantled LICENCE RAJ; opened to FDI + trade; liberalised industrial policy.
